title: Epistulae
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: Almighty Father of all things, to whom supreme power belongs, hear, if I pray aright. Let no day be passed by me in sadness, no night disturb my calm repose. Let others' goods not attract me, but rather let my own avail such as implore my aid: may none have a wish to hurt me or the means to hurt me. Let me have no occasion to will ill and let the unruffled power to do well be with me. Let my mind, content with its own and not given to base gains, overcome bodily enticements keeping the conscience of chaste conduct. Let that offending member, the ever-guilty tongue, well-pleasing to malicious ears for the poison it sheds, hate lewd jesting and unseemly words. Let me not be overcome by any man's decease, nor prosper through the death of any; let me never envy any man nor ever tell a lie. Be mine a cheerful home, and at my unpurchased 1 repasts may a well-fed slave bred in my house, my trusty comrade and prosperous henchman, serve blithely; and mine an obedient wife with children born of my clear wife. Upon pure conduct God bestows such gifts: such conduct assures itself of life unending against the world to come.
style: late antique latin prayer-hymn, unaccompanied plainchant with soft drone, low male voice, slow, reverent, sparse
why: A complete morning prayer — 'let no day be passed by me in sadness' — self-contained and quietly devastating.

title: Epistulae
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: Hut why weave I such sad refrain in mournful verse, why does my heart not turn to nobler prayers? Ear be that fear! Sure is my confidence that, if the Father and the Son of God accept the reverent words of those who seek, thou canst be restored at my prayer, that I may weep not for a home scattered and ravaged, for the realm rent in pieces between a hundred owners, once Paulinus's, and for thee, that, wandering with a range as wide as the extent of Spain, unmindful of old friends thou dost trust in strangers. O hasten hither, my pride, my chiefest care, summoned with vows, good omens, and with prayers speed thee hither, while thou art young and while my old age to win thy favour preserves its vigour unconsumed. Ah, when shall this news break on my ears? Lo, thy Paulinus is at hand: now he leaves the snowy towns of Spain, now reaches the fields of Tarbellae, now approaches the homesteads of Hebromagus, now enters his brother's domains hard by, now glides down stream, and now is in sight: now the prow is being swung out into the stream:1 now he has passed the thronged entrance of his home-port, outstrips the whole host of folk who hurry to meet him, and passing his own doors now, even now beats at thine. Do I believe, or do those who love feign dreams for their own selves. 2
style: late roman elegiac song, cithara and low strings, warm tenor, building anaphora, yearning, rubato
why: The 'now he leaves Spain, now he approaches, now he beats at thy door' build is pure refrain, ending on a heartbreak.

title: Epistulae
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: THIS is the fourth letter in which I have laid bare to thee, Paulinus, my familiar complaint, and with caressing words sought to stir thee from thy lethargy. But never a page comes to repay my loving attentions, no propitious words writ at the head of sheets which bring me greeting.5 How has my luckless letter, for which your long neglect shows such disdain, deserved this rebuff? Yet foe from foe receives greeting 6 in savage speech and hail comes between opposed arms. Even rocks make answer to mankind and speech beating back from caves returns, returns too the vocal mimicry of the woods; cliffs by the sea-shore cry out, streams utter their murmurs, the hedges, whereon bees of Hybla feed,1 are ever whispering. Reed-grown banks also have their tuneful harmonies, and the pine's foliage in trembling accents talks with its beloved winds. So oft as the light eastern breeze leans on the shrill-voiced leaves, strains of Dindymus respond to the grove of Gargara. 2 Nature made nothing dumb. Birds of the air and four-footed beasts are not mute, even the serpent has its own hissing note, and the herds of the deep sigh with faint semblance of a voice. Cymbals give sound at a clash, stages at beat of bounding feet, the taut skins of hollow drums give back a booming; Mareotie 3 sistra raise rattling din in Isis' honour nor does Dodona's brazen tinkling cease as oft as the lavers at the clappers' measured stroke obediently reply with rhythmic beat.1 2,; Thou, as though thou wert a mute citizen of Oebalian Amyclae,5 or Egyptian Sigalion 6 were sealing thy lips, stubbornly keepest silence, Paulinus. I recognise shame in thee, for continued negligence cherishes her own defeet, and in shame for long silenee thou dost resolve not to maintain interchange of courtesies; and lengthened idleness loves its own fault. Who forbids you to write hail and farewell with studied brevity, and to commit to paper these words of greeting? I do not demand that thy page should weave a long drawn out web of verse and burden thy letter with a multitude of words. Twas but one letter wherewith the Spartans made reply and, though refusing, pleased the angry king.1 For indeed terseness is courteous; so, report says, taught reborn Pythagoras.2 While babblers would be stringing indecisive words, in all cases he would answer only Yes or No. O stable rule of speech! For nothing is shorter and more adequate than these, which approve the valid or reject the invalid. None pleased by silence; many by brief reply. 45"But I, whither with foolish amplitude of speech have I been long careering? How distant from itself and yet how near is error! I with long speech, thou with utter silence, we both displease. Yet can not keep silence, for free affection never bears yoke, nor loves to screen truth with glozing words. Hast thou, dearest Paulinus, changed thy nature? Do Biscayan glades and sojourns in the snowy Pyrenees and doth forgetfulness of our clime work thus? What curse shall I not righteously call down on thee, O land of Spain? May Carthaginians ravage thee, may faithless Hannibal waste thee with fire, may banished Sertorius again seek in thee the seat of war! Shall then Birbilis or Calagorris clinging to its crags, or parched Ilcrda3 whose ruins, littered over rugged hills, look down on brawling Sicoris, possess him who is mine and his country's pride, the mainstay of the Senate? Here dost thou, Paulinus, establish thy robe consular and Roman curule chair, and wilt thou bury there thy native honours? But who is that unhallowed wretch who has urged you to so long silence? May he turn no sound to any advantage, may no joys enliven him, no sweet poets' lays, no melting harmonies of seductive elegy, may no cry of beast nor low of cattle nor song of bird cheer him, nor yet Echo, who hidden in shepherds' bosky groves consoles us while repeating our complaints. Sad, needy let him dwell in waste places and in silence roam the borders of Alpine hills, even as, 'tis said, in days of old Beller-ophon, distraught, avoided the company of men and wandered straying through untrodden places.1 This is my prayer, this cry, Boeotian Muses divine, receive ye and with Latin strains call back your bard!
style: latin rhetorical lament, lyre and frame drum, declamatory male voice, insistent, gathering, measured
why: 'Nature made nothing dumb' — a whole catalogue of the world's noises marshalled against one friend's silence.

title: Apocolocyntosis
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
O weep for the man! This world never saw
One quicker a troublesome suit to decide,
When only one part of the case had been tried,
(He could do it indeed and not hear either side).
Who'll now sit in judgment the whole year round?
Now he that is judge of the shades underground
Once ruler of fivescore cities in Crete,
Must yield to his better and take a back seat.
Mourn, mourn, pettifoggers, ye venal crew,
And you, minor poets, woe, woe is to you!
And you above all, who get rich quick
By the rattle of dice and the three card trick."
Claudius was charmed to hear his own praises sung,
and would have stayed longer to see the show. But the Talthybius of the gods laid a hand on him, and led him across the
Campus Martius, first wrapping his head up close that no one might know him, until
style: mock funeral dirge, roman satire, low brass and reedy flutes, ironic massed chorus, processional, slow and swaggering
why: A parody lament with real dirge shape — 'Mourn, mourn, pettifoggers, ye venal crew' is a made refrain.

title: Apocolocyntosis
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
any of the old stagers, lest Claudius should dare to hope for any such relief. It
was agreed that some new punishment must be devised: they must devise some new task,
something senseless, to suggest some craving without result. Then Aeacus decreed he
should rattle dice for ever in a box with no bottom. At once the poor wretch began
his fruitless task of hunting for the dice, which for ever slipped from his
fingers.
"For when he rattled with the box, and thought he now had got 'em,
The little cubes would vanish thro' the perforated bottom.
Then he would pick 'em up again, and once more set a-trying:
The dice but served him the same trick: away they went a-flying.
So still he tries, and still he fails; still searching long he lingers;
And every time the tricksy things go slipping thro' his fingers.
style: sardonic latin cabaret, plucked lyre and hand percussion, dry male voice, jaunty, looping, unresolved
why: The bottomless dice-box is the sharpest image in the satire and the verse already circles like the punishment.

title: Apocolocyntosis
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
style: classical spinning-song, kithara and light strings, bright interlacing female voices, lilting, incantatory
why: The Fates pulling golden thread while Phoebus plays — a genuine lyric interlude in a prose satire.

title: Birds
author: Aristophanes
lyrics:
The runaway slave, whom you brand, is only a spotted francolin with us. Are you Phrygian like Spintharus? Among us you would be the Phrygian bird, the goldfinch, of the race of Philemon. Are you a slave and a Carian like Execestides?
Among us you can create yourself forefathers; you can always find relations. Does the son of Pisias want to betray the gates of the city to the foe? Let him become a partridge, the fitting offspring of his father; among us there is no shame in escaping as cleverly as a partridge.
Second Semi-Chorus:
Singing.
So the swans on the banks of the Hebrus, tiotiotiotiotiotinx, mingle their voices to serenade Apollo, tiotiotiotinx, flapping their wings the while, tiotiotiotinx; their notes reach beyond the clouds of heaven; they startle the various tribes of the beasts; a windless sky calms the waves, totototototototototinx;
style: ancient greek comic chorus, aulos and lyre, frame drum, layered voices with birdcall syllables, lively, dancing
why: The swan chorus on the Hebrus with its tiotiotiotinx refrain — the play's one true song, already built to be sung.

title: Birds
author: Aristophanes
lyrics:
Give me wings and I will fly into the topmost airs to gather fresh songs in the clouds, in the midst of the vapors and the fleecy snow.
Pisthetaerus:
Gather songs in the clouds?
Cinesias:
'Tis on them the whole of our latter-day art depends. The most brilliant dithyrambs are those that flap their wings in empty space and are clothed in mist and dense obscurity.
To appreciate this, just listen.
Pisthetaerus:
Oh! no, no, no!
Cinesias:
By Hermes! but indeed you shall.
Cinesias:
He sings.
I shall travel through thine ethereal empire like a winged bird, who cleaveth space with his long neck...
Pisthetaerus:
Stop! Way enough!
Cinesias:
style: mock dithyramb, aulos and shimmering strings, high wavering male voice, floating, airy, absurdly grand
why: 'Give me wings and I will fly into the topmost airs to gather fresh songs in the clouds' — the line the play is remembered by.

title: Poems
author: Richard Jago
lyrics:
While horrid flames surround her children's room!
On heav'n she calls, and wrings her trembling hands,
Constrain'd to see, but not prevent their doom.
"O grief of griefs! with shrieking voice she cry'd,
"What sight is this that I have liv'd to see?
"O! that I had a maiden-goldfinch died,
"From love's false joys, and bitter sorrows free!
"Was it for this, alas! with weary bill,
"Was it for this, I pois'd th' unwieldy straw?
"For this I pick'd the moss from yonder hill?
"Nor shun'd the pond'rous chat along to draw?
"Was it for this, I cull'd the wool with care;
"And strove with all my skill our work to crown?
"For this, with pain I bent the stubborn hair;
"And lin'd our cradle with the thistle's down?
"Was it for this my freedom I resign'd;
style: english pastoral elegy, harpsichord and recorder, plaintive soprano, strophic, grieving, unhurried
why: The goldfinch's lament built on a hammering 'Was it for this' — refrain, grief, and concrete nest-making detail.

title: Poems
author: Richard Jago
lyrics:
Attend with pity to my strain,
And grant my love a kind return.
For see the wintry storms are flown,
And gentle Zephyrs fan the air;
Let us the genial influence own,
Let us the vernal pastime share.
The raven plumes his jetty wing
To please his croaking paramour;
The larks responsive ditties sing,
And tell their passion as they soar.
But trust me, love, the raven's wing
Is not to be compar'd with mine;
Nor can the lark so sweetly sing
As I, who strength with sweetness join.
O! let me all thy steps attend!
I'll point new treasures to thy sight;
style: georgian pastoral air, baroque guitar and flute, warm tenor, courting, lilting, springlike
why: The blackbird's wooing song — 'the wintry storms are flown, and gentle Zephyrs fan the air' — a clean, singable love lyric.

title: Poems
author: Richard Jago
lyrics:
See, Delia, on my roof your guests to-day;
To-morrow on my roof your guests no more!
Ere yet 'tis night, with haste they wing away,
To-morrow lands them on some safer shore.
How just the moral in this scene convey'd!
And what without a moral wou'd we read?
Then mark what Damon tells his gentle maid,
And with his lesson register the deed.
'Tis thus life's chearful seasons roll away;
Thus threats the winter of inclement age;
Our time of action but a summer's day;
And earth's frail orb the sadly-varied stage!
And does no pow'r its friendly aid dispense,
Nor give us tidings of some happier clime?
Find we no guide in gracious Providence
Beyond the stroke of death, the verge of time!
style: english georgian hymn-air, chamber organ and viola, reflective tenor, slow, valedictory
why: 'To-morrow on my roof your guests no more' turns departing swallows into a whole theory of mortality in four lines.

title: Poems
author: Henry Carey
style: english broadside ballad, fiddle and hurdy-gurdy, comic male-female duet, bouncing, nonsense refrain, brisk
why: Roger tapping at Dolly's window with thumpaty-thump — the nonsense refrain is already a hook.

title: Poems
author: Henry Carey
lyrics:
I'll bear it all for Sally.
She is the Darling of my Heart,
And she lives in our Alley.
Of all the Days that are in the Week,
I dearly love but one Day.
And that's the Day that comes betwixt
The Saturday and Monday.
For then I'm drest all in my Best,
To walk abroad with Sally.
She is the Darling of my Heart,
And she lives in our Alley.
My Master carries me to church,
And often am I blamed,
Because I leave him in the lurch,
As soon as Text is named.
I leave the church in Sermon-time,
style: georgian ballad-opera air, harpsichord and violin, plain sincere tenor, tender, strophic with refrain
why: Sally of our Alley — the refrain repeats, the devotion is comic and real, and it was written to be sung.

title: Poems
author: Henry Carey
lyrics:
Oh! then I'll marry Sally.
Oh! then we'll wed, and then we'll bed,
But not in our Alley.
Pretty Sally's Answer.
OF all the Lads in London Town,
There's none I love like Johnny.
He walks so stately o'er the Ground,
I like him for my Honey.
And none but him I e'er will wed,
As my Name is Sally:
And I will dress me in my Best,
In spite of all our Alley.
Because that Nan and Sue did say,
That live in our Alley,
Unto Bess Franklin, do but see,
Look there goes pretty Sally.
style: london street ballad, fiddle and tabor, bright saucy female voice, brisk, defiant, strophic
why: Sally's answering ballad gives the woman the voice and the same 'in spite of all our Alley' refrain.

title: Poems
author: 4th Earl of Chesterfield
lyrics:
For whilst he teaches us to die,
He cheats us of our living.
To die's a lesson we shall know
Too soon without a master;
Then let us only study now
How may we live the faster.
To live's to love, to bless, be blest
With mutual inclination;
Share then my ardour in your breast,
And kindly meet my passion.
But if thus bless'd I may not live,
And pity you deny,
To me at least your Sherlock give,
'Tis I must learn to die.
SONG.
WHEN Fanny blooming fair
style: georgian drawing-room song, harpsichord and cello, wry baritone, elegant, moderate, lightly mocking
why: 'To die's a lesson we shall know too soon without a master' — a complete, epigrammatic argument against sermons on death.

title: Poems
author: 4th Earl of Chesterfield
lyrics:
WHenever, Chloe, I begin
Your heart like mine to move,
You tell me of the crying sin
Of unchaste lawless love.
How can that passion be a sin,
Which gave to Chloe birth?
How can those joys but be divine,
Which make a heaven on earth?
To wed, mankind the priest trepann'd,
By some sly fallacy,
And disobey'd God's great command,
Increase and multiply.
You say that love's a crime; content:
Yet this allow you must,
More joy's in heav'n if one repent,
Than over ninety just.
style: restoration catch, lute and viol, sly tenor, light, teasing, dance-like
why: The Chloe song is a whole seduction argument in four neat stanzas, blasphemous and self-contained.

title: De communibus notitiis adversus Stoicos
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
DIADUMENUS. But lest these things should seem to have too much of logical difficulty, let us proceed to such as pertain more to natural philosophy. Since then, as themselves say, Jove is of all beginning, midst, and end, they ought chiefly to have applied themselves to remedy, redress, and reduce to the best order the conceptions concerning the Gods, if there were in them any thing confused or erroneous; or if not, to have left every one in those sentiments which they had from the laws and custom concerning the Divinity: For neither now nor yesterday These deep conceits of God began; Time out of mind they have been aye, But no man knows where, how, or when.
But these men, having begun (as it were) from Vesta to disturb the opinions settled and received in every country concerning the Gods, have not (to speak sincerely) left any thing entire and uncorrupted. For what man is there or ever was, except these, who does not believe the Divinity to be immortal and eternal? Or what in the common anticipations is more unanimously chanted forth concerning the Gods than such things as these: There the blest Gods eternally enjoy Their sweet delights;
style: ancient greek philosophical chant, lyre and low drone, grave male voice, slow, declamatory, austere
why: Carries the Sophoclean quatrain — 'neither now nor yesterday these deep conceits of God began' — the best line available in this work.

title: De Sera Numinis Vindicta
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
And in another place, He that his neighbors harm contrives, his art Contrives the mischiefgainst his own false heart.
Or can you believe but that in this particular God is wiser than Hesiod, admonishing and exhorting us in this manner: Nor mind the pleasures of the genial bed, Returning from th interment of the dead; But propagate the race, when heavenly food And feasting with the Gods have warmed the blood;
style: greek gnomic verse, kithara and hand drum, stern male voice, measured, oracular, sparse
why: Only candidate, but a real gnomic couplet: the man who plots his neighbour's harm plots it against his own heart.

title: de consulatu Stilichonis
author: Claudian
lyrics: In so short a time didst thou win so many battles without loss of blood, and, setting out with the moon yet new, thou didst return or ever it was full; so didst thou compel the threatening Rhine to learn gentleness with shattered horns, that the Salian now tills his fields, the Sygambrian beats his straight sword into a curved sickle, and the traveller, as he looks at the two banks, asks over which Rome rules. The Belgian, too, pastures his flock across the river and the Chauci heed it not; Gallic herds cross the middle Elbe and wander over the hills of the Franks. Safe it is to hunt amid the vast silence of the distant Hercynian forest, and in the woods that old-established superstition has rendered awful our axes fell the trees the barbarian once worshipped and nought is said.
style: late roman peace-hymn, cithara and soft low strings, clear tenor, flowing, pastoral, unhurried
why: The sword beaten into a curved sickle and the traveller asking which bank Rome rules — the one passage here that is an image rather than a boast.

title: de consulatu Stilichonis
author: Claudian
lyrics: Meanwhile a maiden of years full ripe for marriage troubled a father's heart, and the emperor doubted whom to select as her husband and as future ruler of the world; right anxiously did he search east and west for a son-in-law worthy of being wedded to Serena. Merit alone had to decide; through camps, through cities, through nations roamed his poised and hesitating thoughts. But thou wast chosen, thus in the opinion and judgement of him who selected thee surpassing all the candidates of the whole world and becoming a son-in-law in the imperial family where thou wast shortly to become a father-in-law. The marriage - bed was ablaze with flashing gold and regal purple. The maiden steps forth accompanied by her parents clad in scarlet. On one side stood her sire, famed for his triumphs, on the other was the queen, fulfilling a mother's loving office and ordering the bridal veil beneath a weight of jewels. Then, so men say, the horses of the sun and the stars of heaven danced for joy, pools of honey and rivers of milk welled forth from the earth. Bosporus decked his banks with vernal flowers, and Europe, entwined with rosy garlands, uplifted the torches in rivalry with Asia.
style: late antique epithalamium, aulos and lyre with light hand drums, bright massed voices, processional, joyful
why: A wedding song complete in itself: pools of honey, rivers of milk, and Europe and Asia lifting torches against each other.

title: de consulatu Stilichonis
author: Claudian
lyrics: Neither Vulcan's fabulous shield nor such armour as that of which poets sing the forging assisted thine efforts. Single-handed thou didst succeed in penning within the narrow confines of a single valley the vast army of barbarians that were long since ravaging the land of Thrace. For thee the fearful shriek of the onrushing Alan had no terrors nor the fierceness of the nomad Hun nor the scimitar of the Geloni, nor the Getae's bow or Sarmatian's club. These nations would have been destroyed root and branch had not a traitor by a perfidious trick abused the emperor's ear and caused him to withhold his hand; hence the sheathing of the sword, the raising of the siege, and the granting of a treaty to the prisoners.
style: late roman martial ode, war horns and deep frame drums, declamatory bass, cold, driving, stark
why: Winter campaign verse that ends on ploughshares ringing against the bones of buried kings — concrete and terrible.

title: Achilleis
author: Statius
lyrics:
The mother sees him wavering and willing to be forced,
and threw the robes upon him; then she softens his stiff
neck and lowers his heavy shoulders and loosens his strong
arms and tames his unkempt hair into a fixed order
and transfers her own necklaces to his beloved neck;
and, restraining his steps within an embroidered hem,
she teaches him his gait and motion and the modesty of speech,
even as the wax that shall live beneath an artist's thumb
takes its forms and follows the fire and the hand:
such was the image of the goddess transforming her son,
nor did she struggle long; for very much grace remains to him
even in his unwilling manhood, and he deceives the gazers,
his sex doubtful and hidden by a slender difference.
They go forth, and warning him again and again, and wearying him,
style: latin epic recitation, kithara and bowed strings, warm baritone, supple, tender, hushed
why: Thetis dressing her son as a girl, 'even as the wax that shall live beneath an artist's thumb' — a whole transformation in one image.

title: Achilleis
author: Statius
lyrics:
the sleep that is for boys, from the rocks of the Haemonian cave
to the calm waters and to the shores bidden to be silent:
the Cynthian goddess shows the way and flashes over the whole orb,
and Chiron escorts the goddess and, untroubled, asks for swift
returns over the sea, and hides his streaming
eyes, and watches, on his reared horse, the two
snatched away suddenly and now already hidden, where for a little while
the grey signs of their flight foam and the wake dies in the liquid deep.
Him, never to return again to Thessalian Tempe,
now sad Pholoe, now cloudy Othrys bemoans,
and Spercheos thinner in his waters, and the cave
of the learned old man, struck dumb; the Fauns ask for the boyish songs,
and the Nymphs lament the marriage long hoped for.
Now day presses upon the stars, and from the low sea Titan
style: greek-latin pastoral lament, panpipe and low lyre, mournful mixed voices, slow, receding, elegiac
why: Chiron watching the wake die on the water while the Fauns ask for the boy's songs — the saddest thing in the poem.

title: Achilleis
author: Statius
lyrics:
and the Argolic ships.' So having begun, he sprang
into the alder-ship, and, the south wind whistling deep, is swept
far from the neighbouring lands: and now it begins to draw the lofty
clouds, and Scyros to depart across the long sea.
Far off on the topmost tower, attended by the tears of her sisters,
and holding the child entrusted to her, which bears the name of Pyrrhus,
his wife hung, and with her eyes fixed on the sails
she went, herself too, with the strait, and now alone saw the poop;
he too turns his sidelong looks to the beloved walls
and ponders the widowed home and the groans of the forsaken one:
the hidden fire is born again beneath his heart,
and valour gives place. The Laertian hero perceives
him grieving, and, approaching, sets to bend him with placid words:
style: latin farewell aria, harp and sustained strings, grieving soprano, slow, swelling, salt-heavy
why: Deidamia on the tower going out with the strait until only the poop is left — a departure scene that needs no context.

title: Poems
author: William Melmoth
lyrics:
To want abandon'd and by wrongs opprest?
Who shall the wretched out-cast's teen befriend?
Live's mercy then, if not in parent's breast?
At Jove's right hand, to Jove for ever dear,
Yes, MERCY lives, the gentle goddess blest,
Aye at his feet she pleads the cause distrest,
To Sorrow's plaints she turns his equal ear,
And wafts to heaven's star-throne fair Vertue's silent tear.
'Twas SHE that bade Euphormius quell each thought
That well mote rise to check his generous aid.
Tho high the torts which Lycon him had wrought,
Tho few the flocks his humble pastures fed,
When as he learn'd Pastora's hapless sted,
His breast humane with wonted pity flows.
He op'd his gates, the naked exile led
Beneath his roof: a decent drapet throws
style: english renaissance-revival hymn, viol consort and recorder, pure tenor, stately, archaic, strophic
why: Mercy at Jove's right hand wafting Virtue's silent tear to heaven's star-throne — a complete Spenserian stanza that stands alone.

title: Poems
author: William Melmoth
lyrics:
A wolf in form as erst a wolf in soul!
To Pholoe, forest wild, he hy'd away,
The horrid haunt of savage monsters soul.
There helpless innocence is still his prey,
Thief of the bleating fold, and shepherd's dire dismay.
Tho Jove to good Euphormius' cot did wend,
Where peaceful dwelt the man of virtue high,
Each shepherd's praise and eke each shepherd's friend,
In every act of sweet humanity.
Him Jove approaching in mild majesty,
Grected all hail! then bade him join the throng
Of glit'rand lights that gild the glowing sky.
There shepherds nightly view his orb yhong,
Where bright he shines eterne, the brightest stars emong.
A TALE.
BY THE SAME.
style: archaic pastoral ballad, lute and bowed lyre, plain male voice, measured, fable-telling, cool
why: Two transformations in one breath: 'A wolf in form as erst a wolf in soul' and the good man set among the stars.

title: Poems
author: William Melmoth
lyrics:
The slightest trifles solid sorrows prove,
And the long ling'ring wheel of life scarce seems to move.
Useless in business, yet unfit for ease,
Nor skill'd to mend mankind, nor form'd to please,
Such spurious animals of worthless race
Live but the publick burthen and disgrace:
Like mean attendants on life's stage are seen,
Drawn forth to fill, but not conduct the scene.
The mind not taught to think, no useful store
To fix reflection, dreads the vacant hour.
Turn'd on its self its num'rous wants are seen,
And all the mighty void that lies within
Yet cannot wisdom stamp our joys complete;
'Tis conscious virtue crowns the blest retreat.
Who feels not that, the private path must shun.
And fly to publick view t' escape his own;
style: georgian reflective air, harpsichord and cello, grave baritone, measured, sombre, inward
why: 'The mind not taught to think ... dreads the vacant hour' — the mighty void within, in clean couplets.

title: Poems
author: Joseph Warton
lyrics:
Where woodbines cluster round the door,
Where shells and moss o'erlay the floor,
And on whose top an hawthorn blows,
Amid whose thickly-woven boughs
Some nightingale still builds her nest,
Each evening warbling thee to rest:
There lay me by the haunted stream,
Rapt in some wild, poetick dream,
In converse while methinks I rove
With SPENSER thro' a fairy grove;
Till suddenly awoke, I hear
Strange whisper'd musick in my ear,
And my glad soul in bliss is drown'd
By the sweetly-soothing sound!
Me, Goddess, by the right-hand lead,
Sometimes thro' the yellow mead,
style: english pastoral folk ballad, acoustic guitar and low flute, warm female vocal, lilting, dreaming, unhurried
why: The moss-floored cottage, the nightingale on the roof, roving with Spenser through a fairy grove — octosyllabics already built to be sung.

title: Poems
author: Joseph Warton
lyrics:
YE green-rob'd Dryads, oft' at dusky eve
By wondering shepherds seen, to forests brown,
To unfrequented meads, and pathless wilds,
Lead me from gardens deck'd with art's vain pomps.
Can gilt alcoves, can marble-mimic gods,
Parterres embroider'd, obelisks, and urns
Of high relief; can the long, spreading lake,
Or vista lessening to the sight; can Stow,
With all her Attic fanes, such raptures raise,
As the thrush-haunted copse, where lightly leaps
The fearful fawn the rustling leaves along,
And the brisk squirrel sports from bough to bough,
While from an hollow oak, whose naked roots
O'erhang a pensive rill, the busy bees
Hum drowsy lullabies? The bards of old,
Fair Nature's friends, sought such retreats, to charm
style: georgian pastoral ode, chamber strings and oboe, declamatory tenor, spacious, blank-verse cadence, sunlit
why: 'Ye green-rob'd Dryads' — the thrush-haunted copse and the bees humming drowsy lullabies out of a hollow oak.

title: Poems
author: Joseph Warton
lyrics:
Still takes at eve his silent round,
Or sits yon new-made grave beside,
Where lies a frantic Suicide:
While labouring sighs my heart-strings break,
Thus to the sullen Power I speak:
"Haste, with thy poison'd dagger, haste,
" To pierce this sorrow-laden breast;
"Or lead me at the dead of night,
" To some sea-beat mountain's height,
"Whence with headlong haste I'll leap
" To the dark bosom of the deep;
"Or shew me far from human eye,
" Some cave to muse in, starve, and die,
"No weeping friend or brother near,
" My last fond, faultering words to hear? "
'Twas thus with weight of woes opprest,
style: gothic lament, solo viola and dark harp, low troubled voice, slow, unsettled, funereal
why: The address to Despair: the poisoned dagger, the sea-beat mountain's height, the cave to starve and die in.

title: Poems
author: John Gay
lyrics:
INTRODUCTION TO THE FABLES.
The Shepherd and the Philosopher.
Remote from citys liv'd a Swain,
Unvex'd with all the cares of gain,
His head was silver'd o'er with age,
And long experience made him sage;
In summer's heat and winter's cold
He fed his flock and pen'd the fold,
His hours in cheerful labour flew,
Nor envy nor ambition knew;
His wisdom and his honest fame
Through all the country rais'd his name.
A deep Philosopher (whose rules
Of moral life were drawn from schools)
The Shepherd's homely cottage sought,
And thus explor'd his reach of thought.
style: english ballad air, fiddle and plucked cittern, plain warm tenor, brisk, strophic, storytelling
why: 'Remote from citys liv'd a Swain' — four-beat couplets, a whole portrait in ten lines, an opening that opens.

title: Poems
author: John Gay
lyrics:
Who cherishes a brutal mate
Shall mourn the folly soon or late.
FABLE [49] XLIX.
The Man and the Flea.
Whether on earth, in air, or main,
Sure ev'ry thing alive is vain!
Does not the hawk all fowls survey,
As destin'd only for his prey?
And do not tyrants, prouder things,
Think men were born for slaves to kings?
When the crab views the pearly strands,
Or Tagus, bright with golden sands,
Or crawles beside the coral grove,
And hears the ocean roll above;
Nature is too profuse, says he,
Who gave all these to pleasure me!
style: wry moral ballad, harpsichord and pizzicato strings, sly baritone, trotting, epigrammatic, light
why: The crab beside the coral grove deciding the ocean was made for his pleasure — the fable's whole point in one image.

title: Poems
author: John Gay
lyrics:
Bespoke him thus. When coxcombs prate,
They kindle wrath, contempt, or hate.
Thy teazing tongue had judgment ty'd,
Thou hadst not, like a puppy, dy'd.
FABLE [47] XLVII.
The Court of Death.
Death, on a solemn night of state,
In all his pomp of terrors sate:
Th' attendants of his gloomy reign,
Diseases dire, a ghastly train,
Croud the vast court. With hollow tone
A voice thus thunder'd from the throne.
This night our minister we name,
Let ev'ry servant speak his claim;
Merit shall bear this eban wand.
All, at the word, stretch'd forth their hand.
style: macabre processional ballad, low organ and muffled drum, dark chorus, slow, tolling, ceremonious
why: Death holding court in his pomp of terrors with Diseases crowding the hall — a court scene that sings itself.

title: Poems
author: Richard Berenger
lyrics:
Not so, said one who stood behind,
And heard him thus disclose his mind;
Consider well pray what you do,
And think what numbers live in you:
If you go drown, your woes to ease,
Pray who will keep your lice and fleas?
On yours alone their lives depend,
With you they live, with you must end.
On great folks thus the little live,
And in their sunshine bask and thrive:
But when those suns no longer shine,
The hapless insects droop and pine.
Oh GRENVILLE then this tale apply,
Nor drown yourself lest I should die:
Compassionate your louse's case,
And keep your own to save his place.
style: english comic ballad, fiddle and hurdy-gurdy, dry mocking tenor, bouncing, brisk, punchline-timed
why: The suicide talked out of the pond because his lice depend on him — a complete joke with a real sting: 'On great folks thus the little live.'

title: Poems
author: Richard Berenger
lyrics:
As if it had been sown. What a piece of work!
How noble in faculty! infinite in reason!
A combination and a form indeed,
Where every God did seem to set his seal.
Heav'n has him now  yet let our idolatrous fancy
Still sanctify his relicts; and this day
Stand aye distinguish'd in the kalendar
To the last syllable of recorded time:
For if we take him but for all in all
We ne'er shall look upon his like again.
style: renaissance art song, lute and viol, countertenor, reverent, chamber, gently building
why: The Shakespeare cento closing on 'we ne'er shall look upon his like again' — borrowed lines, but it lands as a finished elegy.

title: Facta et Dicta Memorabilia
author: Valerius Maximus
lyrics:
7e.4. Phidias too played upon Homer's verses with an excellent saying: for, when the statue of Olympian Jupiter was finished, than which no work of human craftsmanship is more eminent or more admirable, being asked by a friend whither directing his mind he had embraced in lines of ivory the countenance of Jupiter, all but fetched from heaven itself, he answered that he had used those verses as his master:
'He spoke, and with his dark brows the son of Cronos nodded; and the ambrosial locks of the lord flowed streaming from his immortal head; and he made great Olympus tremble.'
style: ancient greek hymnic chant, lyre and deep drone, grave male voice, slow, awestruck, sparse
why: Phidias naming his master: the nod of Cronos' son, the ambrosial locks streaming, Olympus made to tremble.

title: Bergson and His Philosophy
author: John Alexander Gunn
lyrics:
"Our past still travels with us from afar And what we have been makes us what we are."
"O, Lord, my heart is sick, Sick of this everlasting change, And Life runs tediously quick Through its unresting race and varied range. Change finds no likeness of itself in Thee, And makes no echo in Thy mute eternity."
"For a thousand years in Thy sight Are but as yesterday when it is past, And as a watch in the night."
style: victorian devotional hymn, chamber organ and viola, plaintive alto, slow, aching, congregational
why: 'Our past still travels with us from afar' into 'a thousand years in Thy sight are but as yesterday' — three quotations that make one song about time.

title: San Hyan Tattvajnana
author: Unknown
lyrics:
*sakatopamam pradhanam puruso vrsabhopamah /*
*isasarathisamyuktam jagat bhramitacakravat //*
style: balinese kidung chant, gender wayang metallophones and bamboo flute, low male recitation, slow, hypnotic, ritual
why: The only candidate, but a true sloka: matter the cart, the soul the bull, the Lord the charioteer, the world a spinning wheel.

title: Panegyricus de sexto consulatu Honorii Augusti
author: Claudian
lyrics:
With what cunning, with what skill, did Stilicho, that ever fatal enemy, ensnare me! His pretended mercy did but blunt my warlike spirit, and availed him to shift the war backwards across the Po. A curse on that armistice, more damaging than the yoke of slavery. 'Twas then the cause of the Getae was undone, then that I signed my own deathwarrant. More rudely than any weapon did mercy destroy our people, beneath that semblance of peace lay the deadliest form of war, and I myself fell into the snare I had laid for others. I am weary of it all; where shall I find comfort or counsel? I fear my friends more than my foes.
Would God I had lost them all on that field. He is ever mine that has fallen in hard conflict. Better all had perished by the sword; less bitter had been my grief for losses inflicted by a victorious foe than for those brought upon me by treachery. Is there not left one faithful follower? My comrades have turned against me, my friends hate me. My life is a burden; why prolong it? Where hide the remnants of my shipwrecked fortunes? To what land shall I flee where the names of Stihcho and all too powerful Italy shall not sound for ever in mine ears?
style: late antique lament, low bowed strings and sparse frame drum, weary baritone, slow, bitter, unresolved
why: Alaric alone after the rout: 'I fear my friends more than my foes ... my life is a burden; why prolong it?' — the one human voice in the panegyric.

title: Panegyricus de sexto consulatu Honorii Augusti
author: Claudian
lyrics: Too long, my emperor, have I, thy mother, borne in silence the hurt thy refusal to return hath done me. How long shall favoured Liguria possess that for which I desire? How long shall the Rubicon, separating me from the object of my prayers by so narrow a space, torture the Tiber by the all-but-presence of that divine being whose nearer sojourn it is not allowed to enjoy? Was it not enough to have scorned me once when Africa, again at war, mocked the city with hopes of its emperor's coming, nor could we move thine obstinate ears with all our prayers? Yet did I harness for thee two steeds whiter than snow to draw the chariot wherein thou shouldst ride; already had I builded in thy name a triumphal arch through the which thou shouldst pass clad in the garb of victory, and I was dedicating it as a memorial of the war with an inscription to be the undying witness of the salvation of Libya. Even then were being prepared for Jove to see from the Tarpeian rock models for the coming triumph; a fleet of ships was cast in metal, ships whose oar-blades smote the golden sea; the cities of Africa were made to go before thy chariot and
style: roman civic invocation, cithara and low horns, commanding female voice, stately, reproachful, processional
why: Rome herself speaking as a slighted mother, counting the white horses and the arch she built for a son who would not come.

title: Thebais
author: Statius
lyrics:
have ceased, when Capaneus is heard amid the stars.
'Do you stand, you powers, for trembling Thebes?' he cried.
'Where are the sluggish nurslings of that unspeakable land,
Bacchus and Alcides? It shames me to provoke the lesser ones.
You rather come  for who is worthier to clash
with us? Look, the ashes and the tomb of Semele are held
now come, now strive against me with all your flames,
Jupiter! Or are you braver to trouble timid girls with thunder
and to raze the towers of Cadmus, your father-in-law?'
The grief of the gods groaned at his words; Jove himself laughed
at the raving man, and shaking the mass of his sacred hair:
'What hope is there for men after the battles of swelling Phlegra!
Must you too be struck?' he says. On every side the crowd of gods
presses the slow one, gnashing, and demands the avenging weapons,
style: latin epic defiance, war horns and thunderous drums, roaring bass over massed voices, driving, blasphemous, building to a crack
why: Capaneus shouting at Jupiter to come down and fight him, and Jove laughing — the most electric moment in the poem.

title: Thebais
author: Statius
lyrics:
his garments exhale a vapour, and beneath his sluggish body
the bedding grows warm, and above the couch a black mist breathes out
from his panting mouth; one hand sustains the hair
fallen from his left temple, the other has let slip, forgotten, the horn;
around him stray the countless Dreams with their wandering faces,
true mingled with false, and grim with soothing,
the shadowy host of night, and they cling to the beams and doorposts,
or lie on the ground; faint, where the gleam circles the hall,
is the light and feeble, and the languid lamps that lure on
the first slumbers breathe out from their sinking flames.
Here from the blue ether the many-coloured maiden
balanced herself down: the woods shine out, the shadowy Tempe
smiled upon the goddess, and the house, struck by her gleaming girdle,
style: dream-shadow lullaby, bowed vibraphone and soft harp, breathy low voice, very slow, drifting, narcotic
why: The House of Sleep: dreams true and false clinging to the doorposts, lamps breathing out from their sinking flames.

title: Thebais
author: Statius
lyrics:
The unhappy woman would have spoken still more, and filled all things
with her complaints: her companions and the handmaids lead her away,
loathing them, consoling, and hold her in her chamber; she sits, her cheeks
gouged with much nail; she heeds not the day, not the words
of those who pray, nor turns the gaze she has left fixed on the ground,
now bereft of voice, now of mind; so the fierce tigress,
her young snatched away, abandoned beneath a Scythian cave,
lies and licks the traces of the warm rock;
nowhere her wrath, the savagery and hunger of her raging
mouth has settled; the untroubled herds and flocks pass by:
she looks at them as she lies; for where, on what shall she feed her teats,
or whom, awaited, shall she crush with her huge prey?
Thus far arms, trumpets, iron, and wounds: but now
style: latin grief-lament, solo viola and skin drum, raw contralto, slow, keening, animal
why: The tigress licking the warm rock where her cubs lay, watching herds walk past unhunted — grief made into a hunger with nothing to eat.

title: Andreas
author: Cynewulf
lyrics:
We have heard of heroes in ages past,
of twelve true thanes under the turning stars,
the Lords own champions. Their glory lived on
in the grim struggle where standards clashed.
Their lots were laid out as the Lord Himself,
Heavens High King, handed them their fates.
Famed were those men across the fields of earth,
bold-hearted leaders, keen in the battle-press,
where hand guarded helmet on the field of doom,
and the broad shield was broken in the bitter fray.
One of them was Matthew, who first with might
preached the pure gospel, proclaiming Gods law.
Fate had assigned him that far-off country,
the grim land of Mermedonia, a place of dread,
where no guest could journey for gold or for love,
nor find any welcome in that hateful nation.
style: nordic folk, bowed lyre and frame drum, low male chant, stark, cold, alliterative and measured
why: 'We have heard of heroes in ages past, of twelve true thanes under the turning stars' — the opening does everything an opening should.

title: Andreas
author: Cynewulf
lyrics:
holy near his heart, his spirit untiring.
When the holy man was under the dark shadow,
the courage-hard hero, the livelong night
beset with sorrows. Snow bound the earth
in winters drifts. The weather grew cold
with hard hail-showers, likewise rime and frost,
the hoar-frost warriors, locked the heroes homeland,
the seats of the people. The lands were frozen
with cold icicles, the waters power clamored
over the ice-streams, it bridged with ice
the pale brine-road. The blithe-hearted hero dwelled,
the uncorrupted man, mindful of his might,
bold and enduring in his dire needs
that winter-cold night. He did not cease in his wits,
nor quail at the terror, from what he began before,
that he would ever most gloriously praise the Lord,
style: old english winter chant, bowed lyre and bone flute, hoarse male voice, very slow, glacial, sparse
why: Rime and frost as 'the hoar-frost warriors' locking the homeland, ice bridging the pale brine-road — pure Old English cold.

title: Andreas
author: Cynewulf
lyrics:
at the days dawning covered the earth,
the mere-flood grew. A mead-pouring sorrow
came after the feast-day; they awoke from their sleep,
the cunning-minded. The sound took the ground,
deeply disturbed. The host was terrified
by the floods sudden rush. The fated died,
the young in the ocean the war-rush took
through the salt-way. That was a sorrowful burden,
a bitter beer-serving. The cup-bearers did not fail,
the serving-thanes. There was for each one enough
from the days start, a drink ready at once.
The waters power grew. The men lamented,
the old ash-bearers. Their desire was to get out,
to flee the fallow stream, they wanted to save their lives,
to seek a dwelling in the down-caves,
a refuge on the earth. An angel blocked them,
style: grim mead-hall dirge, bowed lyre and deep drum, layered male voices, heavy, ironic, tolling
why: The drowning told as a feast: 'a bitter beer-serving. The cup-bearers did not fail ... a drink ready at once.'

title: Epigrams
author: Callimachus
lyrics:
And as that man led the lesser bride home to his dwelling,
so you too, Dion, drive the one that matches you.
2. Someone told me of your death, Heraclitus, and it brought
a tear to my eye; and I remembered how often
the two of us sank the sun in talk together. But you, I suppose,
my Halicarnassian friend, are long since ash;
yet your nightingales live on, and on them Hades,
who carries off all things, shall never lay his hand.
4. Timonfor you are no longerwhich is hateful to you,
the dark or the light?
"The dark; for more of you are in Hades."
5. A shell am I, Lady of Zephyrium, a wonder of old; but now you,
Cypris, hold me, the first offering of Selenaea,
a nautilus that sailed upon the seas: if there were winds,
spreading my sail from my own forestays;
but if Calm, that gleaming goddess, then rowing hard with my feet
style: hellenistic lyre song, solo kithara, clear tenor, gentle, elegiac, unhurried
why: 'Your nightingales live on, and on them Hades ... shall never lay his hand' — the most quoted couplet in Greek epigram.

title: Epigrams
author: Callimachus
lyrics:
12. If you come to Cyzicus, it is little trouble to find Hippacus
and Didyme; for their family is in no way obscure.
And you will tell them a grievous word, yet say
this all the same: that here I hold Critias, their son.
13. "Is it under you that Charidas rests?" "If you mean the son
of Arimmas of Cyrene, he is under me."
"O Charidas, what is below?" "Deep darkness." "And the ways up?"
"A lie." "And Pluto?" "A tale." "We are undone."
"This is my true word to you; but if you want
the pleasant kind: a great ox in Hades costs a Pellaean penny."
14. Who knows well the daemon of tomorrow? When even you,
Charmisyou who were before our eyes but yesterday
we buried, weeping, on the next day. Nothing more grievous
than this did your father Diophon ever see.
15. "Timonoe." "Who are you? By the gods, I should not have known you,
style: greek call-and-response dirge, low aulos and hand drum, two alternating voices, spare, uncanny, dry
why: The dialogue with the dead Charidas: 'And the ways up?' 'A lie.' 'And Pluto?' 'A tale.' — already written as call and response.

title: Epigrams
author: Callimachus
lyrics:
you goats, since the goddess has made a truce.
63. So may you sleep, Conopion, as you make me
lie down by these cold porches.
So may you sleep, most unjust one, as you lull your lover
to sleep, and have met not even pity in a dream.
The neighbours pity me; but younot even in a dream.
And soon the grey hair will remind you of all this.
style: greek doorstep serenade, plucked lyre and soft reed, wounded tenor, slow, insomniac, repeating
why: 'So may you sleep, Conopion' — the sleepless lover on the cold porch, with a refrain and a curse for an ending.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Craven
lyrics:
I thank thee God, that I have lived
In this great world and known its many joys:
The songs of birds, the strong sweet scent of hay,
And cooling breezes in the secret dusk;
The flaming sunsets at the close of day,
Hills and the lovely, heather-covered moors;
Music at night, and moonlight on the sea,
The beat of waves upon the rocky shore
And wild white spray, flung high in ecstasy;
The faithful eyes of dogs, and treasured books,
The love of Kin and fellowship of friends
And all that makes life dear and beautiful.
I thank Thee too, that there has come to me
A little sorrow and sometimes defeat,
A little heartache and the loneliness
That comes with parting and the words 'Good-bye';
style: english thanksgiving hymn, acoustic guitar and chamber strings, warm female vocal, unhurried, grateful, building
why: A litany of concrete blessings — hay, moonlight on the sea, the faithful eyes of dogs — that reads as one long grace.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Craven
lyrics:
" Vainly imagin'd I cou'd ne'er deny
"Whate'er thy fancy ask'd  Alas! but now
" I find thy wants my ev'ry sense outgrow;
"And ever having, ever wanting more,
" A power to please, to give, or to adore.
"Say, why like other Hearts dost thou not bear
" With callous apathy each worldly care?
"Why dost thou shriek at Envy's horrid cries?
" In thee Compassion, Hatred's place supplies,
"Why not with malice treat malicious Men?
" Why ever pity when thou shou'dst condemn?
"Why, at the hearing of a dismal tale,
" Dost thou with sorrow turn my Beauty pale?
"Why, when distress in any shape appears,
" Dost thou dissolve my very soul in Tears?
"Why in thy secret folds is Friendship bred?
style: georgian dramatic air, harpsichord and cello, agitated soprano, insistent, questioning, quickening
why: The heart interrogated at her own feet: a whole stanza of 'Why dost thou...' — anaphora already written for singing.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Craven
lyrics:
His Holiness deranged and ill
Was often heard to mutter
Throw to the dogs your nasty pill
I only long for butter.
St. Dominic said in a dream
Leo away with plaisters
And trust to butter and to cream
For curing your disasters.
Each doctor long his art had tried
To drive away the spleen
Whoever spoke  the Pope replied
"Butter and Margravine."
'Tis now resolved to wait no more
"Her butter to my knowledge"
The Pontiff cried, "is worth a score
Such quacks and all the College."
style: comic drawing-room ballad, fortepiano and pizzicato strings, arch soprano, brisk, deadpan, quatrain-strophic
why: The Pope refusing his pills: 'Whoever spoke — the Pope replied, Butter and Margravine.' A complete joke in singable quatrains.

title: Poems
author: Constantine Barber
lyrics:
Recalls him from the bright, delusive Scene;
With Grief he then perceives th' enchanting Sight,
The fleeting Creature of oblivious Night.
When some fine Voice delights the raptur'd Heart,
By Nature pleasing, yet improv'd by Art;
Tho' trembling each Seraphic Sound decay,
And with melodious Cadence melt away;
The faithful Echo still revives the Strain,
And sweetly charms the list'ning Ear again:
But Life, once vanish'd, will return no more;
No mimic Thought its Presence can restore.
Say then, my Soul, how must I now survey
So many Years, so quickly snatch'd away?
Awake, my Muse! Thou only canst impart
Ease to my Griefs, and heal the wounded Heart:
What Theme shall now employ my youthful Lays?
style: georgian reflective air, chamber organ and viola, grave tenor, slow, wistful, measured
why: The echo that revives a dying note set against the life that cannot be revived — one clean image carrying the whole poem.

title: Poems
author: Constantine Barber
lyrics:
But O! may Heav'n give Thine a longer Date.
To Mrs. Frances-Arabella Kelly, with a Present of Fruit.
By the Same.
Tho' the Plumb, and the Peach, with Apollo conspire,
To present you their Softness, and Sweetness, and Fire;
Their Aid is in vain; for what can they do,
But blush, and confess them selves vanquish'd by you?
Where Virtue and Wit with such Qualities blend,
What Mortal, what Goddess, would dare to contend?
Verses ty'd about a Fawn's Neck, which was presented to a very young Lady, call'd by her Friends the Ivory Maid.
By the Same.
As thro' this sylvan Scene I stray'd,
I saw and lov'd the Iv'ry Maid:
And hearing that she fled from Man,
I begg'd this Form of mighty Pan;
To try, by ev'ry winning Art,
style: english anapaestic compliment-song, baroque guitar and flute, light tenor, tripping, gallant, brisk
why: 'The Plumb, and the Peach, with Apollo conspire' — a four-line compliment that dances in its own metre.

title: Opilius Macrinus
author: Scriptores Historiae Augustae
lyrics: 11. Yet in his imperial life Macrinus was somewhat rigid and austere, hoping that he could consign all his past deeds to oblivion, when his very severity opened the way for reproaching and tearing at him. For he had wished to be called both Severus and Pertinax, which two names seemed to him names of harshness; and when the senate had called him Pius and Felix, he received the name of Felix but was unwilling to have that of Pius; whence there seems to survive against him an elegant epigram of a certain Greek poet, which in Latin is contained in this sense: "An actor now grown old, base, heavy, harsh, unjust, impiousand 'Felix'he wishes thus to be at once, so that he is unwilling to be Pius, yet wishes to be blessed, which Nature denies and Reason does not admit; for he could both be called and seem Pius and Feliximpious and unfortunate he is, and so he will be to himself." These verses someone or other, of those who were Latin, placed in the forum beside those which were Greek; and Macrinus, having received them, is said to have replied with these verses: "If the fates had borne such a Greek poet as that Latin gibbet-bird was, the people would have known nothing, the senate would have known nothing, you slave-dealer; no one would have written foul songs against me." With these verses, far worse than those Latin ones, Macrinus believed he had replied; but he was held no less for a laughingstock than that poet who attempted to write in Latin from the Greek.
style: roman street lampoon, reedy pipes and hand drum, sneering male voice, jaunty, mocking, quick
why: Only candidate, but it carries a real forum-lampoon: the emperor who wanted to be Felix and refused to be Pius, and his worse reply.

title: Non Posse Suaviter Vivi Secundum Epicurum
author: Plutarch
lyrics: and these: But from our lips the vital spirit fled Returns no more to wake the silent dead.
style: ancient greek lament, single lyre and low drone, solo male voice, very slow, hollow, sparse
why: Two lines only, but they are the Homeric ones: the breath that leaves the lips and never comes back to wake the dead.

title: Satyricon
author: Petronius Arbiter
lyrics:
At all times and in all places I have lived such a life that I spent each passing day as though that light would never return...
"The hair that is the whole glory of the body is fallen, dull winter has carried away the bright locks of spring. Now the temples are bare of their shade and are downcast, and the wide naked space on my old head shines where the hair is worn away. Ye Gods that love to cheat us; ye rob us first of the first joys ye gave to our youth.
Poor wretch, a moment ago thy hair shone bright and more beautiful than Phbus and the sister of Phoebus. Now thou art smoother than bronze or the round garden mushroom that is born in rain, and turnest in dread from a girl's mockery. To teach thee how quickly death shall come, know that a part of thine head hath died already."
style: roman drinking-song elegy, plucked lyre and low pipe, rueful tenor, moderate, wry, intimate
why: The bald head as a season: 'dull winter has carried away the bright locks of spring ... a part of thine head hath died already.'

title: Satyricon
author: Petronius Arbiter
lyrics: I marvelled at the resources of poverty, and the art displayed in each particular. 'No Indian ivory set in gold shone here, the earth did not gleam with marble now trodden upon and mocked for the gifts she gave, but the grove of Ceres on her holiday was set round with hurdles of willow twigs and fresh cups of clay shaped by a quick turn of the lowly wheel. There was a vessel for soft honey, and wicker-work plates of pliant bark, and a jar dyed with the blood of Bacchus. And the wall round was covered with light chaff and spattered mud; on it hung rows of rude nails and slim stalks of green rushes. Besides this, the little cottage roofed with smoky beams preserved their goods, the soft service-berries hung entwined in fragrant wreaths, and dried savory and bunches of raisins; such a hostess was here as was once on Athenian soil, worthy of the worship of Hecale, of whom the Muse testified for all ages to adore her, in the years when the poet of Cyrene sang.'
style: rustic latin pastoral, reed pipe and hand drum, plain warm voice, gentle, unhurried, hearthside
why: The poor cottage inventoried — clay cups off a fast wheel, service-berries in wreaths, savory and raisins — all concrete, all singable.

title: Satyricon
author: Petronius Arbiter
lyrics:
'Even so I suppose the birds of Stymphalus fled into the sky when the power of Hercules compelled them, and the Harpies whose reeking wings made the tantalizing food of Phineus run with poison. The air above trembled and shook with unwonted lamentation, and the palace of heaven was in an uproar.'..
Whoever has money sails in a fair wind, and directs his fortune at his own pleasure. Let him take Danae to wife, and he can tell Acrisius to believe what he told Danae. Let him write poetry, make speeches, snap his fingers at the world, win his cases and outdo Cato. A lawyer, let him have his 'Proven' and his Not proven,' and be all that Servius and Labeo were. I have said enough: with money about you, wish for what you like and it will come. Your safe has Jupiter shut up in it....
style: sardonic roman cabaret, plucked strings and light percussion, dry mocking baritone, jaunty, clipped, looping
why: 'Whoever has money sails in a fair wind ... Your safe has Jupiter shut up in it' — a complete cynical creed with a punchline.

title: Punica
author: Silius Italicus
lyrics:
of the gods sought out, by lot and fate, the offspring of Hannibal.
But a nearer fear was from the wrath of the armed leader,
and great before their eyes stood the image of his return.
This Imilce makes harsher, her cheeks befouled and her hair torn,
and fills the city with the clamour of her grief,
as an Edonian woman on Pangaeus, stirred by the triennial rite,
goes over the ridges and sighs within her breast for the enclosed Bacchus.
So among the Tyrian mothers, as if set beneath the torches,
she cries: "Ah, husband, in whatever quarter of the world
you wage your wars, hither bear your standards. More violent is the foe here,
here nearer. You now perhaps beneath the very
walls of the Dardan city receive the quivering weapons
upon your shield, unafraid, and brandishing the savage
style: carthaginian lament, frame drum and double reed, wailing female voice, ecstatic, keening, ritual
why: Imilce tearing her hair among the Tyrian mothers, calling her husband home from the wrong war — the poem's one true cry.

title: Punica
author: Silius Italicus
lyrics:
Was it thought unworthy that this life be cut off by a brave
right hand? Give me back, O son, to dangers,
give me back to the foe! Let it be allowed me, in battle, to summon a death
that I may approve to my country and my brother." Then, stirred by his words,
Venus groaned and turned upon the river the swift
might of her unconquered husband. The scattered fire drives flames
on every side along the banks, and burning lays waste
the shades nursed for many years by the river.
The whole grove burns, and Vulcan, poured into the high woods
in victory, crackles with loosened reins.
And now the fir is scorched in its foliage, now the pine and the alders,
now the poplar, standing on its bare trunk alone, has let fall on high
the birds wont to dwell among its branches.
The greedy flame drinks up the waters drawn from the deepest
style: latin epic conflagration, low brass and crackling percussion, declamatory bass, driving, blazing, relentless
why: The grove burning limb by limb until the bare poplar lets its birds fall from the sky.

title: Punica
author: Silius Italicus
lyrics:
his yellow hair and his locks for you, Gradivus,
rivalling gold, and the ruddy knot upon his crown.
But the Fates, not hearing him vow his unshorn hair,
dragged him by it to the shades. Over his white limbs
the gore goes steaming, and the drenched earth grows red.
But Ligaunus, not slowed by the javelin that met him,
rushes in and, facing the man, wheels his sword to meet him,
and rising strikes where the sinews bind the supple arm
to the shoulder, and the right hand, cut off by the wound,
hung dying a little while from the loosened reins,
and while it gleams, with a trembling effort it grasps again the strap
and, knowing nothing, imitates one guiding the accustomed bridle.
Then Vosegus reaps the neck of the turned man, and bearing
the helmet hung up with its plume, and the enclosed face
style: grim battle chant, war horns and heavy drum, hoarse male voice, hard, unflinching, stamping
why: The severed hand that gropes back to the rein and, knowing nothing, imitates a man still driving.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Campbell
lyrics:
THE Pleasures of Hope. PART FIRST.
Pleasures of Hope.
PART I.
AT summer eve, when Heav'n's aerial bow
Spans with bright arch the glittering hills below,
Why to yon mountain turns the musing eye,
Whose sunbright summit mingles with the sky?
Why do these cliffs of shadowy tint appear
More sweet than all the landscape smiling near?
'Tis Distance lends enchantment to the view,
And robes the mountain in its azure hue.
Thus, with delight, we linger to survey
The promis'd joys of life's unmeasur'd way;
Thus, from afar, each dim-discover'd scene
More pleasing seems than all the past hath been;
And every form that fancy can repair
style: english romantic lyric, acoustic guitar and soft strings, warm tenor, unhurried, wide-open, pastoral
why: 'Tis Distance lends enchantment to the view' — the line the poet is remembered by, sitting in a landscape that opens the song for you.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Campbell
lyrics:
My Absalom! the voice of Nature cried!
Oh! that for thee thy father could have died!
For bloody was the deed, and rashly done,
That slew my Absalom!  my son!  my son!
Unfading Hope! when life's last embers burn,
When soul to soul, and dust to dust return!
Heav'n to thy charge resigns the awful hour!
Oh! then, thy kingdom comes! Immortal Power!
What though each spark of earth-born rapture fly
The quivering lip, pale cheek, and closing eye!
Bright to the soul thy seraph hands convey
The morning dream of life's eternal day
Then, then, the triumph and the trance begin!
And all the Phoenix spirit burns within!
Cease, every joy, to glimmer on my mind,
But leave  oh! leave  the light of hope behind!
style: romantic hymn-anthem, chamber organ and swelling strings, soaring soprano, slow, exalted, luminous close
why: The Absalom cry giving way to 'leave — oh! leave — the light of hope behind' — grief and consolation in one arc.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Campbell
style: scottish border ballad, fiddle and harp, plaintive female voice, strophic, mournful, unhurried
why: Gilderoy's ballad — drum, bell, gallows tree, and the memory of Roslin's glen. Ballad metre, ready to sing.

title: Podagra
author: Lucian of Samosata
lyrics:
GOUT-SUFFERER
O hateful name, O name detested by the gods,
Gout, much-lamented, child of Cocytus,
whom in the deep-shadowed hollows of Tartarus
Megaera the Fury bore forth from her womb
and nursed at her breast, and into your bitter infant lips
Alecto let her milk drip down
which of the powers, then, sent you up
into the light, ill-named as you are? You came to mankind as a curse.
For if upon the dead there followed some requital
for the sins they did in the light of day,
then Tantalus need not be punished with his drink,
nor Ixion whirled upon his wheel, nor Sisyphus
with his stone, there in the house of Pluto;
no  all who have done evil should simply
be handed over to your joint-racking torments,
style: mock greek tragedy, aulos and low drone with frame drum, grave declaiming male voice, slow, portentous, absurdly solemn
why: A tragic curse aimed at gout: nursed in Tartarus by Megaera, milk dripped in by Alecto. Perfect straight-faced parody.

title: Podagra
author: Lucian of Samosata
lyrics:
and the king of the dead below, Hades, trembles
you who love the bandage, who bring men to their couches,
who hobble the runner, who rack the ankle-bones,
who set the ankles ablaze, who scarce let the foot touch ground,
who make a man dread the pestle, who keep the burning knee awake,
who love the knobs and swellings about the joints,
you who bow the knee and bend it crooked, Gout.
MESSENGER
Mistress  for at a timely moment you have met my foot
hear me, for the word I bring is not in vain,
but the deed travels as companion to the word.
For I, as you commanded, with quiet foot
went tracking through the cities, searching every house,
longing to learn whether any man dishonours your power.
And among the rest I found their minds at peace,
overcome, my queen, by the force of your two hands;
style: greek cult hymn, layered voices over lyre and hand drum, incantatory, building, insistent
why: The litany of epithets — 'who hobble the runner, who rack the ankle-bones, who keep the burning knee awake' — pure singable anaphora.

title: Podagra
author: Lucian of Samosata
lyrics:
CHORUS
Salmoneus's might did not contend with the thunders of Zeus,
but he died, subdued in his mind by the god's smoky bolt.
The satyr Marsyas did not rejoice when he contended with Phoebus,
but to this day his skin quivers shrilly about that pine.
For the sake of her strife, Niobe the mother won unforgettable grief,
but even now, still mourning, she pours much weeping on Sipylus.
Maeonian Arachne came into strife with the Tritonian goddess,
but, having lost her form, even now she weaves her threads;
for the daring of mortals is no match for the wrath of the blessed ones,
of Zeus, of Leto, of Pallas, of the Pythian.
Gentle, O goddess of all the people, may you bring an affliction, Gout,
light, easy, not sharp, doing little harm, free of pain,
easy to bear, easy to be rid of, weak, letting a man walk about.
style: ancient chorus, lyre and frame drum, layered voices, solemn, building, then softening to prayer
why: Salmoneus, Marsyas, Niobe, Arachne — a real tragic ode on mortals who contended with gods, ending in a bargaining prayer to Gout.

title: Poems
author: Eliza Day
lyrics:
Upon a lady losing a sprig of Myrtle, presented to her by her husband, on the morning of their marriage.
NOW beneath pale Luna's beam,
Fairies sport, while mortals dream;
Cruel schemes they plan to-night,
Mischief charms each pigmy sprite;
Hear, enraged, their frowning queen,
Thus exclaim, with jealous spleen;
Shall a mortal dare be blest,
When sad Titania cannot rest?
Thwart their marriage, fairy elves,
Or scorn and hate pursue yourselves.
Thrice I wave my magic wand,
Your signal to prepare;
Obedient to your queen's command,
Ascend the ambient air.
Five times compass round the earth
style: fairy incantation, harp and small bells with soft frame drum, silvery female voice, quick, conspiratorial, chanting
why: Titania's jealous spell against a marriage — 'Thrice I wave my magic wand' — a charm already written in charm-metre.

title: Poems
author: Eliza Day
lyrics:
Black Eurus chill'd thy infant wing,
Dread wastes affright thine eye;
Opening the vocal choir of spring,
Stern winter bid thee die.
Ah! what avails a bounteous store,
Or what a heart to give;
When the important minute's o'er,
That sufferers might receive?
ON FINDING A STRAYED CHILD.
A STEM blown from its parent tree,
I planted in my humble bower;
Sure it may grow to shelter me,
From scorching sun and dripping shower.
Stay Madelina, child of woe,
Thy little feet no more shall roam,
I said, and fast as tears could flow,
style: english ballad lament, acoustic guitar and low strings, tender female vocal, slow, tearful, strophic
why: The strayed child taken in as a broken stem replanted — 'Stay Madelina, child of woe, thy little feet no more shall roam.'

title: Poems
author: Eliza Day
lyrics:
For kindness a soft charm disclosing,
Best its fury can subdue.
The sun and wind their power contesting,
(A tale in sop's moral page)
Which the traveller divesting,
Of his mantle could engage.
The wind his storms then fiercely blowing,
Saw him his cloak more closely fold;
But he to the sun warm glowing,
Yields the prize, and quits his hold.
Where cold suspicions are misleading,
And with contempt and hatred bind;
Gentleness for truth best pleading,
Melts the fetters of the mind.
The frigid blast the shepherd's mourning,
More firmly bound his streams to see;
style: moral fable song, harpsichord and viol, clear alto, lilting, trochaic, gently instructive
why: The sun and wind contending for the traveller's cloak, ending on 'Gentleness ... melts the fetters of the mind.'

title: Poems
author: William Woty
lyrics:
WHAT! tho' thou com'st in sable mantle clad,
Yet, Winter! art thou welcome to my eye:
Thee here I hail, tho' terrors round thee wait,
And winds tempestuous howl along the sky.
But shall I then so soon forget the days
When Ceres led me thro' her wheaten mines!
When autumn pluck'd me, with his tawny hand,
Empurpled clusters from ambrosial vines!
So soon forget, when up the yielding pole
I saw ascend the silver-bearded hop!
When Summer, waving high her crown of hay,
Pour'd o'er the mead her odoriferous crop!
I must forget them  and thee too, O Spring!
Tho' many a chaplet thou hast weav'd for me:
For, now prepar'd to quit th' enchanting scenes,
Cold, weeping Winter! I come all to thee.
style: english winter ode, chamber strings and low flute, grave tenor, measured, austere, welcoming the cold
why: 'Winter! art thou welcome to my eye' — the seasons remembered in turn, autumn plucking clusters with a tawny hand.

title: Poems
author: William Woty
lyrics:
Ye lillies chaste! with silver heads
As my Cleora's bosom fair:
No more I court your balmy sweets;
For I, and I alone, can prove,
How sweeter, when each other meets,
The kisses are of her I love.
Her tempting eyes my gaze inclin'd,
Their pleasing lesson first I caught;
Her sense, her friendship next confin'd
The willing pupil she had taught.
Should fortune, stooping from her sky,
Conduct me to her bright alcove;
Yet, like the turtle, I should die,
Denied the kiss of her love.
TO WINTER.
BY MR. WOTY.
style: georgian love song, baroque guitar and recorder, warm tenor, lilting, strophic with a returning refrain
why: Lilies, roses, and the refrain 'the kisses are of her I love' coming round twice — a song that already has its hook.

title: Poems
author: William Woty
lyrics:
Hail to thy rolling clouds, and rapid storms!
Tho' they deform fair Nature's lovely face:
Hail to thy winds, that sweep along the earth!
Tho' trees they root up from their solid base.
How sicklied over is the face of things!
Where is the spice kiss of the southern gale!
Where the wild rose, that smil'd upon the thorn,
The mountain flower, and lilly of the vale!
How gloomy 'tis to cast the eye around,
And view the trees disrob'd of every leaf,
The velvet path grown rough with clotting showers,
And every field depriv'd of every sheaf!
How far more gloomy o'er the rain-beat heath,
Alone to travel in the dead of night!
No twinkling star to gild the arch of heaven,
No moon to lend her temporary light:
style: bleak pastoral elegy, solo viola and sparse guitar, low voice, slow, wind-blown, desolate
why: 'Where is the spice kiss of the southern gale?' — an ubi sunt for summer, ending alone on a rain-beaten heath with no star.

title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith
lyrics: The worst of all the multitude Did something for the common good. This was the states craft, that maintaind The whole, of which each part complaind: This, as in musick harmony, Made jarrings in the main agree; Parties directly opposite, Assist each othr, as twere for spight; And temprance with sobriety Serve drunkenness and gluttony. The root of evil, avarice, That damnd ill-naturd baneful vice, Was slave to prodigality, That noble sin; whilst luxury Employd a million of the poor, And odious pride a million more: Envy itself and vanity Were ministers of industry; Their darling folly, fickleness In diet, furniture, and dress, That strange ridiclous vice, was made The very wheel that turnd the trade.
style: english satirical broadside, fiddle and hurdy-gurdy with tabor, brisk chorus of voices, driving, ironic, relentless
why: The Fable of the Bees in four-beat couplets — envy and vanity as ministers of industry, ending with the poor living better than the rich before.

title: Crassus
author: Plutarch
lyrics: The Parthians lifted it up with clapping of hands and shouts of joy, and at the kings bidding his servants gave Sillaces a seat at the banquet. Then Jason handed his costume of Pentheus to one of the chorus, seized the head of Crassus, and assuming the role of the frenzied Agave, sang these verses through as if inspired: We bring from the mountain A tendril fresh-cut to the palace, A wonderful prey.
style: greek bacchic chant, aulos and tambourine, wild high voice, ecstatic, unsettling, quickening
why: The actor playing Agave with the real severed head: 'We bring from the mountain a tendril fresh-cut to the palace, a wonderful prey.'

title: Consolatio ad Apollonium
author: Plutarch
style: greek consolation ode, lyre and low strings, grave tenor, slow, measured, autumnal
why: The leaves simile — 'Another race the following spring supplies; they fall successive, and successive rise' — the oldest image we have for mortality.

title: Consolatio ad Apollonium
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
And to fly out the crowding mischief strove;
But slender hope upon the brims did stay,
Ready to vanish into air away;
She with retrieve the haggard in did put,
And on the prisoner close the box did shut;
But plagues innumerable abroad did fly,
Infecting all the earth, the seas, and sky,
Diseases now with silent feet do creep,
Torment us waking, and afflict our sleep.
These midnight evils steal without a noise,
For Jupiter deprived them of their voice.
After these the comedian, talking of those who bear afflictions uneasily, speaks consonantly to this purpose: If we in wet complaints could quench our grief,
At any rate wed purchase our relief;
With proffered gold would bribe off all our fears,
And make our eyes distil in precious tears.
But the Gods mind not mortals here below,
style: dark chamber ballad, viol and muted harp, low female voice, slow, hushed, creeping
why: Pandora's plagues creeping on silent feet because Jupiter took away their voices — a nightmare with a beautiful mechanism.

title: Consolatio ad Apollonium
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
But for a day it doth endure.
And also: From small beginnings our misfortunes grow,
And little rubs our feet do overthrow;
A single day is able down to cast
Some things from height, and others raise as fast.
Demetrius Phalereus affirms that this was truly said, but that the poet had been more in the right if for a single day he had put only a moment of time. For earthly fruits and mortal mens estate
Turn round about in one and selfsame rate;
Some live, wax strong, and prosper day by day,
While others are cast down and fade away.
And Pindar hath it in another place, What are we, what are we not?
Man is but a shadows dream.
He used an artificial and very perspicuous hyperbole to draw human life in its genuine colors; for what is weaker than a shadow? Or what words can be found out whereby to express a shadows dream? Crantor hath something consonant to this, when, condoling Hippocles upon the loss of his children, he speaks after this manner:
style: ancient greek gnomic chant, single lyre and drone, plain male voice, unhurried, aphoristic, sparse
why: 'What are we, what are we not? Man is but a shadow's dream' — Pindar's hyperbole set against a wheel that turns in a single day.

title: Amphitruo
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
AMPHITRYON:
May the Gods grant, that, in the event, what you have said may prove untrue.
(They stand apart.)
(Enter ALCMENA, from the house, attended by THESSALA.)
ALCMENA:
Is not the proportion of pleasures in life and in passing our existence short in comparison with what is disagreable? So it is allotted to each man in life;
so has it pleased the Gods that Sorrow should attend on Pleasure as her companion; but if aught of good befalls us, more of trouble and of ill forthwith attends us. For this do I now feel by experience at home and in relation to myself, to whom delight has been imparted for a very short time, while I had the opportunity of seeing my husband for but one night; and now has he suddenly gone away hence from me before the dawn.
style: roman stage aria, tibia pipes and light strings, warm female voice, flowing, resigned, dignified
