why: Alcmena alone: pleasure allotted sorrow for a companion, one night of a husband, and valour named the best reward — a real solo speech.

title: Amphitruo
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
Is he amorously disposed? He is wise; he does right, inasmuch as he follows his inclination; a thing that all men ought to do, so long as it is done in a proper manner. Now, my father wishes Amphitryon to be cajoled; Ill take care, Spectators, that he shall be rarely cajoled, while you look on. Ill place a chaplet on my head, and pretend that I am drunk.
And up there (pointing to the top of the house) will I get; from that spot, at the top of the house, Ill cleverly drive this person off when he comes hither: Ill take care that, sober, he shall be drenched. Afterwards, his own servant Sosia will presently be suffering the punishment for it; hell be accusing him of doing, this day, the things which I myself have done whats that to me? Its proper for me to be obedient to my father; its right to be subservient to his pleasure.
style: comic patter song, plucked lyre and hand drum, sly light tenor, quick, conspiratorial, mischievous
why: Mercury planning to fake a drunk and pelt a man from his own rooftop — a self-contained aside told straight to the audience.

title: Amphitruo
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
MERCURY:
As, in purchasing and selling your merchandize, you are desirous to render me propitious to your bargains, and that I should assist you in all things; and as both in foreign countries and at home, you desire me to turn to the best advantage the business and the accounts of you all, and that with fair and ample profit, without end, I should crown the venture both which you have begun, and which you shall begin; and as you wish me to delight you and all yours with joyous news these tidings will I bring, that I may announce them to you, things which in especial are for your common interest
(for already do you know, indeed, that it has been given and assigned to me by the other Divinities, to preside over news and profit): as you would wish me to favour and promote these things, that lasting gain may ever be forthcoming for you, so shall you give silence for this play, and so shall you be fair and upright judges here, all of you. Now, by whose command, and for what reason I am come, Ill tell you, and at the sane time, myself, I will disclose my name. By the command of Jupiter I am come; my name is Mercury.
style: roman market-god prologue, reedy pipes and tambourine, brash showman's voice, brisk, wheedling, rhythmic
why: The god of profit bargaining with the crowd for their silence before naming himself — a prologue that is already a performance.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Tickell
lyrics:
Ah! have you seen a lily pale
When beating rains descend?
So droop'd this slow-consuming maid,
Her life now near its end.
By LUCY warn'd, of flatt'ring swains
Take heed, ye easy fair;
Of vengeance due to broken vows,
Ye flatt'ring swains beware!
Three times all in the dead of night,
A bell was heard to ring;
And at her window shrieking thrice,
The raven flap'd his wing.
Full well the love-lorn maiden knew
The solemn boding sound,
And thus in dying words bespake
The virgins weeping round.
style: english supernatural ballad, fiddle and harp, plaintive female voice, strophic, ominous, unhurried
why: Colin and Lucy — the bell tolling three times and the raven at the window. Ballad metre with a curse in it.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Tickell
lyrics:
Nor e'er was to the bowers of bliss convey'd
A fairer spirit, or more welcome shade.
In what new region, to the just assign'd,
What new employments please th' unbody'd mind?
A winged virtue, through th' etherial sky,
From world to world unweary'd does he fly,
Or curious trace the long laborious maze
Of heav'n's decrees, where wond'ring angels gaze?
Does he delight to hear hold seraphs tell
How Michael battled, and the dragon fell?
Or, mix'd with milder cherubim, to glow
In hymns of love, not ill essay'd below?
Or dost thou warn poor mortals left behind,
A task well suited to thy gentle mind?
Oh, if sometimes thy spotless form descend,
To me thy aid, thou guardian genius, lend!
style: georgian elegy-hymn, chamber organ and strings, clear tenor, slow, questioning, ascending
why: 'In what new region, to the just assign'd, what new employments please th' unbody'd mind?' — a whole song of questions to the dead.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Tickell
lyrics:
Secure of fame, and justice in the grave.
Ah! no  when once the mortal yields to fate,
The blast of Fame's sweet trumpet sounds too late,
Too late to stay the spirit on its flight,
Or sooth the new inhabitant of light;
Who hears regardless, while fond man, distress'd,
Hangs on the absent, and laments the blest.
Farewel then fame, ill sought thro' fields of blood,
Farewel unfaithful promiser of good:
Thou musick, warbling to the deafen'd ear!
Thou incense wasted on the fun'ral bier!
Through life pursu'd in vain, by death obtain'd,
When ask'd, deny'd us, and when giv'n, disdain'd.
AN ODE Inscrib'd to the Right Honourable the EARL of SUNDERLAND at WINDSOR.
By the Same.
THOU dome, where Edward first enroll'd
style: solemn valediction, muted strings and low flute, grave baritone, slow, bitter, spare
why: 'Thou musick, warbling to the deafen'd ear! Thou incense wasted on the fun'ral bier!' — fame indicted in four unanswerable lines.

title: Poems
author: Ann Batten Cristall
lyrics:
But most his future life his gratitude display'd.
SONG.
COME, let us dance and sing,
While our spirits lightly wing;
Youth's gay fantastic spring
Wreathes the mystic bow'rs!
Bend here thy quivering feet,
Fancy thy smiles shall greet,
Dimples 'mid roses sweet,
And fruits with glowing flowers!
Glide along,
Join my song,
Meet me in the varied throng;
Crown'd with May,
Laughing gay,
Hailing like a lark the day!
style: english dance-song, tabor and pipe with fiddle, bright female voice, quick, whirling, refrain-driven
why: 'Come, let us dance and sing' — short lines, internal rhyme, a built-in chorus. It is already a song and says so.

title: Poems
author: Ann Batten Cristall
lyrics:
BEFORE TWILIGHT.
DAWN had not streak'd the spacious veil of night,
When EYEZION, the light poet of the spring,
Hied from his restless bed, to sing,
Impatient for the promis'd beams of light:
Sweetly his voice through woods and vallies rang,
While fleeting o'er the hills, these anxious notes he sang:
Swift, swift, ye lingering hours,
And wake the morning star;
Rouse from the dew-fraught flowers
The shades, and drive them far.
Quick on the wings of morning,
Dart the young glimmering light,
Th' horizon's verge adorning,
With blushing radiance dight.
Rise, Phoebus, from yon mountain,
style: dawn aubade, harp and soft flute, high clear voice, gathering, expectant, luminous
why: The poet of spring calling the hours on: 'Swift, swift, ye lingering hours, and wake the morning star.'

title: Poems
author: Ann Batten Cristall
lyrics:
Still o'er each sun-burnt furzy hill,
Wild, playful, gay, and free,
She laugh'd and scorn'd, I chas'd her still,
And still she banter'd me.
When autumn waves her golden ears,
And wafts o'er fruits her pregnant breath,
The sprightly lark its pinions rears,
I chas'd her o'er the daisy'd heath;
Sweet hare-bells trembled in the vale,
And all around was glee;
Still, wanton as the timid hart,
She swiftly flew from me.
Now winter lights its chearful fire,
While jests with frolic mirth resound,
And draws the wand'ring beauty nigher,
'Tis now too cold to rove around:
style: pastoral chase ballad, acoustic guitar and fiddle, warm mixed voices, lilting, teasing, seasonal
why: The girl who laughs and runs across three seasons of hills — a pursuit song with the year built into its verses.

title: Poems
author: Matthew Green
lyrics:
Nymph-like the sister chiefs surround;
Nature shall smile, and round this cell
The turf to your light pressure swell,
And knowing beauty by her shoe,
Well air its carpet from the dew.
The Oak, while you his umbrage deck
Lets fall his acorns in your neck:
Zephyr his civil kisses gives,
And plays with curls, instead of leaves:
Birds, seeing you, believe it spring,
And during their vacation sing;
And flow'rs lean forward from their seats
To traffic in exchange of sweets;
And angels bearing wreaths descend,
Preferr'd as vergers to attend
This fane, whose deity intreats
style: witty georgian air, harpsichord and recorder, light tenor, tripping, charming, four-beat
why: The oak dropping acorns down your neck, birds taking their vacation to sing, flowers leaning out to trade sweets — invention on every line.

title: Poems
author: Matthew Green
lyrics:
In one, no object of our sight,
Immutable and infinite,
Who can't be cruel, or unjust,
Calm and resign'd, I fix my trust;
To him my past and present state
I owe, and must my future fate.
A stranger into life I'm come,
Dying may be our going home,
Transported here by angry Fate,
The convicts of a prior state.
Hence I no anxious thoughts bestow
On matters, I can never know;
Thro' life's foul way, like vagrant pass'd,
He'll grant a settlement at last,
And with sweet ease the wearied crown,
By leave to lay his being down.
style: reflective english hymn, chamber organ and viola, calm baritone, slow, settled, consoling
why: 'A stranger into life I'm come, dying may be our going home' — the whole argument for peace of mind in twelve lines.

title: Poems
author: Matthew Green
lyrics:
Poor little, pretty, fluttering thing,
Thy pains the sex display,
Who only to repair a ring
Could take thy life away;
Drive av'rice from your breasts, ye fair,
Monster of foulest mien:
Ye would not let it harbour there,
Could but its form be seen.
It made a virgin put on guile,
Truth's image break her word,
A Lucia's face forbear to smile,
A Venus kill her bird.
JOVE and SEMELE.
By the Same.
JOVE for amusement quitted oft his skies,
To visit earth, contracted to our size;
style: drawing-room lament, harpsichord and solo violin, tender soprano, gentle, reproachful, strophic
why: The sparrow killed to mend a ring, closing on 'A Lucia's face forbear to smile, a Venus kill her bird.'

title: Against Leocrates
author: Lycurgus
lyrics:
Should I not send them forth into the fight,
Though fearing for them? May my children then
Fight also, vie with men, and not become
Mere shapes of vanity within the state.
And yet, when mothers send their sons to war
With tears, they often daunt them as they leave.
I hate the women who above all else
Prefer their sons to live and put this thought
Before their honor, urging cowardice.
But if they fall in battle they obtain
A common grave and glory which they share
With many others; whereas she, my child,
By dying for this city will attain
A garland destined solely for herself.
And she will save her mother and you too
And both her sisters. Is it right to scorn
style: greek tragic monody, aulos and low lyre, resolute female voice, measured, unwavering, austere
why: The mother giving her daughter to be sacrificed, scorning the women who urge cowardice — a garland destined for her alone.

title: Against Leocrates
author: Lycurgus
lyrics:
Before the youths, with grey beard, hair grown white,
To breathe out in the dust his valiant life,
Clasping his bloody groin with clinging hands,
(Fit sight indeed to kindle wrath and shame!)
His body bared. But those whom youths sweet flower
Adorns unfaded nothing can defame.
Honor of men is theirs, in life, and womens love;
Fair are they too when in the van laid low.
Then clench your teeth and, with both feet astride,
Firm planted on the ground withstand the foe.
And so over their graves a testimony to their courage can be seen, faithfully engraved for every Greek to read: to the Spartans: Go tell the Spartans, thou who passest by, That here obedient to their laws we lie.
And to your ancestors: Athenians, guarding Greece, subdued in fight At Marathon the gilded Persians might.
style: spartan war chant, deep drum and bronze percussion, massed male voices, hard, driving, stamping
why: Tyrtaeus at full pitch, closing on the greatest epitaph ever cut: 'Go tell the Spartans ... that here obedient to their laws we lie.'

title: Against Leocrates
author: Lycurgus
lyrics:
Unwelcome will he be whereer he goes,
Bowed dawn with hardship and by want defiled.
Bringing his house dishonor, he belies
His noble mien, a prey to fear and shame.
Thus roams the waif unpitied and unloved,
He and the line that after bears his name.
Be stalwart then. Think not of life or limb;
Shielding our land and children let us die.
Youths, brave the fight together. Be not first
To yield to craven cowardice and fly.
Make large your hearts within you. Undismayed
Engage in battle with grown men. Be bold;
And standing fast forsake not those whose feet
No longer keep their swiftness. Guard the old.
For shame it is to see an elder fall,
Down in the forefront, smitten in the strife,
style: greek marching song, double pipe and frame drum, low male chorus, insistent, grim, steady
why: The exile roaming unpitied with his whole line behind him, turned into a reason to stand and guard the old.

title: Ion
author: Plato
lyrics: For as they were eager to pass over, a bird had crossed them, an eagle of lofty flight, pressing the host at the left hand, and bearing a blood-red monster of a snake, alive and still struggling; nor had it yet unlearnt the lust of battle. For bending back it smote its captor on the breast by the neck, and the bird in the bitterness of pain cast it away to the ground, and dropped it down in the midst of the throng; and then with a cry flew off on the wafting winds.
style: homeric recitation, single lyre and low drone, declaiming male voice, deliberate, ominous, spare
why: The eagle and the still-fighting snake that bites its captor and is dropped into the army — a complete omen in one breath.

title: Mosella
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: Hail, river, praised by the fields, praised by the husbandmen, to whom the Belgae owe the walls honoured with imperial rank! River, your vine-clad ridges planted with fragrant Bacchus, your grassy banks planted too, O greenest of rivers! Ship-bearing like the sea, you slope downward into your descending waters; like a river you flow, yet with your glassy depth you rival the lakes, and you can match the brooks with your quick course, and surpass the cold springs in the clearness of your draught. You alone possess all that a spring has, all that a brook and a river have, and a lake, and the tidal sea that ebbs back with twofold flow. You glide past with placid waters, and you suffer no murmur of the wind, no struggle of any hidden rock. You are not forced to hurry your rapid currents over a foaming shoal; nor, broken by jutting lands in mid-channel, do you let an island sever your excluded stream, lest it rob you of the honour of your rightful name. You have been allotted a double path: both when you glide down with the favouring current, so that the swift oars strike the troubled shallows, and when the sailors, the towrope nowhere slackening along the banks, strain the cables of the masts against their necks. How often do you yourself marvel at your own eddies in the stream, and think your lawful course flows almost too sluggishly? You do not fringe your bank with marsh-bred sedges, nor sluggishly drench your shores with foul mire: the footprints go down to the water's very edge and stay dry. Go now, and inlay your smooth floors with Phrygian marbles, stretching a marble plain through panelled halls! But I, scorning what wealth and riches have given, will marvel at the work of Nature, not at that ruinous extravagance in which a spendthrift poverty, glad to squander, runs riot. Here solid sands carpet the moist shores, and the pressed footprints keep no remembering shapes.
style: late antique river hymn, cithara and low flute with soft water percussion, warm tenor, flowing, celebratory, unhurried
why: 'Hail, river ... O greenest of rivers!' — a direct address that gathers spring, brook, lake and tide into one praise.

title: Mosella
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: Nor does the scenery of the place delight men alone: here I could believe that even the rustic Satyrs and the grey-eyed Naiads gather on the farthest banks, when wanton mischief drives the goat-footed Pans, and they leap upon the shallows and terrify the trembling sisters beneath the stream, beating the water with their unschooled blows; and often Panope of the river, having stolen the grapes from the midst of the hills, flees amid her Oread friends from the wanton Fauns, the rustic powers. It is said, too, that when the fiery sun has stood in mid-orbit, at the common stream the Satyrs and the glassy sisters celebrate their shared dances together, when the more burning heat has granted hours secret from the gathering of men. Then the Nymphs sport, leaping over their own waters, and plunge the Satyrs in the shallows, and slip out, who know not how to swim, through their very hands, while they grasp at the slippery limbs of the deceiver and the watery waves yield to them in place of a body. But let it not be lawful for me to tell of these things, seen by none nor known to sight, except in part; let that hidden reverence be veiled, and lie concealed, entrusted to its own streams.
style: pastoral idyll, panpipes and light frame drum, mixed voices, playful, sunlit, then hushed at the close
why: Nymphs ducking the Satyrs at noon while nobody watches, ending on the poet refusing to say more — mischief with a veil drawn over it.

title: Mosella
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: Gazing through the smooth surface into the glassy deep, the river keeps nothing hidden; and just as the kindly air spreads itself open to the unobstructed gaze, and no calm winds bar the eyes as they range through the void, so we discern things sunk far below, our sight enduring to the inmost depth, and the secret recess of the hidden deep lies open, when the shallows move gently and the flow of the clear waters reveals the shapes scattered in the blue light: how the furrowed sand ripples in a light eddy, how the bending grasses tremble on the green bottom. Down beneath the native springs the swaying water-weeds endure the quivering waters; the pebble now gleams, now hides, and the gravel sets off the green moss. Such is the whole shore that lies open to the Caledonian Britons, when the tide lays bare green seaweeds and red corals and the whitening pearls, the spawn of shells, men's delights; and beneath the wealthy waves the imitating necklaces counterfeit our own adornments. Not otherwise does the discoloured weed reveal, beneath the glad shallows of the placid Moselle, the variegated pebbles mingled there.
style: meditative water song, harp and glassy bowed strings, soft high voice, slow, transparent, drifting
why: Looking down through clear water: the furrowed sand rippling, the pebble that gleams and hides, the gravel setting off green moss.

title: Satires
author: Aulus Persius Flaccus
lyrics:
pr. Prologue
I never wet my lips at the nag's spring,
nor do I remember dreaming on two-peaked Parnassus,
that I should step forth all at once a poet so.
The Heliconian Muses and pale Pirene
I leave to those whose portraits the clinging
ivy licks: I myself, half a rustic outsider,
bring my own song to the holy rites of the bards.
Who taught the parrot his "good morning,"
and schooled the magpie to attempt our speech?
That master of skill, that lavisher of talent,
the belly, an artist at chasing voices once denied;
for let the hope of treacherous coin glitter,
and you would believe that raven-poets and magpie-poetesses
were singing the very nectar of Pegasus.
1. O the cares of men! O how much emptiness there is in things!
style: roman satirical prologue, plucked lyre and dry hand percussion, wry conversational baritone, brisk, sardonic, clipped
why: 'I never wet my lips at the nag's spring' — hunger taught the parrot to say good morning, and that is the whole theory of poetry.

title: Satires
author: Aulus Persius Flaccus
lyrics:
then they groan that their thick days are past, and the swampy light,
and that, too late now, the life they have left behind is gone.
But you delight to grow pale over the leaves by night;
for, a tiller of the young, you graft their cleansed ears
with the fruit of Cleanthes. Seek from here, boys and old men,
a fixed goal for the mind, and provisions for wretched grey hairs.
"Tomorrow this shall be done." The same tomorrow it will be done. "What?
Is it a great thing, then, that you grant me a day?" But when the next light comes,
we have already used up yesterday's tomorrow; behold, another tomorrow
carries off the years, and is always a little beyond,
for though it be close beside you, though it be under the same pole,
in vain will you chase the rim that turns upon itself,
style: insistent moral chant, low strings and ticking percussion, urgent tenor, driving, circling, unresolved
why: 'Tomorrow this shall be done.' The same tomorrow it will be done — the rim that turns upon itself and is never caught.

title: Satires
author: Aulus Persius Flaccus
lyrics:
what should you fear?and a dish that guards the hearth in safety."
Is that enough? Or is it fitting to burst your lung with windy pride
because you draw your branch as the thousandth on a Tuscan stock,
or because you greet your own censor in your festal robe?
Off to the rabble with your trappings! I know you inside and to the skin.
Are you not ashamed to live by the loose ways of unbelted Natta?
But he is numb in his vice, and the fat has grown thick over his vitals;
he feels no fault, knows not what he is losing, and sunk deep below
no longer rises to bubble at the surface.
Great father of the gods, may it please you to punish cruel tyrants
in no other way than this, when dread lust,
steeped in burning venom, has stirred their nature:
let them see virtue, and pine for having forsaken it.
style: stern latin invective, low brass and deep drum, hard declaiming voice, weighty, accusing, building to a curse
why: The prayer against tyrants: let them see virtue, and pine for having forsaken it. The best line Persius ever wrote.

title: Sonnets
author: William Shakespeare
lyrics:
How like a winter hath my absence been
From thee, the pleasure of the fleeting year!
What freezings have I felt, what dark days seen!
What old Decembers bareness everywhere!
And yet this time removed was summers time;
The teeming autumn, big with rich increase,
Bearing the wanton burden of the prime,
Like widowd wombs after their lords decease:
Yet this abundant issue seemd to me
But hope of orphans, and unfatherd fruit;
For summer and his pleasures wait on thee,
And, thou away, the very birds are mute:
Or, if they sing, tis with so dull a cheer,
That leaves look pale, dreading the winters near.
From you have I been absent in the spring,
When proud-pied April, dressd in all his trim,
style: renaissance art song, lute and viol, countertenor, gentle, chamber, wintry and aching
why: Sonnet 97 entire — 'How like a winter hath my absence been' — an autumn that feels like December because one person is missing.

title: Sonnets
author: William Shakespeare
lyrics:
Full many a glorious morning have I seen
Flatter the mountain tops with sovereign eye,
Kissing with golden face the meadows green,
Gilding pale streams with heavenly alchemy;
Anon permit the basest clouds to ride
With ugly rack on his celestial face,
And from the forlorn world his visage hide,
Stealing unseen to west with this disgrace:
Even so my sun one early morn did shine,
With all triumphant splendour on my brow;
But out! alack! he was but one hour mine,
The region cloud hath maskd him from me now.
Yet him for this my love no whit disdaineth;
Suns of the world may stain when heavens sun staineth.
Why didst thou promise such a beauteous day,
And make me travel forth without my cloak,
style: elizabethan lute song, solo lute and bass viol, warm tenor, unhurried, radiant then clouding over
why: Sonnet 33 entire — the sun flattering the mountain tops, then hidden by the basest clouds, then forgiven.

title: Sonnets
author: William Shakespeare
lyrics:
Since brass, nor stone, nor earth, nor boundless sea,
But sad mortality oersways their power,
How with this rage shall beauty hold a plea,
Whose action is no stronger than a flower?
O! how shall summers honey breath hold out,
Against the wrackful siege of battering days,
When rocks impregnable are not so stout,
Nor gates of steel so strong but Time decays?
O fearful meditation! where, alack,
Shall Times best jewel from Times chest lie hid?
Or what strong hand can hold his swift foot back?
Or who his spoil of beauty can forbid?
O! none, unless this miracle have might,
That in black ink my love may still shine bright.
Tired with all these, for restful death I cry:
As to behold desert a beggar born,
style: renaissance consort song, viol consort and lute, grave countertenor, slow, embattled, resolving to a single bright line
why: Sonnet 65 entire — brass, stone, earth and sea against time, and only black ink left standing at the end.

title: Eunuchus
author: Terence
lyrics:
(Enter PHAEDRIA and PARMENO.)
PHAEDRIA:
What then, shall I do? Ought I not to go, not now even, when I am sent for of her own accord? Or ought I rather so to behave myself as not to put up with affronts from Courtesans? She shut her door against me; she now invites me back. Ought I to return? No; though she should implore me.
PARMENO:
lfaith, if indeed you only can, theres nothing better or more spirited; but if you begin, and can not hold out stoutly, and if, when you can not endure it, while no one asks you, peace being not made, you come to her of your own accord, showing that you love her, and can not endure it, you are done for; its all over with you;
style: roman comic aria, tibia and plucked strings, worldly baritone, conversational, quickening, rueful
why: Parmeno's catalogue of love — 'wrongs, suspicions, enmities, reconcilements, war, then peace' — and the folly of being mad with reason.

title: Eunuchus
author: Terence
lyrics:
What! said I, do you suppose it is managed by those means? You are quite mistaken. Once upon a time, in the early ages, there was a calling for that class; this is a new mode of coney-catching; I, in fact, have been the first to strike into this path. There is a class of men who strive to be the first in every thing, but are not; to these I make my court; I do not present myself to them to be laughed at;
but I am the first to laugh with them, and at the same time to admire their parts: whatever they say, I commend; if they contradict that self-same thing, I commend again. Does any one deny? I deny: does he affirm? I affirm: in fine, I have so trained myself as to humor them in every thing. This calling is now by far the most productive.
PARMENO:
(apart.)
A clever fellow, upon my faith! From being fools he makes men mad outright.
style: comic patter song, pizzicato strings and woodblock, sly tenor, fast, antithetical, self-delighted
why: The parasite's manifesto: 'Does any one deny? I deny: does he affirm? I affirm.' Built on a rhythm that sings itself.

title: Eunuchus
author: Terence
lyrics:
(ironically.)
Poor fellow!
CHAEREA:
(continuing.)
I am going out, said she, to dinner.
She took her maids with her; a few novices of girls remained, to be about her. These immediately made preparations for her to bathe. I urged them to make haste. While preparations were being made, the damsel sat in a room looking up at a certain painting, in which was represented how Jove is said once to have sent a golden shower into the bosom of Danae.
I myself began to look at it as well, and as he had in former times played the like game, I felt extremely delighted that a God should change himself into money, and slily come through the tiles of another persons house, to deceive the fair one by means of a shower. But what God was this? He who shakes the most lofty temples of heaven with his thunders.
style: roman narrative song, lyre and soft drum, hushed conspiratorial voice, unhurried, wondering, sensual
why: The boy studying the painting of Danaë's golden shower and delighting that a god would turn himself into money to get in through the roof tiles.

title: Fabulae
author: Phaedrus
lyrics:
WHAT from the founder Esop fell,
In neat familiar verse I tell:
Twofold's the genius of the page,
To make you smile and make you sage.
But if the critics we displease,
By wrangling brutes and talking trees,
Let them remember, ere they blame,
We're working neither sin nor shame;
'Tis but a play to form the youth
By fiction, in the cause of truth.
BY thirst incited; to the brook
The Wolf and Lamb themselves betook.
The Wolf high up the current drank,
The Lamb far lower down the bank.
Then, bent his ravenous maw to cram,
The Wolf took umbrage at the Lamb.
style: english fable ballad, fiddle and plucked cittern, bright storytelling tenor, brisk, four-beat, wry
why: 'Twofold's the genius of the page, to make you smile and make you sage' — a prologue that states its own terms, then walks straight into the wolf and the lamb.

title: Fabulae
author: Phaedrus
lyrics:
A Daw, ambitious and absurd,
Pick'd up the quills of Juno's bird;
And, with the gorgeous spoil adorn'd,
All his own sable brethren scorn'd,
And join'd the peacocks-who in scoff
Stripp'd the bold thief; and drove him off
The Daw, thus roughly handled, went
To his own kind in discontent:
But they in turn contemn the spark,
And brand with many a shameful mark.
Then one he formerly disdain'd,
"Had you," said he, "at home remain'd
Content with Nature's ways and will,
You had not felt the peacock's bill;
Nor 'mongst the birds of your own dress
Had been deserted in distress."
style: comic beast fable, harpsichord and tabor, mocking mixed voices, trotting, strophic, punchline-timed
why: The jackdaw in borrowed peacock quills, stripped by both flocks and told he should have stayed at home. A complete fable with its sting intact.

title: Fabulae
author: Phaedrus
lyrics:
A Pearl upon the dunghill found:
"O splendid thing in foul disgrace,
Had there been any in the place
That saw and knew thy worth when sold,
Ere this thou hadst been set in gold.
But I, who rather would have got
A corn of barley, heed thee not;
No service can there render'd be
From me to you, and you to me."
I write this tale to them alone
To whom in vain my pearls are thrown.
Up in a lofty oak the Bees
Had made their honey-combs: but these
The Drones asserted they had wrought.
Then to the bar the cause was brought
Before the wasp, a learned chief,
style: dry epigrammatic air, plucked lute and light percussion, deadpan baritone, measured, ironic, clipped
why: The cock finding a pearl on the dunghill and preferring a grain of barley, closing on 'to whom in vain my pearls are thrown.'

title: The Philosophy of Despair
author: David Starr Jordan
lyrics:
And fear not lest Existence, closing your Account, and mine, shall know the like no more; The Eternal Saki from that bowl hath pour'd Millions of bubbles like us, and will pour.
When you and I behind the veil are past, Oh, but the long, long while the world shall last, Which of our coming and departure heeds As the Sev'n Seas shall heed a pebble-cast.
A moment's halt--a momentary taste Of Being from the Well amid the waste, And lo!--the phantom caravan has reach'd The Nothing it set out from--O, make haste!
There was the door to which I found no key; There was the veil through which I could not see: Some little talk awhile of Me and Thee There was--and then no more of Thee and Me.
Why, all the Saints and Sages who discuss'd Of the two worlds so learnedly are thrust Like foolish prophets forth; their words to scorn Are scatter'd and their mouths are stopt with dust.
style: persian-inflected art song, santur and low strings with soft frame drum, dark warm voice, slow, fatalistic, circling
why: Rubaiyat quatrains at their bleakest: the phantom caravan reaching the Nothing it set out from, and the door with no key.

title: The Philosophy of Despair
author: David Starr Jordan
lyrics:
A darkening sky and a whitening sea, And the wind in the palm trees tall; Soon or late comes a call for me, Down from the mountain or up from the sea, Then let me lie where I fall.
And a friend may write--for friends there be, On a stone from the gray sea wall, "Jungle and town and reef and sea-- I loved God's Earth and His Earth loved me, Taken for all in all."
So when the angel of the darker Drink At last shall find you by the river-brink, And offering you his cup, invite your Soul Forth to your lips to quaff, you shall not shrink.
Why, if the soul can fling the Dust aside, And naked on the air of Heaven ride, Wert not a shame--wert not a shame for him In this clay carcase crippled to abide?
'Tis but a tent where takes his one-day's rest A Sultan to the realm of Death addrest; The Sultan rises, and the dark Ferrash Strikes, and prepares it for another guest.
style: island elegy, acoustic guitar and low flute, weathered male voice, unhurried, salt-worn, valedictory
why: 'A darkening sky and a whitening sea' — a man writing his own epitaph on a stone from the grey sea wall.

title: The Philosophy of Despair
author: David Starr Jordan
lyrics:
I gazed into the mist, and fear came on me, Then said the mist: "I weep for the lost sun."
"With her the seed of Wisdom did I sow, And with mine own hands wrought to make it grow; And this is all the harvest that I reap'd, 'I come like water, and like wind I go.'"
The "dragons of the prime, That tore each other in the slime,"
"Can it be, O Christ in Heaven, That the highest suffer most, That the strongest wander farthest And most hopelessly are lost?--
That the mark of rank in Nature Is capacity for pain, And the anguish of the singer Marks the sweetness of the strain?
"The city is of night but not of sleep; There sweet sleep is not for the weary brain. The pitiless hours like years and ages creep-- A night seems termless hell. This dreadful strain Of thought and consciousness which never ceases, Or which some moment's stupor but increases."
style: victorian hymn-lament, chamber organ and viola, plaintive alto, slow, questioning, unresolved
why: 'That the mark of rank in Nature is capacity for pain, and the anguish of the singer marks the sweetness of the strain' — a whole thesis in one stanza.

title: Solon
author: Plutarch
lyrics: And as for the ridicule which many heaped upon him for refusing the tyranny, he has written as follows; Solon was a shallow thinker and a man of counsel void; When the gods would give him blessings, of his own will he refused. When his net was full of fish, amazed, he would not pull it in, All for lack of spirit, and because he was bereft of sense. I had certainly been willing, for the power, and boundless wealth, And to be tyrant over Athens no more than a single day, Then to have a pouch flayed from me, and my lineage blotted out.
style: greek self-mocking lyric, lyre and hand drum, dry knowing male voice, moderate, ironic, conversational
why: Solon quoting his own critics — the fool who would not haul in a net full of fish — and answering with a flayed pouch and a blotted line.

title: Solon
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
But that he classed himself among the poor rather than the rich, is clear from these verses: For often evil men are rich, and good men poor; But we will not exchange with them Our virtue for their wealth since one abides always, While riches change their owners every day.
None of these things shook Solon from his resolution. To his friends he said, as we are told, that a tyranny was a lovely place, but there was no way down from it. And in his poems he writes to Phocus: And if, he says, I spared my land, My native land, and unto tyranny and violence implacable Did not set hand, polluting and disgracing my fair fame, Im not ashamed; in this way rather shall my name be set above That of all other men. From this it is clear that even before his legislation he was in high repute.
style: greek gnomic chant, plucked lyre and low drone, steady grave voice, measured, plain, resolute
why: 'Our virtue for their wealth — since one abides always, while riches change their owners every day.'

title: The Coal Question
author: William Stanley Jevons
lyrics:
"These iron times breed none that mind posterity"
"The havoc and the spoyle, Which, even within the measure of my days, Is made through every quarter of this Isle In woods and grooves which were this Kingdom's praise."
"The yron mills are excellent for that; I have a patent draune to that effect; If they goe up, downe goe the goodly trees. I'll make them search the earth to find new fire."
style: elizabethan broadside lament, bowed lyre and tabor, grim baritone, measured, foreboding, plain
why: 'These iron times breed none that mind posterity' — and the patent-holder's boast: if the mills go up, down go the goodly trees.

title: De consolatione philosophiae
author: Boethius
lyrics:
I THAT with youthful heat did verses write, Must now my woes in doleful tunes indite. My work is framed by Muses torn and rude, And my sad cheeks are with true tears bedewed: For these alone no terror could affray from being partners of my weary way. The art that was my young life's joy and glory Becomes my solace now i m old and sorry; Sorrow has filched my youth from me, the thief! My days are numbered not by time but Grief. a Untimely hoary hairs cover my head, And my loose skin quakes on my flesh half dead. o happy death, that spareth sweetest years, And comes in sorrow often called with tears. Alas, how deaf is he to wretch's cries; And loath he is to close up weeping eyes;
While trustless chance me with vain favours crowned, that saddest hour my life had almost drowned Now she hath clouded her deceitful face, My spiteful days prolong their weary race. My friends, why did you count me fortunate? He that is fallen, ne'er stood in settled state.
style: late antique consolation lament, bowed viol and small harp, grave low male voice, slow, elegiac, sparse
why: The book's opening cry — 'My days are numbered not by time but Grief' — the most famous lament in the work and complete in itself.

title: De consolatione philosophiae
author: Boethius
lyrics: The guilty souls with pains opprest, Moved with his song began to weep. Ixion's wheel now standing still Turns not his head with motions steep. Though Tantalus might drink at will, To quench his thirst lie would forbear, The vulture full with music shrill Doth not poor Tityus' liver tear. 'We by his verses conquered are,' Saith the great King whom spirits fear. 'Let us not then from him debar His wife whom he with songs doth gain, Yet lest our gift should stretch too far, We will it with this law restrain, That when from hell he takes his flight, He shall from looking back refrain.' Who can for lovers laws indite? Love hath no law but her own will. Orpheus, seeing on the verge of night Eurydice, doth lose and kill Her and himself with foolish love. But you this feigned tale fulfil, Who think unto the day above To bring with speed your darksome mind. For if, your eye conquered, you move Backward to Pluto left behind, All the rich prey which thence you took, You lose while back to hell you look.
style: orphic ballad, solo lyre and low drone, keening tenor, unhurried, spellbinding, building to a break
why: The Orpheus meter, ending on 'Love hath no law but her own will' and the fatal backward look.

title: De consolatione philosophiae
author: Boethius
lyrics: If thou would st see God's laws with purest mind, Thy sight on heaven must fixed be, Whose settled course the stars in peace doth bind. The sun's bright fire Stops not his sisters team, Nor doth the northern bear desire Within the ocean s wave to hide her beam. Though she behold The other stars there couching, Yet she uncessantly is rolled About high heaven, the ocean never touching. The evening light With certain course doth show The coming of the shady night, And Lucifer before the day doth go.
style: cosmic hymn, chamber organ and viols, layered choir over a held drone, measured, luminous, processional
why: 'This mutual love courses eternal makes' — the concord of the elements laid out season by season, pure refrain material.

title: Satires
author: Juvenal
lyrics:
1. Satire I
Must I be always only a listener? Never strike back,
so often racked by hoarse Cordus and his Theseid?
Shall this one read me out his comedies unpunished,
that one his elegies? Shall some monstrous Telephus
burn up my whole day unavenged, or an Orestes
written to the margin's edge and onto the back, still not finished?
No man knows his own house better than I know
the grove of Mars and Vulcan's cave hard by the Aeolian crags.
What the winds are at, what shades Aeacus
is racking, from what spot another sneaks off the gold
of the stolen fleece, how huge the ash-trees Monychus hurls
Fronto's plane-trees and battered marble shriek it
forever, his columns cracked by the relentless reciter.
You may expect the same from poet greatest and least.
I too have pulled my hand back from the schoolmaster's cane, I too
style: roman satiric declamation, plucked lyre and hand drum, sardonic biting male voice, brisk, driving, insolent
why: 'Must I be always only a listener? Never strike back' — the line that opens satire as a genre, and it opens itself.

title: Satires
author: Juvenal
lyrics:
Here many a sick man dies of sleeplessness (but the languor
itself is bred by undigested food clinging
to the burning stomach); for what rented rooms
allow sleep? Only with great wealth can one sleep in the city.
There lies the source of the disease: the passing of carts
in the narrow winding lanes, and the curses of the halted drove,
would rob sleep from a Drusus or the seals of the sea.
If duty calls, the rich man will be borne over the people's heads
as the crowd gives way, and will run on his great Liburnian litter,
and on the way will read, or write, or sleep inside;
for the closed window of the litter brings on sleep.
Yet he will arrive first: as we hurry, the wave ahead
blocks us, and the throng that follows presses our loins
in a great column; one strikes me with his elbow, another
style: urban street rant, low strings and clattering percussion, hoarse restless male voice, hurried, jostling, claustrophobic
why: Rome by night — carts, curses, elbows — landing on 'Only with great wealth can one sleep in the city.'

title: Satires
author: Juvenal
lyrics:
So you admit you did not know what was to be wished:
for he who craved excessive honours
and demanded excessive wealth was piling up the many
storeys of a lofty tower, from which the fall would be
the higher, the sheer plunge of the toppled ruin the more vast.
What overthrew the Crassi, the Pompeys, and the man
who broke the Romans and led them tamed to his own lash?
The topmost place, sought of course by every art,
and great prayers granted by the malignant gods.
Few kings go down to Ceres' son-in-law without
slaughter and wound, few tyrants by a bloodless death.
Eloquence and the fame of Demosthenes or Cicero
each man begins to long for, and longs for through the whole festival,
whoever still worships at his thrifty penny's Minerva,
attended by a slave to guard his little satchel.
style: grave latin moral chant, cello drone and struck bronze, stern baritone, slow, admonitory, gathering weight
why: The tower image from Satire X: the higher the wish, the vaster the fall — the passage the whole vanity-of-wishes tradition rests on.

title: Poems
author: Edward Jerningham
lyrics:
I tread this dome to misery allied.
No wakening joy informs my sullen breast,
Thro' opening skies no radiant seraph smiles,
No saint descends to sooth my soul to rest,
No dream of bliss the dreary night beguiles.
Here haggard discontent still haunts my view;
The sombre genius reigns in ev'ry place,
Arrays each virtue in the darkest hue,
Chills ev'ry prayer, and cancels ev'ry grace.
I meet her ever in the chearless cell,
The gloomy grotto and unsocial wood;
I hear her ever in the midnight bell,
The hollow gale, and hoarse resounding flood.
This caus'd a mother's tender tears to flow,
(The sad remembrance time shall ne'er erase)
When having seal'd th' irrevocable vow,
style: gothic elegy, sustained strings and distant bell, cold clear soprano, slow, desolate, echoing
why: The nun's despair told through what she hears — the midnight bell, the hollow gale, the hoarse resounding flood.

title: Poems
author: Edward Jerningham
lyrics:
AN ELEGY WRITTEN AMONG THE RUINS OF AN ABBEY.
BY MR. JERNINGHAM.
WHERE sighs the zephyr to yon lonely tree,
A solemn grove its leafy mantle spread:
Where bend yon mouldering turrets o'er the sea,
A venerable dome once rear'd its head.
The solemn grove, the venerable dome,
Were erst frequented by a numerous train,
Ev'n chaste as they who Dian's mountain roam,
But not subjected to her gentle reign:
Far other Goddess did this train obey,
Far other temples, other altars rais'd,
Far other meaning breath'd their choral lay,
Far other incense on their altars blaz'd:
Veil'd Superstition wak'd her magic sound,
Bad Albion's sons forsake the splendid court,
style: graveyard-school elegy, harpsichord and viola da gamba, plaintive tenor, unhurried, solemn, sea-wind atmosphere
why: Ruined abbey above the sea with a fourfold 'Far other' refrain already built into the stanza.

title: Poems
author: Edward Jerningham
lyrics:
Their harmless joys disease too soon effac'd:
One fatal morn, her Turturella's mate
She found, with flagging wing subdued, oppress'd,
And just, just sinking at the blow of fate:
While down her cheek compassion's shower distill'd,
She gently rais'd it to her anxious breast;
But death's cold blast life's crimson current chill'd,
And thus the fair her breathless bird address'd:
"Ill-fated turtle, round whose peaceful bower
" The jocund loves so lately wont to play:
"How sunk, alas! in youth's exulting hour,
" To fell disease, to death th' untimely prey:
"How silent is the voice, which, void of art,
" Along the tender day was heard to coo!
"How still, how frozen is the constant heart,
" Which to its dear companion beat so true!
style: sentimental english air, guitar and flute, tender mezzo, gentle, grieving, strophic
why: The lament over the dead turtle-dove — 'How silent is the voice... How still, how frozen is the constant heart'.

title: Poems
author: William Whitehead
lyrics:
'Twas both perhaps, or neither;
In short, 'twas that provoking charm
Of CAELIA altogether.
SONG for RANELAGH.
By Mr. W. WHITEHEAD.
YE belles, and ye flirts, and ye pert little things,
Who trip in this frolicksome round,
Pray tell me from whence this indecency springs,
The sexes at once to confound:
What means the cock'd hat, and the masculine air,
With each motion design'd to perplex?
Bright eyes were intended to languish, not stare,
And softness the test of your sex.
The girl who on beauty depends for support,
May call ev'ry art to her aid:
The bosom display'd, and the petticoat short,
style: georgian pleasure-garden song, harpsichord and violin, arch witty soprano, brisk, dancing, teasing
why: Written as a song for Ranelagh, with the cocked hat and the masculine air — the one candidate built to be sung.

title: Poems
author: William Whitehead
lyrics:
THE ENTHUSIAST: AN ODE.
BY WM. WHITEHEAD, ESQ.
ONCE, I remember well the day,
'Twas ere the blooming sweets of May
Had lost their freshest hues,
When every flower on every hill,
In every vale, had drank its fill
Of sunshine, and of dews.
In short, 'twas that sweet season's prime
When Spring gives up the reins of Time
To Summer's glowing hand,
And doubting mortals hardly know,
By whose command the breezes blow
Which fan the smiling land.
'Twas then, beside a green-wood shade,
Which cloath'd a lawn's aspiring head
style: english pastoral ode, recorder and lute, warm tenor, lilting, springlike, unhurried
why: 'When Spring gives up the reins of Time to Summer's glowing hand' — clean singable six-line stanzas and a real image.

title: Poems
author: William Whitehead
lyrics:
And make their fields more gay?
Where is the villa's rural pride,
The swelling dome's imperial gleam,
Which lov'd to grace thy verdant side,
And tremble in thy golden stream?
Where are the bold, the busy throngs,
That rush'd impatient to the war,
Or tun'd to peace triumphal songs,
And hail'd the passing car?
Along the solitary road,
Th' eternal flint by Consuls trod,
We muse, and mark the sad decays
Of mighty works, and mighty days!
For these vile wastes, we cry, had Fate decreed
That Veii's sons should strive, for these Camillus bleed?
Did here, in after-times of Roman pride,
style: ruins ode, low strings and chamber organ, declamatory baritone, slow, questioning, hollow
why: An ubi sunt over the Roman campagna — 'Where are the bold, the busy throngs' — repeated question as refrain.

title: Poems
author: David Mallet
lyrics:
She shivering sigh'd, and died.
WILLIAM AND MARGARET.
By DAVID MALLET, Esq
'TWAS at the silent, solemn hour,
When night and morning meet;
In glided MARGARET's grimly ghost,
And stood at WILLIAM's feet.
Her face was like an April-morn,
Clad in a wintry cloud:
And clay-cold was her lilly-hand,
That held her sable shroud.
So shall the fairest face appear,
When youth and years are flown:
Such is the robe that kings must wear,
When death has rest their crown.
Her bloom was like the springing flower,
style: border ghost ballad, fiddle and bodhrán, stark unaccompanied opening female voice, slow, uncanny, strophic
why: 'In glided Margaret's grimly ghost, and stood at William's feet' — the most famous ballad opening in the book.

title: Poems
author: David Mallet
lyrics:
Thy pledge and broken oath:
And give me back my maiden-vow,
And give me back my troth.
Why did you promise love to me,
And not that promise keep?
Why did you swear my eyes were bright,
Yet leave those eyes to weep?
How could you say my face was fair,
And yet that face forsake?
How could you win my virgin heart,
Yet leave that heart to break?
Why did you say, my lip my sweet,
And made the scarlet pale?
And why did I, young witless maid,
Believe the flattering tale!
That face, alas! no more is fair;
style: accusing ballad, plucked harp and drone, wounded female voice, insistent, rising, strophic
why: The ghost's reproach is a hammering chain of 'Why did you' questions — refrain-shaped already.

title: Poems
author: David Mallet
lyrics:
BY THE SAME.
FAR in the windings of a vale,
Fast by a sh ltering wood,
The safe retreat of Health and Peace,
An humble cottage stood.
There beauteous Emma flourish'd fair
Beneath a mother's eye;
Whose only wish on earth was now
To see her blest, and die.
The softest blush that Nature spreads
Gave colour to her cheek:
Such orient colour smiles thro' heaven,
When vernal mornings break.
Nor let the pride of great ones scorn
This charmer of the plains:
That sun, who bids their diamond blaze,
style: english pastoral ballad, acoustic guitar and whistle, warm clear female vocal, moderate, tender, storytelling
why: Edwin and Emma's opening — cottage, sheltering wood, and a mother whose only wish is to see her blest and die.

title: Poems
author: George Keate
lyrics:
Reflect, that lodg'd within its breast
The modest pearl delights to rest,
While every gem to Neptune known,
Is there with partial bounty sown.
In years, thus ever may we trace
Each sparkling charm, each blushing grace;
To these let judgment value give,
And in that seat of Beauty live!
This Moral keep before your eyes,
Plunge  and a new-born Venus rise.
PROLOGUE TO THE PLAY OF KING JOHN, ACTED AT MR. NEWCOMB'S, AT HACKNEY, IN MARCH MDCCLXIX.
BY THE SAME.
THE Bard whose scenes this night your thoughts engage,
Has somewhere told us, All the world's a stage,
Where all in one great farce their talents try,
Are born, love, wed, grow covetous,  and die.
style: georgian drawing-room air, harpsichord and cello, light amused soprano, moderate, elegant, ending on a wink
why: The moral of the sea-bathing poem, closing on 'Plunge — and a new-born Venus rise'.

title: Poems
author: George Keate
lyrics:
TO A LADY GOING TO BATHE IN THE SEA.
BY GEORGE KEATE, ESQ.
VENUS, most histories agree,
Sprung from the ferment of the sea;
Yet I confess I'm always loth
To think such beauty was but froth,
Or that the ocean, which more odd is,
Should from a bubble spawn a Goddess:
Tho' hence, my Laura, learned fellows
Of such its wonderous powers still tell us,
That every mother brings her daughter
To dip in this specific water,
Expecting from the briny wave
Charms which it once to Venus gave.
These charms, my Laura, strive to gain;
And that you may not bathe in vain,
style: comic english art song, plucked strings and bassoon, dry playful tenor, bouncing, mock-learned
why: Venus out of the sea-froth used to tease a lady into the water — a complete conceit in one turn.

title: Poems
author: George Keate
lyrics:
To bully two such Kings was no small merit.
Around the world to find the wretch I'd search,
Who dares to leave a woman in the lurch.
My son the dupe of regal baseness made,
Myself amus'd by hopes, cajol'd, betray'd,
My jointure lost, a widow, and not young,
I had no weapon left me but my tongue
Should any Fair be here whose nerves are weak,
Who when man blusters, is afraid to speak,
Whose gentle bosom no resentment fires,
But with her eau de luce in hand, expires,
She'll think, no doubt, my voice too loudly thunders;
Trust me, this female instrument does wonders.
Those, who turn o'er the page of ancient story,
Must own the tongue was ever Woman's glory.
Who has not heard of fam'd XANTIPPE's lute?
style: theatrical patter song, fortepiano and pit strings, bold brassy female voice, quick, defiant, comic
why: Constance after the play — 'a bustling woman lives thro' every storm... I had no weapon left me but my tongue'.

title: Proletarian Poetry
author: Alexander Bogdanov
lyrics:
When the morning whistles resound over the workers suburbs, it is not at all a summons to slavery. It is the song of the future. There was a time when we worked in poor shops and started our work at different hours of the morning. And now, at eight in the morning, the whistles sound for a million men. A million workers seize the hammers at the same moment. Our first blows thunder in accord. What is it that the whistles sing? It is the morning hymn to unity.
See the wheels that whirl around, See the mad belts dancing here ... Comrade, comrade, have no fear! Let the chaos of steel resound, Though its many fires be drowned, Quenched by bitter sea of tears  Have no fear!
You have come from peaceful haunts, Quiet fields and brooklets clear. Comrade, comrade, have no fear! Here the limitless is bound, Here the impossible come round ... This is the dawn of coming years  Have no fear!
style: revolutionary industrial anthem, anvil percussion and low brass, massed male chorus, marching, iron, rousing
why: Factory whistles as a morning hymn to unity, then the 'Comrade, comrade, have no fear' refrain arrives.

title: Proletarian Poetry
author: Alexander Bogdanov
lyrics:
Foaming crests of waves resound With our fortune coming near ... On our kingdom gloomy, drear, A new sun is shining down, Burning brighter now than eer Have no fear!
Like a giant carved in stone At the mad belts stand and steer ... Let the wheels go turning still, Closer now the ranks are drawn  Youre a new link forged in here  Have no fear!
Closer now the ranks are drawn  Youre a new link forged in here  Have no fear!
style: workers' chorus, hammered percussion and accordion, layered voices, steady driving pulse, defiant, building
why: The refrain doubles and closes — 'You're a new link forged in here — have no fear!'

title: Paramārthasāra
author: Abhinavagupta
lyrics:
For one who meditates upon this concise [exposition] uttered by Abhinavagupta, [which is] the supreme Brahman, Siva-hood comes, before long, to enter into [pervade] his own heart.
This most profoundly hidden essence of the scriptures has been compressed in a hundred arya (the matra (moraic) meter of all 105 verses) verses by me, Abhinavagupta, made radiant by the remembrance of Siva's feet.
style: shaiva devotional chant, tanpura drone and small bell, deep male voice, very slow, reverent, sparse
why: Only candidate, but a real closing benediction: meditate on this and Śiva-hood enters your own heart.

title: Olympian
author: Pindar
lyrics: Water is best, and gold, like a blazing fire in the night, stands out supreme of all lordly wealth. But if, my heart, you wish to sing of contests, look no further for any star warmer than the sun, shining by day through the lonely sky, and let us not proclaim any contest greater than Olympia, From there glorious song enfolds the wisdom of poets, so that they loudly sing the son of Cronus, when they arrive at the rich and blessed hearth of Hieron, who wields the scepter of law in Sicily of many flocks, reaping every excellence at its peak, and is glorified by the choicest music, which we men often play around his hospitable table. Come, take the Dorian lyre down from its peg, if the splendor of Pisa and of Pherenicus placed your mind under the influence of sweetest thoughts, when that horse ran swiftly beside the Alpheus, not needing to be spurred on in the race, and brought victory to his master, the king of Syracuse who delights in horses. His glory shines in the settlement of fine men founded by Lydian Pelops, with whom the mighty holder of the earth Poseidon fell in love, when Clotho took him out of the pure cauldron, furnished with a gleaming ivory shoulder. Yes, there are many marvels, and yet I suppose the speech of mortals beyond the true account can be deceptive, stories adorned with embroidered lies;
style: doric victory ode, kithara and double aulos, layered male chorus, stately, processional, blazing
why: 'Water is best, and gold, like a blazing fire in the night' — the most famous opening in Greek lyric, and a real hymn to the games.

title: Olympian
author: Pindar
lyrics:
it is a brilliant star, a mans true light, at least if one has and knows the future, that the reckless souls of those who have died on earth immediately pay the penaltyand for the crimes committed in this realm of Zeus there is a judge below the earth; with hateful compulsion he passes his sentence.
But having the sun always in equal nights and equal days, the good receive a life free from toil, not scraping with the strength of their arms the earth, nor the water of the sea, for the sake of a poor sustenance. But in the presence of the honored gods, those who gladly kept their oaths enjoy a life without tears, while the others undergo a toil that is unbearable to look at.
style: ancient greek mystery hymn, lyre and low drone, hushed layered voices, slow, radiant, floating
why: The Isle of the Blessed — equal nights and days, ocean breezes, flowers of gold blazing on land and in water.

title: Olympian
author: Pindar
lyrics:
As when someone takes a goblet, all golden, the most prized of his possessions, foaming with the dew of the vine from a generous hand, and makes a gift of it to his young son-in-law, welcoming him with a toast from one home to another, honoring the grace of the symposium and the new marriage-bond, and thereby, in the presence of his friends, makes him enviable for his harmonious marriage-bed;
I too, sending to victorious men poured nectar, the gift of the Muses, the sweet fruit of my mind, I try to win the gods favor for those men who were victors at Olympia and at Pytho, That man is prosperous, who is encompassed by good reports. Grace, which causes life to flourish, looks with favor now on one man, now on another, with both the sweet-singing lyre and the full-voiced notes of flutes.
style: symposium ode, lyre and soft flutes, warm generous tenor, unhurried, celebratory, golden
why: The golden goblet foaming with wine passed to a son-in-law, and song poured out the same way — one perfect extended simile.

title: Metamorphoses
author: Ovid
lyrics:
Of shapes transformde to bodies straunge, I purpose to entreate,
Ye gods vouchsafe (for you are they ywrought this wondrous feate)
To further this mine enterprise. And from the world begunne,
Graunt that my verse may to my time, his course directly runne.
Before the Sea and Lande were made, and Heaven that all doth hide,
In all the worlde one onely face of nature did abide,
Which Chaos hight, a huge rude heape, and nothing else but even
A heavie lump and clottred clod of seedes togither driven,
Of things at strife among themselves, for want of order due.
No sunne as yet with lightsome beames the shapelesse world did vew.
No Moone in growing did repayre hir hornes with borowed light.
Nor yet the earth amiddes the ayre did hang by wondrous slight
Just peysed by hir proper weight. Nor winding in and out
style: renaissance invocation, viol consort and chamber organ, grave declamatory male voice, slow, cosmic, unfolding
why: 'Of shapes transformde to bodies straunge' and then Chaos itself — the poem's opening and its whole programme in one breath.

title: Metamorphoses
author: Ovid
lyrics:
Abate thy flight, and I my selfe my running pace will stay.
Yet would I wishe thee take advise, and wisely for to viewe
What one he is that for thy grace in humble wise doth sewe.
I am not one that dwelles among the hilles and stonie rockes,
I am no sheepehearde with a Curre, attending on the flockes:
I am no Carle nor countrie Clowne, nor neathearde taking charge
Of cattle grazing here and there within this Forrest large.
Thou doest not know, poore simple soule, God wote thou dost not knowe,
From whome thou fleest. For if thou knew, thou wouldste not flee me so.
In Delphos is my chiefe abode, my Temples also stande
At Glaros and at Patara within the Lycian lande.
And in the Ile of Tenedos the people honour mee.
The king of Gods himselfe is knowne my father for to bee.
style: elizabethan pursuit song, lute and bass viol, urgent pleading tenor, driving fourteener swing, breathless
why: Apollo calling after the fleeing Daphne — 'Thou doest not know, poore simple soule, from whome thou fleest'.

title: Metamorphoses
author: Ovid
lyrics:
A shift to wind hir out of doores, that none that were within
Perceyved hir: and muffling hir with clothes about hir chin,
That no man might discerne hir face, to Ninus Tumb she came
Unto the tree, and sat hir downe there underneath the same.
Love made hir bold. But see the chaunce, there comes besmerde with blood
About the chappes a Lionesse all foming from the wood
From slaughter lately made of kine to staunch hir bloudie thurst
With water of the foresaid spring. Whome Thisbe spying furst,
Afarre by moonelight, thereupon with fearfull steppes gan flie,
And in a darke and yrkesome cave did hide hirselfe thereby.
And as she fled away for hast she let hir mantle fall
The whych for feare she left behind not looking backe at all.
Now when the cruell Lionesse hir thurst had stanched well,
style: elizabethan tragic ballad, lute and viol, dark storytelling voice, moonlit, foreboding, moderate
why: Thisbe at Ninus' tomb, the bloody-jawed lioness, the dropped mantle — the turn on which the whole tragedy hinges.

title: Poems
author: John Scott
style: english pastoral elegy, harpsichord and flute, clear tenor, unhurried, hopeful with a shadow, strophic
why: 'Stern Winter hence with all his train removes' — a clean spring quatrain sequence that checks its own optimism.

title: Poems
author: John Scott
lyrics:
They pass serene th' appointed hours that bring
The day that wafts them to the realms on high;
The day that centers in eternal spring.
ELEGY.
WRITTEN IN THE HOT WEATHER, JULY MDCCLVII.
BY THE SAME.
THREE hours from noon the passing shadow shows,
The sultry breeze glides faintly o'er the plains,
The dazzling aether fierce and fiercer glows,
And human nature scarce its rage sustains.
Now still and vacant is the dusty street,
And still and vacant where yon fields extend,
Save where those swains, oppress'd with toil and heat,
The grassy harvest of the mead attend.
Lost is the lively aspect of the ground,
Low are the springs, the reedy ditches dry;
style: languid summer air, viola and guitar, hazy warm voice, slow, heat-struck, still
why: Three hours past noon, the street empty, the ditches dry — concrete, sensory, and unusual as a subject for song.

title: Poems
author: John Scott
lyrics:
Whene'er the weight of Want's afflicting hand
Wakes o'er thy vales the Poor's persuasive cry:
When Slaves in office Freemen's rights withstand,
When Wealth enormous sets th' Oppressor high,
And Bribes thy ductile Senators command;
Then mourn, for then thy Fate approacheth nigh.
Not from perfidious Gaul, or haughty Spain,
Nor all the neighbouring nations of the main,
Tho' leagu'd in war tremendous round thy shore,
But from thyself, thy Ruin must proceed;
Nor boast thy Power, for know it is decreed,
Thy Freedom gone, thy Power shall be no more.
ON READING MRS. MACAULAY'S HISTORY OF ENGLAND.
BY THE SAME.
TO Albion's Bards, the Muse of History spoke;
"Record the glories of your native land,
style: patriotic warning ode, low strings and muffled drum, stern baritone, measured, gathering, ominous
why: A complete sonnet whose sting is the ending: not Spain nor France, 'but from thyself, thy Ruin must proceed'.

title: Poems
author: Mary Jones
lyrics:
Long may her widow'd age by heav'n be lent
Among my blessings! and I'm well content.
I ask no more, but in some calm retreat,
To sleep in quiet, and in quiet eat.
No noisy slaves attending round my room;
My viands wholesome, and my waiters dumb.
No orphans cheated, and no widow's curse,
No houshold lord, for better or for worse.
No monstrous sums to tempt my soul to sin,
But just enough to keep me plain, and clean.
And if sometimes, to smooth the rugged way,
Charlot should smile, or You approve my lay,
Enough for me. I cannot put my trust
In lords; smile lies, eat toads, or lick the dust.
Fortune her favours much too dear may hold:
An honest heart is worth its weight in gold.
style: georgian chamber song, harpsichord and cello, plain warm female voice, moderate, contented, settled
why: A whole life's wish in a dozen lines — quiet retreat, no widow's curse, 'an honest heart is worth its weight in gold'.

title: Poems
author: Mary Jones
lyrics:
But Nelly, and Molly, and Charlot so fair.
The swain, who to beauty had never been blind,
Thought this was the season to tell 'em his mind:
But first he debated, to which lovely lass
He should offer his tenders, and open his case.
That Nelly was pretty he could not deny,
But Molly, he thought, had the sprightliest eye;
So on her his affections they rested awhile,
'Till Charlot appear'd, with a look and a smile:
With a look and a smile which sure mischief had done,
Had the swain been encounter'd by Charlot alone.
Perplext in his thought, and disturb'd in his breast,
And unable to tell which bright lass he lov'd best;
He folded his arms, to the grove he retir'd,
And decently on the green willow expir'd.
To Damon's sad fate lend a pitying ear,
style: comic pastoral ballad, fiddle and guitar, mischievous soprano, brisk anapestic lilt, tripping, deadpan
why: The swain who cannot choose between three girls and so 'decently on the green willow expir'd'.

title: Poems
author: Mary Jones
lyrics:
On her BIRTH-DAY, Being the 11th of December.
Why this day's shorter than the rest,
A modern bard full well has guest.
The sun who shines the year about,
And ev'ry lesser light puts out,
This day submits, and will not rise,
But lends his rays to Stella's eyes.
ANOTHER.
Since this day comes but once a year,
Let ev'ry joy with it appear.
Come then, and let us laugh and sport,
And merry be it, tho' 'tis short.
Nor will I, Stella, now advise;
A word's sufficient to the wise.
Yet Beauty's reign, the learned say,
Is shorter than the shortest day.
style: birthday air, spinet and recorder, bright light soprano, quick, affectionate, toasting
why: The shortest day of the year explained — the sun stays down and lends his rays to Stella's eyes.

title: Poems
author: Susanna Centlivre
style: augustan satiric march, snare and harpsichord, dry mocking female voice, brisk, strutting, comic
why: Charles XII demolished by his table manners — dirty thumbs on the butter, and 'Eat, and Drink, and Live and Reign in Boots'.

title: Poems
author: Susanna Centlivre
lyrics:
To set the Favourite, and the Patch to place;
To bow, and glance it, with becoming Grace
To melt the Hero's Heart and charm his Eyes,
Fall to thy Gothick Rage a Sacrifice?
No, to thy Terror learn, our British Youth
Are fam'd for Honour, Constancy and Truth:
Each wou'd as soon consent thy Cause to aid,
As yield the Fair to whom his Vows are paid.
Unlike the Passive Females of thy Land,
The Arbitrators of the War we stand.
At Flurt of Fan, our armed Legions fly,
And they who dare offend, must dare to die.
We know thy daring Heart is nurs'd in Blood,
Wild as the fiercest Savage of the Wood;
With Fame like this, in Northern Slaughter shine,
Rough as the frozen Bear, thy neighb'ring Sign:
style: mock-martial song, trumpet and strings, bold arch female voice, marching, teasing, spirited
why: British women as the real standing army — 'At Flurt of Fan, our armed Legions fly'.

title: Poems
author: Susanna Centlivre
lyrics:
Or drive thee back, or sink thee in the Main:
Tho' Boisterous as the Winds at Sea they roar,
They're gentle all, as Southern Gales on Shore.
Th' Engagement past, the tender Thoughts return,
And for the Fair in Love's foft Fires they burn;
In Beauty's dear Embraces lull'd they lie,
But when their Country calls, Her strongest Foes defie.
THESE hoist their Sails, and wait thy Coming o'er,
And if thou dar'st to touch Britannia's Shore,
Ne'er hope to see thy Native Sweden more.
How wilt thou dare these Hearts of Oak to meet
Shou'd Young Augustus deign to lead the Fleet?
Augustus! He! who striding o'er the Slain,
Hunted thy New Ally o'er Flandria's Plain:
The Boy, whose Cause forsaken now by all,
Calls for a Madman to prevent his Fall.
style: english naval ballad, hornpipe fiddle and drum, hearty chorus voice, rolling, confident, salt-air
why: The sailors 'boisterous as the winds at sea' but 'gentle all, as Southern Gales on Shore' — a ready-made ballad couplet.

title: Epitaphius Adonis
author: Bion of Smyrna
lyrics:
I cry "alas" for Adonis: fair Adonis is dead.
"Fair Adonis is dead," the Loves cry in answer.
No longer, Cypris, sleep in your purple robes;
wake, wretched one, and clad in dark, beat
your breast and tell all: "Fair Adonis is dead."
I cry "alas" for Adonis: the Loves cry in answer.
Fair Adonis lies in the mountains, his thigh by the tusk,
his white thigh struck by the white tusk, and he grieves Cypris
as he breathes out faintly; the black blood drips
down his snowy flesh, and beneath his brows his eyes grow dim,
and the rose flees from his lip; and about him
dies too the kiss that Cypris will never carry away again.
To Cypris the kiss is dear even of one no longer living,
but Adonis does not know that she kissed him as he died.
I cry "alas" for Adonis: the Loves cry in answer.
style: hellenistic ritual lament, double aulos and frame drum, keening female voice with answering chorus, slow, processional, grieving
why: 'I cry alas for Adonis: fair Adonis is dead' — a refrain that is already a refrain, with the white tusk in the white thigh.

title: Epitaphius Adonis
author: Bion of Smyrna
lyrics:
Fair as you were, why did you so madly wrestle with a beast?"
So Cypris lamented; the Loves cry in answer,
"Alas for Cytherea, fair Adonis is dead."
The Paphian sheds as many tears as Adonis
sheds blood; and all upon the ground become flowers.
The blood begets the rose, and the tears the anemone.
I cry "alas" for Adonis: fair Adonis is dead.
No longer in the thickets mourn your husband, Cypris.
No fit couch is a lonely bed of leaves for Adonis;
let Adonis, dead though he is, have your own bed, Cytherea.
Even a corpse he is fair, a fair corpse, as one asleep.
Lay him in the soft robes in which he used to slumber,
in which by night beside you he wrought his sacred sleep
upon the all-golden couch; it too longs for grim Adonis.
And cast upon him garlands and flowers; let all things with him,
style: greek funeral hymn, lyre and low reed, layered mourning voices, slow, tender, ceremonial
why: Blood becoming the rose and tears the anemone, then 'even a corpse he is fair, a fair corpse, as one asleep'.

title: Epitaphius Adonis
author: Bion of Smyrna
lyrics:
The Graces weep for the son of Cinyras,
saying to one another, "Fair Adonis is dead,"
and shrilly they cry "alas" far more than the paean.
And the Fates call Adonis back, "Adonis,"
and chant their spell over him; but he does not hearken to them;
not that he is unwilling, but the Maiden will not release him.
Cease your moaning, Cytherea, for today; refrain from beating your breast;
you must weep again, again in another year shed your tears.
style: closing threnody, solo aulos and soft drum, single low female voice fading, very slow, spent, resigned
why: The lament tells itself to stop and promises to begin again next year — the perfect last verse.

title: Pescennius Niger
author: Scriptores Historiae Augustae
lyrics: 8. Finally, the prophet of Delphic Apollo, in the greatest commotion of the state, when it was announced that there were three emperorsSeverus Septimius, Pescennius Niger, Clodius Albinusbeing consulted whom it would profit the state to have rule, is said to have poured forth a Greek verse of this kind: "Best is Fuscus, good the African, worst the White man." From which it was understood that Fuscus, by the prophecy, meant Niger; the African, Severus; and the White man, Albinus. Nor was there lacking another inquiry, by which it was asked who would obtain the state; to which the oracle replied with another verse such as this: "The blood of the White and the Black living creature shall be shed; the empire of the world shall a Punic man rule, having set out from the city." Likewise, when it was asked who would succeed him, it is said to have replied likewise with a Greek verse: "He to whom the gods grant to have the name of Pius"which was not at all understood until Bassianus received the name of Antoninus, which was the true sign of Pius. Likewise, when it was asked how long he would reign, it is said to have replied in Greek: "Twice ten times shall he mount the Italian sea with ships, if yet one raft shall cross the deep." From which it was understood that Severus would complete twenty years.
style: oracular chant, struck bronze and hollow drone, cavernous whispering male voice, slow, riddling, unsettling
why: Only candidate, but it carries four real Delphic verses — 'best is Fuscus, good the African, worst the White man'.

title: Demosthenis encomium
author: Pseudo-Lucian
lyrics:
Debate and strife had not divided men;
Ismenus? Melias distaff golden-bright?
Cadmus? the race from dragons teeth that came?
Thebes dark circlet? the all-daring might Of Heracles? great Bacchus merry fame?
White-armed Harmonias bridal?Ay, but which?
My Muse, were poor in that we are too rich.
But even at the point of death
She forethought took to fall in seemly wise.
style: greek rhapsodic fragment, solo lyre, questioning tenor, sparse, hesitant, unresolved
why: Only candidate: a chain of Theban questions that turns on 'My Muse, we're poor in that we are too rich'.

title: Quomodo adolescens poetas audire debeat
author: Plutarch
style: ancient greek threnody, lyre and low reed, grave male voice, slow, pleading, shadowed
why: Almost pure quoted verse — the unburied dead begging for a grave and a tear, and the boy pleading to keep the light.

title: Quomodo adolescens poetas audire debeat
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
At whats expedient, and no more require.
For it is an unhappy thing and not to be wished, for a man to obtain and be master of what he desires if it be inexpedient. Again this saying, Thou, Agamemnon, must thyself prepare
Of joy and grief by turns to take thy share:
Thy father, Atreus, sure, neer thee begat,
To be an unchanged favorite of Fate:
we may thus invert: Thy father, Atreus, never thee begat,
To be an unchanged favorite of Fate:
Therefore, if moderate thy fortunes are,
Thou shouldst rejoice always, and grief forbear.
Again it is said, Alas! this ill comes from the powers divine,
That oft we see whats good, yet it decline.
style: gnomic chant, kithara and hand drum, stern measured voice, moderate, admonitory, turning
why: The Atreus lines inverted into their better form — joy and grief by turns, and no one an unchanged favourite of Fate.

title: Elegiae
author: Tibullus
lyrics:
1. Let another heap up riches for himself in tawny gold
and hold many acres of well-tilled soil,
let ceaseless toil terrify him with the enemy near,
the blare of the war-trumpet driving sleep from him:
let my own poverty lead me through a quiet life,
so long as my hearth shines with a steady fire.
With my own hand I would set the tender vines in their due season,
a countryman, and the tall fruit-trees with practised ease;
nor let Hope fail me, but always grant me heaps of grain
and rich new wine in a brimming vat.
For I pay my reverence, whether a lonely stump in the fields
or an old stone at the crossroads bears a garland of flowers,
and whatever fruit the new year ripens for me
is set, an offering, before the farmer's god.
Golden Ceres, for you let there be a crown of grain-ears
style: roman rustic elegy, lyre and soft double pipe, warm intimate male voice, unhurried, pastoral, contented
why: 'Let another heap up riches' against a life of quiet poverty and a steady hearth-fire — the whole Tibullan creed, and his most famous opening.

title: Elegiae
author: Tibullus
lyrics:
How often have I sworn never to return to her threshold!
When I have sworn it well, yet my foot of itself returns.
Fierce Love, would that I might see your weapons broken, the arrows,
and, if it be allowed, the torches put out!
You torment my misery, you compel me to call down
curses on myself and to speak unspeakable things with maddened mind.
By now I would have ended my ills with death, but credulous
Hope nurses my life and ever says tomorrow will be better.
Hope feeds the farmers, Hope entrusts to the ploughed furrows
the seeds that the field will repay with great interest:
this catches birds with the snare, this fish with the rod,
when the slender hooks have hidden the bait before:
Hope too consoles the one bound with a stout fetter:
his legs ring with iron, but he sings amid his work:
style: latin elegy of consolation, plucked lyre and low drone, weary tender voice, slow, building through repetition
why: Hope feeds the farmers, catches the birds, consoles the fettered man who sings at his work — anaphora made for a refrain.

title: Elegiae
author: Tibullus
lyrics:
his wife and his children in the wagon.
But then the wars of Venus grow hot, and the woman laments
her torn hair and her broken-down doors.
She weeps, her tender cheeks bruised, but the victor himself
weeps that his maddened hands had such strength.
But wanton Love supplies the bitter words to the quarrel,
and sits, indifferent, between the two angry ones.
Ah, he is stone and iron, whoever strikes
his girl: he drags the gods down from heaven.
Let it be enough to tear the thin robe from her limbs,
let it be enough to undo the ordering of her hair,
let it be enough to have moved her to tears: four times blessed is he
at whom a tender girl can weep when he is angry.
But let him who is savage with his hands bear shield and stake,
and let him stay far from gentle Venus.
But to us, kindly Peace, come, and hold the corn-ear,
style: roman peace-hymn, aulos and frame drum, pleading male voice with soft chorus, moderate, aching, resolving
why: 'Four times blessed is he at whom a tender girl can weep' turning into the invocation of Peace with her corn-ear.

title: Remedia amoris
