author: Ovid
lyrics:
The title of this book when Cupid spied,
"Treason! a plot against our state," he cried.
Why should you thus your loyal poet wrong,
Who in your war has serv'd so well and long?
So savage and ill-bred I ne'er can prove,
Like Diomede, to wound the queen of love.
Others by fits have felt your am'rous flame,
I still have been, and still your martyr am;
Rules for your vot'ries I did late impart.
Refining passion, and made love an art.
Nor do I now of that or thee take leave,
Nor does the muse her former web unweave.
Let him who loves, where love success may find,
Spread all his sails before the prosp'rous wind;
But let poor youths who female scorn endure,
And hopeless burn, repair to me for cure:
style: augustan comic recitative, harpsichord and pizzicato strings, sly conversational tenor, brisk, mock-serious
why: Cupid reading the title and crying 'Treason!' — a complete comic scene that sets up the whole poem.

title: Remedia amoris
author: Ovid
lyrics:
Far out to sea she cast her prying eyes;
Now stretched upon the sandy beach she lies:
"Faithless Demophoon!" to deaf waves she cried,
While sighs her interrupted words divide,
Hard by a lonesome tree its shadow cast,
As if for solitary mischief plac'd:
'Twas now her ninth sad visit to the shore;
No sail appears, and she'll expect no more:
Her nuptial girdle round her waist was tied,
Just o'er herhead a stretching bough she spied;
She offers, and flies back, dreads what she dares;
And, thus confus'd, the fatal knot prepares.
Now, wretched Phillis, while this deed was done,
I could have wish'd thou hadst not been alone.
Let disappointed lovers warning take
By thee, and never company forsake.
style: tragic ballad, solo cello and guitar, low grieving female voice, slow, unsteady, hushed
why: Phyllis on the ninth day at the shore — 'She offers, and flies back, dreads what she dares' — devastating and self-contained.

title: Remedia amoris
author: Ovid
lyrics:
But both by Venus' presence were disarm'd.
Nor manhood yet must you so far disgrace
As to become the vassal of a face,
Nor to mere beauty your devotion pay;
Her breeding, humor, and her manners weigh;
But in the scale of an impartial mind,
Or inclination will your judgment blind.
What more I have to say will lie compris'd
In little room, but must not be despis'd.
Those short receipts have cures on many done,
And of that number, I myself am one.
The letters sent you when your nymph was kind,
Revise not, for they'll shake your constant mind:
But say, when you commit them to the fire,
"Be this the fun'ral pile of my desire;
Perish, my love, in this just flame expire."
style: resolute farewell air, lute and viol, firm baritone, measured, ceremonial, cold
why: Burning the old love-letters: 'Be this the fun'ral pile of my desire; Perish, my love, in this just flame expire.'

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Hands
lyrics:
'Tis sometime ago though; her mistress said then,
The girl was excessively fond of a pen;
I saw her, but never convers'd with her  though
One can't make acquaintance with servants, you know.
'Tis pity the girl was not bred in high life,
Says Mr. Fribbello:  yes,  then, says his wife,
She doubtless might have wrote something worth notice:
'Tis pity, says one,  says another, and so 'tis.
O law! says young Seagram, I've seen the book, now
I remember, there's something about a mad cow.
A mad cow!  ha, ha, ha, ha, return'd half the room;
What can y' expect better, says Madam Du Bloom?
They look at each other,  a general pause
And Miss Coquettella adjusted her gauze.
The Rector reclin'd himself back in his chair,
And open'd his snuff-box with indolent air;
style: georgian satirical patter song, harpsichord and pizzicato strings, arch narrating soprano, brisk, gossipy, biting
why: The drawing-room demolishing a servant's book — 'there's something about a mad cow' — the poem she is remembered for.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Hands
lyrics:
Says Mrs. Domestic, and when they were done,
I can't see for my part, what use they were on;
Had she wrote a receipt, to've instructed you how
To warm a cold breast of veal, like a ragou,
Or to make cowslip wine, that would pass for Champaign;
It might have been useful, again and again.
On the sofa was old lady Pedigree plac'd,
She own'd that for poetry she had no taste,
That the study of heraldry was more in fashion,
And boasted she knew all the crests in the nation.
Says Mrs. Routella,  Tom, take out the urn,
And stir up the fire, you see it don't burn.
The tea things remov'd, and the tea-table gone,
The card-tables brought, and the cards laid thereon,
The ladies ambitious for each others crown,
Like courtiers contending for honours sat down.
style: drawing-room comedy song, spinet and clattering percussion, quick wry female voice, chattering, clipped, ironic
why: The tea-party opening of the same satire — cowslip wine that would pass for Champaign, and crests instead of poetry.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Hands
lyrics:
Dear Nelly, I make bold to send
My love to you, and am your friend;
I think you are a pretty maid,
And wonder much that you don't wed;
If you can like a country man,
I'll come and see you, if I can,
When roads are good, and weather fine,
But first I hope you'll send a line.
Then he in haste this letter sent,
Also two apples did present,
Which Nell receiv'd, and read the letter,
(But she lik'd the apples better);
When read she into the fire threw it,
And never sent an answer to it.
When spring drew on, the cuckow sung,
The roads were dry, and days were long,
style: rustic courtship ballad, fiddle and hammered dulcimer, plain country voice, jog-trot, dry, strophic
why: The clumsy love letter and two apples: 'Which Nell receiv'd, and read the letter, (But she lik'd the apples better)'.

title: Poems
author: David Garrick
lyrics:
He feels the passion void of art,
The pure, the constant flame.
Tho' sighing swains their torments tell,
Their sensual love contemn;
They only prize the beauteous shell,
But slight the inward gem.
Possession cures the wounded heart,
Destroys the transient fire;
But when the mind receives the dart,
Enjoyment whets desire.
By age your beauty will decay,
Your mind improves with years;
As when the blossoms fade away,
The rip'ning fruit appears:
May heav'n and Sylvia grant my suit,
And bless the future hour,
style: georgian theatre song, harpsichord and flute, sincere clear tenor, gentle, strophic, courting
why: A real song to Sylvia, turning on blossoms falling so the ripening fruit appears — beauty decaying while the mind improves.

title: Poems
author: David Garrick
lyrics:
DEATH and the DOCTOR.
Occasioned by a Physician's lampooning a Friend of the AUTHOR.
By the Same.
AS Doctor ** musing sate,
Death saw, and came without delay:
Enters the room, begins the chat
With, "Doctor, why so thoughtful, pray?"
The Doctor started from his place,
But soon they more familiar grew:
And then he told his piteous case,
How trade was low, and friends were few.
"Away with fear," the phantom said,
As soon as he had heard his tale:
"Take my advice and mend your trade,
"We both are losers if you fail.
"Go write, your wit in satire show,
style: comic macabre ballad, bassoon and plucked strings, dry conspiratorial baritone, moderate, sardonic, sidling
why: Death drops in on a struggling doctor for a friendly chat — 'we both are losers if you fail'.

title: Poems
author: David Garrick
style: mock-epitaph air, spinet and recorder, light mischievous soprano, quick, teasing, birdlike
why: The dead bullfinch promising to haunt the household as a tell-tale bird and sing every tale to Lucy.

title: Poems
author: John Ellis
lyrics:
By Mr. ELLIS.
LOOK round the wide world each profession, you'll find,
Hath something dishonest, which myst'ry they call;
Each knave points another, at home is stark blind,
Except but his own, there's a cheat in them all:
When tax'd with imposture the charge he'll evade,
And like Falstaff pretend he but lives by his trade.
The hero ambitious (like Philip's great son,
Who wept when he found no more mischief to do)
Ne'er scruples a neighbouring realm to o'er-run,
While slaughters and carnage his sabre imbrue.
Of rapine and murder the charge he'll evade,
For conquest is glorious, and fighting his trade.
The statesman, who steers by wise Machiavel's rules,
Is ne'er to be known by his tongue or his face;
They're traps by him us'd to catch credulous fools,
style: english satirical ballad, fiddle and hurdy-gurdy, sardonic male voice, rolling anapestic swing, strophic with refrain
why: Every profession excused by the same closing line — 'he but lives by his trade' — a refrain that is already written.

title: Poems
author: John Ellis
lyrics:
The patient past cure visit thrice in a day,
Write largely the Pharmacop league to uphold,
While poverty's left to diseases a prey;
Are held in repute for their glitt'ring parade:
Their practice is great, and they shine in their trade.
Since then in all stations imposture is found,
No one of another can justly complain;
The coin he receives will pass current around,
And where he is cousen'd he cousens again:
But I, who for cheats this apology made,
Cheat myself by my rhyming, and starve by my trade.
SONG.
By the Same.
AS Chloe ply'd her needle's art,
A purple drop the spear
Made from her heedless finger start,
style: broadside ballad finale, fiddle and drum, wry male voice, rolling, resigned, closing hard
why: The satire turns on its author — 'Cheat myself by my rhyming, and starve by my trade'.

title: Poems
author: John Ellis
lyrics:
And from her eyes a tear.
Ah! might but Chloe by her smart
Be taught for mine to feel;
Mine caus'd by Cupid's piercing dart,
More sharp than pointed steel!
Then I her needle would adore,
Love's arrow it should be,
Indu'd with such a subtle pow'r
To reach her heart for me.
Another.
By the Same.
SUE venal Belinda to grant you the blessing
As Jove courted Danae, or vain's your addressing;
For love, she asserts, all that's generous inspires,
And therefore rich tokens of love she requires.
Such suitors as nothing but ardours are boasting,
style: georgian parlour song, lute and viola, tender light tenor, gentle, courting, small-scale
why: Chloe's pricked finger made into Cupid's arrow, then the sharper joke of venal Belinda and Charon's fee.

title: Sāṃkhyakārikā
author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
lyrics: Therefore this treatise, [though] seen in brief, is not deficient in meaning  like the reflection [transferred] into a mirror of the vast-bodied [original] doctrine. [Non-canonical appendix: this verse occurs only in V1 and M, after the word "samaptam" ("completed"); excluded from the canonical seventy.]
style: sanskrit philosophical chant, tanpura drone and small cymbals, deep steady male voice, slow, austere, sparse
why: The one candidate with a real image — the whole vast doctrine held brief and undiminished, as in a mirror.

title: Eclogarum Liber
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: 2. FROM THE GREEK: A PYTHAGOREAN SAYING ON THE UNCERTAINTY OF CHOOSING A WAY OF LIFE. What path of life shall I follow, if the courts are full of uproar, if the home is anxious with cares, if cares for his household pursue the man abroad, if ever-new losses await the merchant, if base poverty forbids one to rest; if toil harasses the farmer, if shipwreck's terror gives the sea ill repute, and there are heavy penalties in the celibate life, and a heavier and futile watchfulness for the cautious husband; if the work of Mars is bloody, if the gains of usury are base and swift interest cuts down the destitute? Every age has its care; to all, their own time of life displeases them. Sense is absent from little ones who boast, and the rudiments of boys are hard, and the youth of young men is rash. Fortune afflicts men through wars, through the sea, with wraths and snares and chained labours, ever to be exchanged for heavier ones. Old age itself, long awaited and longed for in our prayers  to ill purpose  exposes the body, easily torn, to countless diseases. We all alike despise the present; some, it is agreed, are unwilling to become gods. Juturna cries out: To what end did he give me eternal life? Why was the condition of death taken from me? So beneath the Caucasian crag Prometheus calls Saturn's son to witness, and ceases not by name to accuse Jove, because perennial life has been given him. Look too to the cultivation of the mind: thus, surely, an unhappy care for chastity destroyed chaste Hippolytus. On the other hand, whoever delights to spend a life stained by allurements, let him look upon the punishments and crimes of kings  of incestuous Tereus or soft Sardanapalus. The three Punic wars warn us to avoid treachery; but the destruction of Saguntum forbids us to keep faith. Live, and ever cultivate friendships.  For such a charge the learned school of Pythagorean sages perished.  Fearing this, then, cultivate none.  For such a charge Timon was once stoned in Pallas's Athens. The mind, ever beset, is divided amid uncertain wishes; nor is it enough for a man to have wished: he rejects what he longed for. To be held in honour pleases him; soon he repents; and that they may rule, men wish to serve. The same man, exalted by honour, is exposed to envy. Care keeps the eloquent wakeful all night; but the unpolished man lacks the adornment of life. Be a patron and defend the accused: but the gratitude of a client is rare. Be a client: the patron's person is grievous with its demands. The prayers of fathers urge this man on; soon harsh anxiety steals in with its cares. Childless old age is despised, and the heirless man is the prey of the legacy-hunter. Live thriftily: you shall be torn by report as a miser, and a heavier censure shall brand the lavish giver. All things are contrary to you in adverse chances. Therefore best is the saying of the Greeks: indeed they say that for man it is good not to be born, or, once born, to gain death quickly. This indeed is the Pythagorean apophasis, according to the distich here set below: First, not to have been born among men is best; second, once born, to pass as quickly as possible through the gates of Hades. But, against this, the follower of the other doctrine, disapproving what that teaches, learn what he says by reading below: Therefore, since there is nothing in this life that we should love, yet it is not right that we believe ourselves born to no purpose, if we believe the author of life to be just: another life must be prepared for us by living for him, with whom, after this life, we may live; let them indeed hasten to descend to the Stygian shades, who, following the foolish doctrine of the Pythagoreans, prefer not to have been born rather than, being born, to live.
style: late antique gnomic chant, plainchant over a soft drone, weary male voice, slow, questioning, sparse
why: 'What path of life shall I follow' — every trade and every age indicted in turn, and none of them bearable.

title: Eclogarum Liber
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: 5. ON THE AGES OF LIVING THINGS: AFTER HESIOD. Thrice two and ten times nine and more the years run on, which the just life fills for men as they grow old. These the chattering crow surpasses nine times over in living, and the stag goes four times beyond the crow's generations; the raven thrice outdoes the wing-footed stag, and the Phoenix, the bird that renews itself, multiplies him nine times. Him we Hamadryad Nymphs surpass ten times over in our perpetual age  we whose life is longest. This limit confines the long-lived fates of living things. The rest, God, the arbiter of the hidden age, knows: what times Stilbon (Mercury) rolls round, what ages Phaenon (Saturn), what circuits Pyrois (Mars) holds, what Jupiter with his kindly fire, with what return kindly Venus hastens, who guides the Moon, what toils await Titan (the Sun), until, the year that is called Great being completed, the wandering stars come again into their ancient course, such as they stood from the origin of the ordered world.
style: riddling incantation, plucked lyre and small bell, low measured voice, unhurried, mounting, mythic
why: The ladder of long lives — crow over man, stag over crow, raven, phoenix, and the nymphs above them all.

title: Eclogarum Liber
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: 3. ON THE GOOD MAN: A PYTHAGOREAN SAYING. The good and wise man  such a one as Apollo, when consulted, scarcely found a single one among all the thousands of men  is himself the judge of himself, and examines his whole self to the fingernail. What the nobles think, and what the fickle opinion of the empty crowd, he is unconcerned, like a sphere of the universe, smooth and round, that nothing of an external blemish may settle upon his polished surface. He reflects how long the day will be under the sign of Cancer, and how great the night stretches itself in the tropic of Capricorn; and he weighs himself in the just balance of the scale, lest anything sag, lest anything jut out, that the corner may meet in equal parts, that the level may nowhere swerve, that whatever lies beneath be solid, and that the blow, applied with knocking fingers, betray no hollows beneath. He does not bend his eyes to sweet sleep before he has reckoned over all the deeds of the long day: what things he has passed by, what was done in due season, what was not? Why did grace or reason fail this deed or that? What have I overlooked? Why did this opinion settle, which it had been better to change? Why, pitying some needy man, did I feel a grief with broken spirit? What did I will that it would be good not to have willed? Why, base, did I set the useful before the honourable? Was anyone wounded by a word or, in short, by a look? Why does nature draw me more than discipline? Thus, going through all his words and deeds, and reviewing all from evening's rise, offended at the crooked, he gives the palm and rewards to the upright.
style: stoic hymn, bowed strings and held drone, calm grave voice, slow, level, polished
why: The good man as a sphere of the universe, smooth and round, so nothing external can settle on him.

title: The Fall of Troy
author: Quintus Smyrnaeus
lyrics:
with howling, and a hateful cry rushes through the air;
so Hecuba, wailing, cried aloud over her daughter:
"Ah me, what first, what last, grieving in heart,
shall I wail, encompassed with many evils,
my sons or my husband, who have suffered dire and unlooked-for things,
or my city or my disgraced daughters, or my own
day of necessity and slavery? Because the terrible
Fates have entangled me in many evils.
My child, for you too, dire and unlooked-for things
the Fates have spun, even for yourself; and from your marriage they have cast
the Wedding-song, though it was near, and have brought about destruction,
unbearable and grievous and unspeakable; for indeed Achilles
even in death still warms his heart with our blood;
would that, with you, my dear child, on this day
the earth had gaped and covered me, before I saw your doom."
style: greek tragic lament, aulos and frame drum, raw keening female voice, slow, wailing, unresolved
why: Hecuba over Polyxena — 'Achilles even in death still warms his heart with our blood'.

title: The Fall of Troy
author: Quintus Smyrnaeus
lyrics:
then the strong heart of godlike Achilles
stood over the head of his son, just as he was
when alive, when he was a grief to the Trojans, a joy to the Achaeans.
And he kissed his neck and his gleaming eyes
gladly, and, comforting him, spoke:
"Hail, my child, and do not rend your heart with grief
because of my death, since with the blessed gods
I am now a fellow at the hearth; but restrain your heart, sore-tried
for me, and set my strength to the full in your spirit.
Ever stand as foremost of the Argives, yielding to none
in manhood; but in the assembly to the elder men
give heed; and then all will call you wise.
Honour the blameless men, all whose mind is steadfast;
for to the noble a noble man is dear, and to the harsh, grievous.
If you think good thoughts, you will achieve good deeds too;
style: epic apparition song, lyre and low drone, warm ghostly male voice, slow, tender, counselling
why: The dead Achilles standing over his son's head to bless and instruct him — an entire farewell in one speech.

title: The Fall of Troy
author: Quintus Smyrnaeus
lyrics:
and she groaned greatly, when the day of slavery enwrapped her,
dragged off against her will; and one led one wailing woman,
another another, of the Trojan women, by force to their ships;
and they, wailing piteously, cried aloud, one here, one there,
lamenting most grievously together with their infant children;
as when, together with white-tusked swine, men drive the young
from the former steading to another steading
in the rising of a storm, and they, grievously
mingled together, squeal continually to one another;
so the women of Troy, subdued, groaned beneath the Danaans;
and queen and handmaid alike bore equal necessity.
But Helen no wailing enwrapped; rather shame
sat upon her dark eyes, and above
her fair cheeks blushed red; and within her the heart
beat unspeakably in her breast, lest, as she went
style: processional lament, layered female voices over low drone, slow, heavy, tidal
why: The captive Trojan women driven to the ships, and Helen alone not weeping, only burning with shame.

title: Pseudolus
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
(Exit.)
(Enter a BOY from the house of BALLIO.)
A BOY:
On that Boy on whom the Gods bestow servitude under a procurer, when they add a base occupation as well, assuredly do they, so far as I now understand in my mind, bestow upon him a great misfortune and miseries manifold. Just as this servitude has turned out to me, where I am set over duties great and small; nor am I able to find any admirer to love me, so that at length I might be fitted out in a little better guise.
Now this day is the birthday of this procurer. The procurer has made a determination, from the lowest to the highest, that if each one does not this day send him a present, he shall perish to-morrow with the greatest torments. Now, faith, I know not what to do in my line, for, unless I shall send a present to the procurer this day, to-morrow must I swallow down fullers produce. And yet I cannot do that which they who can are wont to do. Alas! how little am I, even still for this vocation. And by my troth, now, to my misfortune how fearfully do I dread punishment.
style: roman comic complaint, reed pipe and hand drum, put-upon boyish voice, quick, grumbling, patter
why: The slave boy's solo lament — servitude under a pimp, and a birthday present he cannot pay for.

title: Pseudolus
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
SIMO:
Be it so.
CALLIPHO:
You may have your way,
PSEUDOLUS:
But I want you to keep close at home.
SIMO:
Well, that assistance I promise you.
CALLIPHO:
But I shall be off to the Forum. Ill be back here presently.
(Exit CALLIPHO. SIMO goes into his house.)
PSEUDOLUS:
Be back directly. (To the AUDIENCE.) I have a suspicion, now, that you are suspecting that I have been promising these so great exploits to these persons for the purpose of amusing you, while I am acting this play, and that I shall not do that which I said I will do. I will not change my design; so far as that then I know for certain; by what means Im to carry it out not at all do I know as yet; only this, that so it shall be. For he that appears upon the stage in a new character, him it befits to bring something that is new.
style: theatrical patter song, tibia and clacking percussion, sly conspiratorial voice, brisk, winking, direct-address
why: Pseudolus turning to the audience: he does not yet know how he will do it, only that it shall be done.

title: Pseudolus
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
PSEUDOLUS:
Vagabond!
BALLIO:
Pooh! pooh!
CALIDORUS:
Defrauder of the public!
BALLIO:
Most decidedly so.
PSEUDOLUS:
Cheating scoundrel!
CALIDORUS:
Filthy pander!
PSEUDOLUS:
Lump of filth!
BALLIO:
A capital chorus.
style: comic abuse chorus, double pipe and clappers, trading voices, fast, escalating, gleeful
why: A ladder of insults answered by the pimp agreeing with every one, capped by 'a capital chorus'.

title: Poems
author: Susanna Blamire
lyrics:
THE WAEFU' HEART.
GIN living worth could win my heart,
You would na speak in vain;
But in the darksome grave it's laid,
Never to rise again.
My waefu' heart lies low wi' his,
Whose heart was only mine;
And, O! what a heart was that to lose,
But I maun no repine.
Yet, O! gin heaven in mercy soon
Would grant the boon I crave,
And take this life, now naething worth,
Since Jamie's in his grave.
And see! his gentle spirit comes
To show me on my way;
Surpris'd, nae doubt, I still am here,
style: scots lament, solo fiddle and small harp, plain unadorned female voice, very slow, bare, grieving
why: 'My waefu' heart lies low wi' his' — a widow's song complete in itself, no ornament anywhere.

title: Poems
author: Susanna Blamire
lyrics:
He'll cater for me while he's health,
GoodnightI'm off then wi' my laddie.
I'M TIBBY FOWLER O' THE GLEN.
I'M Tibby Fowler o' the glen,
And nae great sight to see, sirs;
But 'cause I'm rich, these plaguy men
Will never let me be, sirs.
There's bonny Maggy o' the brae
As gude as lass can be, sirs;
But 'cause I'm rich these plaguy men
Hae a' run wud for me, sirs.
There's Nabob Jock comes strutting ben,
He thinks the day's his sin, sirs;
But were he a' hung round wi' goud,
He'd find himsel mista'en, sirs.
There's Wat aye tries to glowr and sigh
style: scots comic strophic song, fiddle and bodhrán, bright sardonic female voice, brisk, dancing, refrain-driven
why: Tibby Fowler rich and pestered — 'but 'cause I'm rich these plaguy men' comes back every stanza.

title: Poems
author: Susanna Blamire
lyrics:
Of aw things that is I think thout is meast queer,
It brings that that's by-past and sets it down here;
I see Willy as plain as I dui this bit leace,
When he tuik his cwoat lappet and deeghted his feace.
The lasses aw wonder'd what Willy cud see
In yen that was dark and hard featur'd leyke me;
And they wonder'd ay mair when they talk'd o' my wit,
And slily telt Willy that cudn't be it:
But Willy he laugh'd, and he meade me his weyfe,
And whea was mair happy thro' aw his lang leyfe?
It's e'en my great comfort, now Willy is geane,
That he offen said  nea pleace was leyke his awn heame!
I mind when I carried my wark to yon steyle
Where Willy was deykin, the time to beguile,
He wad fling me a daisy to put i' my breast,
And I hammer'd my noddle to mek out a jest.
style: cumbrian dialect ballad, concertina and fiddle, warm old female voice, unhurried, fond, conversational
why: The widow remembering Willy throwing her a daisy over the wall, and 'nea pleace was leyke his awn heame'.

title: Poems
author: John Wesley
lyrics:
Supplication for Grace.
PUBLICK WORSHIP.
From the German.
LO GOD is here! Let us adore
And own, how dreadful is this Place!
Let all within us feel his Pow'r,
And silent bow before his Face.
Who know his Pow'r, his Grace who prove
Serve Him with Awe, with Rev'rence love.
Lo, GOD is here! Him Day and Night
Th' united Quires of Angels sing:
To Him enthron'd above all Height
Heavn's Hosts their noblest Praises bring:
Disdain not, LORD, our meaner Song,
Who praise Thee with a stamm'ring Tongue.
Gladly the Toys of Earth we leave,
style: methodist hymn, chapel organ and unaccompanied congregation, massed voices, steady, awed, swelling
why: 'Lo God is here! Let us adore' — built for a congregation, with the angel choirs answering the stammering tongue.

title: Poems
author: John Wesley
lyrics:
I groan, I strive, I watch, I pray:
But ah! how soon it dies away!
The deadly Slumber soon I feel
Afresh upon my Spirit steal:
Rise, Lord; stir up thy quick'ning Pow'r,
And wake me that I sleep no more.
Single of Heart O may I be,
Nothing may I desire but Thee:
Far, far from me the World remove,
And all that holds me from thy Love!
DIVINE LOVE.
From the German.
THOU hidden Love of GOD, whose Height,
Whose Depth unfathom'd no Man knows,
I see from far thy beauteous Light,
Inly I sigh for thy Repose.
style: german pietist hymn, harmonium and low strings, longing solo voice, slow, inward, aching
why: 'I groan, I strive, I watch, I pray: but ah! how soon it dies away' running into 'Thou hidden Love of God'.

title: Poems
author: John Wesley
lyrics:
Yea let Man rage! since Thou wilt spread
Thy shadowing Wings around my Head:
Since in all Pain thy tender Love
Will still my sweet Refreshment prove.
Saviour of Men! thy searching Eye
Does all my inmost Thoughts descry:
Doth ought on Earth my Wishes raise;
Or the World's Favour, or its Praise?
The Love of CHRIST does me constrain
To seek the wandring Souls of Men:
With Cries, Intreaties, Tears, to save,
To snatch them from the gaping Grave.
For this let Men revile my Name,
No Cross I shun, I fear no Shame:
All hail, Reproach, and welcome Pain!
Only thy Terrors, LORD, restrain.
style: revival hymn, hand-clapped rhythm and open-air voices, fervent male voice, driving, defiant, rousing
why: 'All hail, Reproach, and welcome Pain!' — the missionary's whole nerve in four lines.

title: Poems
author: Joseph Giles
lyrics:
Cheering, as evening shades prevail,
The soft remains of closing day.
O welcome to my homely board!
There unmolested shalt thou stand;
Were it with choicest dainties stor'd,
For thee I'd ope a liberal hand.
Since thou, of all the warbling throng,
Who now in silence far retire,
Remain'st to sooth me with a song,
And many a pleasing thought inspire.
An EPITAPH.
By the same.
IF e'er sharp sorrow from thine eyes did flow,
If e'er thy bosom felt another's woe,
If e'er fair beauty's charms thy heart did prove,
If e'er the offspring of thy virtuous love
style: english winter air, guitar and recorder, gentle tenor, unhurried, hearth-warm, small
why: The robin hopping over the threshold to peck crumbs, the one singer left when the rest have gone silent.

title: Poems
author: Joseph Giles
lyrics:
Some Reflections upon hearing the Bell toll for the Death of a FRIEND.
By Mr. J. G.
HARK!  what a mournful solemn sound
Rolls murm'ring thro' the cloudy air:
It strikes the soul with awe profound,
Affects the gay,  alarms the fair.
With what a pathos does it speak!
Affecting deep the thoughtful mind:
The golden schemes of folly break,
That hold in glittering snares mankind.
'Tis Death's dread herald calls aloud,
Proclaims his conquest thro' the skies:
The sun retires behind a cloud,
And Nature seems to sympathize.
Reflect, ye restless sons of care!
Your vain designs his hand can spoil,
style: passing-bell elegy, tolling bell and low strings, solemn baritone, slow, arresting, spacious
why: 'Hark! — what a mournful solemn sound' — the bell itself is the refrain and the whole occasion.

title: Poems
author: Joseph Giles
lyrics:
Let opening roses, drooping lillies tell,
Like those she bloom'd, and ah! like these she fell.
In circling wreaths let the pale ivy grow,
And distant yews a sable shade bestow;
Round her, ye Graces, constant vigils keep,
And guard (fair Innocence!) her sacred sleep:
Till that bright morn shall wake the beauteous clay,
To bloom and sparkle in eternal day.
style: graveside air, viola and harp, clear soprano, slow, tender, valedictory
why: 'Like those she bloom'd, and ah! like these she fell' — roses and lilies made to say the whole epitaph.

title: Gordiani Tres
author: Scriptores Historiae Augustae
lyrics: 20. When the elder Gordian once consulted an astrologer about this man's nativity, that man is said to have answered that he would be both the son of an emperor and the father of one, and himself an emperor. And when the elder Gordian laughed, the astrologer, they say, showed the constellation and dictated from old books, so that he proved he had spoken truly; and he indeed foretold, with obstinate firmness from the truth, both the day and the manner of death and the places in which the old man and the young man would perish; all of which the elder Gordian afterward, when he was now emperor in Africa and feared nothing, is reported to have related, even telling of his own death and his son's, and of the manner of death. The old man, moreover, used to sing these verses, when he had seen his son Gordian, very often: "The fates shall but show this man to the earth, nor suffer him to be longer. Too powerful, ye gods above, did the Roman stock seem to you, had these gifts been its own to keep." There survive sayings of the younger Gordian both in prose and in verse, which today are repeated by his kinsmen, neither great nor very small but middling, and such as appear to be those of a man of talent, but one running riot and deserting his own genius.
style: roman prophetic dirge, low strings and struck bronze, grave male voice, slow, fated, hollow
why: Only candidate, but it carries the Marcellus lines the old emperor sang over his own son — shown to the earth and no longer.

title: Nemean
author: Pindar
lyrics: There is one race of men, one race of gods; and from a single mother we both draw our breath. But all allotted power divides us: man is nothing, but for the gods the bronze sky endures as a secure home forever. Nevertheless, we bear some resemblance to the immortals, either in greatness of mind or in nature, although we do not know, by day or by night, towards what goal fortune has written that we should run.
style: doric victory ode, kithara and low drone, layered male chorus, stately, awed, spacious
why: 'One race of men, one race of gods' — and man is nothing, while the bronze sky stands forever. Pindar's most quoted lines.

title: Nemean
author: Pindar
lyrics:
Swiftly Polydeuces the son of Tyndareus went back to his mighty brother, and found him not yet dead, but shuddering with gasps of breath.
Shedding warm tears amid groans, he spoke aloud: Father, son of Cronus, what release will there be from sorrows? Order me to die too, along with him, lord. A mans honor is gone when he is deprived of friends; but few mortals are trustworthy in times of toil to share the hardship. So he spoke. And Zeus came face to face with him, and said these words: You are my son. But Castor was begotten after your conception by the hero, your mothers husband, who came to her and sowed his mortal seed. But nevertheless I grant you your choice in this. If you wish to escape death and hated old age, and to dwell in Olympus yourself with me and with Athena and Ares of the dark spear, you can have this lot. But if you strive to save your brother, and intend to share everything equally with him, then you may breathe for half the time below the earth, and for half the time in the golden homes of heaven. When Zeus had spoken thus, Polydeuces did not have a second thought.
style: greek heroic lament, lyre and frame drum, grieving tenor answered by a low voice, slow, tender, dialogic
why: Polydeuces weeping over the dying Castor and asking Zeus to let him die too — a complete scene with a god's reply.

title: Nemean
author: Pindar
lyrics:
if, by the grace of Mnemosyne with her splendid headdress, one finds a recompense for toils in glorious song.
Skillful men know the wind that will come on the day after tomorrow, and they do not suffer loss through the love of gain. The rich man and the poor man alike travel together to the boundary of death.
style: gnomic ode, plucked lyre and soft aulos, wry knowing male voice, measured, sardonic, level
why: Homer's lies given their solemnity, Ajax undone by a vote, and rich and poor travelling together to the boundary of death.

title: Dionysiaca
author: Nonnus of Panopolis
lyrics:
I want no other burning; but you, girl,
only pour sweet dust over me when I am dead
with your own hand, a last small grace, that one may say:
'The maiden pitied as she killed the man she slew.' And of the dead
let no flute of mine, no harp lie about my tomb,
do not throw down the shepherd's crook, witness of my craft;
but fix your shaft of the slain one high over my tomb,
still bathed in the gore of my love-sickness.
And grant me one last other grace high over my tomb:
let the flowers of love-stricken Narcissus arise,
or lovely crocus or the bindweed flower of the Loves,
and plant the springtime short-lived anemone
proclaiming to all my short-lived youth.
And if no pitiless sea or hills bore you,
shed a little tear for me, only so much as with dews
to wet the rosy tips of your lovely cheek,
style: late antique pastoral lament, solo reed pipe and soft harp, dying tenor, very slow, tender, fading
why: The dying shepherd asking for anemones over his grave and one tear, enough to wet her cheek — flawless and self-contained.

title: Dionysiaca
author: Nonnus of Panopolis
lyrics:
lying in the dust he cried again with a mournful voice:
"Father Zeus, if you love me, and if you know the toil of loves,
set Ampelos speaking again for one hour,
a last hour and only, that he may utter one word:
'Why do you grieve, Dionysus, the one you do not raise with groanings?
I have ears, and I do not hear you crying out,
I have eyes, and I do not see you grieving;
grief-soothing Dionysus, do not shed tears for me,
but leave off your grief, since beside the murderous spring
the Naiads groan and Narcissus does not hear,
Phaethon does not know the mournful grief of the Heliades.'
Alas, that my father did not beget me a mortal, that I might be
a companion of the youth even in Hades, nor in Lethe
leave lovely Ampelos, fallen, alone.
In longing for a youth, Apollo is more blessed,
style: greek elegiac aria, lyre and low strings, raw grieving voice, slow, imploring, broken
why: Dionysus begging Zeus for one hour of Ampelos's speech — 'I have eyes, and I do not see you grieving'.

title: Dionysiaca
author: Nonnus of Panopolis
lyrics:
the earth, scored by the iron that woos the corn-ears,
bore the dry fruit of the sheaf-bearing ploughland.
Now my glorious-gifted child shall fix in the ground
the moist, fragrant fruit of pain-soothing autumn,
Dionysus the griefless, rearing the grief-dispelling cluster,
rival of Demeter; and you will praise me when you behold
the vine reddening with its wine-bearing dews,
the herald of gladness, and the country-folk beside the wine-press
treading the harvest with their heavy-laden feet,
and the phalanx of the Bassarids, lovers of the cry of Euoi,
shaking their loosened, frenzied hair into the air above their shoulders;
and, made frantic in mind by cup after cup,
all will raise the shout of Euoi at the loud-resounding table,
hailing Dionysus, the defender of the human race.
style: dionysiac hymn, double aulos, hand drums and cymbals, ecstatic massed voices, driving, whirling, ecstatic
why: The prophecy of wine: the reddening vine, the treaders at the press, the Bassarids shaking their hair and shouting Euoi.

title: Poems
author: George Crabbe
style: english elegiac air, cello and harpsichord, grave tenor, slow, brooding, unresolved
why: 'Where shall affliction from itself retire?' — care blotting the sun, sighing in the grove, murmuring in the stream.

title: Poems
author: George Crabbe
lyrics:
The bare arms broken from the withering tree,
On which, a boy, he climb'd the loftiest bough,
Then his first joy, but his sad emblem now.
He once was chief in all the rustic trade;
His steady hand the straightest furrow made;
Full many a prize he won, and still is proud
To find the triumphs of his youth allow'd;
A transient pleasure sparkles in his eyes,
He hears and smiles, then thinks again and sighs:
For now he journeys to his grave in pain;
The rich disdain him; nay, the poor disdain:
Alternate masters now their slave command,
Urge the weak efforts of his feeble hand,
And, when his age attempts its task in vain,
With ruthless taunts, of lazy poor complain.
Oft may you see him, when he tends the sheep,
style: rural ballad, fiddle and low guitar, weathered male voice, slow, plain, unsparing
why: The old ploughman who once made the straightest furrow, now disdained by the rich and by the poor alike.

title: Poems
author: George Crabbe
lyrics:
Thus on her name though all disgrace attend,
In every creature she beholds a friend.
REFLECTIONS UPON THE SUBJECT
When all the fiercer passions cease
(The glory and disgrace of youth);
When the deluded soul, in peace,
Can listen to the voice of truth;
When we are taught in whom to trust,
And how to spare, to spend, to give,
(Our prudence kind, our pity just,)
'T is then we rightly learn to live.
Its weakness when the body feels,
Nor danger in contempt defies;
To reason when desire appeals,
When, on experience, hope relies;
When every passing hour we prize,
style: english hymn-tune, chamber organ and viola, plain steady voice, moderate, reflective, settled
why: 'When all the fiercer passions cease' — proper quatrains, and the whole of late wisdom in eight lines.

title: Poems
author: Anna Laetitia Barbauld
lyrics:
Crown'd with flowers, her careless tresses
Loosely floating on the air.
Then, when next the star of evening
Softly sheds the silent dew,
Let me in this rustic temple,
LISSY! meet the Muse and you.
The MOUSE's PETITION, Found in the TRAP where he had been confin'd all Night.
OH! hear a pensive captive's prayer,
For liberty that sighs;
And never let thine heart be shut
Against the prisoner's cries.
For here forlorn and sad I sit,
Within the wiry grate;
And tremble at th' approaching morn,
Which brings impending fate.
If e'er thy breast with freedom glow'd,
style: english ballad, guitar and flute, small clear female voice, gentle, pleading, strophic
why: The mouse's petition from the trap — 'never let thine heart be shut against the prisoner's cries' — her best-known poem.

title: Poems
author: Anna Laetitia Barbauld
style: dissenting hymn, unaccompanied voices with soft organ, warm alto, slow, resolute, building
why: Every crop and flock and rain taken away, and the last line still 'love thee — for thyself alone'.

title: Poems
author: Anna Laetitia Barbauld
lyrics:
To point our path, and light us to our home.
How soft they slide along their lucid spheres!
And silent as the foot of time, fulfil
Their destin'd courses: Nature's self is hush'd,
And, but a scatter'd leaf, which rustles thro'
The thick-wove foliage, not a sound is heard
To break the midnight air; tho' the rais'd ear,
Intensely listening, drinks in every breath.
How deep the silence, yet how loud the praise!
But are they silent all? or is there not
A tongue in every star that talks with man,
And wooes him to be wise; nor wooes in vain:
This dead of midnight is the noon of thought,
And wisdom mounts her zenith with the stars.
At this still hour the self-collected soul
Turns inward, and beholds a stranger there
style: night meditation, sustained strings and soft bells, hushed contralto, very slow, spacious, luminous
why: 'How deep the silence, yet how loud the praise!' and a tongue in every star — the midnight as the noon of thought.

title: Poems
author: Richard Shepherd
lyrics:
Where o'er the joyless plain
The aether sheds its blackest hue,
And here and there a lonely yew
Marks Melancholy's reign.
Where chearful gales forget to blow,
Pellucid currents cease to flow,
The cloud-capt mountain's height
All avenues of the dreary way
Secures from each pervading ray
Of soul-enlivening light.
Where Grief sad social solace seeks,
The rose has fled her meagre cheeks,
And hollow is her eye;
Care on her lap reclines his head,
Whilst hovering round the restless bed
The wing'd chimeras fly.
style: gothic ode, low strings and distant horn, dark contralto, slow, airless, oppressive
why: Melancholy's country where gales forget to blow and currents cease to flow, and Care lies down on Grief's lap.

title: Poems
author: Richard Shepherd
lyrics:
BENEATH yon chain of barren rocks,
Where niggard Nature ne'er unlocks
One hoard of chearful green;
The brown yew forms a gloomy shade,
The blasted oak erects its head,
A dreary wasteful scene.
O haste, O fly th' accursed cell,
Where Envy's fiendly faction dwell!
Else shall her glance, malignant cast,
The fairest shoots of Merit blast:
He risks his ease, who ventures nigh
The baleful witchcraft of her eye.
Ev'n now from her infernal dark abyss,
At Merit's name she lifts her head,
At Merit's name prepar'd to shed
Their influence all her snaky tresses hiss.
style: dramatic ode, tremolo strings and hissing percussion, urgent male voice, taut, sinister, building
why: Envy's cell under the barren rocks — 'at Merit's name prepar'd to shed their influence all her snaky tresses hiss'.

title: Poems
author: Richard Shepherd
lyrics:
From Truth's indisputable ray
Remote, as pole from pole.
So shuts the moping bird of night
Her feeble eyes against the light,
That glads the chearful day;
And when prevailing darkness reigns;
Thro' groves obscene, or dreary plains,
She wings her dubious way.
Consult the blue expanse on high,
The blush that paints the morning sky;
The cloud that nimbly rides,
The orbs that mark with lustre bright
The spangled mantle of the night,
Who there supreme resides.
Question the gaudy flowers around,
That scent the air, or paint the ground,
style: english devotional ode, chamber organ and strings, declamatory tenor, measured, mounting, questioning
why: The owl shutting its eyes against the day, then the sky and the flowers each summoned to answer who made them.

title: Paramārthasāra
author: Ādiśeṣa
lyrics:
The knower of the Self crosses beyond grief; therefore the wise one fears nothing from any quarter. For him there is not even the fear of death from death itself  whence, then, any other [fear]?
Eternally free of decrease and increase, of the slain and the slayer, of bondage and release  this is the truth of {{paramartha|supreme reality}}. Whatever is other than this is all untrue.
Having thus discerned {{prakrti / mulaprakrti|nature}} and the {{purusa|conscious self}}, [the sage,] with the net of [conceptual] construction cast off, delighting in the Self, established in [perfect] quietude, becomes the Alone (kevalin  see {{kaivalya / kevalin|absolute aloneness; the liberated one}}).
As the reed, the plantain, the bamboo, and the [hollow] cane perish once they have come to their own flowering, so [the upadhis,] become [merely] one's [transient] nature, perish on attaining [their fulfilled] nature.
style: vedantic chant, tanpura drone and small cymbals, deep male voice, very slow, austere, sparse
why: No fear even of death from death itself, and the reed and plantain that perish once they have flowered.

title: Paramārthasāra
author: Ādiśeṣa
lyrics:
When the knot of ignorance is split, when the host of doubts is cut through, when [the store of] merit is exhausted and the seed of birth is burnt up, one goes to the supreme Self, Hari.
{{moksa|release, redefined here non-spatially}} has no abode whatever, nor any going-away to some other place. The splitting of the knot [woven] of ignorance  that they know as release (moksa).
Having awakened thus [to the fact] that this form of the world, made of Visnu's {{maya|deluding power}}, is unreal, one should become tranquil, free of the pairs of opposites, of limiting adjuncts ({{upadhi|limiting adjuncts}}s), and of attachment to enjoyment.
Having understood {{prakrti / mulaprakrti|nature}} as [a thing] apart [from himself], the {{purusa|conscious self}}, [though] moving in the midst of transmigration, becomes wholly freed from all actions, as the lotus-leaf [is untouched] by the waters.
style: sanskrit devotional recitation, drone and soft bell, calm low voice, slow, unfolding, still
why: Release with no place to go to — only the knot of ignorance split — and the lotus-leaf untouched by the water.

title: On the Nature of Animals
author: Claudius Aelianus
lyrics: 45. That the tribe of dolphins is fond of song and of the flute, Arion of Methymna is a sufficient witness, both from the statue at Taenarum and from the epigram written upon it. And the epigram is: "By the escort of the immortals, this conveyance saved Arion the son of Cycleus from the Sicilian sea." And a hymn of thanksgiving to Poseidon, witness to the dolphins' love of music, Arion wrote, paying these too, as it were, a ransom for his life. And this is the hymn: "Highest of gods, lord of the sea, gold-tridented Poseidon, earth-holder, through the teeming brine; round you the swimming beasts dance in a ring with their fins, with light tossings of their feet lightly leaping, snub-nosed, bristle-necked, swift-running whelps, the music-loving dolphins, sea-nurslings of the maiden Nereid goddesses, whom Amphitrite bore; you who brought me to the land of Pelops, to the Taenarian shore, as I wandered in the Sicilian sea, carrying me on your arched backs, cleaving the furrow of the Nereid plain, an untrodden path, when treacherous men cast me from their hollow sea-faring ship into the sea-purple swell of the deep." Peculiar to dolphins, surely, in addition to what has been said above, is their love of music too.
style: greek sea-hymn, lyre and hand drum, clear ringing male voice, rolling, buoyant, ceremonial
why: Only candidate, but it carries Arion's whole hymn to Poseidon — the dolphins dancing in a ring and carrying him ashore.

title: Logic, Inductive and Deductive
author: William Minto
lyrics:
Where timid knowledge stands considering Audacious ignorance has done the deed.
Through foul we follow fair For had the world one face And earth been bright as air We had known neither place. Indians smell not their nest The Swiss and Finn taste best The spices of the East.
Spur boldly on, and dash through thick and thin, Through sense and nonsense, never out nor in.
style: english gnomic air, lute and hand drum, bold plain voice, brisk, epigrammatic, spurring
why: Only candidate: three epigraphs that happen to agree — audacious ignorance beats timid knowledge, so spur boldly on.

title: Carmina
author: Catullus, C. Valerius
lyrics: These, with clear-sounding voice, as they combed out the wool, out-poured fates of such kind in sacred song, in song which no age yet to come could tax with untruth. O with great virtues augmenting your exceeding honour, mainstay of Emathia, most famous in your issue, receive what the sisters make known to you on this happy day, a truth-naming oracle! But run, you spindles, drawing the thread which the fates follow, run, spindles! Now Hesperus will come to you bearing what is longed for by bridegrooms, with that fortunate star will your bride come, who steeps your soul with the sway of softening love, and prepares with you to conjoin in languorous slumber, spreading her smooth arms beneath your sinewy neck. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! No house ever yet enclosed such loves, no love bound lovers with such pact, as abides with Thetis, as is the concord of Peleus. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! To you will Achilles be born, a stranger to fear, to his foes known not by his back, but by his strong breast, who, often the victor in the uncertain struggle of the foot-race, will outrun the fire-fleet footsteps of the speedy doe. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! None in war with him may compare as a hero, when the Phrygian streams trickle with Trojan blood, and when besieging the walls of Troy with a long, drawn-out warfare perjured Pelops third heir lays that city waste. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! Often will mothers attest over funeral-rites of their sons his glorious acts and illustrious deeds, when the white locks from their heads are unloosed amid ashes, and they bruise their discoloured breasts with feeble fists. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! For as the reaper, plucking off the dense wheat-ears before their time, mows the harvest yellowed beneath ardent sun, so will he cast prostrate the corpses of Troys sons with grim swords. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! His great valour will be attested by Scamanders wave, which ever pours itself into the swift Hellespont, narrowing its course with slaughtered heaps of corpses he shall make tepid its deep stream by mingling warm blood with the water. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! And finally she will be a witness: the captive-maid handed to death, when the heaped-up tomb of earth built in lofty mound receives the snowy limbs of the stricken virgin.
style: roman wedding prophecy, kithara and low frame drum, layered male and female voices, spinning-wheel pulse, incantatory, building to dread
why: The Fates' song with its hammering refrain 'run, drawing the thread, run, spindles!' — a built-in chorus wrapped around the birth of Achilles.

title: Carmina
author: Catullus, C. Valerius
lyrics:
Maidens:
Hesperus, comrades, has stolen one girl away from us, [Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!]
Youths:
For at your approach a guard always keeps watch. Thieves lie in wait by night, often on your return with your name changed,
Hesperus, you catch the same men. Yet it pleases the unwedded girls to criticize you with false complaints. But what if they criticize the one whom with silent mind they long for? Hymen O Hymenaeus, Hymen come O Hymenaeus!
Maidens:
As grows the hidden flower in a walled garden, unknown to cattle, uprooted by no plow, which the breezes caress, the sun strengthens, and the rain gives growth: many boys and many girls have longed for it: this same flower when plucked by a delicate fingernail sheds its blossoms: no boys and no girls long for it:
style: latin epithalamium, antiphonal choirs of youths and maidens, aulos and lyre, alternating, evening-lit, tender then keen
why: The walled-garden flower — untouched, then plucked and wanted by no one — Catullus's most quoted image, inside an answering-song already built for two choirs.

title: Carmina
author: Catullus, C. Valerius
lyrics:
Was no thought able to bend the intent of your ruthless mind? had you no clemency there, that your pitiless bowels might show me compassion? But these were not the promises you gave me idly of old, this was not what you bade me hope for, but the blithe bride-bed, hymenaeal happiness: all empty air, blown away by the breezes. Now, now, let no woman give credence to mans oath, let none hope for faithful vows from mankind;
for while their eager desire strives for its end, nothing fear they to swear, nothing of promises forbear they: but instantly their lusting thoughts are satiate with lewdness, nothing of speech they remember, nothing of perjuries care. In truth I snatched you from the midst of the whirlpool of death, preferring to suffer the loss of a brother rather than fail your need in the supreme hour, O ingrate. For which I shall be a gift as prey to be rent by wild beasts and the carrion-fowl, nor dead shall I be placed in the earth, covered with funeral mound. What lioness bore you beneath lonely crag?
style: latin tragic lament, solo female voice, lyre and low bowed strings, rubato, bitter, keening
why: Ariadne abandoned: 'let no woman give credence to man's oath' — a complete, furious aria that needs no context.

title: Idylls
author: Theocritus
lyrics:
turning to the house of Phrasidamus, lay down
among deep beds of sweet rushes,
rejoicing in the newly stripped vine-leaves.
Many poplars and elms waved above
over our heads; and close by, the holy water
trickled murmuring from the cave of the Nymphs.
In the shady boughs the sun-burnt cicadas
kept their chattering toil; and far off the tree-frog
cried among the thick thorns of the brambles.
The larks and goldfinches sang, the turtle-dove moaned,
and the tawny bees flitted about the springs.
All breathed of rich summer, all breathed of harvest-time.
Pears at our feet, and apples by our sides
rolled in abundance; and the boughs hung down to the ground
weighted with sloes;
and the four-year-old seal was loosed from the wine-jars' mouths.
style: greek pastoral idyll, syrinx and lyre over soft drone, warm tenor, unhurried, sunlit, drowsy
why: The harvest-home grove — cicadas, bees, pears at the feet, 'all breathed of rich summer' — the most beautiful landscape in Greek pastoral.

title: Idylls
author: Theocritus
lyrics:
come with his heifers, may he have no less.
You springs and pastures, sweet growth, if Daphnis
makes music like the nightingales,
fatten this herd of mine; and if Menalcas
brings any here, may he too feed all in plenty, and rejoice.
Here are the ewes, here the goats that bear twins, here the bees
fill their hives, and here the oaks grow taller,
here the fair Milon sets his feet; but if he goes away,
then dry are both the shepherd and the pastures there.
Spring everywhere, everywhere the meadows, everywhere with milk
the udders swell, and the young are reared,
wherever the fair girl walks; but if she goes away,
then withered are both the cowherd and his cattle.
O he-goat, husband of the white she-goats, O depth of the woodland
without end(O snub-nosed kids, come here to the water)
style: amoebean shepherd's song, twin panpipes and hand drum, two answering male voices, call-and-response, lilting, rustic
why: 'Spring everywhere, everywhere the meadows' — an antiphonal duet with the refrain shape already in the text, each stanza turning on 'but if she goes away'.

title: Idylls
author: Theocritus
style: sicilian pastoral air, single reed pipe and plucked lyre, plain low voice, slow, sea-facing, contented
why: 'May I not have the land of Pelops, nor talents of gold... but under this rock will I sing, holding you in my arms' — a whole ethic of love in one refusal.

title: Poems
author: Mary Tighe
lyrics:
Mourn for ourselves! Secure thy lot must be,
With those who pure in heart their God shall see.
Verses Written in Sickness.
December, 1804.
O THOU, whom Folly's votaries slight,
Domestic Love! assuasive power!
Life's ruby gem, which sheds its light
Through age and sorrow's darkest hour,
Sweeter than Pleasure's syren lay,
Brighter than Passion's, fevered dream!
Still round my pillow soothing stay,
Still spread thy kindly lambent beam.
Alas! for him whose youth has bowed
Beneath the oppressive hand of pain;
Whose claim to pity disallowed
Bids him the unheeded groan restrain.
style: georgian devotional air, chamber organ and viola da gamba, frail warm soprano, slow, hymn-like, consoling
why: 'Domestic Love! assuasive power! Life's ruby gem' — an invocation written from a sickbed, plain and steady where the epic verse is ornate.

title: Poems
author: Mary Tighe
lyrics:
A night of horrors, only less than death.
The Vartree.
SWEET are thy banks, O Vartree! when at morn
Their velvet verdure glistens with the dew;
When fragrant gales by softest Zephyrs borne
Unfold the flowers, and ope their petals new.
How bright the lustre of thy silver tide,
Which winds, reluctant to forsake the vale!
How play the quivering branches on thy side,
And lucid catch the sun-beam in the gale!
And sweet thy shade at Noon's more fervid hours,
When faint we quit the upland gayer lawn
To seek the freshness of thy sheltering bowers,
Thy chesnut glooms, where day can scarcely dawn.
How soothing in the dark sequestered grove
To see thy placid waters seem to sleep;
style: english pastoral lyric, harp and flute, clear female voice, flowing, gentle, riverine
why: The Vartree at morning and noon — dew, silver tide, chesnut glooms; a clean landscape song with real light in it.

title: Poems
author: Mary Tighe
lyrics:
"Soldier, farewel! To thee should power
Commit the fate of lives obscure,
Remember still in fury's hour
The murdered youths of Glenmalure.
"And chief, if civil broils return,
Though vengeance urge to waste, destroy;
Ah! pause! .... think then on Bryan Byrne,
Poor Ellen, and her orphan boy!"
Imitated from Jeremiah.  Chap: xxxi. v. 15.
HARK, the voice of loud lament
Sounds through Ramah's saddened plain!
There cherished grief, there pining discontent,
And desolation reign.
There, mid her weeping train
See Rachel for her children mourn
Disconsolate, forlorn!
style: irish ballad, uilleann pipes and bodhran, keening female voice, modal, mournful, strophic
why: 'Remember still in fury's hour the murdered youths of Glenmalure' — a rebellion ballad that ends on a plea a listener can carry away whole.

title: Poems
author: Mark Akenside
lyrics:
Love is with sweet success beguil'd
And sad remorse forgets her secret wound;
O whither hast thou flown, indulgent God?
God of kind shadows, and of healing dews,
O'er whom dost thou extend thy magic rod?
Around what peaceful couch thy opiate airs diffuse?
Lo, midnight from her starry reign
Looks awful down on earth and main.
The tuneful birds lie hush'd in sleep,
With all that crop the verdant food,
With all that skim the crystal flood,
Or haunt the cayerns of the rocky steep.
No rushing winds disturb the tufted bowr's;
No wakeful sound the moonlight valley knows,
Save where the brook its liquid murmur pours,
And lulls the waving scene to more profound repose.
style: english nocturne, chamber organ and muted strings, hushed baritone, very slow, floating, becalmed
why: A hymn to Sleep: midnight looking down on earth and main, birds hushed, only the brook still murmuring — the quietest thing in the book.

title: Poems
author: Mark Akenside
lyrics:
ODE I. Allusion to HORACE.
AMID the garden's fragrance laid,
Where yonder limes behold their shade
Along the glassy stream,
With HORACE and his tuneful ease
I'll rest from crouds, and care's disease,
And summer's piercing beam.
Behold the busy, wand'ring BEE!
From bloom to bloom, from tree to tree
She sweeps mellifluous dews;
For her the silken gems arise,
For her display their shining dyes,
Their balmy breath diffuse.
Sweet murmurer! may no rude storm
This pleasurable scene deform
To check thy gladsome toils;
style: georgian ode setting, harpsichord and oboe, light tenor, pastoral, lilting, chamber
why: Horace in the garden with the wandering bee — a clean opening, concrete, and short-lined enough to sing.

title: Poems
author: Mark Akenside
lyrics:
Then ofter to thy name attun'd,
And rising to diviner sound,
I'll wake the free HORATIAN song:
Old TYNE shall listen to my tale,
And ECHO, down the bord'ring vale,
The liquid melody prolong.
ODE III. Against SUSPICION.
O Fly! 'Tis dire SUSPICION'S mien;
And, meditating plagues unseen,
The sorc'ress hither bends:
Behold her torch in gall imbrued:
Behold  her garments drop with blood
Of lovers and of friends.
Fly far! Already in your eyes
I see a pale suffusion rise;
And soon thro' every vein,
style: baroque dramatic aria, agitated strings and continuo, urgent alto, minor key, stalking, unsettled
why: Suspicion arriving as a sorceress with her torch steeped in gall and her garments dripping — a real personification with menace.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Carter
lyrics:
Wak'd from the sleep of death with joy survey
The opening splendors of eternal day.
ODE to WISDOM.
By a LADY.
THE solitary bird of night
Thro' the thick shades now wings his flight,
And quits his time-shook tow'r;
Where, shelter'd from the blaze of day,
In philosophick gloom he lay
Beneath his ivy bow'r.
With joy I hear the solemn sound,
Which midnight echoes waft around,
And sighing gales repeat.
Fav'rite of PALLAS! I attend,
And faithful to thy summons, bend
At WISDOM'S aweful seat.
style: eighteenth-century hymn-ode, harpsichord and strings, clear soprano, stately, nocturnal, measured
why: The Ode to Wisdom — 'the solitary bird of night... quits his time-shook tow'r' — Carter's best-known lyric, and it was set to music in her own century.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Carter
lyrics:
Angelic forms shall visit this retreat,
And opening heaven diffuse its glories round.
WRITTEN EXTEMPORE ON THE SEA SHORE.
BY THE SAME.
THOU restless fluctuating deep,
Expressive of the human mind,
In thy for ever varying form
My own inconstant self I find.
How soft now flow thy peaceful waves,
In just gradations to the shore:
While on thy brow unclouded shines
The regent of the midnight hour.
Blest emblem of that equal state,
Which I this moment feel within:
Where thought to thought succeeding rolls,
And all is placid and serene.
style: english art song, fortepiano and cello, reflective mezzo, gently rocking, tidal, introspective
why: 'Thou restless fluctuating deep... in thy for ever varying form my own inconstant self I find' — the whole conceit lands in four lines.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Carter
lyrics:
ODE TO MELANCHOLY.
BY MISS CARTER.
COME, Melancholy! silent power,
Companion of my lonely hour,
To sober thought confin'd;
Thou sweetly sad ideal guest,
In all thy soothing charms confest,
Indulge my pensive mind.
No longer wildly hurried thro'
The tides of mirth, that ebb and flow
In folly's noisy stream:
I from the busy crowd retire,
To court the objects that inspire
Thy philosophic dream.
Thro' yon dark grove of mournful yews
With solitary steps I muse,
style: georgian ode, viola da gamba and chamber organ, contralto, slow, shadowed, processional
why: 'Come, Melancholy! silent power, companion of my lonely hour' — a clean invocation with the yew grove and the retreat from folly's noisy stream.

title: Res Rustica
author: Columella, Lucius Junius Moderatus
lyrics:
If wool is your desire, above all else
Avoid the prickly woods and burs and caltropses.
When after shearing sweat unwashen clings And prickly briers tear away their flesh.
At Lucifer's first rising let us haste To the cool fields, while yet the dawn is new, And turf still hoary, and on tender grass The dew is sweetest to the feeding herd. Then, when the sky's fourth hour brings thirst to all, Let's lead the flocks to wells and deep-dug pools,a and in the middle of the day, as the same poet says, let us conduct them to a valley,
Where haply Jove's great oak with hardwood old Stretches its giant branches or a grove Black -with thick holm-oaks broods with holy shade. b
Till sun-set, when chill evening cools the air And Luna's dews the thirsty glades refresh. a
Learn too to burn the fragrant cedar-wood And from the stalls to drive dread water-snakes With fumes of Syrian gum; a a viper oft, Dangerous to the touch, 'neath unmoved pens Has lurked and, frightened, shunned the light of heaven,
style: roman georgic, shepherd's pipe and plucked lyre, warm baritone, unhurried, sunlit, rustic
why: Driving the flock out at first light while the turf is still hoary, then into the shade of Jove's great oak — the one passage here that is pure landscape.

title: Res Rustica
author: Columella, Lucius Junius Moderatus
lyrics:
And let a palm or vast wild-olive tree
O'ershade the porch, that when new kings lead forth
The infant swarms and the young bees make sport
In their own spring, from honey-combs set free; Then let the neighbouring bank invite retreat From mid-day heat, and let the sheltering tree Hold them in leafy hospitality. a
That upon frequent bridges they may rest And spread their wings to catch the summer sun, If swift east winds have caught them loitering And rained on them or plunged them in the deep. a
You can foreknow the purpose of the herd; The martial roar of the hoarse brass reproves The loiterers, and a voice is heard whose notes The broken sound of trumpets imitates. a
As two-fold are the features of the kings,
So are the bodies of their subjects-; one Will gleam with markings rough with gold, and bright
style: latin bee-hymn, soft aulos and shaken rattle, murmuring male voices, humming drone, light, midsummer
why: New kings leading out the infant swarms under a wild-olive, bees resting on bridges to dry their wings — concrete and strangely tender.

title: The Condition of the Working Class in England
author: Frederick Engels
lyrics:
There is a King, and a ruthless King; Not a King of the poets dream; But a tyrant fell, white slaves know well, And that ruthless King is Steam.
He hath an arm, an iron arm, And tho he hath but one, In that mighty arm there is a charm, That millions hath undone.
Like the ancient Moloch grim, his sire In Himmons vale that stood, His bowels are of living fire, And children are his food.
His priesthood are a hungry band, Blood-thirsty, proud, and bold; Tis they direct his giant hand, In turning blood to gold.
For filthy gain in their servile chain All natures rights they bind; They mock at lovely womans pain, And to manly tears are blind.
The sighs and groans of Labours sons Are music in their ear, And the skeleton shades, of lads and maids, In the Steam Kings hell appear.
style: chartist protest ballad, industrial folk, anvil percussion and fiddle, gritty male chorus, driving, marching
why: The Steam King as a one-armed Moloch fed on children — a factory-age ballad already written in singable quatrains.

title: The Condition of the Working Class in England
author: Frederick Engels
lyrics:
Those hells upon earth, since the Steam Kings birth, Have scatterd around despair; For the human mind for Heavn designd, With the body, is murdered there.
Then down with the King, the Moloch King, Ye working millions all; O chain his hand, or our native land Is destind by him to fall.
And his Satraps abhord, each proud Mill Lord, Now gorgd with gold and blood, Must be put down by the nations frown, As well as their monster God.
style: workers' anthem, hammered percussion, massed unison voices, insurgent, accelerating, defiant
why: 'Then down with the King, the Moloch King, ye working millions all' — the rallying half of the same song, built to be shouted back.

title: History of Modern Philosophy from Nicolas of Cusa to the Present Time
author: Richard Falckenberg
lyrics: "The friends whom I love I gladly would serve, but to this inclination incites me; And so I am forced from virtue to swerve since my act, through affection, delights me. The friends whom thou lovest thou must first seek to scorn, for to no other way can I guide thee; 'Tis alone with disgust thou canst rightly perform the acts to which duty would lead thee."
style: german classical lied, fortepiano and light strings, wry baritone, epigrammatic, brisk, chamber
why: Schiller's joke on Kantian duty — serve your friends only after learning to despise them — a complete two-voice epigram.

title: Works and Days
author: Hesiod
lyrics:
And now I will tell a fable for princes who themselves understand. Thus said the hawk to the nightingale with speckled neck, while he carried her high up among the clouds, gripped fast in his talons, and she, pierced by his crooked talons, cried pitifully. To her he spoke disdainfully: Miserable thing, why do you cry out? One far stronger than you now holds you fast, and you must go wherever I take you, songstress as you are. And if I please, I will make my meal of you, or let you go.
He is a fool who tries to withstand the stronger, for he does not get the mastery and suffers pain besides his shame. So said the swiftly flying hawk, the long-winged bird.
But you, Perses, listen to right and do not foster violence; for violence is bad for a poor man.
Even the prosperous cannot easily bear its burden, but is weighed down under it when he has fallen into delusion. The better path is to go by on the other side towards Justice; for Justice beats Outrage when she comes at length to the end of the race. But only when he has suffered does the fool learn this. For Oath keeps pace with wrong judgements.
style: archaic greek fable-chant, single lyre and hand drum, storyteller's baritone, sparse, hard, unsettling
why: The hawk carrying the nightingale in his talons and telling her why she should not cry out — the oldest fable in Greek, and it needs nothing around it.

title: Works and Days
author: Hesiod
style: greek gnomic chant, plucked lyre over low drone, stern male voice, measured, climbing, austere
why: 'Badness can be got easily and in shoals... but between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows' — the long steep path, the line the poem is remembered for.

title: Works and Days
author: Hesiod
lyrics:
Muses of Pieria who give glory through song, come hither, tell of Zeus your father and chant his praise. Through him mortal men are famed or unfamed, sung or unsung alike, as great Zeus wills.
For easily he makes strong, and easily he brings the strong man low; easily he humbles the proud and raises the obscure, and easily he straightens the crooked and blasts the proud,Zeus who thunders aloft and has his dwelling most high. Attend thou with eye and ear, and make judgements straight with righteousness.
And, Perses, I would tell of true things.
So, after all, there was not one kind of Strife alone, but all over the earth there are two. As for the one, a man would praise her when he came to understand her; but the other is blameworthy: and they are wholly different in nature. For one fosters evil war and battle, being cruel:
style: archaic greek hymn-proem, phorminx and drone, grave male voice, slow, invocatory, swelling
why: The opening call to the Muses, with its hammering 'easily... easily... easily' — Zeus raising and levelling men, built as anaphora already.

title: Apotheosis
author: Aurelius Prudentius Clemens
lyrics:
which taught the true God, the manger, the swaddling-clothes,
the mother's lap adored by the burning torch of the star:
let the very power of his deeds and the marvels speak God.
I see the raging winds suddenly grow gentle
when Christ commands; I see the seas, struggling
with great whirlwinds, stretched into a calm marble plain
at Christ's command; I see, when he is trodden, the very
gulf, while it suffers it, solidify its surface with hardening water.
He himself walks over the flowing waves on shining
soles, and steadies his footsteps on the pressed-down flood;
he himself rebukes the south winds, and bids the gusts be still.
Who would command the savage north winds, "Go, be silent
in your prison-cells, and quit the wide sea,"
unless it were the same heaven-mighty founder of the north winds?
style: latin christian hymn, plainchant over organum drone, male schola, slow, luminous, awed
why: 'I see the raging winds suddenly grow gentle... he himself walks over the flowing waves on shining soles' — an anaphoric catalogue of miracles that is already a hymn.

title: Apotheosis
author: Aurelius Prudentius Clemens
lyrics:
visible, through whom the Father himself may be seen
and not by the eyes of saints alone, but to the light-bereft
eyes of the blind; I speak of the blind, whose dull sloth
in a darkened heart cannot weigh the truth,
whom, if you deny him plain to mortals,
come, say, whom did the tyrant see from Babylon's tower
ranging far amid harmless flames,
treading the swift fires with his brethren unscorched?
Surely he says: "O nobles, three men the vast burning
received into its panting furnaces; one added,
behold, laughing, cuts apart the steaming fires.
That is the Son of God; I confess it, and, vanquished, I adore.
Take away the mocked torches, and withdraw the warm
brands; the heat of the kindled brimstone grows cold.
The Son  there is no doubt  works these wonders of nature,
style: late antique narrative chant, low male voices and struck bell, kindling, dramatic, fire-lit
why: The furnace: three men thrown in, a fourth walking laughing through the flames, and the king's 'I confess it, and, vanquished, I adore.'

title: Apotheosis
author: Aurelius Prudentius Clemens
lyrics:
which from small things we see brought to completion?
And lest, after men were fed, the leavings, trodden, should perish,
nor lie a prey, left to wolves or foxes or little
mice, with no keeper,
twice six baskets were set by, which heaped up should keep
the good things of Christ, displayed afar from the laden hampers.
But why do I unfold these things with faltering voice,
unworthy to sing what is holy? Come forth from the tomb,
Lazarus, tell whose voice beneath the deepest earth
you heard, what power penetrated the hidden things of death;
that, when Christ, you being plunged in the blackening deep,
calls you to return, you hear as if close by,
and without delay are present? What Charybdis so near
joins to the world above the kingdoms of darkness, parted
by a thin boundary? Where are the gloomy Taenarian gates
style: latin funerary chant, deep unison voices and sparse drone, hollow, echoing, slow with a sudden call
why: 'Come forth from the tomb, Lazarus, tell whose voice beneath the deepest earth you heard' — direct address to a dead man, and the gates of darkness opening.

title: Poems
author: Daniel Defoe
lyrics:
She Great in them, and they as Great in Her;
Sure Heaven will such Illustrious Praises hear.
The crouding Millions Hearty Blessings pour:
Saint Paul ne'er saw but one such Day before.
The Vision, A POEM.
Being an ANSWER to the Lord Beilhaven's SPEECH.
By a Person of Quality.
COme hither ye Dreamers of Dreams,
Ye Soothsayers, Vizards and Witches,
That puzzle the World with hard Names,
And without any meaning make Speeches:
Here's a Lord in the North,
Near Edinburgh Frith;
Tho little has been said of his Name or his Worth;
He's seen such a Vision, no Mortal can reach it,
I challenge the Clan of Egyptians to match it.
style: english broadside ballad, fiddle and side drum, mocking male voice, jaunty, brisk, jeering
why: 'Come hither ye Dreamers of Dreams, ye Soothsayers, Vizards and Witches' — a proper street-ballad opening with a hook in the first line.

title: Poems
author: Daniel Defoe
lyrics:
Whom neither Name Invites nor Hopes Inspire:
Yet this she claims, she can Your Fame rehearse,
Unbiass'd in Your Praise, Impartial in her Verse.
This Character sh' has kept, and this she brings,
She always scorn'd to flatter, tho' she sung to Kings.
Satyr has been her Talent, Truth her Song,
Truth who can bear it! sung too loud, too long.
Bright Truth! that Stranger to the Jingling Train,
Makes all their Praises Satyrs, all their Satyrs vain,
While Truth can neither this nor that explain.
Th' Unspotted Standard has been all her Aim,
For this she has felt her Fate, and sunk her Fame:
For this they've damn'd the Poet and his Rimes,
And slain th' unhappy Muse for want of Crimes
Adapted thus to Sacred Truth and Fame,
She never sung but they were both her Theam
style: georgian ballad of defiance, plain guitar and bass viol, weathered baritone, slow, unrepentant, plainspoken
why: Defoe on his own muse: 'Satyr has been her Talent, Truth her Song... For this they've damn'd the Poet and his Rimes' — the pillory speaking.

title: Poems
author: Daniel Defoe
lyrics:
The furious Elements in vain contend,
Unmov'd the mighty natural Breast-works stand.
Their awful Hights in threatning Grandeur shine,
Emblems of mightier Hearts of Stone within.
Th' Instructing Rocks, Invincible and Strong,
Describe the Race that to these Rocks belong,
And bid the quick retreating Waves declare,
And warn the World against a Northern War.
Tell them the Hopes of Conquest must be vain;
When Hands of Steel shall Rocks of Flint maintain.
These are th' eternal Bounds of Providence,
The Oceans Bridle, and the Lands Defence.
The Warts and Wrinkles plac'd on Natures Brow
That her Maternal Care and Conduct show.
The meanest parts of Nature have their Use,
And some to Terror, some to Strength conduce:
style: north-sea hymn, low strings and bodhran, granite bass voice, slow, immovable, storm-battered
why: Sea-cliffs as the ocean's bridle and 'the Warts and Wrinkles plac'd on Natures Brow' — one sustained image, and it holds.

title: Poems
author: Robert Craggs Nugent
lyrics:
But beware with bolder flight,
Tempt not heaven's unequal height;
But beware! with impious strain,
Mock not freedom's hallow'd train!
Sacred, here, O! ever be
Heaven, and heaven-born liberty!
Let the slaves of lawless sway,
Let the stupid flock obey!
Pent within a narrow fold,
Ty'd, and stript, and slain, and sold.
Happier stars the brave befriend,
Britons know a nobler end.
Theirs it is to temper laws,
Theirs to watch in freedom's cause,
Theirs one common good to share,
Theirs to feel one common care;
style: english liberty ode, martial drum and trumpet, ringing baritone with chorus, driving trochaic pulse, defiant
why: 'Let the stupid flock obey! Pent within a narrow fold, / Ty'd, and stript, and slain, and sold' — short lines, hard consonants, made for shouting.

title: Poems
