And taught the doubtful Battel where to rage.
So when an Angel by Divine Command
With rising Tempests shakes a guilty Land,
Such as of late o'er pale Britannia past,
Calm and Serene he drives the furious Blast;
And, pleas'd th' Almighty's Orders to perform,
Rides in the Whirl-wind, and directs the Storm.
But see the haughty Houshold-Troops advance!
The Dread of Europe, and the Pride of France.
style: baroque martial ode, natural trumpets and full strings, commanding tenor, stately, grand, processional
why: Contains Addison's most quoted lines — the angel who 'Rides in the Whirl-wind, and directs the Storm'.

title: Poems
author: Joseph Addison
lyrics:
The dreadful Crack alarms the Skies:
Whose Arches rent, their Weight forego,
And plunge in opening Gulphs below.
Now rushing from their watry Bed,
The driving Waves disdain a shore;
And with resistless Force o'erspread
That Orb, which check'd their Rage before:
While scattered o'er the foamy Tide,
All Nature's floating Ruins ride.
New Heavens disclos'd, the Silver Train
The SUN beneath their Waves admire;
And gliding thro' th' enlight'ned Main,
Gaze at each STAR'S diminish'd Fire.
Well pleas'd, the MOON'S bright Orb survey,
Trembling along their Azure Way.
How strong each Line, each Thought how great
style: english baroque ode, harpsichord and viol consort, clear countertenor, surging, awestruck, quickening
why: A deluge in tetrameter quatrains — 'All Nature's floating Ruins ride' — already shaped like a hymn stanza.

title: Poems
author: Joseph Addison
lyrics:
With their big Cheeks the deaf'ning Clarions wind,
Whose dreadful Clangors startle all Mankind;
Ev'n the Dead hear; the Lab'ring Graves Conceive,
And the swoln Clod in Picture seems to heave:
Ten thousand Worlds revive to better Skies,
And from their Tombs the thronging Coarses rise.
So when fam'd Cadmus sow'd the fruitful Field,
With pregnant Throws the quicken'd Furrow swell'd;
From the warm Soil sprung up a warlike Train,
And Human harvests cover'd all the Plain.
And now from ev'ry Corner of the Earth
The scatter'd Dust is call'd to second Birth;
Whether in Mines it form'd the rip'ning Mass,
Or humbly mix'd, and flourish'd in the Grass:
The sever'd Body now unites again,
And kindred Atoms rally into Men;
style: sacred oratorio chorus, organ and trumpets, massed voices, majestic, thunderous, slow build
why: The last trump and the graves conceiving; 'kindred Atoms rally into Men' is a startling image for 1700.

title: Poems
author: Robert Lloyd
lyrics:
TO THE MOON.
BY MR. ROBERT LLOYD.
ALL hail! majestic Queen of Night,
Bright Cynthia! sweetest Nymph, whose presence brings
The pensive pleasures, calm delight,
While Contemplation smooths her ruffled wings,
Which Folly's vain tumultuous joys,
Or business, care, and buzz of lusty day
Have all too ruffled.  Hence away
Stale Jest, and flippant Mirth, and Strife-engendering Noise.
When Evening dons her mantle grey,
I'll wind my solitary way,
And hie me to some lonely grove
(The haunt of Fancy and of Love)
Whose social branches, far outspread,
Possess the mind with pleasing dread.
style: english pastoral art song, flute and harpsichord, clear soprano, nocturnal, unhurried, moonlit
why: A proper invocation — 'All hail! majestic Queen of Night' — opening a nocturne that stands alone.

title: Poems
author: Robert Lloyd
style: 18th century fairy dance-song, pizzicato strings and tambourine, light bright voices, quick, tripping, mischievous
why: Fairies 'beating the pansie-paven ground in frolic measures round and round' — the rhythm is already a dance.

title: Poems
author: Robert Lloyd
lyrics:
Of Phyllis was always my song,
For she was my pride and my care;
And the folks, as we wander'd along,
Would call us the conjugal pair.
They mark'd how I walk'd at her side,
How her hand to my bosom I prest,
Each tender endearment I try'd,
And I thought none was ever so blest.
But now the delusion is o'er,
These day-dreams of pleasure are fled,
Now Her Damon is pleasing no more,
And the hopes of her shepherd are dead.
May he that my fair shall obtain,
May He, as thy Damon, be true;
Or haply thou'lt think of that swain,
Who bids thee, dear maiden, adieu.
style: georgian pastoral ballad, acoustic guitar and fiddle, plain tenor, lilting triple time, wistful
why: Complete ballad stanzas ending on a clean farewell to the maiden — singable as written.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Seward
lyrics:
Take ev'ry knowledge in of ev'ry kind:
Still on perfection fix thy steady eye,
Be ever rising, rise thou ne'er so high.
But oh reflect, that in th' advent'rous flight,
Thou mount'st a glorious, but a dangerous height:
When ev'ry science ev'ry grace shall join,
When most thy wit, when most thy beauties shine,
When thickest crowds enamour'd press around,
When loudest ev'ry tongue thy praise shall sound,
When verse too offers incense to thy shrine,
And adoration breathes in ev'ry line,
Then let my friendly Muse express her care,
Then most will danger spread her viewless snare:
Then let this truth possess thy inmost soul,
"One drop of Vanity may spoil the whole."
Not self-secure on earth can Knowledge dwell,
style: georgian ode of encouragement, chamber strings and harpsichord, bright soprano, rising, stately, hopeful
why: 'Be ever rising, rise thou ne'er so high' — the argument for a woman's learning at its most direct and lifted.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Seward
lyrics:
Why, CLOE, there's a fond delight
Our former dangers to recite,
And let our neighbours know 'em.
After the thunder of the wars,
The veteran thus displays his scars,
And tells you of his pains;
The galley-slave, enslav'd no more,
Shews you the shackles which he wore,
And where their mark remains.
I talk, 'cause talking gives delight,
I please myself not CLOE by't,
Nor care if she believe;
And when myself she deigns to name,
Whether she praise my song or blame,
I neither joy nor grieve.
For me I quit a fickle fair,
style: italianate 18th century canzonetta, harpsichord and pizzicato strings, dry wry tenor, brisk, light-footed
why: The veteran showing his scars and the freed galley-slave showing his shackles — a witty song with a real sting.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Seward
lyrics:
I press'd to breathe my amorous pain,
Her lips spoke nought but cold despair,
Her eyes shot ice through ev'ry vein.
Thus in ITALIA'S lovely vales
The sun his genial vigour yields,
Reviving heat each sense regales,
And plenty crowns the smiling fields.
When nearer we approach this ray,
High on the Alps' stupendous brow,
Surpriz'd we see pale sun-beams play
On everlasting hills of snow.
CHISWICK.
By the Same.
THE potent Lord, that this bright villa plann'd,
Exhibits here a Paradise regain'd;
Whate'er of Verdure have Hills, Lawns, or Woods,
style: english baroque love song, lute and viola da gamba, plaintive countertenor, slow, cool, aching
why: Warm Italian valleys, then pale sunbeams on everlasting snow — one clean simile for a woman's coldness.

title: Poems
author: William Somervile
style: english pastoral art song, cello and guitar, warm baritone, unhurried, contemplative, evening
why: The pensioned sailor safe ashore, meditating on 'his great voyage, to the world unknown' — a quiet, complete ending.

title: Poems
author: William Somervile
lyrics:
By the late WILLIAM SOMERVILE, Esq;
KIND relief in all my pain,
Jolly Bacchus! hear my pray'r,
Vengeance on th' ingrateful fair!
In thy smiling cordial bowl,
Drown the sorrows of my soul,
All thy deity employ,
Gild each gloomy thought with joy,
Jolly Bacchus! save, oh save
From the deep devouring grave,
A poor, despairing, dying swain.
Haste away,
Haste away,
Lash thy tigers do not stay,
I'm undone if thou delay.
If I view those eyes once more,
style: 18th century drinking song, boisterous strings and hand drum, rowdy male voice with chorus, fast, swaggering, refrain-driven
why: 'Haste away, haste away, lash thy tigers do not stay' — a built-in refrain and a genuine bacchic pulse.

title: Poems
author: William Somervile
lyrics:
The blissful seat of peace and love,
Ten thousand beauties round me rise,
And mingle pleasure with surprize.
By nature blest in every part,
Adorn'd with every grace of art,
This paradise of blooming joys
Each raptur'd sense, at once, employs.
But when I view the radiant queen,
Who form'd this fair enchanting scene;
Pardon ye grots! ye crystal floods!
Ye breathing flow'rs! ye shady woods!
Your coolness now no more invites;
No more your murmuring stream delights;
Your sweets decay, your verdure's flown;
My soul's intent on her alone.
PARAPHRASE upon a FRENCH SONG.
style: georgian pastoral song, flute and harpsichord, sweet soprano, flowing, tender
why: A whole small song: the paradise catalogued, then dismissed the moment she appears.

title: Self-Help
author: Samuel Smiles
lyrics:
"If what shone afar so grand, Turn to nothing in thy hand, On again, the virtue lies In the struggle, not the prize."R. M. Milnes.
"Not for to hide it in a hedge, Nor for a train attendant, But for the glorious privilege Of being independent."Burns.
"Neither a borrower nor a lender be; For loan oft loses both itself and friend; And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry."Shakspeare.
"If every one would see To his own reformation, How very easily You might reform a nation."
"Real glory Springs from the silent conquest of ourselves, And without that the conqueror is nought But the first slave."
"His only labor is to kill the time, And labor dire it is, and weary woe."
"Knowledge dwells In heads replete with thoughts of other men; Wisdom in minds attentive to their own. Knowledge, a rude unprofitable mass, The mere materials with which wisdom builds, Till smoothed and squared, and fitted to its place, Does but encumber, whom it seems t' enrich."
style: victorian parlour hymn, upright piano and fiddle, plain earnest male voice, steady march, resolute
why: Only candidate available; 'the virtue lies in the struggle, not the prize' and Burns's 'glorious privilege of being independent' carry it.

title: Noctes Atticae
author: Gellius, Aulus
lyrics:
All evil thought and profane be still: far hence, far hence from our choirs depart, Who knows not well what the Mystics tell, or is not holy and pure of heart; Who ne'er has the noble revelry learned, or danced the dance of the Muses high; * * * * * I charge them once, I charge them twice, I charge them thrice, that they draw not nigh To the sacred dance of the Mystic choir. But YE, my comrades, awake the song, The night-long revels of joy and mirth which ever of right to our feast belong.
In silence came the Achaeans, breathing rage, Resolved in mind on one another's aid.
When from his breast his mighty voice went forth and:
NEARLY everyone reads these lines from the Georgics of Virgi in this way: At sapor indicium faciet manifestus et ora Tristia temptantum sensu torquebit amaro.
style: ancient mystery-cult processional, double aulos and frame drums, lead cantor answered by massed voices, incantatory, torchlit, building
why: 'I charge them once, I charge them twice, I charge them thrice' — a mystic chorus with the repetition already written into it.

title: Noctes Atticae
author: Gellius, Aulus
lyrics:
I care not if my cloak resplendent be, or spot.
What's wrong?This cloak doth wrinkle (rugat), I'm ill clad. Also Plautus uses pulveret, not of making dusty, but of being dusty:
Go, sprinkle, slave; I'd have this entrance neat. My Venus comes, don't let the place show dust (pulveret). In the Asinaria he uses contemples for contempleris:
O my delight, my darling (delicia). Furthermore Quintus Ennius, in that most famous book of his, said:
Shaping the silver, Hephaestus, Make me no panoply, pray; What do I care for war's combats? Make me a drinking cup rather, Deep as you ever can make it; Carve on it no stars and no wains; What care I, pray, for the Pleiads, What for the star of Bootes? Make vines, and clusters upon them, Treading them Love and Bathyllus, Made of pure gold, with Lyaeus.
style: anacreontic drinking song, lyre and light hand percussion, warm tenor, lilting, convivial, unhurried
why: Ennius's Anacreontic — no shield, no Pleiads, just a deep cup with vines carved on it. A complete little song.

title: Noctes Atticae
author: Gellius, Aulus
lyrics:
My soul has left me; it has fled, methinks, To Theotimus; he its refuge is. But what if I should beg that he refuse The truant to admit, but cast it out? I'll go to him; but what if I be caught? What shall I do? Queen Venus, lend me aid.
That man in truth who knows not leisure's use More trouble has than one by tasks pursued; For he who has a task must be performed, Devotes himself to that with heart and soul; The idle mind knows not what 'tis it wants. With us it is the same; for not at home Are we nor in the field; from place to place We haste; and once arrived, we would be gone. Aimless we drift, we live but more or less (praeterpropter).
When with my parted lips my love I kiss, And quaff the breath's sweet balm from open mouth, Smitten with love my soul mounts to my lips, And through my love's soft mouth its way would take, Passing the open gateway of the lips. But if our kiss, delayed, had been prolonged, By love's fire swayed my soul that way had ta'en, And left me. Faith, a wondrous thing it were, If I should die, but live within my love.
style: latin lyric miniature, solo cithara, intimate close-mic voice, hushed, rubato, suspended
why: The soul climbing to the lips during a kiss and nearly escaping — the most beautiful thing in the whole compilation.

title: Miles Gloriosus
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
(Enter PYRGOPOLINICES, ARTOTROGUS, and Soldiers.)
PYRGOPOLINICES:
Take ye care that the lustre of my shield is more bright than the rays of the sun are wont to be at the time when the sky is clear; that when occasion comes, the battle being joined,mid the fierce ranks right opposite it may dazzle the eyesight of the enemy.
But, I wish to console this sabre of mine, that it may not lament nor be downcast in spirits, because I have thus long been wearing it keeping holiday, which so longs right dreadfully to make havoc of the enemy. But where is Artotrogus?
ARTOTROGUS:
Here he is; he stands close by the hero, valiant and successful, and of princely form. Mars could not dare to style himself a warrior so great, nor compare his prowess with yours.
PYRGOPOLINICES:
Him you mean whom I spared on the Gorgonidonian plains, where Bumbomachides Clytomestoridysarchides, the grandson of Neptune, was the chief commander?
style: roman comic canticum, double tibia and hand drum, blustering baritone, strutting march tempo, mock-heroic
why: The braggart's opening boast about his dazzling shield and homesick sabre — the play's signature and instantly funny.

title: Miles Gloriosus
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
I could have married a dowered wife of the best family; but I dont choose to introduce an everlasting female barker at me into my house.
PLEUSICLES:
Why dont you choose? Fortis a delightful thing to be the father of children [ liberos].
PERIPLECOMENUS:
Troth,tis very much sweeter by far to be free [ liberum] yourself.
For a good wife, if it is possible for her to be married anywhere on earth, where can I find her? But am I to take one home who is never to say this to me, Buy me some wool, my dear, with which a soft and warm cloak may be made, and good winter under-clothes, that you maynt catch cold this winter-weather; such an expression as this you can never hear from a wife, but, before the cocks crow, she awakes me from my sleep, and says, Give me some money, my dear, with which to make my mother a present on the Calends, give me some money to make preserves; give me something to give on the Quinquatrus to the sorceress, to the woman who interprets the dreams, to the prophetess, and to the female diviner;
style: patter comic song, tibia and plucked strings, fast wry male voice, breathless, escalating, farcical
why: The wife waking him before cockcrow — 'give me some money, my dear' — a rant that builds like a chorus.

title: Miles Gloriosus
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
PALAESTRIO:
I faith, that really has been plain for some time now; as she was here in-doors all the while.
SCELEDRUS:
Not a word of certainty have I to utter; I did not see her, although I did see her.
PALAESTRIO:
By my troth, through this folly of yours you certainly have nearly ruined us; while you have wished to prove yourself faithful to your master, you have been almost undone.
But the door of our next neighbour makes a noise; Ill be silent.
(Enter PHILOCOMASIUM, dressed in another habit, from the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.)
PHILOCOMASIUM:
(to a servant SERVANT.)
Put fire on the altar, that in my joy I may return praises and thanks to Diana of Ephesus, and that I may send up for her a grateful smoke with odours of Arabia: she who has preserved me in the realms of Neptune and amid the boisterous temples, where with raging billows I have been so recently dismayed.
style: temple invocation, soft aulos and finger cymbals, clear female voice, slow, sweet, ceremonial
why: Fire on the altar and Arabian smoke for Diana of Ephesus — a genuine lyric moment inside the farce.

title: Poems
author: William Lisle Bowles
lyrics:
AT TYNEMOUTH PRIORY,
AFTER A TEMPESTUOUS VOYAGE.
As slow I climb the cliff's ascending side,
Much musing on the track of terror past,
When o'er the dark wave rode the howling blast,
Pleased I look back, and view the tranquil tide
That laves the pebbled shore: and now the beam
Of evening smiles on the gray battlement,
And yon forsaken tower that time has rent:
The lifted oar far off with transient gleam
Is touched, and hushed is all the billowy deep!
Soothed by the scene, thus on tired Nature's breast
A stillness slowly steals, and kindred rest;
While sea-sounds lull her, as she sinks to sleep,
Like melodies that mourn upon the lyre,
Waked by the breeze, and, as they mourn, expire!
style: english pastoral art song, piano and cello, gentle tenor, slow, tidal, elegiac
why: A whole sonnet, storm to stillness, ending on melodies that mourn upon the lyre and expire as they mourn.

title: Poems
author: William Lisle Bowles
lyrics:
Meantime the clouds, impressed with livelier beams,
Roll, in the lucid track of air,
Arrayed in coloured brede, with semblances more fair.
The airy troop, as on they sail,
Thus the pensive stranger hail:
In the pure and argent sky,
There our distant chambers lie;
The bed is strewed with blushing roses,
When Quietude at eve reposes,
Oft trembling lest her bowers should fade,
In the cold earth's humid shade.
Come, rest with us! evanishing, they cried
Come, rest with us! the lonely vale replied.
Then Fancy beckoned, and with smiling mien,
A radiant form arose, like the fair Queen
Of Beauty: from her eye divinely bright,
style: ethereal choral lullaby, harp and glassy layered voices, weightless, floating, refrain-driven
why: 'Come, rest with us! evanishing, they cried — Come, rest with us! the lonely vale replied' — the refrain is already there.

title: Poems
author: William Lisle Bowles
style: gothic ballad, low strings and harp, dramatic mezzo, hushed then opening out, slow release
why: Terror pointing forever at a stony coffin, then the prisoner released into the smell of spring — one clean turn.

title: Poems
author: Thomas D'Urfey
lyrics:
Fixing my Eyes upon your Face,
I slight the glittering Planets round.
And as to Shrines when Pilgrims go,
Such awful Reverence I feel,
That though I'm sure 'tis only show,
I scarcely can forbear to kneel.
To CLORIS: An ODE set to the New RIGGADON.
I Love thee well,
But not so well to wed thee,
Lest blood rebel,
And Appetite should cloy;
Whilst free and kind,
Each hour I long to bed thee:
But if consin'd,
Should scarce believ't a Joy.
Second Movement.
style: restoration theatre song, harpsichord and baroque violin, rakish tenor, dance lilt, teasing
why: 'I love thee well, but not so well to wed thee' — a real stage song with short lines built for a tune.

title: Poems
author: Thomas D'Urfey
lyrics:
Whatever dull Gown men or Sages may think,
There's no Man grows old till he ceases to drink;
Then Health to Sir Thomas, and that he may be,
As well as sixscore as at sixty and three.
The KING'S Health: A CATCH Sung in Parts.
NOW Second Hannibal is come,
O'er frozen Lakes and mounts of Snow,
To found our Faith on conquer'd Rome,
And give Proud France a fatal Blow.
Well may our Phaebus disappear,
And set his Glory in the Sea;
If Planets of a lower Sphere,
Can give us greater light than he.
Fryars and Monks, and all those bald-pate Fools,
With Wafers, Oyntments, Beads and Shams,
Pardons and Antichristian Bulls.
style: english catch in parts, tavern voices in rounds, fiddle and tabor, boisterous, quick, communal
why: A catch sung in parts, opening on 'there's no man grows old till he ceases to drink'.

title: Poems
author: Thomas D'Urfey
lyrics:
I calmly did her foible shew,
Where e'er he came, abus'd him:
I call'd him Fool, I prov'd him so,
Yet she the better us'd him.
I hate, she cry'd, your God of Wit,
Our Sex should all oppose him;
'Tis he that Charms my Appetite,
Shall sleep upon my Bosom:
This senseless stuff my love withdrew,
And cur'd my Melancholly;
I kick'd her brute, then bid adieu
To every Female folly.
A SONG set to a pleasant Scotch Tune.
A Lad o' th' Town thus made his moan
One Winter Morning early,
Alas, that I must lie alone,
style: scotch-air ballad, fiddle and small pipes, plain tenor, brisk, wry, cold-morning
why: Set to a Scotch tune by the author himself; the lad making his moan alone on a winter morning.

title: Poems
author: King of Prussia Frederick II
lyrics:
And time to me shall be no more;
No more the sun these eyes shall view,
Earth o'er these limbs her dust shall strew,
And life's fantastic dream be o'er.
Alas! I touch the dreadful brink,
From nature's verge impell'd I sink,
And endless darkness wraps me round!
Yes, Death is ever at my hand,
Fast by my bed he takes his stand,
And constant at my board is found.
Earth, air, and fire, and water, join
Against this fleeting life of mine,
And where for succour can I fly?
If art with flatt'ring wiles pretend
To shield me like a guardian friend,
By Art, ere Nature bids, I die.
style: solemn baroque death-ode, string orchestra and muted brass, grave baritone, slow, measured, funereal
why: 'Yes, Death is ever at my hand, fast by my bed he takes his stand, and constant at my board is found.'

title: Poems
author: King of Prussia Frederick II
lyrics:
That heard th' insatiate vow rebel,
Would e'er have thought them mortal born?
See the world's victor mount his car,
Blood marks his progress wide and far,
Sure he shall reign while ages fly;
No, vanish'd like a morning cloud,
The hero was but just allow'd
To fight, to conquer, and to die.
And is it true, I ask with dread,
That nations heap'd on nations bled
Beneath his chariot's fervid wheel,
With trophies to adorn the spot,
Where his pale corse was left to rot,
And doom'd the hungry reptile's meal?
Yes, Fortune weary'd with her play,
Her toy, this hero, casts away,
style: martial elegy, timpani and low strings, declamatory bass, processional, darkening, abrupt close
why: The world's victor vanishing like a morning cloud, 'allow'd to fight, to conquer, and to die' — written by a king.

title: Poems
author: King of Prussia Frederick II
lyrics:
By which is measur'd human worth.
Voltaire, within his private cell
In realms where ancient honesty
Is patrimonial property,
And sacred Freedom loves to dwell,
May give up all his peaceful mind,
Guided by Plato's deathless page,
In silent solitude resign'd
To the mild virtues of a Sage;
But I, 'gainst whom wild whirlwinds wage
Fierce war with wreck-denouncing wing,
Must be, to face the tempest's rage,
In thought, in life, in death a king.
style: prussian court ode, horns and harpsichord, resolute tenor, stately, defiant, storm-driven
why: Voltaire may retire to Plato; the writer must be 'in thought, in life, in death a king'. A perfect closing line.

title: Poems
author: Anthony Whistler
style: georgian parlour song, harpsichord and cello, light soprano, gentle triple time, tender
why: Four 'twas nots and then the turn — 'No — 'twas your generous nature' — anaphora made for singing.

title: Poems
author: Anthony Whistler
lyrics:
Yes, do be angry  'tis a Riddle.
SONG.
By the Same.
LET wisdom boast her mighty pow'r,
With passion still at strife,
Yet love is sure the sov'reign flow'r,
The sweet perfume of life.
The happy breeze that swells the sail,
When quite becalm'd we lie;
The drop, that will the heart regale,
And sparkle in thy eye.
The sun that wakes us to delight,
And drives the shades away;
The dream that chears our dreary night,
And makes a brighter day.
But if, alas! it wrongly seize,
style: english pastoral air, flute and guitar, warm mezzo, flowing, sunlit, hymn-like
why: Love as the breeze in a calm and the drop that sparkles in the eye — a short song of pure images.

title: Poems
author: Anthony Whistler
lyrics:
FLOWERS.
By ANTHONY WHISTLER, Esq;
LET sages, with superfluous pains,
The learned page devour;
While Florio better knowledge drains
From each instructive flow'r.
His fav'rite Rose his fear alarms,
All opening to the sun;
Like vain coquettes, who spread their charms,
And shine, to be undone.
The Tulip, gaudy in its dress,
And made for nought but show,
In every sense, may well express
The glittering, empty beau!
The Snow-drop first but peeps to light,
And fearful shews its head;
style: 18th century emblem song, viol and harpsichord, bright arch soprano, dainty, stepwise, witty
why: The rose like a coquette, the tulip like an empty beau — a flower-emblem catalogue that actually has jokes.

title: On Fate
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
lyrics:
35. Of this kind is that passage of Ennius: Would that in the grove of Pelion the fir-trees, hewn by the axe, had never fallen to the ground! He might have gone even higher: Would that no tree had ever grown on Pelion!and higher still: Would that no Mount Pelion existed at all!and so, fetching back the earlier antecedents in like manner, one may go back without end. Nor thence had the ship taken its first beginning. To what purpose are these past events? Because there follows that: For never would my erring mistress have set foot from her homeMedea, sick at heart, wounded by savage lovenot as though those things furnished the cause of her love.
fr3. Those verses of Homer also lend support to this opinion, which Cicero rendered into Latin: Such are the minds of men as is the light with which the Father himself, Jupiter, has flooded the fruitful lands. (Augustine, City of God 5.8)
style: latin tragic recitative, solo lyre over a low drone, grave male voice, slow, incantatory, receding
why: Only candidate; the regress of wishes — no felled firs, no tree, no Mount Pelion at all — reads as a built chain.

title: Travels in France during the Years 1787, 1788, 1789
author: Arthur Young
lyrics:
Deepens the murmurs of the falling floods, And breathes a browner horror o'er the woods.
The feast of reason and the flow of soul.
"Be sure yourself and your own reach to know".POPE.
"How to build ships and dreadful ordnance cast, Instruct the artist and reward their haste."
style: english pastoral ode, horn and harpsichord, measured baritone, stately, shadowed, unhurried
why: Only candidate; it opens on 'breathes a browner horror o'er the woods', which is worth the song by itself.

title: Parentalia
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: pr2. Likewise, a preface set down in verse. The names of my dear ones, now buried with due funeral, wept before with tears, I shall now commemorate in measures  bare, without ornament, and lacking the cultivation of fine speech: the funeral honour suffices for the dead. O dirge, dutiful enough with funereal complaints, do not pass over the yearly gifts with silence  those rites which Numa dedicates to kindred shades, as the degree of death or of birth demands. This is enough for the tombs, enough for those who lack earth: to summon the souls by voice has the worth of a funeral. The buried ashes rejoice to have their own names spoken; the monuments too command this with their inscribed fronts. He too, for whom the urn of a sad sepulchre was wanting, will be almost buried when his name is thrice spoken. But you, whoever you are, reader, who deign to commemorate the fates of my own in sad elegies, may you run through the unshaken times of your life, and weep no deaths beyond what is just.
style: late antique funeral rite, unaccompanied male voice over a low drone, slow, ceremonial, name-calling cadence
why: 'The buried ashes rejoice to have their own names spoken' — the whole argument for a book of the dead, in one breath.

title: Parentalia
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: 9. ATTUSIA LUCANA SABINA, MY WIFE. Thus far our dirge, performing its rites in pious measures, has sung of those dear, and likewise wept with due funeral. Now my grief and torments and the wound not to be touched  the death of my wife, snatched away, must be commemorated by me. Noble from your forefathers and of the bright origin of the senate, but more bright, Sabina, for your good character: you I, a young man, mourned, cheated in my first years, and for nine Olympiads, widowed, I weep you. Nor is it permitted to lull the grief, overlaid with age, to sleep; for it ever grows raw for me, almost fresh. Others admit the solaces of a grieving time: long days make these wounds heavier. I torment my grey hairs, cheated by a celibate life; and the more alone I am, the more sorrowful I pass my days. The wound is fed by the silent, mute house and the cold bed, because I share my ills with none, my goods with none. I grieve if another's wife is good; I grieve, on the other hand, if she is bad: as a pattern you are ever before me. From either side you come to me as a torment: whether she is bad, because you would have been unlike her; or good, because like. I do not lament empty wealth and idle joys, but that you, young, were snatched from me, your young husband. Glad, chaste, dignified, renowned in race and renowned in beauty, both the grief and the glory of Ausonius your husband: you, about now to complete four times seven Decembers, left behind two children, our pledges. They, by the favour of God, as your prayers were, flourish, heaped with the goods you desired; and I pray that they thrive, and that at last, both surviving, my embers may announce this to your ash.
style: latin lament, solo viol and low drone, aching baritone, very slow, bare, unresolved
why: Thirty-six years a widower: the silent house, the cold bed, and every other wife a torment whether good or bad.

title: Parentalia
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: 10. AUSONIUS, MY LITTLE SON. I will not defraud you, unwept, of a mindful complaint, you, my firstborn son, called a boy by my name: whom, while you were practising to loose your murmurs in your first words, of full promise, we mourned with funeral rites. You, set in your great-grandfather's bosom, a shared funeral, that you might not suffer the reproach of a tomb of your own.
style: pastoral dirge, single shepherd's pipe and low strings, quiet tenor, halting, tender, broken off
why: The grandson named Pastor, killed by a tile from a roof — 'that tile, hurled, sought my own head'.

title: Carmina
author: Sidonius Apollinaris
lyrics:
When Nature set the youthful Jove above the stars
and the new god took up the ancient realm,
the divine powers vied to honour their own divinity,
and in unequal measures sang an equal wisdom.
Mars, with blaring trumpet, proclaimed his father's praise
and lauded the thunderbolts with thunderous sound;
the Arcadian and the Bowman thrummed on resonant strings,
this one more skilled at the cithara's stroke, that at the lyre;
the chorus of the Castalides applauded in varied measure,
with songs, with reeds, with thumb, with voice, with foot.
Yet after the heaven-dwellers, even the demigods' middling
chants the god is said to have borne with patience.
Then the Dryads, fit for the Fauns, and the Maenads for the Satyrs,
a rustic throng, poured out a charming melody.
The pipe-blowing Pans left the high Maenala,
style: late roman hymnic processional, lyre and reed pipes with light percussion, layered voices, ceremonial, festive, building
why: The gods competing in song for the new Jove — 'with songs, with reeds, with thumb, with voice, with foot'.

title: Carmina
author: Sidonius Apollinaris
lyrics:
The Bassarids, the Satyrs, the Pans, and the Fauns Silenus
was teaching to sport, now full of his nursling's godhead,
yet adorned as to his head; for, his crown bare,
with garlands he strives to excuse his lost hair.
Then horned Ganges becomes the pomp of the new triumph;
head bowed, he stood, his unkempt face with dripping mouth,
and aided the dry waves with glassy tears;
his hands, cast into bonds, the vine bound behind his back;
here, little by little, the captive moisture flowing again,
of its own accord the shoot puts forth leaves along his dewy arms.
Likewise there the bound wife of the snatched husband
goes, her saffron cheeks lowered, and, the lamp forbidden
to be hidden, Aurora blushed with the rays of the Sun.
Here too was present, after his lost cinnamon, the Phoenix,
style: bacchic triumphal procession, frame drums, cymbals and double pipes, ecstatic massed voices, driving, intoxicated
why: Horned Ganges led in chains while the vine that binds him sprouts leaves along his wet arms.

title: Carmina
author: Sidonius Apollinaris
lyrics:
thick onyx crusts the threshold, and near it the blue
of jacinth casts a concordant colour into the pools.
The outer rock is unadorned, but the pumice, rough
from the unceasing lash of the waters, juts up high.
In the inner place Mulciber feigned in gold
the rocks standing forth widely, and by his mistress-art
he deceived the uncultivated nature with vast culture,
intent on this work, which she did not yet know
who afterward condemned the stolen love with Lemnian chains.
Hither the scaly Triton, where the borders of his twofold back
meet above the windings of his coiled belly,
bore Dione through the waters with warm heart.
But Galatea presses, with the added weight of a shining
shell, the side of the half-beast, which, her thumb fixed,
she plucks, and by a secret touch promises marriage;
style: late antique sea idyll, harp and soft flutes, shimmering female voice, languid, glittering, slow swell
why: Triton carrying Venus through the water while Galatea plucks his side and promises a marriage in secret.

title: Poems
author: John Dennis
lyrics:
THE EMPIRE Sav'd, AND EUROPE Deliver'd.
UP, Rouze your selves, ye Nations, praise the Lord,
Sing, ye deliver'd Nations, to your God,
A lofty Song of Thankfulness and Praise;
For his Almighty Arm o'erthrew the Proud,
His be the Triumph, as the Conquest his.
And thou, O God, rais'd High above all Gods,
Thou God of great Revenge, true God of War,
Who when the injur'd World to thee appeal'd,
Descending bow'd the very Heav'n of Heav'ns,
And with Ten Thousand Terrors arm'd cam'st down
On Bleinheim's dreadful Day, t'avenge the wrong'd,
Upon their mighty and their proud Oppressor:
Thou gav'st the Victory, do thou inspire the Praise,
If thou in Sacred Harmony delight'st;
Or if thou lov'st to pass eternal Day
style: baroque victory anthem, massed choir with organ and trumpets, majestic, thunderous, processional
why: 'Up, rouze your selves, ye Nations' — the poem opens by demanding to be sung, which settles it.

title: Poems
author: John Dennis
lyrics:
Not Michael Angelo's stupendous Work;
Where the last dreadful Doom sends guilty Souls
Down to eternal Punishments in Hell;
Hell seizes them, Hell meets them on the Way,
For in their Air and in their Looks is Hell,
And endless Torments in their Baleful Eyes.
Thus fell the French before the Victor's Wrath,
They who had stood so many Storms of War,
Yet still unshaken kept their Ground in all.
Thus of tall Oaks I've known a goodly Row,
That grac'd the winding Margin of the Floud,
Defy the Rage of many a wintry Blast,
The Tempest saw their Strength, and sigh'd, and past them by.
But when a Hurrican by Wrath divine
Came lately bellowing o'er the Western Main,
That with immortal Fury on them fell,
style: english blank-verse elegy, low strings and solo horn, sombre baritone, slow, wind-swept
why: 'The Tempest saw their Strength, and sigh'd, and past them by' — the one line here worth a whole song.

title: Poems
author: John Dennis
lyrics:
But yet, we fought, ye Stygian Gods, we fought
With Spirit equal to the vast Design.
Fate gave our Enemy the Field, but Ours,
Ours was the Triumph, and the Glory Ours
Of great, aspiring, unexampled Minds
Who dar'd against the Omnipotent to War.
Can ye remember this? Can ye reflect
That ye for Angels were an equal Match,
And yield at last to Man, to Woman yield?
For 'tis a Woman, O ye Pow'rs, destroys
This mighty Champion of our Cause and Us;
For she directs, she animates, she fires
Those who o're Earth the Rule of Heav'n extend.
'Tis she who out of pure Despight to me,
Contemns a boundless Arbitrary Reign,
And thinks it lovelier Empire, fairer Fame,
style: infernal recitative, dark brass and timpani, growling bass, brooding, defiant, ominous
why: Satan in council: 'we fought, ye Stygian Gods, we fought' — Miltonic and genuinely stormy.

title: Poems
author: Isabella Kelly
lyrics:
Shield thee from the least alarms.
Lov'd already, little blessing,
Kindly cherish'd, tho' unknown,
Fancy forms thee sweet and lovely,
Emblem of the rose unblown:
Though thy father is imprison'd,
Wrong'd, forgotten, robb'd of right,
I'll repress the rising anguish,
Till thine eyes behold the light.
Start not, babe! the hour approaches
That presents the gift of life;
Soon, too soon thoul't taste of sorrow
In these realms of care and strife:
Share not thou a mother's feelings,
Hope vouchsafes a pitying ray;
Tho' a gloom obscures the morning,
style: georgian cradle song, harp and soft strings, tender soprano, gentle rocking, hopeful beneath grief
why: A song to an unborn child while its father sits in prison — 'emblem of the rose unblown'. Trochaic and singable.

title: Poems
author: Isabella Kelly
style: english ballad lament, fiddle and guitar, plain female voice, anapaestic sway, resigned, wounded
why: 'Though I die, may thy pleasure increase! Thy Mary will never repine' — a wronged wife's farewell in clean ballad stanzas.

title: Poems
author: Isabella Kelly
lyrics:
Ah! sad remembrance, why exert thy power,
Why, why recal the past endearing hour,
When thy sweet frame upon my breast repos'd,
And opening beauty every look disclos'd?
Each happier mother, vain of her delight,
Still, still obtrudes her darling on my sight;
Then in the harmless smile, the feeble cry,
I hear the voice, I see thy languid eye:
Oh! still my child, if in thy perfect state,
Thou hast a knowledge of my suffering fate,
In gentle dreams thy beauteous form display,
And bring me tidings from the realms of day;
Tell thy sad mother when the hour draws near,
That we shall meet, nor other parting fear;
And Heaven, still gracious to the mourning kind,
Oh! deign to send me peace, a will resign'd;
style: mourning parlour song, piano and cello, low female voice, slow, intimate, breaking
why: The mother asking her dead child to visit her in dreams and bring word of when they will meet.

title: Frogs
author: Aristophanes
lyrics:
FROGS
Brekekekex koax koax,
brekekekex koax koax!
Children of the marsh and springs,
let us raise the tuneful cry of our hymns,
my sweet-voiced song,
koax koax,
which around the Nysaean
Dionysus, son of Zeus,
in the Marshes we shrieked,
when the hung-over revel-crowd
of the people streams
through my sacred precinct on the holy Feast of Pots.
Brekekekex koax koax!
FROGS
Brekekekex koax koax!
style: comic ritual chant, croaking layered male voices over frame drum and reed pipe, insistent, looping refrain, marshy
why: Brekekekex koax koax — the most famous refrain in Greek comedy, already built as a song.

title: Frogs
author: Aristophanes
lyrics:
the fruit-laden, blossoming
wreath of myrtle, and with bold
foot beating out
the unbridled, frolic-loving rite,
that holds the greatest share of grace, the pure and sacred
dance for the holy initiates.
CHORUS
Wake the blazing torches, for in your hands he comes brandishing,
Iacchus, O Iacchus,
the light-bringing star of the nocturnal rite.
The meadow shines with flame;
the old men's knees leap up;
they shake off their griefs
and the long years of ancient time,
beneath the sacred worship.
And you, blazing with your torch,
style: torchlight processional hymn, double aulos, cymbals and massed voices, ecstatic, quickening, radiant
why: 'The meadow shines with flame; the old men's knees leap up; they shake off their griefs' — a real initiation hymn.

title: Frogs
author: Aristophanes
lyrics:
Iacchus, lover of the dance, escort me.
CHORUS
For just now I caught sight, with a sidelong glance,
of the lovely-faced face of a young girl,
a playmate of mine,
with her little tunic torn,
and a little breast peeping out.
Iacchus, lover of the dance, escort me.
CHORUS
Go now
round the sacred circle of the goddess, through the flowery grove,
sporting, you who share in the god-loved feast;
and I'll go with the girls and women,
to where they keep the all-night vigil for the goddess, to bear the holy light.
CHORUS
Let us go to the rosy
style: greek festival dance-song, lyre and hand drums, mixed voices with call-and-response refrain, lilting, mischievous, warm
why: 'Iacchus, lover of the dance, escort me' three times over, with the glimpsed girl and the all-night vigil.

title: The Religion of the Samurai: A Study of Zen Philosophy
author: Kaiten Nukariya
lyrics:
"O brother man, fold to thy heart thy brother; Where pity dwells, the peace of God is there; To worship rightly is to love each other, Each smile a hymn, each kindly word a prayer." --Whittier.
"Virtue may be assailed, but never hurt; Surprised by unjust force, but not enthralled. But evil on itself shall back recoil, And mix no more with goodness. If this fail, The pillared firmament is rottenness, And earth's base built on stubble."
"I can but trust that good shall fall At last-far off-at last, to all."
"I do not see my cow, But trees and grass, And hear the empty cries Of cicadas."
"The grove is deep, and so Is my desire. How glad I am, O lo! I see her tracks."
"Her loud and wild mooing Has led me here; I see her form afar, Like a dark shadow."
"Alas! it's hard to keep The cow I caught. She tries to run and leap And snap the cord."
style: zen chant-song, shakuhachi and koto, spare male voice, slow, wandering, unadorned
why: The ox-herding stanzas — the empty cries of cicadas, the deep grove, the tracks, the cord about to snap.

title: The Religion of the Samurai: A Study of Zen Philosophy
author: Kaiten Nukariya
lyrics:
"I'm glad the cow so wild Is tamed and mild. She follows me, as if She were my shadow."
"Slowly the clouds return To their own hill, Floating along the skies So calm and still.
"The cow goes out by day And comes by night. I care for her in no way, But all is right."
"There's no cowherd nor cow Within the pen; No moon of truth nor clouds Of doubt in men."
"There is no dyer of hills, Yet they are green; So flowers smile, and titter rills At their own wills."
"The cares for body make That body pine; Let go of cares and thoughts, O child of mine!"
style: zen folk verse, solo shakuhachi and light hand drum, warm quiet voice, gentle, settled, resolved
why: The other half of the sequence and a complete quatrain on its own: the wild cow tamed, following like a shadow.

title: De Virtute Morali
author: Plutarch
style: greek symposium song, lyre over a low drone, wry male voice, measured, ironic, brooding
why: Only candidate; 'we know those virtues, which we ne'er pursue' and the anchor dragging on loose ground both land.

title: Epigrammaton Liber
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: Whose work art thou? Pheidias's: his who made Pallas' statue, who made Jove's: his third masterpiece am I. I am a goddess seldom found and known to few, Opportunity my name. Why stand'st thou on a wheel? I cannot stand still. Why wearest thou winged sandals? I am ever flying. The gifts which Mercury scatters at random I bestow when I will. Thou coverest thy face with thy hair. I would not be recognised. Butwhat!art thou bald at the back of thy head? That none may catch me as 1 flee. Who is she who bears thee company? Let her tell thee. Tell me, I beg, who thou art. I am a goddess to whom not even Cicero himself gave a name. I am a goddess who exacts penalties for what is done and what undone, to cause repentance. So I am called Metanoea.1" " Do thou 2 now tell me what does she along with thee? When I have flown away she remains: she is retained by those I have passed by. Thou also whilst thou keepest asking, whilst thou tarriest with questioning wilt say that I have slipped away out of thy hands.
style: late antique riddle-dialogue, plucked lyre and light frame drum, two alternating voices, quick, restless, quicksilver
why: Opportunity on her wheel, winged, bald behind — and gone from your hands while you stand there asking questions.

title: Epigrammaton Liber
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics:
Meroe.; but because thou never slakest wine with water, being used to drink draughts unallayed of wine, pure wine.1
AS a stone the Persians once brought me here to be a trophy of war; now am I Nemesis. And even as I stand here a trophy of Greek victory., so as Nemesis I requite the idly-boasting Persians.3
FELL FIGHTING MOST BRAVELY 4 THAT thou receivest seven gashes all in front, that thou art borne, Thrasybulus, upon thy shield, this grieves not thy sire, but adds greater glory to Pitana.5 Rare is the opportunity of so fair a death. After thy comrades laid thee upon the mournful bier, these words did thy stout-hearted sire pronounce: Weep ye for others: a son needs not any tears, being mine, so glorious, and a Spartan.
A Spartan mother slinging her son's shield, Return with this, said she, or upon it.
style: doric war epitaph, low male voices in unison, bone flute and slow drum, austere, stony, unhurried
why: 'Return with this, or upon it' — and the father who tells the mourners to weep for other men's sons.

title: Epigrammaton Liber
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics:
I USED to say to thee: Galla, we grow old, Time Hies away, enjoy thy life: a chaste girl is an old woman. Thou didst scorn my warning. Age has crept upon thee unperceived, nor canst thou call back the days that are gone. Now thou art sorry and dost lament, either because then thou wert disinclined, or because now thou hast not that former beauty. Yet give me thine embrace and share forgotten joys with me. Give: I will take, albeit not what I would, yet what I once would.
ONCE on the strand of Sicily a sea-dog snapped up a hare speeding before the hounds. Then said the hare: Against me both sea and land direct their ravages, perchance heaven also; since there is a Dog among the stars.
AS lazy a scribe as a sluggish runner, thou, Pergamus, didst run away and wert caught at the first lap. Therefore thou hast felt letters 1 branded, Pergamus, upon thy face, and those which thy right hand neglected thy brow endures.
style: late roman love elegy, soft cithara and low strings, ageing wistful voice, slow, rueful, intimate
why: 'Galla, we grow old' — and the terrible closing bargain: I will take, not what I would, but what I once would.

title: Ajax
author: Sophocles
lyrics:
And may they seize those wicked men with most wicked destruction, just as they see me. Come, you swift and punishing Erinyes, devour all the assembled army and spare nothing!
And you, Helios, whose chariot-wheels climb the steep sky, when you see the land of my fathers, draw in your rein spread with gold and tell my disasters and my fate to my aged father and to the unhappy woman who nursed me.
Poor mother! Indeed, I think, when she hears this news, she will sing a song of loud wailing throughout the entire city. But it is not for me to weep in vain like this. No, the deed must quickly have its beginning. O Death, Death, come now and lay your eyes on me!
And yet I will meet you also in that other world and there address you. But you, beam of the present bright day, I salute you and the Sun in his chariot for the last time and never again. O light! O sacred soil
style: greek tragic monody, solo male voice with aulos and low drum, slow, resolute, sun-struck, final
why: The last speech: the Erinyes summoned, Helios asked to carry the news home, then 'O light! O sacred soil'.

title: Ajax
author: Sophocles
lyrics:
from Hector, my greatest enemy, I have gotten no good from the Greeks. Yes,
mens proverb is true:
the gifts of enemies are no gifts and bring no good.
And so hereafter I shall, first, know how to yield to the gods, and, second, learn to revere the Atreidae. They are rulers, so we must submit. How could it be otherwise? Things of awe and might
submit to authority. So it is that winter with its snow-covered paths gives place to
fruitful summer; nights dark orbit makes room for day with her white horses
to kindle her radiance; the blast of dreadful winds
allows the groaning sea to rest; and among them all, almighty Sleep releases the fettered sleeper, and does not hold him in a perpetual grasp.
And we menmust we not learn self-restraint? I, at least, will learn it, since I am newly aware that an enemy is to be hated only as far as
style: greek choral meditation, lyre and soft aulos, calm baritone, cyclical, seasonal, deceptively serene
why: Winter yielding to summer, night to day, the winds letting the sea rest — the great deception speech.

title: Ajax
author: Sophocles
lyrics:
Exit Teucer.
Chorus:
Which will be the last year? When will the sum of the years of our many wanderings stop bringing upon me the unending doom of toilful spear-battles
throughout broad Troy, the cause of sorrow and of shame for Greece?
Chorus:
If only that man had first passed into the depths of the sky or into Hades, the common home of all,
before he taught the Greeks the shared plague of Ares detested arms! Ah, those toils of
his invention, which produced so many more toils! Look how that man has
ravaged humanity!
Chorus:
No delight in garlands
or deep wine-cups did that man provide me, no sweet din of flutes, that miserable man, or pleasing rest in the night.
And from lovegod!from love he has totally barred me. Here I lie uncared for, while heavy dews constantly wet my hair,
style: soldiers' lament chorus, frame drum and reed pipe, weary massed male voices, slow, damp, homesick
why: No garlands, no wine-cups, no flutes, no love — only heavy dew wetting their hair year after year at Troy.

title: Poems
author: Soame Jenyns
lyrics:
Spend an inglorious country life;
These are the joys I still pursue,
When absent from the town and you:
Thus pass long summer suns away,
Busily idle, calmly gay;
Nor great, nor mean, nor rich, nor poor,
Not having much, or wishing more;
Except that you, when weary grown
Of all the follies of the town,
And seeing, in all publick places,
The same vain fops and painted faces,
Wou'd sometimes kindly condescend
To visit a dull country friend:
Here you'll be ever sure to meet
A hearty welcome, tho' no treat,
One who has nothing else to do,
style: english pastoral song, guitar and recorder, easy tenor, lilting, contented, unhurried
why: 'Busily idle, calmly gay; nor great, nor mean, nor rich, nor poor' — a whole philosophy in four tetrameters.

title: Poems
author: Soame Jenyns
lyrics:
And then the great celestial dance is done.
Where can the mor'list find a juster plan
Of the vain labours, and the life of man?
Awhile thro' justling crowds we toil, and sweat,
And eagerly pursue we know not what,
Then when our trifling short-liv'd race is run,
Quite tir'd sit down, just where we first begun.
Tho' to your arms kind fate's indulgent care
Has giv'n a partner exquisitely fair,
Let not her charms so much engage your heart,
That you neglect the skilful dancer's part;
Be not, when you the tuneful notes should hear,
Still whisp'ring idle prattle in her ear;
When you should be employ'd, be not at play,
Nor for your joys all others steps delay:
But when the finish'd dance you once have done,
style: minuet turned reflective, harpsichord and strings, wry baritone, dance tempo, circling, resigned
why: The dance as an image of a life: 'quite tir'd sit down, just where we first begun'.

title: Poems
author: Soame Jenyns
lyrics:
The hall-door's lock'd, the key is lost:
These difficulties all o'ercome,
We reach at length the drawing-room,
Then there's such trampling over-head,
Madam you'd swear was brought to bed;
Miss in a hurry bursts the lock,
To get clean sleeves to hide her smock;
The servants run, the pewter clatters,
My lady dresses, calls, and chatters;
The cook-maid raves for want of butter,
Pigs squeak, fowls scream, and green geese flutter.
Now after three hours tedious waiting,
On all our neighbours faults debating,
And having nine times view'd the garden,
In which there's nothing worth a farthing,
In comes my lady, and the pudden:
style: hudibrastic patter song, harpsichord and fiddle, fast comic voice, headlong, clattering, farcical
why: 'Pigs squeak, fowls scream, and green geese flutter' — a country visit as pure comic momentum.

title: Poems
author: Mary Chandler
lyrics:
And such your lov'd Employ;
Who would indulge your noblest Pow'rs,
But know no guilty Joy.
And thus as swift-wing'd Time brings on
Death, nearer to our View;
Tun'd to sweet Harmony our Souls,
We take a short Adieu.
Till the last Trump's delightful Sound
Shall wake our sleeping Clay;
Then swift, to find our Fellow-souls,
As Light, we haste away.
On my Recovery.
God of my Life and lengthen'd Days!
To Thee my Breath I owe.
Teach me my grateful Voice to raise,
In Sounds that sweetly flow.
style: english hymn in common metre, chapel organ and small choir, clear female voice, steady, luminous, ascending
why: 'Then swift, to find our Fellow-souls, as Light, we haste away' — already in hymn metre and already a hymn.

title: Poems
author: Mary Chandler
style: georgian retirement song, guitar and flute, warm alto, gentle amble, homely, contented
why: The whole wish for a life: a hill, a brook, good neighbours, a useful book, and time to mend one's ways.

title: Poems
author: Mary Chandler
lyrics:
Fountain of Light, and God of Love;
Do thou my Breast inspire!
'Tis not the Politician's Art,
Who makes his injur'd Country smart,
To fill his Chests with Gold;
Nor all his cunning Craft, to gain
Pleasures and Honours false and vain,
For which his Peace is sold.
No, I would sing a nobler Theme:
His Wisdom is an idle Dream,
That flies him when awake.
The guilty Soul with keen Remorse
Finds all his Gains repaid with Loss,
And curses his Mistake.
WISDOM is Truth without Disguise:
Clear as the Sun in cloudless Skies,
style: devotional ode, harpsichord and viol, bright soprano, measured, plain, radiant
why: 'Wisdom is Truth without Disguise: clear as the Sun in cloudless Skies' — plain and hard to improve on.

title: Catalepton
author: Appendix Vergiliana
lyrics:
O who on earth speaks more pleasantly than you alone?
For surely bright Clio herself does not so speak.
Wherefore it is enough, if you permit yourself to be loved;
for that the love be mutual in returnwhence is that to come to me?
Away from here, you empty bombasts of the rhetoricians, away,
words puffed up with no Achaean dew,
and you, Selius and Tarquitius and Varro,
the race of schoolmen, dripping with grease,
away from here, you cymbal of empty youth.
And you, O Sextus, the care of my cares,
farewell, Sabinus; now farewell, fair ones.
We are setting our sails for the blessed harbours,
seeking the learned sayings of great Siro,
and we will free our life from all care.
Away from here, Camenae; you too, awayand yet farewell,
sweet Camenae, for we will confess the truth,
style: latin farewell song, solo cithara over a low drone, young resolved male voice, steady, valedictory, brightening
why: Away with the rhetoricians — sails set for the blessed harbours, and the reluctant goodbye to the sweet Camenae.

title: Catalepton
author: Appendix Vergiliana
lyrics:
sweet you were, and yet revisit my pages,
but modestly and seldom.
Father-in-law, blessed neither to yourself nor to another,
and son-in-law Noctuinus, you rotten head,
has such a girl, then, by your stupor and by yours,
been crushed and gone off to the country? Ah me,
how that verse fits, on every side:
"Father-in-law and son-in-law, you have ruined everything."
This indeed without offence, sweetest Varius, I will say:
may I perish, if that pretty boy has not undone me.
But if the precepts forbid me to say it, then truly
I will not say it, but that boy has undone me.
Little farm, that were Siro's, and you, poor little field,
yet to that master you too were riches,
I commend to you myself and these, along with me, whom I have ever loved,
if I shall hear anything sadder of my fatherland,
style: roman pastoral miniature, single reed pipe and soft strings, quiet tenor, tender, small-scale, homely
why: 'Little farm, that were Siro's, and you, poor little field' — a poet commending his father to a scrap of land.

title: Catalepton
author: Appendix Vergiliana
lyrics:
this man was bringing grievous slavery to you, now to you, Rome,
(for the rest had fallen by the hero's spear-point):
when suddenly, in the midst of the contest of affairs, headlong
he collapsed, driven from his fatherland into exile.
Such is the power of the goddess; by such a nod the deceitful
hour, in a moment of time, wears away mortal things.
Wherever the seasons of our varied life bid us go,
whatever lands to touch, whatever men to see,
may I perish, if any other shall be dearer to me than you.
For what other can be sweeter than you,
to whom, a youth before others, the gods and the gods' sisters,
the Muse too, gave all good things, and not undeservedly,
all things in which the chorus of Phoebus and Phoebus himself rejoice?
O who could have been more learned than you, Muse?
style: roman moral elegy, low strings and slow drum, grave baritone, stately then abrupt, stark
why: The man who had shaken the globe collapsing headlong: 'the deceitful hour, in a moment of time, wears away mortal things'.

title: Constitution of the Athenians
author: Aristotle
lyrics:
To this, in the court of Time, might bear me witness
the greatest mother of the Olympian gods,
the best, the black Earth, from whom I once
tore up the boundary-stones fixed in many places;
before enslaved, she is now free.
And to Athens, their god-built fatherland, I brought back
many who had been sold, one unjustly,
another justly, and those who through forced necessity
had fled, no longer speaking the Attic tongue,
as men who had wandered far and wide;
and those who here at home endured a shameful slavery,
trembling at their masters' moods,
I set free. These things by the power of law,
fitting together force and justice,
I wrought, and carried through as I had promised.
Ordinances alike for the base and the noble,
style: archaic greek elegy, lyre over a low drone, grave male voice, measured, declamatory, earth-rooted
why: Solon calling black Earth as witness that he tore up her boundary-stones and brought the sold-away home.

title: Constitution of the Athenians
author: Aristotle
lyrics:
I mark, and grief lies deep within my heart,
as I behold the eldest land of Ionia
sinking down;
But you, who have driven on to a surfeit of many good things,
calm the strong heart within your breasts,
and set your proud minds upon moderate things. For neither shall we
submit, nor will these things be fitting for you.
Anthemion son of Diphilus dedicated this to the gods,
having exchanged the labourer's class for the knight's.
To the people I gave such privilege as is sufficient,
neither taking from their honour nor reaching out for more;
and as for those who had power and were admired for their wealth,
for these too I took thought that they should suffer nothing unseemly.
I stood casting my strong shield about both,
and allowed neither to win an unjust victory.
The people would best follow its leaders thus,
style: archaic greek elegy, aulos and lyre, sorrowing male voice, slow, admonitory, unresolved
why: 'I stood casting my strong shield about both, and allowed neither to win an unjust victory.'

title: Constitution of the Athenians
author: Aristotle
lyrics:
until he had stirred up the milk and taken out the cream.
But I stood, as it were in the no-man's-land between them,
a boundary-stone.
Alas, Leipsydrion, betrayer of comrades,
what manner of men you destroyed, good fighters
and of noble birth,
who then showed of what fathers they were sprung.
Pour for Cedon too, servant, and do not forget,
if one must pour wine for good men.
style: athenian drinking skolion, lyre passed hand to hand, lead voice with answering chorus, short, convivial, defiant
why: Two real drinking songs — the lament for Leipsydrion and 'pour for Cedon too, servant, and do not forget'.

title: Titus Flamininus
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
Of these the one most in vogue was the following epigram in elegiac verses: Unwept and without graves are we, O traveller, who on this ridge of Thessaly lie dead, in number thirty thousand, subdued by the sword of the Aetolians, and of the Latins whom Titus led from spacious Italy, Emathias great bane. And the bold spirit that Philip had displayed was gone; it showed itself more agile than swift deer.
Moreover, even down to our own day a priest of Titus is duly elected and appointed, and after sacrifice and libations in his honour, a set hymn of praise to him is sung: it is too long to be quoted entire, and so I will give only the closing words of the song: And the Roman faith we revere, which we have solemnly vowed to cherish; sing, then, ye maidens, to great Zeus, to Rome, to Titus, and to the Roman faith: hail, Paean Apollo! hail, Titus our saviour!
style: greek cult hymn, girls' chorus with lyre and aulos, bright unison voices, processional, joyous, refrain-driven
why: Only candidate, but it ends on a real cult refrain: 'hail, Paean Apollo! hail, Titus our saviour!'

title: Epinicians
author: Bacchylides
lyrics:
Fortunate in your fate, commander of the Syracusans, riders of whirling horses: you, if any man on earth today, will rightly understand this honor, sweet gift of the violet-garlanded Muses. Now, calm your righteous mind; rest it from cares, and consider: a hymn, woven with the help of the deep-waisted Graces, is sent from the holy island to your glorious city by your guest-friend, the brilliant servant of Ourania with her golden headband. He wants to pour forth his voice from his heart to praise Hieron. High above, slicing the deep air with his swift golden wings, the eagle, messenger of loud-thundering, wide-ruling
Zeus, trusts boldly in his powerful strength, and thin-voiced birds crouch in fear. The peaks of the great earth do not restrain him, nor the rough, choppy waves of the untiring sea. In the everlasting void he shifts his delicate wings, riding the gusts of the west wind, a conspicuous sight for men.
style: greek choral ode, kithara and aulos, layered voices, soaring, expansive, wind-borne
why: The eagle slicing the deep air on golden wings while thin-voiced birds crouch — the cleanest, grandest passage here.

title: Epinicians
author: Bacchylides
style: greek choral narrative ode, lyre and low drum, solo voice with choral answers, tense then transfigured, slow release
why: Croesus on the pyre, Zeus quenching the golden flame with a rain-cloud, Apollo carrying the old man to the Hyperboreans.

title: Epinicians
author: Bacchylides
lyrics:
My mother, the hostile daughter of Thestius, did not take this into account; she brought about my evil fate, the fearless woman, and planned my destruction.
She took the log of my swift doom out of the ornate chest, and burned it. Fate had marked off that this should be the boundary of my life. I happened to be slaying
Clymenus, Daipylus' valiant son, whose body was flawless; I had overtaken him in front of the towers. The others were fleeing to the well-built ancient city of Pleuron. And my sweet soul diminished; I knew that my strength was gone, aiai! I breathed my last breath in tears, as I left behind splendid youth.
They say that was the only time that the son of Amphitryon, fearless in battle, ever wetted his eyes with tears, pitying the fate of the man who endured grief. And he answered him in this way:
style: underworld lament, single aulos over a deep drone, hollow male voice, slow, ghostly, tear-struck
why: Meleager's shade telling how his mother burned the log — and the only time Heracles ever wept.

title: Helen
author: Euripides
lyrics:
Menelaos:
O Zeus, called father and god of wisdom, look on us and alter our woes! As we drag our fortunes to the rocky hill, make haste to join with us; if you touch us with your finger-tip only, we shall reach our longed-for goal. There has been enough distress in what we have suffered before. I have invoked you, gods, with many names, good and painful; I am not bound to be unfortunate forever, but to advance in a straight course. If you grant me one favor, you will make me fortunate hereafter. Exeunt Menelaos and Helen.
Chorus:
O swift Phoenician ship of Sidon, dear to the surging waves, mother of the oar, leader of the lovely dancing of dolphins, when the sea is clear of breezes and Oceans gray-green daughter, spirit of calm, says these words: Spread your sails to the sea-breezes, as you go on your way, grasp your oars of pine, oh! sailors, sailors, speeding Helen on her way to the shore with good harbor, where once Perseus lived..
style: greek sea-chorus, lyre and light frame drum, layered female voices, rowing pulse, bright, hopeful
why: 'O swift Phoenician ship of Sidon... mother of the oar, leader of the lovely dancing of dolphins' — a sailing song outright.

title: Helen
author: Euripides
lyrics:
If you were only moderate, in other ways you are by nature the sweetest of gods for men; I dont deny it. Exeunt Helen and Menelaos.
Chorus:
Let me call on you, beneath leafy haunts, sitting in your place of song, you, the most sweetly singing bird, tearful nightingale, oh, come, trilling through your tawny throat, to aid me in my lament, as I sing the piteous woes of Helen and the tearful fate of Trojan women under the Achaeans spears; when he sped over the surging plains with foreign oar, when he came, came bringing to Priams race from Lacedaemon you, Helen, his unhappy bride Paris, fatally wedded, under the guidance of Aphrodite.
Chorus:
style: greek choral threnody, solo aulos and soft kithara, mournful female voices, slow, trilling, keening
why: The nightingale summoned from her leafy haunts to help carry the lament — one of Euripides' loveliest openings.

title: Helen
author: Euripides
lyrics:
and Castor and his brother, twin glory of their native land, have vanished, vanished, leaving the plains that shook to their galloping horses, and the schools of reed-fringed Eurotas, scene of youthful labors.
Chorus:
Alas, alas! for your mournful fate and destiny, lady! You were fated, fated to have a life full of pain, when Zeus begot you on your mother, shining through the air on the wings of a snow-white swan. What evil is not yours? What life have you not endured? Your mother is dead;
the twin beloved sons of Zeus do not enjoy happiness; and you do not see your fatherland, while through the cities a rumor goes, mistress, which hands you over to the bed of a barbarian; your husband has lost his life in the salty waves, and never again will you bring glee to your fathers halls and Athene of the Bronze House.
style: greek tragic chorus, lyre over a low drone, massed female voices, incantatory, sorrowing, ceremonial
why: Zeus shining through the air on the wings of a snow-white swan, and the doubled 'fated, fated' of Helen's life.

title: Heautontimorumenos
author: Terence
lyrics:
(Pointing at CLINIA.)
SYRUS:
He will stay here.
CLITIPHO:
O happy man!
SYRUS:
Take yourself off.
(Exit CLITIPHO.)
(Enter BACCHIS and ANTIPHILA at a distance.)
BACCHIS: Upon my word, my dear Antiphila, I commend you, and think you fortunate in having made it your study that your manners should be conformable to those good looks of yours: and so may the Gods bless me, I do not at all wonder if every man is in love with you. For your discourse has been a proof to me what kind of disposition you possess.
And when now I reflect in my mind upon your way of life, and that of all of you, in fact, who keep the public at a distance from yourselves, it is not surprising both that you are of that disposition, and that we are not; for it is your interest to be virtuous; those, with whom we are acquainted, will not allow us to be so. For our lovers, allured merely by our beauty, court us for that;
style: roman canticum turned reflective, single tibia and soft strings, warm female voice, unhurried, candid, bittersweet
why: The courtesan telling the good girl why virtue is possible for her and not for us — the play's most honest speech.

title: Heautontimorumenos
author: Terence
lyrics:
CLITIPHO:
I believe so.
CHREMES:
Ill now go hence in-doors, to see what we have for dinner. Do you, seeing what is the time of day, mind and take care not to be any where out of the way.
(Goes into his house, and exit CLITIPHO.)
(Enter CLITIPHO.)
CLITIPHO:
(to himself.)
What partial judges are all fathers in regard to all of us young men, in thinking it reasonable for us to become old men all at once from boys, and not to participate in those things which youth is naturally inclined to. They regulate us by their own desires,such as they now are,not as they once were. If ever I have a son, he certainly shall find in me an indulgent father. For the means both of knowing and of pardoning his faults shall be found by me; not like mine, who by means of another person, discloses to me his own sentiments.
style: roman comic canticum, tibia and plucked lyre, quick bright tenor, restless, wry
why: 'What partial judges are all fathers' — and the vow that if he ever has a son he will be an indulgent father.

title: Heautontimorumenos
author: Terence
lyrics:
Ill lend my endeavors. This little business is in my way. Our neighbors Simus and Crito are disputing here about boundaries;
they have chosen me for arbitrator. Ill go and tell them that I can not possibly give them my attention to-day as I had stated I would. Ill be here immediately.
(Exit.)
MENEDEMUS:
Pray do. (To himself.) Ye Gods, by our trust in you! That the nature of all men should be so constituted, that they can see and judge of other mens affairs better than their own! Is it because in our own concerns we are biased either with joy or grief in too great a degree? How much wiser now is he for me, than I have been for myself!
(Re-enter CHREMES.)
CHREMES:
I have disengaged myself, that I might lend you my services at my leisure. Syrus must be found and instructed by me in this business.
style: roman stage monologue, low tibia and hand drum, weathered baritone, measured, rueful
why: 'That they can see and judge of other men's affairs better than their own' — the whole play's moral in one line.

title: Poems
author: William Julius Mickle
lyrics:
Amid the secret windings of the wood,
With solemn meditation let me stray;
This is the hour, when, to the wise and good,
The heavenly Maid repays the toils of day.
The river murmurs, and the breathing gale
Whispers the gently waving boughs among,
The star of evening glimmers o'er the dale,
And leads the silent host of heaven along.
How bright, emerging o'er yon broom-clad height,
The silver empress of the night appears!
Yon limpid pool reflects a stream of light,
And faintly in its breast the woodland bears.
The waters tumbling o'er their rocky bed,
Solemn and constant, from yon dell resound;
The lonely hearths blaze o'er the distant glade;
The bat, low-wheeling, skims the dusky ground.
style: scottish pastoral nocturne, fiddle and guitar over a soft drone, warm baritone, slow, moonlit, hushed
why: The silver empress of the night, the limpid pool, the low-wheeling bat — a complete evening in four quatrains.

title: Poems
author: William Julius Mickle
lyrics:
The Snowdrop bows the head.
Yet parting life one struggle gave,
She lifts her languid eyes;
"Return, my Hengist, oh return,
" My slaughter'd love! "she cries.
"Oh  still he lives  he smiles again,
" With all his grace he moves:
"I come  I come, where bow nor spear
" Shall more disturb our loves.  "
She spake  she died. The Saxon dart
Was drawn from Elmer's side;
And thrice he call'd his sister Mey,
And thrice he groan'd, and died.
Where in the dale a moss-grown cross
O'ershades an aged thorn,
Sir Elmer's and young Hengist's corse
style: border ballad, harp and low fiddle, plain female voice, modal, steady, mournful
why: 'I come — I come, where bow nor spear shall more disturb our loves' — the ballad's death-scene, in true ballad metre.

title: Poems
author: William Julius Mickle
lyrics:
Oft with the rising sun, when life was new,
Along the woodland have I roam'd with Thee;
Oft by the moon have brush'd the evening dew,
When all was fearless innocence and glee.
The sainted well, where yon bleak hill declines,
Has oft been conscious of those happy hours;
But now the hill, the river crown'd with pines,
And sainted well have lost their cheering powers.
For Thou art gone  My guide, my friend, oh where,
Where hast thou fled, and left me here behind!
My tenderest wish, my heart to Thee was bare,
Oh, now cut off each passage to thy mind!
How dreary is the gulph, how dark, how void,
The trackless shores that never were repast!
Dread separation! on the depth untry'd
Hope faulters, and the soul recoils aghast.
style: elegiac air, cello and piano, low male voice, slow, bare, aching
why: 'For thou art gone — my guide, my friend, oh where' — grief measured against the hills and the sainted well.

title: Institutio Oratoria
author: Quintilian
lyrics:
And all my blood is curdled cold with fear;
And trembling mothers clasped
Their children to their breast.
Thence like fierce wolves beneath the cloud of night, or
Like the bird that flies
Around the shore and the fish-haunted reef,
Skimming the deep.
As when Apollo wintry Lycia leaves,
And Xanthus' streams, or visits Delos' isle,
Thence like fierce wolves beneath the cloud of night, precedes its subject. On the other hand, an example of the simile following its subject is to be found in the first Georgic, where, after the long lamentation over the wars civil and foreign that have afflicted Rome, there come the lines:
As when, their barriers down, the chariots speed
Lap after lap; in vain the charioteer
Tightens the curb: his steeds ungovernable
Sweep him away nor heeds the car the rein.
style: latin epic recitation, low strings and driving frame drum, urgent male voice, gathering, headlong, storm-lit
why: An unbroken chain of similes — wolves under cloud, the skimming sea-bird, and the runaway chariots that end it.

title: Institutio Oratoria
author: Quintilian
lyrics:
Neptune admitted to the land
Protects the fleets from blasts of Aquilo.
Ucalegon burns next.
Pale death with equal foot knocks at the poor man's door and
There pale diseases dwell and sad old age;
The arms which he, the traitor, left
Fixed on the chamber wall.
To Aigialeus
His sire bears funeral offerings,
Anchises, worthy deigned
Of Venus' glorious bed, [beloved of heaven,
Twice rescued from the wreck of Pergamum.]
O ship, new waves will bear thee back to sea.
But now
A mighty length of plain we have travelled o'er;
'Tis time to loose our horses' steaming necks.
style: roman elegiac song, lyre and soft flute, grave tenor, slow, valedictory, evening
why: 'Pale death with equal foot knocks at the poor man's door', closing on the unhitching of the steaming horses.

title: The Sexual Life of the Child
author: Albert Moll
lyrics:
"Wie Du mit den kleinen Kindern, Will ich alles mit ihr tun, Und sie soll in ihrer Wiege Neben meinem Bette ruhn. Schlaeft sie, werd' ich von ihr traeumen, Schreit sie auf, erwach' ich gleich,-- Mein himmlisch gute Mutter, O, wie bin ich dock so reich!"
"All you do for your children, For my Doll I do instead, And in her little cradle She lies beside my bed. When she sleeps, I dream about her, When she cries, I wake up too. My own, dear, darling Mother, I'm just as rich as you!"
"Es gibt nichts schoeneres auf der Welt, Als wenn einem ein Wesen besonders gefaellt; Und fuehlt man sich gezogen hin Zu einer suessen Lehrerin, Das ist ein Glueck. Und liebt man sie so inniglich, Dann fuerchtet wohl gar sehr man sich Vorm Abschiedtag..."
"Of all things sweet beneath the sun, The sweetest is to love but one; And when the object of one's fondness Is one's darling governess, Supreme the joy. And if one love her so intensely, Then, of course, one dreads immensely The day of parting...."
style: german kinderlied, music box and simple piano, light child's soprano, gentle, lilting, tender
why: A child's song about her doll in its cradle, ending 'I'm just as rich as you' — complete, innocent, and singable in either language.

title: Quomodo adulator ab amico internoscatur
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
Well then, let us enquire regularly into this affair. We have already asserted, that friendship generally takes its rise from a conformity of tempers and dispositions, whereby different persons come to have the same taste of the like humors, customs, studies, exercises, and employs, as these following verses import:; Old men with old, and boys with boys agree; And womens clack with womens company. Men that are crazy, full of sores and pain, Love to diseased persons to complain. And they who labor under adverse fate, Tell their sad stories to th unfortunate.
and as another speaking of Ulysses, How can I doubt, while great Ulysses stands To lend his counsel and assist our hands?
and again, when he sees correction requisite, he will check him severely, as, Whither, O Menelaus, wouldst thou run, And tempt a fate which prudence bids thee shun?
style: greek proverb-song, lyre and light hand drum, wry male voice, steady, aphoristic, companionable
why: Only candidate, but it opens on a finished rhyming poem: old men with old, boys with boys, and the unlucky telling the unlucky.

title: System of Economical Contradictions: or, The Philosophy of Poverty
author: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
lyrics:
Par dela tous les cieux, le Dieu des cieux reside.
Le rouet est silencieux dans la vallee: C'en est fait des sentiments de famille. Sur un peu de fumee le vieil aieul Etend ses mains pales; et le foyer vide Est aussi desole que son coeur. (3)
style: french romantic chanson, solo piano and cello, low male voice, slow, desolate, hearth-cold
why: Only candidate; the silent spinning-wheel and the old man warming pale hands over smoke at an empty hearth.

title: Prometheus Bound
author: Aeschylus
lyrics:
I will not speak to upbraid mankind but to set forth the friendly purpose that inspired my blessing.
First of all, though they had eyes to see, they saw to no avail; they had ears, but they did not understand; but, just as shapes in dreams, throughout their length of days, without purpose they wrought all things in confusion. They had neither knowledge of houses built of bricks and turned to face the sun nor yet of work in wood; but dwelt beneath the ground like swarming ants, in sunless caves. They had no sign either of winter or of flowery spring or of fruitful summer, on which they could depend but managed everything without judgment, until I taught them to discern the risings of the stars and their settings, which are difficult to distinguish.
Yes, and numbers, too, chiefest of sciences,
