author: Greek Anthology
lyrics:
On the same
The Thespians revere Eros as the only god from Cytherea,
painted from no other original,
but the one Praxiteles knew as a god; whom, gazing about Phryne,
he gave as the ransom of his own longings.
Eros is naked; for this he laughs and is gentle;
for he has no bow nor fiery arrows;
nor in vain does he hold in his hands a dolphin and a flower:
for in the one he holds the earth, in the other the sea.
On Eros sleeping in a bed of pepper
Not even in slumber, nor breathless, nor at a feast
is Eros free from his fire-sown sting.
You who blow upon the brand to light your lamp,
come, light it from my soul; for I am all aflame.
When we came to the deep-shaded grove, we found within
the child of Cythera, like to purple apples.
style: greek erotic lyric, lyre and double flute, light tenor, playful, quickening
why: Naked laughing Eros with earth in one hand and sea in the other, closing on "light it from my soul; for I am all aflame".

title: Greek Anthology
author: Greek Anthology
lyrics:
but on the other he fits his shrivelled foot.
He sings either of lovely Bathyllus, or of Megistes,
swinging in his hand the lovesick lyre.
But, father Dionysus, guard him; for it is not fitting
that a servant of Bacchus should fall from Bacchus.
See how the old man Anacreon, from drink,
is tripped up, and his cloak drags
down to his limbs; and of his slippers the one
he still keeps, but the other he has lost.
And he sings, plucking the tortoise-shell,
of either Bathyllus, or fair Megistes.
Guard the old man, Bacchus, lest he fall.
Him who was reared with the honey-sweet Desires,
Lyaeus, Anacreon, the Teian swan,
you tripped with the liquid care of nectar.
For his sidelong glance, and the hem of his cloak cast
style: greek symposium drinking song, barbitos lyre, tambourine, ragged warm male voice, tipsy, swaying
why: Anacreon staggering with one slipper lost — the refrain "Guard the old man, Bacchus, lest he fall" is already a chorus.

title: Poems
author: William Cowper
lyrics:
He sprang impetuous forth,
Secure of conquest where the prize
Attends superior worth.
So the best courser on the plain
E'er yet he starts is known,
And does but at the goal obtain
What all had deem'd his own.
ODE TO PEACE.
COME, peace of mind, delightful guest!
Return and make thy downy nest
Once more in this sad heart:
Nor riches I, nor pow'r pursue,
Nor hold forbidden joys in view,
We therefore need not part.
Where wilt thou dwell if not with me,
From av'rice and ambition free,
style: english hymn, chamber organ, viola da gamba, gentle tenor, slow, consoling
why: "Come, peace of mind, delightful guest!" — a complete stanzaic ode by the author of the Olney Hymns, made to be sung.

title: Poems
author: William Cowper
lyrics:
Reclaim the wand'ring thousands, and bring home
A flock so scatter'd and so wont to roam,
Then place it once again between my knees,
The sound of truth will then be sure to please,
And truth alone, where'er my life be cast,
In scenes of plenty or the pining waste,
Shall be my chosen theme, my glory to the last.
HOPE.
ASK what is human life  the sage replies
With disappointment low'ring in his eyes,
A painful passage o'er a restless flood,
A vain pursuit of fugitive false good,
A scene of fancied bliss and heart-felt care,
Closing at last in darkness and despair.
The poor, inur'd to drudgery and distress,
Act without aim, think little and feel less,
style: georgian sacred air, harpsichord and strings, grave baritone, measured, sombre
why: "Ask what is human life" — six couplets that answer the question and close on darkness and despair.

title: Poems
author: William Cowper
lyrics:
That seems to swing uncertain, and yet falls
Full on the destin'd ear. Wide flies the chaff,
The rustling straw sends up a frequent mist
Of atoms sparkling in the noon-day beam.
Come hither, ye that press your beds of down
And sleep not: see him sweating o'er his bread
Before he eats it.  'Tis the primal curse,
But soften'd into mercy; made the pledge
Of chearful days, and nights without a groan.
By ceaseless action, all that is, subsists.
Constant rotation of th' unwearied wheel
That nature rides upon, maintains her health,
Her beauty, her fertility. She dreads
An instant's pause, and lives but while she moves.
Its own revolvency upholds the world.
Winds from all quarters agitate the air,
style: pastoral blank-verse air, acoustic guitar and low strings, plain weathered male voice, steady, turning
why: The threshing floor and "By ceaseless action, all that is, subsists" — a working image that becomes a cosmology.

title: Poems
author: Mary Barber
lyrics:
SONG.
By the Same.
STELLA and Flavia every hour
Do various hearts surprize;
In Stella's soul lies all her power,
And Flavia's in her eyes.
More boundless Flavia's conquests are,
And Stella's more confin'd;
All can discern a face that's fair,
But few a lovely mind.
Stella, like Britain's monarchs, reigns
O'er cultivated lands;
Like eastern tyrants Flavia deigns
To rule o'er barren sands.
Then boast not, Flavia, thy fair face,
Thy beauty's only store;
style: georgian parlour song, harpsichord and cello, bright soprano, lilting, gently mocking
why: An actual song in ballad stanzas, and its point lands clean: all can discern a face that's fair, but few a lovely mind.

title: Poems
author: Mary Barber
lyrics:
Still let her be thy Substitute below,
To raise the sinking Heart, to heal Distress;
To Her was giv'n the Will and Pow'r to bless.
O would Heav'n grant me, ere I cross the Main,
To see thy Face, Hortensia, once again!
But I must hasten to Hibernia's Shore;
And never, never, shall behold thee more.
To Mrs. Frances-Arabella Kelly.
To Day, as at my Glass I stood,
To set my Head-cloaths, and my Hood;
I saw my grizzled Locks with Dread,
And call'd to mind the Gorgon's Head.
Thought I, whate'er the Poets say,
Medusa's Hair was only gray:
Tho' Ovid, who the Story told,
Was too well-bred to call her old;
style: 18th century comic air, fortepiano, wry mezzo-soprano, brisk, conversational
why: The poet at her mirror deciding Medusa's snakes were only grey hair — self-contained and genuinely funny.

title: Poems
author: Mary Darwall
lyrics:
While thy vivid skies appear,
Nature smiles, and all is gay.
Thine the flowery-painted mead,
Pasture fair, and mountain green;
Thine, with infant-harvest spread,
Laughing lies the lowland scene.
Friend of thine, the shepherd plays
Blithsome near the yellow broom,
While his flock, that careless strays,
Seeks the wild thyme's sweet perfume.
May, with thee I mean to rove
O'er these lawns and vallies fair,
Tune my gentle lyre to love,
Cherish hope, and soften care.
Round me shall the village swains,
Shall the rosy nymphs, appear;
style: english pastoral folk ballad, acoustic guitar and recorder, warm female vocal, unhurried, sunlit
why: The Ode to May in trochaic quatrains — shepherd, broom, wild thyme; the most singable thing in the set.

title: Poems
author: Mary Darwall
lyrics:
Variety  in vain I hope to find;
Variety, thou dear, but distant name!
With pleasure cloy'd, and sick of tasteless ease,
No sweet alternatives my spirits chear;
Joys oft repeated lose their power to please,
And harmony grows discord to my ear.
Blest Freedom! how I long with thee to rove,
Where varying Nature all her charms displays;
To range the sun-burnt hill, the rifted grove,
And trace the silver current's winding maze!
Free as the wing'd inhabitants of air,
Who distant climes and various seasons see,
Regions  tho' not, like soft Ambara, fair;
Yet blest with change, and crown'd with Liberty.
Vain wish! these rocks, whose summits pierce the skies,
With frowning aspect tell me  Hope is vain:
style: georgian elegy, harp and muted strings, clear soprano, slow, aching
why: Gilded captivity in the Happy Valley: "Variety, thou dear, but distant name!" — longing with a real image behind it.

title: Poems
author: Mary Darwall
lyrics:
When every earthly care's at rest,
And musing Silence reigns;
Then active Fancy takes her flight
Wide o'er th' etherial plains;
Soars thro' the trackless realms of space,
Sees endless systems roll;
Whilst all harmoniously combine,
To form one beauteous whole.
All hail! sweet Solitude! to thee,
In thy sequester'd bower,
Let me invoke the Pastoral Muse,
And every Sylvan power.
Dear pensive Nymph, the tender thought
And deep research is thine;
'Tis thine to heal the tortur'd breast,
And form the great design.
style: evening hymn, chamber organ and viol, hushed female voice, slow, spacious
why: Silence, Fancy crossing the trackless realms of space, and the hail to Solitude — a devotional stanza set that stands alone.

title: Poems
author: Rev. Mr. Robertson
lyrics:
This mental beam dilates the heart,
And sparkles in the face;
It harmonizes every thought,
And heightens every grace.
One glimpse can sooth the troubled breast,
The heaving sigh restrain;
Can make the bed of sickness please,
And stop the sense of pain.
Its power can charm the savage heart,
The tyrant's pity move;
To smiles convert the wildest rage,
And melt the soul to love.
When Sweetness beams upon the throne,
In majesty benign,
The awful splendors of a crown
With milder lustre shine.
style: 18th century hymn tune, chamber organ, viola, sweet tenor, gentle, flowing
why: Clean common-metre stanzas on the beam that "can make the bed of sickness please, and stop the sense of pain".

title: Poems
author: Rev. Mr. Robertson
lyrics:
THO' thy decrees, great God, are wise,
Thy dispensations right,
Thy darling attribute is love,
Compassion thy delight.
But should thy goodness condescend
To pity my distress,
Offended Justice would each thought
Of lenity suppress.
Yes, righteous God, my daring crimes
For pardon leave no room;
Thy majesty prevents my bliss,
Thy grace demands my doom.
O! then denounce thy sovereign will,
Avenge thy injur'd name;
And let an impious miscreant's tear
Thy sacred wrath inflame.
style: penitential hymn, low organ and cello, dark baritone, slow, severe
why: The Barreaux sonnet's terrible logic — "Thy majesty prevents my bliss, thy grace demands my doom" — and the sinner inviting the bolt.

title: Leucippe and Clitophon
author: Achilles Tatius
lyrics:
1.2. If one were to strip away the modulations of the melody and speak the words bare of their harmony, the words would run thus: "If Zeus had wished to set a king over the flowers, the rose would have reigned over them. It is the ornament of the earth, the glory of the plants, the eye of flowers, the blush of the meadow.
14.1. Meanwhile, the war having broken out and the girl having been sent over to us for safekeeping, he had learned all this, yet none the less held to his plot; and the following thing helped him. The Byzantines received an oracle of this sort: "There is a certain island city that has won a name from a plant, bearing at once an isthmus and a strait upon the mainland. There Hephaestus rejoices to possess gray-eyed Athena; thither I bid you carry sacrifice to Heracles."
style: greek romance idyll, kithara and soft flute, warm tenor, flowing, ornamented
why: Only candidate, but its first half is a genuine set piece: the rose as king of the flowers, blush of the meadow.

title: Homer and Classical Philology
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
lyrics: With subtle wit you took away Our former adoration: The Iliad, you may us say, Was mere conglomeration. Think it not crime in any way: Youth's fervent adoration Leads us to know the verity, And feel the poet's unity.
style: german student lied, upright piano, light male voice with small chorus, brisk, wry
why: Only candidate, and it happens to be a rhymed epigram-quatrain on the Homeric question — short, closed, singable.

title: Vitae philosophorum
author: Diogenes Laertius
lyrics:
Give ear, Pausanias, thou son of Anchitus the wise! Moreover he wrote an epigram upon him: The physician Pausanias, rightly so named, son of Anchitus, descendant of Asclepius, was born and bred at Gela. Many a wight pining in fell torments did he bring back from Persephones inmost shrine. At all events Heraclides testifies that the case of the woman in a trance was such that for thirty days he kept her body without pulsation though she never breathed; and for that reason Heraclides called him not merely a physician but a diviner as well, deriving the titles from the following lines also:
My friends, who dwell in the grcat city sloping down to yellow Acragas, hard by the citadel, busied with goodly works, all hail! I go about among you an immortal god, no more a mortal, so honoured of all, as is meet, crowned with fillets and flowery garlands. Straightway as soon as I enter with these, men and women, into flourishing towns, I am reverenced and tens of thousands follow, to learn where is the path which leads to welfare, some desirous of oracles, others suffering from all kinds of diseases, desiring to hear a message of healing.
style: hieratic greek chant, lyre and low drone, resonant male voice, processional, exalted
why: Empedocles proclaiming himself an immortal god walking into Acragas, garlanded and followed by thousands — the most electric verse in the whole Lives.

title: Vitae philosophorum
author: Diogenes Laertius
lyrics:
This man in violation of the hallowed law of the immortals was unrighteously slain by the king of the bow-bearing Persians, who overcame him, not openly with a spear in murderous combat, but by treachery with the aid of one in whom he trusted.
At Chalcis he died, according to Eumelus in the fifth book of his Histories, by drinking aconite, at the age of seventy. The same authority makes him thirty years old when he came to Plato; but here he is mistaken. For Aristotle lived to be sixty-three, and he was seventeen when he became Platos pupil.
The hymn in question runs as follows:
O virtue, toilsome for the generation of mortals to achieve, the fairest prize that life can win, for thy beauty, O virgin, it were a doom glorious in Hellas even to die and to endure fierce, untiring labours. Such courage dost thou implant in the mind, imperishable, better than gold, dearer than parents or soft-eyed sleep. For thy sake Heracles, son of Zeus, and the sons of Leda endured much in the tasks whereby they pursued thy might.
style: ancient greek paean, aulos and lyre, male chorus in unison, solemn, rising
why: Aristotle's hymn to Virtue: "better than gold, dearer than parents or soft-eyed sleep" — written to be sung, and it still scans as a hymn.

title: Vitae philosophorum
author: Diogenes Laertius
lyrics:
One sire there is, he has twelve sons, and each of these has twice thirty daughters different in feature; some of the daughters are white, the others again are black; they are immortal, and yet they all die. And the answer is, The year.
He died at the ripe age of seventy; and the inscription over him is: Here the wise Rhodian, Cleobulus, sleeps, And oer his ashes sea-proud Lindus weeps.
In mother earth here Periander lies, The prince of sea-girt Corinth rich and wise. My own epitaph on him is: Grieve not because thou hast not gained thine end,
But take with gladness all the gods may send; Be warned by Perianders fate, who died Of grief that one desire should be denied.
Back from his travels Anacharsis came, To hellenize the Scythians all aglow; Ere half his sermon could their minds inflame, A winged arrow laid the preacher low.
style: gnomic greek song, kithara, plain steady male voice, riddling, measured
why: The riddle of the year — twelve sons, sixty daughters, white and black, immortal yet all dying — closed and memorable on its own.

title: Troades
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
Or do we wholly die, and no part of us remains,
when, with the fleeing breath, the spirit,
mingled with the mists, has passed into the air,
and the kindled torch has touched the naked side?
Whatever the rising sun, whatever the setting,
has known, whatever Ocean with its blue straits,
coming and fleeing twice, washes,
time will snatch away with the pace of Pegasus.
With what whirl the twelve constellations fly,
with what course the lord of the stars hastens
to roll round the ages, in what manner Hecate
hastens to run with her slanting curves:
to this we all make our way, the fates; nor is he
who has touched the lake sworn by the gods above
anywhere any more: as smoke from hot fires
vanishes, foul, through a brief space,
style: roman tragic chorus, low strings and hand drum, unison voices, stark, declamatory, slow
why: "Or do we wholly die?" — the great annihilation chorus, ending in smoke vanishing from a hot fire. Fully self-contained.

title: Troades
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
Whoever trusts in a throne and, mighty, lords it
in a great hall, nor fears the fickle gods,
and has given his soul over, credulous, to glad fortune,
let him look on me and on you, Troy: never has chance
given greater proof on how frail a footing
the proud stand. The pillar of powerful Asia,
overthrown, has fallen, the famous handiwork of the gods;
to whose aid came even he who drinks the cold Tanais
that spreads its seven mouths,
and she who, looking out upon her neighbor, the roving Scythians,
strikes the Pontic bank with her husbandless bands,
and he who, first receiving the new-born day,
mingles the warm Tigris with the reddening sea
it has been cut down with the sword, Pergamum has fallen upon itself.
See, the high glories of the heaped-up wall lie low,
the buildings burnt; the flames ring the palace round,
style: latin declamation set to music, cello drone and struck frame drum, grave male voice, weighty, deliberate
why: "Whoever trusts in a throne... let him look on me and on you, Troy" — a complete argument about fortune with the burning city as evidence.

title: Troades
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
captive modesty?
Let the mantle gird your loosened tunics,
let the frenzied hand be free
for the blows of frequent beating  this garb pleases,
it pleases: I recognize the Trojan throng.
Let the old griefs return again,
surpass your wonted custom of weeping:
we weep for Hector.
CHORUS: We have all loosed our hair, torn
with many a death;
the locks are let down free of the knot,
and the hot ash has sprinkled our faces.
The garment falls from our bared shoulders
and, drawn up, covers only the lowest flank;
now the naked breasts call to our right hands:
now, now, grief, bring forth your cheap laments.
style: ritual lament, bare hand drums and keening female voices, beaten rhythm, raw, insistent
why: The chorus loosening hair and striking bare breasts to a beat — "we weep for Hector" is already a refrain with a rhythm attached.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Rowe
lyrics:
How canst thou Fear while I am thy Defence?
Do thou the Spightful Foxes then Destroy,
That would my Young Aspiring Vines Annoy.
Not for the World would I exchange my Bliss,
While my Beloved's Mine, and I am His.
And till the break of that Eternal Day,
Whose Rising Sun shall chase the Shades away;
Turn, my Beloved, turn again; and thy
Dear sight shall make the lazy Moments fly.
CHAP. III.
TWas in the deadness of a Gloomy Night,
My Love, more pleasant than the wishtfor Light,
O're all my Bed I vainly sought; for there
My Arms could Grasp no more than empty air:
Griev'd with my Loss, through all the streets I rove,
And every Ear with soft Complaints I move:
style: baroque sacred love song, theorbo and viol, warm soprano, tender, flowing
why: The Canticles paraphrase — "While my Beloved's Mine, and I am His" and the night search through the streets. Sensuous and complete.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Rowe
lyrics:
Arm'd with thy mighty Bow,
Thou marchedst out against thy daring Foe:
And very terrible thou didst appear
To them, but thus thy darling People cheer.
"Know, Iacob's Sons, I am the God of Truth,
" Your Father Iacob's God, nor can I break my Oath.
The Mountains shook as our dread Lord advanc'd,
And all the little Hills around 'em danc'd:
The neighb'ring Streams their verdant Banks o'reflow,
The Waters saw and trembled at the sight,
Back to their old Abyss they go,
And bear the News to everlasting Night:
The Mother Deep within its hollow Caverns roars.
And beats the silent Shores.
The Sun above no longer dares to strive,
Nor will his frighted Steeds their wonted Iourney drive.
style: english verse anthem, chamber organ and natural trumpet, full choir, majestic, striding
why: Psalm paraphrase where the mountains shake, the little hills dance and the waters run backward to tell the news.

title: Poems
author: Elizabeth Rowe
lyrics:
Oh Son of Venus, Mourn thy baffled Arts,
For I defye the proudest of thy Darts:
Undazled now, I thy weak Taper View,
And find no fatal influence accrue;
Nor would fond Child thy feebler Lamp appear,
Should my bright Sun deign to approach more near;
Canst thou his Rival then pretend to prove?
Thou a false Idol, he the God of Love;
Lovely beyond Conception, he is all
Reason, or Fancy amiable call,
All that the most exerted thoughts can reach,
When sublimated to its utmost streach.
Oh! altogether Charming, why in thee
Do the vain World no Form or Beauty see?
Why do they Idolize a dusty clod,
And yet refuse their Homage to a God?
style: restoration devotional air, harpsichord and violin, bright soprano, ardent, declarative
why: Cupid dismissed as a guttering taper beside the true God of Love — a single sustained turn of thought, no apparatus.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Paine
lyrics:
The sons of the earth, the proud giants of old,
Have broke from their darksome abodes;
And such is the news, that in Heaven tis told,
Theyre marching to war with the gods.
A council was held in the chamber of Jove,
And this was the final decree,
That Wolfe should be calld to the armies above,
And the charge was intrusted to me.
To the plains of Quebec with the orders I flew,
He beggd for a moments delay;
And cried, O forbear! Let me victory hear,
And then the command Ill obey.
With a darkening film I encompassd his eyes,
And conveyd him away in an urn,
Lest the fondness he bore to his own native shore,
Should tempt him again to return.
style: 18th century broadside ballad, fife, snare drum and fiddle, strong male voice, marching, elegiac
why: The Death of General Wolfe — giants storming heaven, a council of Jove, and Wolfe carried off in an urn. A real ballad, complete.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Paine
lyrics:
And the figures that fancy in the clouds can create
Supplied me with garden and ground.
I had grottoes and Fountains and orange-tree groves,
I had all that enchantment has told,
I had sweet shady walks for the Gods and their Loves,
I had mountains of coral and gold.
But a storm that I felt not had risen and rolld,
While wrapt in a slumber I lay,
And when I lookd out in the morning, behold,
My Castle was carried away.
It passd over rivers and vallies and groves,
The World it was all in my view,
I thought of my friends, of their fates, and their loves,
And often, full often, of you.
At length it came over a beautifull scene
That nature in silence has made,
style: colonial parlour ballad, fiddle and hammered dulcimer, gentle tenor, lilting, wistful
why: The castle in the air, with its coral and gold, carried off by a storm the dreamer never felt.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Paine
lyrics:
The land of Love and Liberty.
May ages as they rise proclaim
The glories of thy natal day,
And restless Europe, from thy example learn
To love, to rule, and to obey.
Be thou for ever, for ever, great and free
The land of Love and Liberty.
Let Laureats sing their birth-day odes,
Or how their death-like thunders hurld,
Tis ours the Charter, the Charter, ours alone
To sing the birth-day of a World
Be thou for ever, for ever, great and free
The land of Love and Liberty.
Give Me Kind Heaven
The following lines were written at a tea-table, on the author being asked what kind of woman he should prefer.
Give me kind Heavn  if this wide world has one
style: revolutionary anthem, fife and drums with massed voices, rousing, moderate march
why: "Be thou for ever, for ever, great and free / The land of Love and Liberty" — an actual repeating chorus, and Paine singing the birthday of a world.

title: Poems
author: Richard Roderick
lyrics:
The SHEPHERD'S FAREWEL to his LOVE.
Being the same ODE.
Translated by Mr. RODERICK.
PHoebe, thank thy false heart, it has fix'd my repose,
The gods have had pity at length on my woes;
I feel it, I feel my soul loose from its chain,
And at last freedom comes, often dream'd of in vain.
The flame is burn'd out, and each passion at rest.
Under which love disguis'd still might lurk in my breast;
No more, when thou'rt nam'd, the warm blushes arise,
No more slutters my heart, when I meet with your eyes.
In my sleep now no longer thy image I see,
Nor the first of my thoughts, when I wake, is of thee,
When from thee, no more of thy absence I plain,
When with thee, I feel neither pleasure nor pain.
My heart without fondness can muse on thy charms,
style: georgian anapestic air, guitar and flute, light tenor, brisk, breezily bitter
why: "Phoebe, thank thy false heart" — a clean-limbed farewell in swinging anapests, and the freedom it claims is audibly not believed.

title: Poems
author: Richard Roderick
lyrics:
Nor male nor female is my sex,
You'll scarce believe my troth;
For when I've told you all my tricks
You'll swear 't must needs be both.
For oft my master lies with me,
His wife I oft enjoy;
Yet's she's no whore, no cuckold he,
And true to both am I.
My cloaths nor women fit, nor men,
They're neither coat nor gown;
Yet oft both men and maidens, when
They're naked, have them on.
When I'm upon my legs, I lie,
Yet legs in truth I've none;
And never am I seen so high
To rise as when I'm down.
style: english tavern catch, fiddle and drone, ragged male voices, bawdy, bouncing
why: The riddle of the bed: neither male nor female, master and wife both, up when it lies down. Funny, closed, and made for a round.

title: The Approach to Philosophy
author: Ralph Barton Perry
lyrics:
"A Moment's Halt--a momentary taste Of Being from the Well amid the Waste-- And Lo!--the phantom Caravan has reach'd The Nothing it set out from-- . . ."
"We are no other than a moving row Of Magic Shadow-shapes that come and go Round with the Sun-illumin'd Lantern held In Midnight by the Master of the Show."
"The earth expending right hand and left hand, The picture alive, every part in its best light, The music falling in where it is wanted, and stopping where it is not wanted."
"That you are here--that life exists and identity, That the powerful play goes on, and you may contribute a verse."
"Some for the Glories of This World; and some Sigh for the Prophet's Paradise to come; Ah, take the Cash, and let the Credit go, Nor heed the rumble of a distant Drum."
"Drink for you know not whence you come, nor why; Drink for you know not why you go, nor where."
style: persian-inflected art song, oud and hand drum, husky low voice, swaying, fatalistic
why: Rubaiyat quatrains — the phantom caravan, the row of magic shadow-shapes, take the cash and let the credit go.

title: The Approach to Philosophy
author: Ralph Barton Perry
lyrics:
"To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to Yahweh than sacrifice."[93:9]
"The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."
"For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones."[94:11]
"--a sense sublime Of something far more deeply interfused, Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, And the round ocean and the living air, And the blue sky, and in the mind of man."
"O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: My soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee, In a dry and weary land, where no water is. So have I looked upon thee in the sanctuary, To see thy power and thy glory. For thy loving-kindness is better than life; My lips shall praise thee."
style: quiet devotional hymn, sustained strings and low organ, single clear voice, spacious, awed
why: "Something far more deeply interfused" set beside "my soul thirsteth for thee, in a dry and weary land" — two thirsts, one mood.

title: Antiquitates Romanae
author: Dionysius of Halicarnassus
lyrics: 72.9. And again, saying that there was wrought on it a Cretan chorus of youths and maidens, he has spoken thus: "And a dancing-floor the renowned god of the two strong arms wrought, like to that which once in broad Knossos Daedalus fashioned for fair-haired Ariadne. There youths and maidens worth many oxen danced, holding one another's hands by the wrist." And describing its adornment, that he might make plain to us that the movement of the males was in arms, he says: "And these had fair garlands, and those had daggers of gold from silver baldrics." And introducing the leaders of their dance, who gave the others the lead and led off, he writes: "And a great crowd stood about the lovely dance, taking delight; and two tumblers among them, leading off the song, whirled through the midst."
style: ancient dance tune, double aulos, lyre and clapping frame drum, wordless chorus interjections, quick, circling
why: Only candidate, and it is the dancing-floor of Ariadne: garlands, gold daggers, tumblers whirling through the middle of the ring.

title: Seven Against Thebes
author: Aeschylus
lyrics:
Ah, ah, you gods and goddesses, raise your war cry over our walls to drive away the onrushing evil!
The army of the white shield, ready for battle, rushes at full speed against the city.
Who then will rescue us, which of the gods or goddesses will help?
Or shall I fall in supplication at the feet of our ancestral gods statues?
Ah, blessed gods, firmly enthroned, the time has come to hold fast to your statues. Why do we delay, who are much to be lamented?
Do you hear the clash of shields, or does it escape you? When, if not now, shall we place sacred robes and wreaths on the statues to accompany our prayers?
I see the clashit is not the clatter of a single spear. What will you do? Will you betray your own land, Ares, where you have dwelt since long ago? God of the golden helmet, look, look upon the city that you once cherished!
style: archaic greek chorus, aulos and krotala, agitated female voices overlapping, urgent, driving
why: The panic at the walls — "Do you hear the clash of shields?" — short breathless lines built for a chorus in flight.

title: Seven Against Thebes
author: Aeschylus
lyrics:
Scout:
Another, the fourth, has the gate near Onca Athena and takes his stand with a shout, Hippomedon, tremendous in form and figure. I shuddered in fear as he spun a huge diskthe circle of his shield, I mean
I cannot deny it. The symbol-maker who put the design on his shield was no lowly craftsman: the symbol is Typhon, spitting out of his fire-breathing mouth a dark, thick smoke, the darting sister of fire.
And the rim of the hollow-bellied shield is fastened all around with snaky braids. The warrior himself has raised the war-cry and, inspired by Ares he raves for battle like a maenad, with a look to inspire fear. We must put up a good defense against the assault of such a man, for already Rout is boasting of victory at the gate.
Eteocles:
style: martial greek chant, deep frame drums and horn, low male voices, ominous, heavy tread
why: Hippomedon spinning his shield: Typhon breathing dark smoke, the rim braided with snakes, the warrior raving like a maenad.

title: Seven Against Thebes
author: Aeschylus
lyrics:
Chorus:
Over these poor men it can be said that they did much to harm our citizens and also the ranks of all the foreigners who died in abundance in the fighting.
Ill-fated beyond all women who are called by the name of mother is she who bore them. After she made her own child her own husband, she gave birth to these sons, who have thus ended their lives with kindred hands giving death for death.
Chorus:
Of the same seed, in truth, they were utterly destroyed in unloving divisions, in maddened discord, in the ending of their strife.
Their hatred has ceased. Their life has been mingled in the blood-soaked earth. Now truly their blood is one.
Ruthless is that which resolved their strife, the stranger from across the sea, sharpened iron rushed from the fire. Ruthless, too, was Ares, the cruel divider of their property, who made their fathers curses come true.
style: greek dirge, bowed lyre over a low drone, unison voices, slow, final
why: "Their hatred has ceased... now truly their blood is one" — the iron from across the sea divides the brothers' estate. A closed lament.

title: Bacchides
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics: Then, for the son of the old gentleman, my master here in love, together with whom I drink, with whom I eat and go a-courting, I have procured regal and golden trea sures, that he may take from thence at home, and not go seeking abroad. Those Parmenos and those Syruses, please me not, who filch some two or three minae from their masters. Theres nothing more worthless than a servant without skillworthless, if he has not a breast mightily well-stocked, so that, whenever there is necessity, he may draw his supply from his own breast. No one can be a person well to do unless he understands both how to do good and how to do evil. With rogues he must be a rogue; with thieves let him filch whatever he can. It befits him who is truly wise, to be a person that can shift his very skin.
style: roman comic canticum, double pipe and plucked lyre, brash male voice, fast patter, swaggering
why: The clever slave's manifesto — with rogues a rogue, with thieves a thief, wise enough to shift his very skin.

title: Bacchides
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
if his rods are in the fields, still my backs at home. Now Ill be off, and tell my masters son this contrivance about the gold, and about his mistress Bacchis who has been found.
(Exit.)
(Enter LYDUS from the house of BACCHIS.)
LYDUS:
Open and throw back straightway this gate of hell, I do entreat. For, really, I do deem it nothing else; inasmuch as no one comes here but he whon all hopes have deserted, that he may yet be a decent person. Bacchisno, not Bacchis is their name, but they are most determined Bacchanals. Avaunt from me, you sisters, who suck the blood of men. Richly and elegantly furnished is this housefor destruction. Soon as I beheld all this, at once I straight-way way betook myself to my heels.
style: mock-tragic patter song, tibia and hand drum, indignant declaiming voice, quick, exasperated
why: "Open and throw back this gate of hell" — Bacchis and Bacchanals, sisters who suck the blood of men. A complete comic tirade.

title: Bacchides
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
To this silly old man of ours, in fact, I give the name of Ilium; the Captain is Menelaus; I, Agamemnon; I, too, am Ulysses, the son of Laertes; Mnesilochus is Alexander, who will be the destruction of his fathers fortunes; he has borne off the Helen, on whose account I am now carrying on the siege of Ilium. For there I have heard say that Ulysses was both bold and full of mischief, just as I am.
I have been detected in my trickshe, discovered in a beggars guise, had almost perished, while he was spying out there the doings of the Trojans. Similarly has it happened to myself to-day. I have been bound, but by my devices I have redeemed myself; he, too, preserved himself by artifice. I have heard that there were three destinies attending Troy, which were fatal to it; if the statue should be lost from the citadel; whereas the second was the death of Troilus;
style: burlesque epic recitation, lyre and drum, boastful male voice, strutting, mock-heroic
why: Chrysalus casting himself as Agamemnon and Ulysses and the old man as Troy — the play's most famous conceit, self-explaining.

title: Ars Amatoria
author: Ovid
lyrics:
In Cupid's school, whoe'er would take degree
Must learn his rudiments by reading me,
Seamen with sailing art their vessels move;
Art guides the chariot: art instructs to love.
Of ships and chariots others know the rule;
But I am master in Love's mighty school.
Cupid indeed is obstinate and wild,
A stubborn god; but yet the god's a child:
Easy to govern in his tender age,
Like fierce Achilles in his pupilage:
That hero, born for conquest, trembling
stood
Before the centaur, and receiv'd the rod.
As Chiron mollified his cruel mind
With art; and taught his warlike hands to wind
The silver strings of his melodious lyre;
style: latin elegiac song, lyre and light hand percussion, wry seductive male voice, easy ambling tempo
why: The proem: art guides the chariot, art instructs to love — and Cupid as a child to be schooled like Achilles under Chiron.

title: Ars Amatoria
author: Ovid
lyrics:
In time the steer will to the yoke submit,
In time the restive horse will bear the bit.
E'en the hard ploughshare use will wear away,
And stubborn steel in length of time decay.
Water is soft and marble hard, and yet
We see soft water through hard marble eat.
Though late, yet Troy at length in
flames expir'd;
And ten years more, Penelope had tir'd.
Perhaps she writes, and answers with disdain,
And sharply bids you not to write again:
What she requires, she fears you would accord;
The jilt would not be taken at her word.
Meantime, if she be carried in her chair,
Approach, but do not seem to know she's there:
Speak softly, to delude the standers by;
style: roman love song, cithara and soft flute, coaxing tenor, patient, sinuous
why: "Water is soft and marble hard, and yet we see soft water through hard marble eat" — persuasion by accumulation, made of proverbs.

title: Ars Amatoria
author: Ovid
lyrics:
The first ripe cluster let your mistress eat,
With chesnut, melons, or fair peaches, treat;
Some larger fish, or choicer fowl, present;
They recommend your passion where they're sent.
'Tis with these arts the childless miser's caught,
Thus future legacies are basely bought;
But may his name with infamy be curst,
That practis'd them on love, and women first.
In tender sonnets most your flame rehearse,
But who, alas! of late are mov'd by verse?
Women a wealthy treating fool admire,
Applaud your wit,-but costly gifts require.
This is the golden age, all worship gold;
Honours are purchas'd, love and beauty sold.
Should Homer come with his harmonious train,
And not present, Homer's turn'd out again.
style: satirical roman air, plucked strings and tabor, sardonic voice, brisk, cutting
why: "This is the golden age, all worship gold" — and Homer himself turned out of doors for arriving without a present.

title: Poems
author: Amelia Opie
lyrics:
THE WARRIOR'S RETURN.
THE WARRIOR'S RETURN.
SIR WALTER returned from the far Holy Land,
And a blood-tinctured falchion he bore;
But such precious blood as now darkened his sword
Had never distained it before.
Fast fluttered his heart as his own castle towers
He saw on the mountain's green height;
"My wife, and my son!" he exclaimed, while his tears
Obscured for some moments his sight.
For terror now whispered, the wife he had left
Full fifteen long twelvemonths before,
The child he had claspt in his farewel embrace,
Might both, then, alas! be no more.
Then, sighing, he thought of his Editha's tears
As his steed bore him far from her sight,
style: english narrative ballad, harp and fiddle, storytelling mezzo voice, steady gait, foreboding
why: The Warrior's Return — Sir Walter home from the Holy Land with a strangely bloodied sword. Pure ballad, and it hooks in four stanzas.

title: Poems
author: Amelia Opie
lyrics:
Thy scenes with unobtrusive art
Shall steal the mourner from her heart, ....
The hands in sorrow claspt unclose,
Bid her sick soul on Heaven repose,
And, soothed by time and nature, hail
Health, peace, and hope in Borrowdale.
THE LUCAYAN'S SONG.
THE LUCAYAN'S SONG.
THE LUCAYAN'S SONG.
HAIL, lonely shore! hail, desert cave!
To you, o'erjoyed, from men I fly,
And here I'll make my early grave ....
For what can misery do but die?
Sad was the hour when, fraught with guile,
Spain's cruel sons our valleys sought;
Unknown to us the Christian's wile,
style: island lament, solo female voice over sparse frame drum and low strings, desolate, slow
why: "Hail, lonely shore! hail, desert cave!... For what can misery do but die?" — a song by title and by build.

title: Poems
author: Amelia Opie
lyrics:
Although, alas! he scorns my love.
TO HENRY.
HOW I hail this morn's appearing!
It will thee, my love, restore:
Safety danger past endearing,
Sure we meet to part no more!
Fame is thine, lo! crowds aver it,
And her smile is dear to thee;
But I charge thee, don't prefer it
E'er again to home and me.
Thou, thy country's call obeying,
Hast her battles nobly fought;
And, thy ready zeal repaying,
See, she gives the laurels sought.
But have I no claims, my rover?
Claims as fondly dear to thee?
style: regency parlour song, fortepiano and cello, bright soprano, buoyant, teasing
why: Trochaic welcome-home stanzas that turn into a claim: fame is dear to you, but don't prefer it again to home and me.

title: Poems
author: John Delap
lyrics:
ELEGY I.
AH stay!  thy wand oblivious o'er my eyes
Yet wave, mild power of sleep!  my prayer is vain;
She flies, the partial nurse of nature flies,
With all her soothing visionary train.
Then let me forth; and near yon flowering thorn
Taste heaven's pure breath; while rob'd in amber vest,
Fresh from her watery couch, the youthful morn
Steals on the slumbers of the drowsy east.
Lo, at her presence, the strong arm of toil,
With glittering sickle, mows the prime of May;
While yon poor hirelings, for the mine's rude soil,
Leave to their sleeping babes their cots of clay.
With sturdy step, they cheerly whistle o'er
The path that flings across the reedy plain;
To the deep caverns of that yawning moor,
style: graveyard-school elegy, viola and chamber organ, low measured male voice, slow, grey-lit
why: Sleep refusing to come, then dawn over the flowering thorn and the miners whistling out to the pit. A complete elegiac opening.

title: Poems
author: John Delap
lyrics:
By Mr. DELAP.
HOW blithe the flow'ry graces of the spring
From nature's wardrobe come! and hark how gay
Each glittering insect, hovering on the wing,
Sings their glad welcome to the fields of May!
They gaze, with greedy eye, each beauty o'er;
They suck the sweet breath of the blushing rose;
Sport in the gale, or sip the rainbow show'r;
Their life's short day no pause of pleasure knows.
Like their's, dread pow'r! my chearful morn display'd
The flattering promise of a golden noon,
'Till each gay cloud, that sportive nature spread,
Dy'd in the gloom of thy distemper'd frown.
Yes, ere I told my two-and-twentieth year,
Swift from thy quiver flew the deadly dart;
Harmless it pass'd 'mid many a blithe compeer,
style: 18th century pastoral elegy, harpsichord and strings, plaintive tenor, moderate, wistful
why: Insects sipping the rainbow shower against the dart that found its entrance near the heart before the poet was twenty-two.

title: Carmen Saeculare
author: Horace
lyrics:
1. Phoebus, and Diana, mistress of the woodlands,
bright glory of the sky, O ever to be worshipped
and ever worshipped, grant what we pray for
at this sacred season,
at which the Sibylline verses have admonished
chosen maidens and unblemished boys
to sing a hymn to the gods
to whom the seven hills are dear.
Kindly Sun, who in your shining chariot
bring forth the day and hide it, and rise again
another and yet the same  may you never
look upon anything greater than the city of Rome!
Gentle to bring to term the births now ripe,
Ilithyia, watch over our mothers,
whether you choose to be called Lucina
or Genitalis:
style: roman processional hymn, lyre and double aulos, mixed choir of boys and girls, stately, bright, ceremonial
why: The opening invocation of Phoebus and Diana — this is literally a hymn commissioned to be sung by a chorus.

title: Carmen Saeculare
author: Horace
lyrics:
Mild and gentle, your weapon laid aside,
hear the suppliant boys, Apollo;
queen of the stars, two-horned,
hear, O Moon, the girls:
if Rome is your work, and if Trojan companies
held the Etruscan shore,
that band bidden to change their homes and city
in a saving voyage,
for whom, through burning Troy, with no treachery,
chaste Aeneas, surviving his fatherland,
made ready a free road, destined to give
more than was left behind:
Gods, grant to the teachable young an upright character,
gods, grant to peaceful old age its rest,
and to the race of Romulus give wealth and offspring
and every glory.
style: antiphonal hymn, two answering choirs of boys and girls, kithara and soft drum, alternating, solemn
why: Boys to Apollo, girls to the Moon — the structure of the stanza is already a call and response.

title: Carmen Saeculare
author: Horace
lyrics:
And whatever the renowned blood of Anchises
and of Venus entreats of you with white oxen,
let him obtain it  mightier than the warring foe,
gentle to the one laid low.
Now the Mede fears our hands, powerful
by sea and land, and the Alban axes;
now the Scythians, lately so proud, and the Indians
seek our answers.
Now Faith and Peace and Honour and old-fashioned
Modesty, and Virtue too long neglected,
dare to return, and blessed Plenty appears
with her full horn.
May Phoebus, the augur, splendid with his gleaming bow
and dear to the nine Muses,
who by his healing art relieves
the weary limbs of the body,
style: roman triumph hymn, trumpets and lyre, full choir, broad, radiant, rising
why: Faith, Peace, Honour and Modesty daring to return, and Plenty appearing with her full horn — the ode's great turn.

title: Laws
author: Plato
lyrics:
Ath. Everybody, I believe, gives the name of headship to the government which then existed,and it still continues to exist to-day among both Greeks and barbarians in many quarters. And, of course, Homer mentions its existence in connection with the household system of the Cyclopes, where he says No halls of council and no laws are theirs, But within hollow caves on mountain heights Aloft they dwell, each making his own law.
For wife and child; of others reck they naught.
Ath. The same that Homer himself mentioned next to the second, when he said that the third form arose in this way. His verses run thus Dardania he founded when as yet The Holy keep of Ilium was not built Upon the plain, a town for mortal folk, But still they dwelt upon the highland slopes Of many-fountained Ida.
style: archaic epic recitation, single lyre, grave male voice, sparse, unhurried
why: Only candidate, but it carries the Cyclopes lines: no halls of council and no laws, each man aloft in his cave making his own law.

title: Maximini Duo
author: Scriptores Historiae Augustae
style: roman soldiers' marching chant, stamping feet and low drum, gruff male voices in unison, blunt, repetitive
why: Only candidate, and it is already a chant — elephant, lion, tiger, all killed; beware the many if you do not fear the few.

title: Hecyra
author: Terence
lyrics:
For my sake, admit of this plea, and attend in silence, that he may be encouraged to write other Plays, and that it may be for my advantage to study new ones hereafter, purchased at my own expense.
(Enter PHILOTIS and SYRA.)
PHILOTIS:
I faith, Syra, you can find but very few lovers who prove constant to their mistresses.
For instance, how often did this Pamphilus swear to Bacchishow solemnly, so that any one might have readily believed himthat he never would take home a wife so long as she lived. Well now, he is married.
SYRA:
Therefore, for that very reason, I earnestly both advise and entreat you to take pity upon no one, but plunder, fleece, and rend every man you lay hold of.
PHILOTIS:
What! Hold no one exempt?
SYRA:
No one; for not a single one of them, rest assured, comes to you without making up his mind, by means of his flatteries, to gratify his passion with you at the least possible expense.
style: roman comic canticum, tibia and plucked lyre, sardonic female voice, brisk, worldly
why: Syra's advice to plunder, fleece and rend every man you lay hold of — a complete comic argument in two voices.

title: Hecyra
author: Terence
lyrics:
Myrrhina here recognized it just now, while I had it on my finger. She asked whence it came: I told her all the story. Hence the discovery has been made that it was Philumena ravished by him, and that this new-born child is his. I am overjoyed that this happiness hsa befallen him through my agency; although other courtesans would not have similar feelings; nor, indeed, is it to our interest that any lover should find pleasure in matrimony. But, i faith, I never, for the sake of gain, will give my mind to base actions. So long as I had the opportunity, I found him to be kind, easy, and good-natured. This marriage has fallen out unluckily for me,that I confess to be the fact. But, upon my word, I do think that I have done nothing for it to befall me deservedly.
It is but reasonable to endure inconveniences from one from whom I have received so many benefits.
style: roman monody, soft double pipe and lyre, warm low female voice, reflective, unhurried
why: The courtesan's soliloquy: the ring recognised, the truth out, and "I never, for the sake of gain, will give my mind to base actions".

title: Cyclops
author: Euripides
lyrics:
Chorus:
Offspring of well-bred sires and dams, pray whither wilt thou be gone from me to the rocks? Hast thou not here a gentle breeze, and grass to browse, and water from the eddying stream set near the cave in troughs? and are not thy young ones bleating for thee?
Chorus:
Pst! pst! wilt thou not browse here, here on the dewy slope? Ho? ho! ere long will I cast a stone at thee. Away, away! O horned one, to the fold-keeper of the Cyclops, the country-ranging shepherd.
Chorus:
Loosen thy bursting udder; welcome to thy teats the kids, whom thou leavest in the lambkins pens. Those little bleating kids, asleep the livelong day, miss thee;
wilt then leave at last the rich grass pastures on the peaks of Aetna and enter the fold?
Chorus:
Chorus:
Here we have no Bromian god; no dances here, or Bacchantes thyrsus-bearing;
style: rustic satyr chorus, panpipes and goatskin drum, rough male voices with calls and whistles, lively, pastoral
why: The goat-herding chorus — dewy slope, bursting udder, bleating kids — a genuine work-song with shouts built into it.

title: Cyclops
author: Euripides
lyrics:
Odysseus:
Well, we will give thee money besides.
Silenus:
Only undo the skin, and never mind the money.
Odysseus:
Bring out the cheeses then and lambs.
Silenus:
I will do so, with small thought of any master. For let me have a single cup of that and I would turn madman, giving in exchange for it the flocks of every Cyclops and then throwing myself into the sea from the Leucadian  rock, once I have been well drunk and smoothed out my wrinkled brow. For if a man rejoice not in his drinking, he is mad; for in drinking there is love with all its frolic, and dancing withal, and oblivion of woe. Shall not I then purchase so rare a drink, bidding the senseless Cyclops and his central eye go hang? Exit Silenus.
Chorus:
Hearken, Odysseus, let us hold some converse with thee.
Odysseus:
style: greek drinking song, aulos and clapping hands, slurred lusty male voice, rollicking, accelerating
why: Silenus on wine: love with all its frolic, dancing, and oblivion of woe — "if a man rejoice not in his drinking, he is mad".

title: Cyclops
author: Euripides
lyrics:
Odysseus:
Alas! escaped from the troubles of Troy and the sea, my barque now strands upon the whim and forbidding heart of this savage.
O Pallas, mistress mine, goddess-daughter of Zeus, help me, help me now; for I am come to toils and depths of peril worse than all at Ilium; and thou, O Zeus, the strangers god, who hast thy dwellingmid the radiant stars, behold these things;
for, if thou regard them not, in vain art thou esteemed the great god Zeus, though but a thing of naught. [Follows the Cyclops reluctantly.
Chorus:
Ope wide the portal of thy gaping throat, Cyclops; for strangers limbs, both boiled and grilled, are ready from off the coals for thee to gnaw and tear and mince up small, reclining in thy shaggy goatskin coat.
Chorus:
Relinquish not thy meal for me; keep that boat for thyself alone. Avaunt this cave! avaunt the burnt-offerings, which the godless Cyclops offers on Aetnas altars, exulting in meals on strangers flesh!
style: grotesque satyr chorus, braying pipes and heavy drums, leering voices in unison, gleeful, macabre
why: "Ope wide the portal of thy gaping throat, Cyclops" — a cannibal serenade, self-contained and horribly catchy.

title: Agamemnon
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
THE GHOST OF THYESTES
Leaving the dark places of infernal Dis,
I am here, sent forth from the deep cavern of Tartarus,
uncertain which abode I hate the more:
I, Thyestes, flee the underworld; I put the upper world to flight.
Lo, my soul shudders and fear shakes my limbs:
I see my father's, nay rather my brother's house;
this is the ancient threshold of the Pelopian home;
here it is the Pelasgian custom to take the first auspices
of the royal crown for the head; here on a lofty couch they sit
who bear the proud sceptre in their hand;
here is the place for holding councilhere the place for feasts.
I would gladly turn back. Were it not better even to dwell
by the gloomy pools? Were it not better to be the guardian of the Styx,
tossing his three-fold neck with its black manes?
style: underworld invocation, low drones and struck metal, bass male voice, sepulchral, slow, spoken-sung
why: Thyestes' ghost arriving: "I flee the underworld; I put the upper world to flight" — an opening that explains itself entirely.

title: Agamemnon
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
is beaten by the rainy south wind,
and the grove, scattering thick shadows,
sees its aged oaks broken;
thunderbolts strike the lofty hills,
the larger bodies lie open to diseases,
and while the common herds run
to their wandering pastures,
the largest neck is marked for the wound.
Whatever Fortune has raised on high,
she lifts to dash it down. To modest things
belongs a longer age: happy is whoever,
content with the lot of the middle throng,
the breeze brushes his safe shores,
and, fearing to trust his boat to the sea,
skirts the lands with a nearer oar.
CLYTEMNESTRA, NURSE
style: roman chorus, lyre and low strings, unison voices, grave, measured, resigned
why: "Whatever Fortune has raised on high, she lifts to dash it down" — and the safer joy of rowing close to shore.

title: Agamemnon
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
the weapon of Pyrrhus in the old man's throat
scarcely tinged with his scanty blood.
CASSANDRA
Restrain the tears that every time will demand,
Trojan women, and mourn yourselves your own dead
with your lamentable groan: my sorrows
refuse a partner; remove your laments
from my disasters; for my own ills I myself will suffice.
CHORUS
It is sweet to mingle tears with tears:
those whom secret cares lacerate
burn the more; it is sweet to weep
one's own openly. Nor will you, however
a hard heroine and patient of evil,
be able to weep such great ruins,
not the bird that sings its shifting song
style: lament with responding chorus, harp and viol over a drone, solo female voice, slow, aching
why: Cassandra refusing company in her grief against the chorus's "it is sweet to mingle tears with tears" — call and answer already written in.

title: Poems
author: Edward Rolle
lyrics:
Who in a wrath of verse, with all their might
Write on, howe'er unqualify'd to write,
The POWER of POETRY.
WHEN tuneful Orpheus strove by moving strains
To sooth the furious hate of rugged swains:
The list'ning multitude was pleas'd,
Ev'n Rapine drop'd her ravish'd prey,
Till by the soft oppression seiz'd,
Each savage heard his rage away;
And now o'ercome, in kind consent they move,
And all is harmony, and all is love!
Not so, when Greece's chief by heav'n inspir'd,
With love of arms each glowing bosom fir'd:
But now the trembling soldier fled
Regardless of the glorious prize;
And his brave thirst of honour dead,
style: 18th century ode for music, baroque strings and trumpet, tenor with small chorus, alternating grand and tender
why: The Power of Poetry — Orpheus stilling the swains, Rapine dropping her prey. Written in ode stanzas that already ask for setting.

title: Poems
author: Edward Rolle
lyrics:
Hopes for what never was, nor e'er will be:
The nearest ease, since we must suffer still,
Are they, who dare be patient under ill.
Whilom a fool saw where a fiddle lay;
And after pouring round it, strove to play:
Above, below, across, all ways he tries;
He tries in vain, 'tis discord all and noise:
Fretting he threw it by: then thus the lout;
"There's musick in it, could I fetch it out."
If life does not its harmony impart,
We want not instruments, but have not art.
'Tis endless to defer our hopes of ease,
Till crosses end, and disappointments cease.
The sage is happy, not that all goes right,
His cattle feel no rot, his corn no blight;
The mind for ease is fitted to the wise,
style: georgian moral air, harpsichord and violin, wry baritone, brisk, epigrammatic
why: The fool with the fiddle — "There's musick in it, could I fetch it out" — and the moral that we lack not instruments but art.

title: Poems
author: Edward Rolle
lyrics:
Thus gratitude is made to plead for sin;
My trait'rous breast a party forms within:
And inclination brib'd, we never want
Excuse  "'Tis hot, and walking makes one faint."
Now sense gets strength; my bright resolves decay,
Like stars that melt at the approach of day:
Thought dies, and ev'n, at last, your image fades away.
My head grows warm; all reason I despise:
"To-day be happy, and to-morrow wise!"
Betray'd so oft, I'm half persuaded now,
Surely to fail, the first step is to vow.
The country lately, 'twas my wish: oh there!
Gardens, diversions, friends, relations, air:
For London now, dear London, how I burn!
I must be happy, sure, when I return.
Whoever hopes true happiness to see,
style: english drinking-and-repenting song, fortepiano and cello, rueful tenor, easy, self-mocking
why: "To-day be happy, and to-morrow wise!" and the confession that to fail, the first step is to vow.

title: Poems
author: Constantia Grierson
style: georgian song in tetrameter couplets, harpsichord and flute, arch light soprano, playful, trotting
why: Cupid complaining of his own portraits: the patriot enslaved to a jilt, the sage wedded to a shrew, vestals languishing for a beau.

title: Poems
author: Constantia Grierson
style: 18th century ode, strings and oboe, declamatory soprano, stately, indignant
why: Phoebus growing jealous as the Muses build a woman's mind and denying her the universal tongue — the grievance is fully legible.

title: Suasoriae
author: Seneca the Elder
lyrics:
to be torn by the sea-brutes through a sluggish doom.
And one, striving with battling gaze to break through the air,
when, the world snatched from him, he could make out nothing,
poured forth from his choked breast such words as these:
'Whither are we borne? The very day flees, and farthest nature
shuts off the world we have left in perpetual darkness.
Or do we seek nations set beyond, under another pole,
and another world untouched by storm-winds?
The gods call us back, and forbid mortal eyes
to know the end of things. Why do we violate with our oars
alien seas and the sacred waters, and trouble
the gods' quiet abodes?'"
26. "And the faces, all but breathing still, of those great-souled men
lay upon their own Rostra: but the image of snatched Cicero
carried off all, as though it alone were there.
style: sea epic recitation, bowed drone and deep frame drum, resonant male voice, vast, foreboding, slow swell
why: Pedo's Ocean: "Whither are we borne?" — mortals forbidden to know the end of things, troubling the gods' quiet waters with oars.

title: Suasoriae
author: Seneca the Elder
lyrics:
Then come back to men's minds the consul's mighty deeds,
the sworn bands, the plot of guilt detected,
the patrician sacrilege quenched: the punishment of Cethegus,
and Catiline, cast down with his accursed prayers, returns.
What had they availed  an age cultivated with sacred arts?
One day took away the glory of a lifetime, and, smitten with grief,
the sad eloquence of the Latin tongue fell silent.
He who was once the sole protection and salvation of the anxious,
ever the noble head of his country, he the senate's
champion, he of the forum, of the laws, of right and of the toga,
the public voice, fell dumb for ever before savage arms.
The disfigured features, the gray hair spattered with unspeakable gore,
and the sacred hands, ministers of works so great,
cast down before proud feet  a citizen flung at the feet
style: roman funeral declamation, low strings and muffled drum, grave male voice, heavy, mournful
why: Cicero's head on the Rostra — "one day took away the glory of a lifetime" and the Latin tongue fell silent.

title: De Pythiae oraculis
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
together with what was prophesied concerning the island which the sea threw up right against Thera and Therasia; as also the prediction of the war between King Philip and the Romans, When Trojan race shall tame Phoenicians bold, Prodigious wonders shall the world behold; From burning seas shall flames immense ascend; Lightning and whirlwinds hideous rocks shall rend From their foundations, and an island rear, Dreadful to sight and terrible to hear. In vain shall greater strength and valor then Withstand the contemned force of weaker men.
And the said Simonides a little lower calls Clio somewhat more curiously The chaste inspectress of those sacred wells, Whose fragrant water all her cisterns fills; Water, through dark ambrosial nooks conveyed, By which Castalian rivulets are fed.
style: oracular chant, drone and struck bowl, high wavering female voice, hypnotic, portentous
why: Only candidate, but it carries a whole oracle in verse — flames from burning seas, an island reared up dreadful to hear — plus the Castalian springs.

title: Rhetoric
author: Aristotle
lyrics: Sappho rejoined: Hadst thou desired what was good or noble, and had not thy tongue stirred up some evil to utter it, shame would not have filled thine eyes; but thou would'st have spoken of what is right.
style: aeolic lyric, solo lyre, clear unadorned female voice, intimate, spare
why: Only candidate, and it is Sappho answering: if your wish were good, shame would not have filled your eyes. One closed thought.

title: Persians
author: Aeschylus
lyrics:
Chorus:
Yet the insidious guile of godwhat mortal man can escape it? Who with agile foot can lightly overleap and escape its toils?
Chorus:
For Delusion, with her fair appearance, lures men astray into her snares, from which it is not possible to escape without meeting with disaster.
Chorus:
Therefore my heart is wrapped in gloom and is racked with fear for the Persian army lest the state learn that the mighty capital of Susa is empty of men.
Chorus:
Fearful I am too that as bands of women cry aloud woe, the Cissian stronghold will raise a resounding shout responsive to the beating of breasts, and that there will be a tearing of fine linen robes.
Chorus:
For all the men-at-arms, those who urge on steeds and those who march along the plain, have left the city and gone forth, like bees in a swarm, together with the captain of the host.
style: archaic greek chorus, aulos and low drone, elders' voices in unison, foreboding, measured
why: "What mortal man can escape the guile of god?" — Delusion's fair face, the emptied city, the army gone off like bees in a swarm.

title: Persians
author: Aeschylus
lyrics:
and parents, bereft of their children, in their old age bewail their heaven- sent woes (alas!), now that they learn the full measure of their afflictions.
Chorus:
Not now for long will those who dwell throughout the length and breadth of Asia abide under the sway of the Persians, nor will they pay further tribute at the compulsion of their lord, nor will they prostrate themselves to the earth and do him reverence;
for the royal power has perished utterly.
No longer will men keep a curb upon their tongues; for the people are set free to utter their thoughts at will, now that the yoke of power has been broken.
The blood-stained soil of Ajax sea-washed isle holds all that once was Persia.
Enter Atossa
Atossa:
My friends, whoever has experience of misery knows that when a sea of troubles comes upon mortal men, they view all things with alarm; but when fortune flows with prosperous tide, they believe that this same fortune will forever bring them success. Now in my case everything seems full of dread; before my eyes appears the enmity of the gods, and in my ears there rings a sound that has no note of joy; such is my consternation at the evil tidings which terrify my soul.
style: greek threnody, bowed lyre and frame drum, mixed voices, slow, desolate then defiant
why: The empire ending in one image: the blood-stained soil of Salamis holds all that once was Persia, and tongues go free.

title: Persians
author: Aeschylus
lyrics:
Chorus:
Royal lady, august queen of the Persians, pour these libations down to the chambers of the earth, while we, in solemn chant, beseech the guides of the dead beneath the earth to be gracious to our prayers.
O holy divinities of the nether world, Earth and Hermes, and you, Lord of the dead, send up to the light the spirit from below; for if, beyond our prayers, he knows any further remedy for our distress, he alone of mortals can declare how to bring it to accomplishment.
Chorus:
Does our sainted and godlike king hear me as I utter, in obscure barbaric speech, my dismal and dolorous cries? Or must I shout aloud the utter misery of my anguish so that it pierces the earth? Does he hear me from below?
Chorus:
O Earth, and you other rulers of those who dwell in the nether world, ensure, I implore, that the glorious spirit, the god of the Persians, whom Susa bore, may quit his abode.
style: necromantic invocation, deep drone, struck bronze, chanting male voices, ritual, hypnotic
why: The summoning of Darius from the tomb — libations poured, Earth and Hermes called, a chant with its own liturgy.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
O if the breasts of the rich lay open!
What great fears does lofty fortune drive
within! The Bruttian wave, when the Corus
beats the strait, is gentler;
the poor man bears an untroubled breast.
He holds cups of spreading beechwood,
but he holds them not with trembling hand;
he plucks easy and cheap foods,
but does not look back on drawn swords:
blood is mingled with golden cups.
A wife wed to a modest husband
does not bear, bright with the well-set necklace,
the gifts of the reddening sea,
nor does the stone gathered in the Eastern wave
drag down her gem-bearing ears,
nor, soft in the Sidonian cauldron,
style: roman chorus, plucked lyre and low strings, calm unison voices, plain, steady, consoling
why: Beechwood cups held without a trembling hand against blood mingled with golden ones — the whole moral fits in the images.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
and the sad gods of Erebus,
nor did he fear the Stygian lakes
sworn by the gods above.
The unsteady wheel stood still,
languid, its whirling conquered,
the liver of Tityos grew again,
while with song he held the birds;
and the relentless stone
and the rock could follow the bard;
then for the first time the Phrygian old man,
forgetful, with the waters standing still,
shook off his raging thirst
nor set his hands to the apples.
Heard too was the ferryman,
of the infernal water's flood,
he came with no rowing.
style: orphic hymn, solo lyre and soft drone, warm baritone, spellbound, slow
why: Orpheus in the underworld: the wheel stilled, Tityos' liver healed, Tantalus forgetting his thirst while the song lasts.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
received among the stars, will be safe?
Only far from the rugged Lion
let your father give you a seat, and from the burning Crab,
lest the stars, trembling at your face,
confound their laws and Titan be afraid.
While flowers come in the warming spring,
or summer recalls the foliage to the woods,
and the apples yield as autumn flees,
or winter cuts back the foliage of the woods:
you, companion to Phoebus, shall go companion to the stars.
No age shall snatch you from the lands:
sooner shall the harvest be born in the deep,
or the strait resound with sweet water,
sooner shall the star of the icy Bear
descend and enjoy the forbidden sea,
than your praises among the peoples grow still.
style: apotheosis hymn, harp and strings with rising choir, radiant, broad, exalted
why: Spring, summer, autumn, winter turning past a fixed star — "sooner shall the harvest be born in the deep" than his praises fall silent.

title: Poems
author: Gilbert West
lyrics:
THE HYMN OF CLEANTHES.
BY GILBERT WEST, ESQ.
O Under various sacred names ador'd!
Divinity supreme! all-potent Lord!
Author of nature! whose unbounded sway
And legislative power all things obey!
Majestic Jove! all hail! To thee belong
The suppliant prayer, and tributary song:
To thee from all thy mortal offspring due;
From thee we came, from thee our being drew;
Whatever lives and moves, great Sire! is thine,
Embodied portions of the soul divine.
Therefore to thee will I attune my string,
And of thy wondrous power for ever sing.
The wheeling orbs, the wandering fires above,
That round this earthly sphere incessant move,
style: philosophical hymn, chamber organ and strings, noble tenor, broad, reverent
why: The Hymn of Cleanthes in couplets — one god under many names, and every living thing an embodied portion of the soul divine.

title: Poems
author: Gilbert West
lyrics:
From the moon's relucent horn,
From the star that wakes the morn;
From the bow, whose mingling dyes
Sweetly cheer the frowning skies;
From the silver cloud that sails
Shadowy o'er the darken'd vales;
From th' Elysiums of the sky,
Spirits immortal, hither fly!
CHORUS of SPIRITS.
Fly, and through the limpid air
Guard in pomp the sliding car,
Which to his terrestrial throne
Wafts Britannia's Genius down.
Second SPIRIT.
Hither, all ye heav'nly pow'rs!
From your empyreal bow'rs!
style: baroque masque chorus, recorders, harpsichord and light strings, treble voices, airy, quick
why: "From the moon's relucent horn, from the star that wakes the morn" — spirits summoned in trochaics, with a chorus already written in.

title: Poems
author: Gilbert West
lyrics:
Long in primaeval patriarchal state,
The lord, the judge, the father of the plain,
He dwelt; and with him, in the golden chain
Of wedded faith y-link'd, a matron sage
Aye dwelt; sweet partner of his joy and pain,
Sweet charmer of his youth, friend of his age,
Skill'd to improve his bliss, his sorrows to assuage.
From this fair union, not of sordid gain,
But merit similar and mutual love,
True source of lineal virtue, sprung a train
Of youths and virgins; like the beauteous grove,
Which round the temple of Olympick Jove,
Begirt with youthful bloom the parent tree,
The sacred olive; whence old Elis wove
Her verdant crowns of peaceful victory,
The guerdons of bold strength, and swift activity.
style: spenserian pastoral, lute and viol, gentle baritone, flowing, archaic
why: Two clean Spenserian stanzas on a long marriage and the grove of children around the sacred olive.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Gray
lyrics:
To break my iron-sleep again,
Till Lok has burst his tenfold chain;
Never, till substantial Night
Has reassumed her ancient right;
Till wrapped in flames, in ruin hurled,
Sinks the fabric of the world.
Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
The curfew tolls the knell of parting day,
The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea,
The ploughman homeward plods his weary way,
And leaves the world to darkness and to me.
Now fades the glimmering landscape on the sight,
And all the air a solemn stillness holds,
Save where the beetle wheels his droning flight,
And drowsy tinklings lull the distant folds;
Save that from yonder ivy-mantled tower
style: english elegy, solo cello and chamber organ, low unhurried baritone, hushed, twilit
why: The curfew, the lowing herd, the ploughman — the most famous opening in English elegy, and it needs nothing around it.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Gray
lyrics:
He wound with toilsome march his long array.
Stout Gloster stood aghast in speechless trance:
To arms! cried Mortimer, and couch'd his quiv'ring lance.
I. 2.
On a rock, whose haughty brow
Frowns o'er old Conway's foaming flood,
Robed in the sable garb of woe,
With haggard eyes the Poet stood;
(Loose his beard, and hoary hair
Stream'd, like a meteor, to the troubled air)
And with a Master's hand, and Prophet's fire,
Struck the deep sorrows of his lyre.
'Hark, how each giant-oak, and desart cave,
'Sighs to the torrent's aweful voice beneath!
'O'er thee, oh King! their hundred arms they wave,
'Revenge on thee in hoarser murmurs breathe;
style: welsh bardic lament, harp alone then storm of strings, wild declaiming male voice, building, tempestuous
why: The Bard on the rock above Conway, beard streaming like a meteor, striking the deep sorrows of his lyre.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Gray
lyrics:
Join the wayward work to aid:
'Tis the woof of victory.
Ere the ruddy sun be set,
Pikes must shiver, javelins sing,
Blade with clattering buckler meet,
Hauberk crash, and helmet ring.
(Weave the crimson web of war)
Let us go, and let us fly,
Where our Friends the conflict share,
Where they triumph, where they die.
As the paths of Fate we tread,
Wading thro' th' ensanguin'd field:
Gondula, and Geira, spread
O'er the youthful King your shield.
We the reins to slaughter give,
Ours to kill, and ours to spare:
style: nordic war chant, bowed lyre and heavy drums, layered female voices with a repeating refrain, driving, grim
why: The Fatal Sisters weaving: "Pikes must shiver, javelins sing" and the bracketed refrain "Weave the crimson web of war".

title: Poems
author: John Straight
lyrics:
When from his fragrant ambuscade
He thus accosts the weeping maid.
Cease, Chloe, cease; and do not cry,
Nor blame the harmless tree  'twas I.
'Twas I, that caus'd the little pain,
And I  will make it well again.
My mother bad me do't; and said,
This herb would ease the suff'ring maid.
Let it but to the place be bound,
'Twill stop the blood, and heal the wound.
But, Chloe, if so small a dart,
And in the finger, gives such smart,
What, madam  if I'd pierc'd your heart?
Cease then to scorn my pow'r; and know,
By what I've done, what I can do.
Here he assum'd an aweful look;
style: georgian comic air, harpsichord and flute, arch light tenor, trotting, teasing
why: Cupid stepping out of the rose bush: if so small a dart in the finger smarts, what if I had pierced your heart?

title: Poems
author: John Straight
lyrics:
I've seen the sprig where Cupid stood.
I saw his little fragrant nest
And Chloe told me all the rest.
The POET to his false Mistress.
By the same.
WONDER not, faithless woman, if you see,
Yourself so chang'd, so great a change in me.
With shame I own it, I was once your slave,
Ador'd myself the beauties which I gave;
For know, deceiv'd deceitful, that 'twas I
Gave thy form grace, and lustre to thine eye:
Thy tongue, thy fingers I their magic taught,
And spread the net in which myself was caught.
So pagan priests first form and dress the wood,
Then prostrate fall before the senseless God.
But now, curst woman, thy last sentence hear:
style: 18th century dramatic air, strings and continuo, biting baritone, urgent, imperious
why: The poet revoking the beauty he claims to have lent — pagan priests dressing the wood, then falling before the senseless god.

title: Letters
author: Pliny the Younger
lyrics:
knock at her eloquent door;
he gives whole days to austere Minerva,
while he labours for the ears of the Hundred Men
at that which the ages and posterity might
compare even with the pages of Arpinum.
Safer you will go in the late lamplight;
this is your hour, when Lyaeus rages,
when the rose reigns, when the locks are dripping.
Then let even rigid Catos read me.
14.5. I know besides that the truest law of this kind of work is the one Catullus expressed: "For it befits the devoted poet to be chaste himself; his little verses need not be; which then at last have wit and charm if they are somewhat soft and not too modest."
27.4. "I sing my songs in slender verses, those in which once my Catullus too, and Calvus, and the men of old. But what is that to me? One Plinius is to me the men of old: forsaking the forum, he prefers little verses, and seeks what he may love, and thinks he is loved. O that Plinius, how many Catos is he! Go now, whoever loves, and dare not to love."
style: roman drinking epigram set to music, lyre and hand drum, playful tenor, loose, late-night swing
why: Martial sending his Muse only after dark — when Lyaeus rages, the rose reigns and the hair is dripping — then even rigid Catos may read.

title: Heroicus
author: Flavius Philostratus
lyrics:
Vinedresser
Indeed, stranger, many of those who have approached the island say they hear Achilles singing other things too; but this song, I think, he composed last year, most charmingly, holding to the resolution and the meaning. It is composed thus:
"Echo, dwelling by the boundless water
along the side of the great Black Sea,
my lyre sounds you by my hand;
but do you sing me divine Homer,
the glory of men, the glory of our labors,
through whom I did not die, through whom Patroclus is mine,
through whom my Ajax is equal to the immortals,
through whom the city won by the spear, sung by the wise,
took up glory and did not fallTroy."
748. Vinedresser
From old, stranger. For they say that Heracles, having crucified the body of Asbolus the centaur, inscribed upon it this epigram:
style: greek heroic lyric, solo lyre with sea-drone, clear resonant male voice, echoing, slow, luminous
why: Achilles' own song to Echo across the Black Sea, asking her to sing Homer back to him — a complete lyric with a real conceit.

title: Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren
author: John Maynard Keynes
lyrics:
Dont mourn for me, friends, dont weep for me never, For Im going to do nothing for ever and ever.
With psalms and sweet music the heavensll be ringing, But I shall have nothing to do with the singing.
style: music hall ballad, upright piano and banjo, wry working-class voice, jaunty, deadpan
why: Only candidate, and it is a complete four-line epitaph — the heavens ringing with psalms while she does nothing for ever and ever.

title: Suppliants
author: Euripides
lyrics: Shall I to my home, there to see its utter desolation and the blank within my life? or shall I to the halls of that dead Capaneus?halls I smiled to see in days gone by, when yet my daughter was alive. But she is lost and gone, she that would ever draw down my cheek to her lips, and take my head between her hands; for naught is there more sweet unto an aged sire than a daughters love; our sons are made of sterner stuff, but less winning are their caresses. Oh! take me to my house at once, in darkness hide me there, to waste and fret this aged frame with fasting! What shall it avail me to touch my daughters bones? Old age, resistless foe, how do I loathe thy presence! Them too I hate, whoso desire to lengthen out the span of life, seeking to turn the tide of death aside by philtres, drugs, and magic spells,folk that death should take away to leave the young their place, when they no more can benefit the world.
style: ancient greek lament, lyre, low frame drum, aged male voice, slow, unaccompanied passages, desolate
why: Iphis on losing his daughter — tag-free, complete, and the loveliest thing in the play: no aged sire has anything sweeter than a daughter's love.
