At Holy Russia lets fire a shot. At hutted Russia Thick-rumped and solid, Russia, the stolid, Eh, eh, unhallowed, unblessed.  The Twelve
On the square I was told There where the Kremlin stood as a target, They cut the thread and brought fresh hemp for the yarn.
Thus rave all the fed, Thus longs the satisfaction of important bellies, Their trough is overturned, And confusion is in their foul pen.  A. Blok, The Fed)
style: russian revolutionary song, accordion, balalaika, ragged male chorus, marching, raw, defiant
why: Blok's 'At Holy Russia let's fire a shot... eh, eh, unhallowed, unblessed' beside words settling like halcyon birds on branches.

title: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
author: John Maynard Keynes
lyrics:
In each human heart terror survives
The ruin it has gorged: the loftiest fear
All that they would disdain to think were true:
Hypocrisy and custom make their minds
The fanes of many a worship, now outworn.
They dare not devise good for man's estate,
And yet they know not that they do not dare.
The good want power but to weep barren tears.
The powerful goodness want: worse need for them.
The wise want love; and those who love want wisdom;
And all best things are thus confused to ill.
Many are strong and rich, and would be just,
But live among their suffering fellow-men
As if none felt: they know not what they do.
style: english romantic art song, piano, cello, dark baritone, slow, sombre, resigned
why: Shelley on the wise wanting love and the loving wanting wisdom, 'and all best things are thus confused to ill' — whole and quotable.

title: Gallus
author: Lucian of Samosata
lyrics: Cock: This is probably what you want: "Best of all things is water, but gold-like a flaming fire by night it blazes out from all the haughty store of wealth."
style: pindaric victory ode, kithara, aulos, bright male voice with small chorus, stately, radiant, ceremonial
why: Pindar's opening — water best of all things, gold blazing like fire in the night — the most famous line in Greek lyric.

title: Oedipus Tyrannus
author: Sophocles
lyrics:
It is sweet for our thought to dwell beyond the sphere of grief. Alas, Cithaeron, why did you provide a shelter for me? When I was given to you, why did you not slay me straightway, that I might never reveal my origin to men. Ah, Polybus, ah, Corinth, and you that were called the ancient house of my father, how fair-seeming was I, your nurseling, and what evils were festering underneath! Now I am found to be evil and of evil birth. Oh you three roads, and you secret glen, you, thicket, and narrow way where three paths met you who drank my fathers blood from my own handsdo you remember, perhaps, what deeds I
have performed in your sight, and then what fresh deeds I went on to do when I
came here? Oh marriage rites, you gave me birth, and when you had brought me
style: greek tragic monody, solo aulos, low drone, ravaged male voice, very slow, unbearable, sparse
why: The blinded Oedipus addressing Cithaeron, the three roads and the marriage bed — the most famous speech in Greek tragedy.

title: Oedipus Tyrannus
author: Sophocles
lyrics:
Chorus:
Lycean Lord, would that the shafts from your bent bows string of woven
gold might go forth in their might, our champions in the face of the foe, and the flashing fires of Artemis too, with which she darts through the Lycian hills. I call him whose locks are bound with gold, who is named with the name of this land, ruddy Bacchus to whom Bacchants cry, to draw near with the blaze of his shining torch, our ally against the god unhonored among the gods.
Oedipus:
style: ancient chorus hymn, lyre, frame drum, torch-lit layered voices, building, invocatory, urgent
why: The prayer to the Lycean Lord's golden bowstring, Artemis' fires and Bacchus with his blazing torch — a real invocation.

title: Oedipus Tyrannus
author: Sophocles
lyrics:
Teiresias:
Though you are king, the right of reply must be considered the same for both: over that I have control.
For I do not live as your slave, but as Loxias. I will not stand enrolled as Creons
client. And I tell you, since you have taunted my blindness, that though you
have sight, you do not see what a state of misery you are in, or where you
dwell, or with whom.
Do you know who your parents are? You have been an unwitting enemy to your own kin, both
in the Underworld and on the earth above, and the double lash of your mothers
and your fathers curse will one day drive you from this land in dreadful
haste, with darkness upon those eyes of yours which now can see.
What place will be harbor to your cries, what part of all Cithaeron will not ring with them soon, when you have learned the meaning of the nuptials in which, within that house, you found a fatal haven, after a voyage so fair? And you have not guessed at a throng of other ills which will bring you level with your true self and with your own children. Therefore heap your scorn upon Creon and upon my message: for no man will ever be crushed more miserably than you.
style: prophetic chant, deep drone, struck bell, grave old male voice, slow, implacable, gathering dread
why: Teiresias: you have sight and do not see; the double lash of your parents' curse will drive you out with darkness on your eyes.

title: Poems
author: Joel Barlow
lyrics:
To the glad swain proclaims his day's work done,
Night's pleasing shades his various task prolong,
And yield new subjects to my various song.
For now, the corn-house fill'd, the harvest home,
Th' invited neighbours to the Husking come;
A frolic scene, where work, and mirth, and play,
Unite their charms, to chace the hours away.
Where the huge heap lies center'd in the hall,
The lamp suspended from the cheerful wall,
Brown corn-fed nymphs, and strong hard-handed beaux,
Alternate rang'd, extend in circling rows,
Assume their seats, the solid mass attack;
The dry husks rustle, and the corn-cobs crack;
The song, the laugh, alternate notes resound,
And the sweet cider trips in silence round.
The laws of Husking ev'ry wight can tell;
style: american husking-bee tune, fiddle, banjo, hammered dulcimer, hearty male lead with mixed chorus, brisk, communal
why: The husking: rustling husks, cracking cobs, laughter, and cider going round in silence — a whole night in one scene.

title: Poems
author: Joel Barlow
lyrics:
A grain whose rich luxuriant growth requires
Short gentle showers, and bright etherial fires.
But here, tho' distant from our native shore,
With mutual glee we meet and laugh once more.
The same! I know thee by that yellow face,
That strong complexion of true Indian race,
Which time can never change, nor soil impair,
Nor Alpine snows, nor Turkey's morbid air;
For endless years, thro' every mild domain,
Where grows the maize, there thou art sure to reign.
But man, more fickle, the bold licence claims,
In different realms to give thee different names.
Thee the soft nations round the warm Levant
Polanta call, the French of course Polante;
Ev'n in thy native regions, how I blush
To hear the Pennsylvanians call thee Mush!
style: mock-georgic comic air, fiddle, penny whistle, wry tenor, moderate, affectionate, jesting
why: The poet recognising his cornmeal abroad by its yellow face, then blushing that Pennsylvanians call it Mush.

title: Poems
author: Joel Barlow
lyrics:
Hail the mild morning, where the dawn began,
The full fruition of the hopes of Man:
Where sage experience seals the sacred cause;
And that rare union, liberty and laws,
Speaks to the reas'ning race; to freedom rise
Like them be equal, and like them be wise.
THE HASTY-PUDDING: A POEM.
CANTO I.
YE Alps audacious, thro' the Heav'ns that rise,
To cramp the day and hide me from the skies;
Ye Gallic flags, that o'er their heights unfurl'd,
Bear death to kings, and freedom to the world,
I sing not you. A softer theme I chuse,
A virgin theme, unconscious of the Muse,
But fruitful, rich, well suited to inspire
The purest frenzy of poetic fire.
style: mock-heroic invocation, small brass, snare, grandly ironic baritone, stately then winking, moderate
why: 'Ye Alps audacious... I sing not you. A softer theme I chuse' — the joke of the whole poem stated in its opening lines.

title: Poems
author: Horace Walpole
lyrics:
Of some luxurious Satrap's barb'rous lust.
The greatest curses any Age has known,
Have issued from the Temple or the Throne;
Extent of ill from Kings at first begins,
But Priests must aid, and consecrate their sins.
The tortur'd Subject might be heard complain,
When sinking under a new weight of chain,
Or more rebellious might perhaps repine,
When tax'd to dow'r a titled Concubine,
But the Priest christens all a Right Divine.
When at the altar a new Monarch kneels,
What conjur'd awe upon the people steals!
The chosen HE adores the precious oil,
Meekly receives the solemn charm, and while
The Priest some blessed nothings mutters o'er,
Sucks in the sacred grease at ev'ry pore:
style: augustan satirical air, harpsichord, oboe, crisp cutting baritone, brisk, sardonic
why: 'The greatest curses any Age has known, / Have issued from the Temple or the Throne' — with the king sucking in the sacred grease.

title: Poems
author: Horace Walpole
lyrics:
The lovely form of Goddess LIBERTY!
For her in Senates be he train'd to plead,
For her in Battles be he taught to bleed.
Lead him where Dover's rugged cliff resounds
With dashing seas, fair Freedom's honest bounds,
Point to yon azure Carr bedropp'd with gold,
Whose weight the necks of Gallia's sons uphold;
Where proudly sits an iron-scepter'd Queen,
And fondly triumphs o'er the prostrate scene,
Cry, That is Empire! shun her baleful path,
Her Words are Slavery, and her Touch is Death!
Thro' wounds and blood the Fury drives her way,
And murthers half, to make the rest her prey.
Thus spoke each Spartan matron, as she dress'd
With the bright cuirass the young soldier's breast;
On the new warrior's tender-sinew'd thigh,
style: patriotic declamation, martial snare, strings, ringing tenor with chorus, stirring, defiant
why: 'That is Empire! shun her baleful path, / Her Words are Slavery, and her Touch is Death!' — pure singable rhetoric.

title: Poems
author: Horace Walpole
lyrics:
And ZEUXIS' composition-piece,
Where every nymph that could at most
Some single grace or feature boast,
Contributed her favourite charm
To perfect the ideal form.
'Twas CYNTHIA'S brow, 'twas LESBIA'S eye,
'Twas CLOE'S cheeks' vermilion dye;
ROXANA lent the noble air,
Dishevell'd flow'd ASPASIA'S hair,
And CUPID much too fondly press'd
His mimick mother THAIS' breast.
Antiquity, how poor thy use!
A single Venus to produce!
Friend Eckardt, ancient story quit,
Nor mind whatever Pliny writ;
Felibien and Fresnoy declaim,
style: rococo drawing-room song, fortepiano, flute, light elegant tenor, graceful, playful
why: Zeuxis assembling a goddess out of borrowed features — Cynthia's brow, Lesbia's eye, Chloe's vermilion cheek.

title: Poems
author: John Gerrard
lyrics:
And may these bodings ne'er with truth agree,
May grief and anguish be unknown to thee,
May bitter memory ne'er recount with pain,
That e'er you frown'd, or I admir'd in vain.
No more  my spirit is prepar'd to fly,
Supprest my voice, and stiffen'd is my eye:
Death's swimming shadows intercept my view,
Vain world, and thou relentless nymph, adieu!
A SONG.
BY THE SAME.
YE scenes that engag'd my gay youth,
Say, whither so fast do ye fly?
If the lesson you told me was truth,
Ah! why do ye fade from my eye?
That meadow where often I stray'd,
That bank, and yon shadowy tree,
style: pastoral folk song, acoustic guitar, flute, warm tenor, gentle, wistful, with a returning refrain
why: 'Ye scenes that engag'd my gay youth, / Say, whither so fast do ye fly?' — an actual song, with its question coming round again.

title: Poems
author: John Gerrard
lyrics:
How shall I tell the anguish of my Fate!
Teach me, remorseless monsters, not to feel,
Instruct me, fiends and furies, to relate!
Wrathful behind the guilty shade I stole,
I rais'd the tube  the clamorous woods resound
Too late I saw the idol of my soul,
Struck by my aim, fall shrieking to the ground!
No other bliss her soul allow'd but me;
(Hapless the pair that thus indulgent prove)
She sought concealment from a shady tree,
In amorous silence to observe her love.
I ran  but O! too soon I found it true!
From her stain'd breast life's crimson stream'd apace
From her wan eyes the sparkling lustres flew
The short-liv'd roses faded from her face!
Gods!  could I bear that fond reproachful look,
style: english elegy ballad, harp, cello, plaintive tenor, slow, stark, catching at the turn
why: The gun raised at the moving shade, and the idol of his soul falling shrieking to the ground — the ballad's whole hinge.

title: Poems
author: John Gerrard
lyrics:
That strove her peerless innocence to plead!
But partial death awhile her tongue forsook,
To save a wretch that doom'd himself to bleed.
While I distracted press'd her in my arms,
And fondly strove t' imbibe her latest breath;
"O spare, rash love, she cry'd, thy fatal charms,
" Nor seek cold shelter in the arms of death.
"Content beneath thy erring hand I die.
" Our fates grew envious of a bliss so true;
"Then urge not thy distress when low I lie,
" But in this breath receive my last adieu! "
No more she spake, but droop'd her lily head!
In death she sicken'd  breathless  haggard  pale
While all my inmost soul with horror bled,
And ask'd kind vengeance from the passing gale.
Where slept your bolts, ye lingering lightnings say?
style: deathbed lament, solo viol, low harp, tenor with a fading female voice, very slow, tender
why: Her dying words forgiving the hand that killed her — 'Content beneath thy erring hand I die'.

title: On the Nature of the Gods
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
lyrics: 89. And as that shepherd in Accius, who had never before seen a ship, when from a mountain he beheld afar the divine and strange vessel of the Argonauts, at first wondering and terrified speaks in this wise: 'So vast a mass glides roaring from the deep with mighty din and breath: it rolls the waves before it, by force whirls up eddies, plunges headlong, drenches the sea, blows it back; so that now you would believe a broken storm-cloud is rolling, now that some rock, driven by the winds or by tempests, is being snatched aloft, or that round whirlwinds are arising, struck by the clashing waves  unless the sea is stirring up some wreck of the land, or perhaps Triton, overturning with his trident the caverns beneath the very roots, heaves from the depths a mass of rock to the sky in the surging strait': at first he doubts what that nature is which he beholds unknown; and the same man, when the youths are seen and the sailors' song is heard, says, 'Like swift and eager dolphins snorting with their snouts'  and much else besides  that the song is borne to his ears like to the melody of Silvanus
style: latin dramatic recitation with music, aulos, low strings, rising percussion, awed male voice, surging like sea swell
why: The shepherd who has never seen a ship watching the Argo come on — terror, then the sailors' song heard as Silvanus' music.

title: On the Nature of the Gods
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
lyrics:
107. And while its whole shape is splendid, yet above all are to be looked upon the figure of its head and the fire of its eyes: for it not a single star alone that gleams adorning its head, but its temples are marked with a double brightness, and from its fierce eyes two glowing lights flash, and its chin shines with one radiant star; its head is bent aslant, but turned back on its rounded neck, so that you would say it fixed its gaze upon the tail of the Greater Bear.
108. And the rest of the Dragon's body we behold all night long; this its head here a little, and suddenly, hides itself, where rising and setting are mingled in one quarter. And touching this head there turns, as it were the image of one weary and mourning, which the Greeks are wont to call Engonasin (the Kneeler), because it is borne propped on its knees. Here is placed, with surpassing brightness, that Crown. And these things indeed are behind; but near the head is the Serpent-holder, whom the Greeks call by the famous name Ophiuchus.
style: star-hymn, kithara, small bells, sustained drone, low male voice, slow, nocturnal, glittering
why: The Dragon's head with its double-marked temples and two glowing eyes, gazing back at the tail of the Great Bear.

title: Letters to Lucilius
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
14. Nor among the Greek tragedians are there lacking those who barter innocence, safety, a good name, for gain. "Let me be called most base, so I be called rich." "Whether he be rich, we all ask; whether good, no one. Not for what reason or whence, only what you have, do they ask. Everywhere each man has been worth as much as he had. What is it shameful for us to have? Nothing. Either I choose to live rich or to die poor. He dies well, whoever dies while making gain." "Money, the mighty good of the human race, to which neither a mother's pleasure can be equal, nor a fawning child's, nor a father holy by his deserts; if anything so sweet shines in the face of Venus, deservedly does money move the loves of gods and men."
12. When he had recited these verses"Phoebus begins to bring forth his burning flames, the ruddy day to spread itself; now the sad swallow, returning, begins to bring food to her shrill nestlings, and shares it out, serving it from her soft beak"Varus, a Roman knight, a companion of Marcus Vinicius, an attender of good dinners, which he earned by the wickedness of his tongue, exclaimed: "Buta is beginning to sleep." Then, when he had presently recited:
style: sardonic latin chorus, low brass, plucked strings, ironic baritone with answering chorus, marching, swaggering
why: 'Let me be called most base, so I be called rich' — and money outbidding mother, child and father in the face of Venus.

title: Letters to Lucilius
author: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus
lyrics:
16. 'But if you look back to the swift sun and the stars that follow in order, never will tomorrow's hour deceive you, nor will you be ensnared by the treacheries of a cloudless night.' It has been provided fully and abundantly that I should be safe from snares.
5. "Oh, how shall I name you, maiden? For your face is not mortal, nor does your voice sound human. Be propitious, and lighten our toil, whoever you are." She will be present and will lighten it, if we are willing to worship her. But she is worshipped not by the slaughter of fat bulls' bodies, nor by gold and silver hung up, nor by coin poured into her treasury, but by a pious and upright will.
13. "The palace of the Sun was high with lofty columns, bright with flashing gold." Look at his chariot too: "The axle was of gold, the pole of gold, of gold the rim of the topmost wheel, and the row of spokes of silver." In short, the age that men wish to seem the best they call golden.
style: roman hymn to philosophy, lyre, soft chorus, reverent tenor, slow, golden, spacious
why: 'Your face is not mortal, nor does your voice sound human' — a goddess worshipped by an upright will, not slaughtered bulls.

title: Letters of Marcus Tullius Cicero
author: Cicero (Marcus Tullius Cicero)
lyrics:
Compliance gets us friends, plain speaking hate.
He plants his trees to serve a race to come,
For happy though but ill, for ill not worst.
Ashamed to shrink and yet afraid to take.
. . . . For dreams descend from Jove.
Few were his words, but wonderfully strong.
She took great care to fall with decency.
Patroclus lies in death.
Who swayed his people with a fathers love:
Priscus, at thy command
Though my shockd soul recoils, my tongue shall tell.
The brave and mean an equal honour find.
 All Ive foreseen, and oft in thought revolvd;
Reclind on clouds his steed and armour lay.
style: roman epistolary litany, solo lyre, sparse strings, half-spoken male voice, unhurried, one line at a time, reflective
why: A string of quoted tags that reads as a litany — compliance gets us friends, plain speaking hate; he plants trees for a race to come.

title: De Heroditi malignate
author: Plutarch
lyrics: And their honorary sepulchre at the Isthmus has on it this epitaph: When Greece upon the point of danger stood, We fell, defending her with our life-blood.
style: greek funeral epigram, bowed lyre, single low drum, unison male voices, very slow, stone-carved, solemn
why: The Isthmus epitaph entire: 'When Greece upon the point of danger stood, / We fell, defending her with our life-blood.'

title: Aeneid
author: Virgil
lyrics:
Arms and the man I sing, who first made way, predestined exile, from the Trojan shore to Italy, the blest Lavinian strand.
Smitten of storms he was on land and sea by violence of Heaven, to satisfy stern Juno's sleepless wrath; and much in war he suffered, seeking at the last to found the city, and bring o'er his fathers' gods to safe abode in Latium; whence arose the Latin race, old Alba's reverend lords, and from her hills wide-walled, imperial Rome.
O Muse, the causes tell! What sacrilege, or vengeful sorrow, moved the heavenly Queen to thrust on dangers dark and endless toil a man whose largest honor in men's eyes was serving Heaven? Can gods such anger feel?
In ages gone an ancient city stood
Carthage, a Tyrian seat, which from afar made front on Italy and on the mouths of Tiber 's stream; its wealth and revenues were vast, and ruthless was its quest of war.
style: roman epic invocation, lyre and low drone, resonant male recitation, stately, processional
why: The most famous opening in Latin literature, complete from first line to the founding of Carthage.

title: Aeneid
author: Virgil
lyrics:
The oracle foretold thy fate, too well!
Scarce had he spoken, when a pair of doves
Before his very eyes flew down from heaven
To the green turf below; the prince of Troy
Knew them his mother's birds, and joyful cried,
0, guide me on, whatever path there be!
In airy travel through the woodland fly,
To where yon rare branch shades the blessed ground.
Fail thou not me, in this my doubtful hour,
0 heavenly mother! So saying, his steps lie stayed,
Close watching whither they should signal give;
The lightly-feeding doves flit on and on,
Ever in easy ken of following eyes,
Till over foul Avernus' sulphurous throat
Swiftly they lift them through the liquid air,
In silent flight, and find a wished-for rest
style: ancient mediterranean art song, kithara and soft flute, hushed tenor, gentle, questing
why: The doves guiding Aeneas to the golden bough — pure image, a prayer, and a journey in one passage.

title: Aeneid
author: Virgil
lyrics:
No hand could stay Evander. Forth he flew into the midmost tumult, and fell prone on his dead Pallas, on the resting bier;
he clung to the pale corse with tears, with groans, till anguish for a space his lips unsealed:
Not this thy promise, Pallas, to thy sire, to walk not rashly in the war-god's way.
I knew too well how honor's morning-star, and sweet, foretasted glory tempt and woo in a first battle. O first-fruit forlorn of youth so fair! O prelude pitiless of war approaching! O my vows and prayers, which not one god would hear! My blessed wife, how happy was the death that spared thee not to taste this bitterness! But I, the while, by living longer lived to meet my doom, a father sole-surviving. Would I myself had perished by the Rutule's cruel spear, the Trojan's cause espousing! This breath of life how gladly had I given! And O, that now yon black solemnity were bearing home myself, not Pallas, dead! Yet blame I not,
style: latin funeral lament, muted horn and low strings, grieving baritone, slow, keening
why: Evander over the body of Pallas: the strongest self-contained lament in the poem.

title: Stichus
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
SAGARINUS:
(pledging STICHUS.)
Heres to you first of all.
STICHUS:
Tis a droll thing this, for two persons, rivals of each other, to be courting, to be drinking from one goblet, and to be kissing one wench.Tis worthy of remark this: I am you, you are I; of one accord are we. With one mistress are we both in love; when shes with me, still shes with you; and when shes with you, shes with me as well; neither of us envies the other.
SAGARINUS:
Come, come, theres enough of it; I dont want it overdone to weariness. Id now like some other sport.
STICHUS:
Drink on, if you are drinking.
SAGARINUS:
There shall be no skulking in me.
But, troth, Ive had enough of the feast; would but our mistress come here. If she were here, nothing else would be away.
STICHUS:
Should you like us to invite our mistress out? She shall give us a dance.
style: roman comic drinking song, double pipes, hand drum, two rowdy male voices, brisk, tipsy
why: Two rival slaves sharing one cup and one girl — 'I am you, you are I' is the line the play is remembered for.

title: Stichus
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
SAGARINUS:
This banquet, for our means, is quite sufficient, with its nuts, beans, figs, a dish of olives, pounded lupines, and a cake.
STICHUS:
It better becomes a man who is a slave to bring his expenses within moderation than beyond. Each one to his own station; they, who have wealth at home, drink from cups, goblets, and bowls; we, if we are now drinking from our Samian jug, still build our walls according to our means.
SAGARINUS:
But while she who is your mistress and mine is arranging her hair, and bedecking herself, I wish us to have some diversion among ourselves. I appoint you the commander of this feast.
STICHUS:
Very aptly does it suggest itself to your mind.
SAGARINUS:
Wouldnt we be more suitably entertained like Cynics on benches here, than upon couches?
STICHUS:
style: tavern patter song, plucked lyre and wooden clappers, wry male voice, quick, sly
why: Nuts, beans, figs, olives and a Samian jug: concrete, funny, and a whole philosophy of means in eight lines.

title: Poems
author: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
style: georgian parlour lament, harpsichord and viol, clear soprano, slow, bitter
why: Flavia after the smallpox — 'Beauty is fled, and dress is now no more' — her best-known and most unsparing passage.

title: Poems
author: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
style: baroque love complaint, continuo and solo violin, expressive soprano, rubato, intimate
why: A complete love complaint built on rising verbs: 'I sigh, I faint, I tremble at your touch.'

title: Poems
author: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
lyrics:
And no spring your charms renew.
I, like you, was born a woman,
Well I know what vapours mean:
The disease, alas! is common;
Single, we have all the spleen.
All the morals that they tell us,
Never cur'd the sorrow yet:
Chuse, among the pretty fellows;
One of honour, youth, and wit.
Prithee hear him every morning,
At the least an hour or two;
Once again at night returning
I believe the dose will do.
Answer to the foregoing Lines.
By the late Lord HERVEY.
TOO well these lines that fatal truth declare,
style: witty georgian ballad, spinet and light strings, arch mezzo voice, trotting, comic
why: Trochaic ballad stanzas prescribing a lover as medicine for the spleen — already half a song.

title: Poems
author: Samuel Whyte
lyrics:
ELEGY I.
'TIS night, dead night; and o'er the plain
Darkness extends her ebon ray,
While wide along the gloomy scene
Deep Silence holds her solemn sway:
Throughout the earth no chearful beam
The melancholic eye surveys,
Save where the worm's fantastic gleam
The 'nighted traveller betrays:
The savage race (so Heaven decrees)
No longer thro' the forest rove;
All nature rests, and not a breeze
Disturbs the stillness of the grove:
All nature rests; in Sleep's soft arms
The village swain forgets his care:
Sleep, that the sting of Sorrow charms,
style: georgian nocturne elegy, chamber strings and low flute, plaintive tenor, slow, hushed
why: 'Tis night, dead night' — a whole nocturne of stilled forest, glow-worm and sleeping village, in clean quatrains.

title: Poems
author: Samuel Whyte
lyrics:
O shun her paths, the traitress shun!
Her voice is death, her smile is fate,
Who hears, or sees her, is undone.
And, when Death's hand shall close my eye,
(For soon, I know, the day will come)
O chear my spirit with a sigh,
And grave these lines upon my tomb!
THE EPITAPH.
Consign'd to dust, beneath this stone,
In manhood's prime is Damon laid;
Joyless he liv'd, and dy'd unknown
In bleak misfortune's barren shade.
Lov'd by the Muse, but lov'd in vain
'Twas beauty drew his ruin on;
He saw young Daphne on the plain;
He lov'd, believ'd, and was undone.
style: graveyard ballad, solo guitar and cello, low male voice, mournful, unhurried
why: Ends on the epitaph itself: 'He lov'd, believ'd, and was undone.'

title: Poems
author: Samuel Whyte
lyrics:
As, taught by heaven's informing power,
From every fruit and every flower,
That nature opens to the view,
The bee extracts the nectar-dew;
A vagrant thus, and free to change
From fair to fair I vow'd to range,
And part from each without regret
As pleas'd and happy as I met.
Then Freedom's praise inspir'd my tongue,
With Freedom's praise the vallies rung,
And every night and every day,
My heart thus pour'd th' enraptur'd lay:
"My cares are gone, my sorrows cease,
"My breast regains its wonted peace,
"And joy and hope returning prove,
"That Reason is too strong for Love. "
style: pastoral ode with refrain, flute and harpsichord, light tenor, lilting, rueful
why: The bee ranging flower to flower, with a genuine four-line refrain to sing back.

title: Poems
author: Samuel Wesley
lyrics:
EUPOLIS' Hymn to the Creator.
AUTHOR of Being, Source of Light,
With unfading Beauties bright,
Fulness, Goodness, rolling round
Thy own fair Orb without a Bound:
Whether Thee thy Supplicants call
Truth, or Good, or One, or All,
Ei or Iao; Thee we hail
Essence that can never fail,
Grecian or Barbaric Name,
Thy stedfast Being still the same.
Thee, when Morning greets the Skies
With rosy Cheeks and humid Eyes;
Thee, when sweet-declining Day
Sinks in purple Waves away;
Thee will I sing, O Parent Jove
style: grand baroque hymn, chapel organ and trumpet, full choir, broad, exalted
why: 'Author of Being, Source of Light' — a hymn opening that names the god by every name and still holds together.

title: Poems
author: Samuel Wesley
lyrics:
Of Jove and Thee We are the Care.
O Father King, whose heav'nly Face
Shines serene on All thy Race,
We thy Magnificence adore,
And thy well-known Aid implore:
Nor vainly for thy Help we call;
Nor can we want: For thou art All!
On the CRUCIFIXION.
BEHOLD the Saviour of Mankind
Nail'd to the shameful Tree!
How vast the Love that Him inclin'd
To bleed and die for Thee!
Hark how he groans! while Nature shakes,
And Earth's strong Pillars bend!
The Temple's Veil in sunder breaks,
The solid Marbles rend.
style: solemn passion hymn, sparse organ and low strings, dark male choir, slow, grave
why: 'Behold the Saviour of Mankind' — Wesley's best-known hymn, with the temple veil tearing at its centre.

title: Poems
author: Samuel Wesley
lyrics:
Pale Death with all his ghastly Train
My Soul encompast round,
Anguish and Sin, and Dread and Pain
On ev'ry Side I found.
To Thee, O LORD of Life, I pray'd,
And did for Succour flee:
O save (in my Distress I said)
The Soul that trusts in Thee!
How good Thou art! How large thy Grace!
How easy to forgive!
The helpless Thou delight'st to raise:
And by thy Love I live.
Then, O my Soul, be never more
With anxious Thoughts distrest,
GOD's bounteous Love doth Thee restore
To Ease and Joy and Rest.
style: psalm paraphrase, gallery choir with viols, warm mixed voices, moderate, consoling
why: Psalm 116 in ballad metre: death encompassing round, then release — a complete arc.

title: Cromwell and Communism: Socialism and Democracy in the Great English Revolution
author: Eduard Bernstein
lyrics:
You noble Diggers all, stand up now, stand up now, You noble Diggers all, stand up now; The waste Land to maintain, seeing Cavaliers by name Your digging does disdaine, and persons all defame. Stand up now, stand up now.
With spades, and hoes, and plowes, stand up now, etc. Your Freedom to uphold, seeing Cavaliers are bold To kill you if they could, and rights from you to hold. Stand up now, diggers all.
The gentry is all round, on each side they are found; Their wisdom is so profound to cheat us from our ground.
The Clergy they come in, and say it is a sin That we should now begin, our freedom for to win.
To conquer them by love, come in now, come in now. To conquer them by love, come in now; To conquer them by love, as it does you behove, For he is king above, no power is like to love, Glory hear Diggers all.
style: seventeenth century english protest ballad, fiddle and bodhran, rough unison male chorus, driving, defiant
why: The Diggers' Song itself — built on a shouted refrain, made to be sung by a crowd.

title: Cromwell and Communism: Socialism and Democracy in the Great English Revolution
author: Eduard Bernstein
lyrics:
The Poore long Have suffered wrong, By the gentry of this Nation, The Clergy they Have bore a great sway By their base insultation. But they shall Lye levell with al They have corrupted our Fountains; And then we shall see Brave Community When Vallies lye levell with Mountains.
The time is nigh That this mystery Shall be no more obscure, And then we shall see Such community As shall alwayes indure The Rich and Poore Shall love each other Respecting of Persons shall fall, The Father alone That sits in his throne Shall be honoured of all.
The glorious Hate, Which I do relate, Unspeakable comfort shall bring, The corn will be greene And the Flowers seene Our Store-houses they will be filld. The Birds will rejoyce With a merry voice All things shall yield sweet increase. Then let us all sing And joy in our King Which causeth all sorrowes to cease.
style: levelling folk hymn, hurdy-gurdy and hand drum, mixed rustic voices, steady, rising
why: 'Brave Community When Vallies lye levell with Mountains' — the vision song of the English radicals.

title: Modern French Philosophy: A Study of the Development Since Comte
author: John Alexander Gunn
lyrics:
_La nature fatale offre a la Liberte Un probleme_.
. . . _Video meliora proboque deteriora sequor_.
_Ce mot si doux au coeur et si cher, Liberte, Jen prefers encore un: cest Solidarite._
Ah, Love! could thou and I with Fate conspire To grasp this sorry Scheme of Things entire, Would we not shatter it to bitsand then Re-mould it nearer to the hearts desire.
Give me the glory of going on and not to die!
Supprimer Dieu, serait-ce amoindrir lunivers?
Children of men! the unseen Power, whose eye For ever doth accompany mankind, Hath lookd on no religion scornfully That men did ever find.
style: contemplative art song, solo piano and cello, restrained baritone, slow, meditative
why: Only candidate; a chain of epigraphs on freedom and fate that reads as a coherent lyric.

title: De astrologia
author: Lucian of Samosata
lyrics:
Nay, be it thine to control the delightsome duties of wedlock, and anent those of warfare,
These shall all be the care of impetuous Mars and Minerva.
style: greek oracular chant, lyre and aulos, single male voice, sparse, incantatory
why: Only candidate; an oracle dividing wedlock from war between the gods — short but whole.

title: Description of Greece
author: Pausanias
lyrics:
These statements she made in her poetry when in a frenzy and possessed by the god. Elsewhere in her oracles she states that her mother was an immortal, one of the nymphs of Ida, while her father was a human. These are the verses: I am by birth half mortal, half divine; An immortal nymph was my mother, my father an eater of corn; On my mother's side of Idaean birth, but my fatherland was red Marpessus, sacred to the Mother, and the river Aidoneus.
However, death came upon her in the Troad, and her tomb is in the grove of the Sminthian with these elegiac verses inscribed upon the tomb-stone: Here I am, the plain-speaking Sibyl of Phoebus, Hidden beneath this stone tomb. A maiden once gifted with voice, but now for ever voiceless, By hard fate doomed to this fetter. But I am buried near the nymphs and this Hermes, Enjoying in the world below a part of the kingdom I had then. The Hermes stands by the side of the tomb, a square-shaped figure of stone. On the left is water running down into a well, and the images of the nymphs.
style: greek oracular chant, lyre and low drone, veiled female voice, slow, incantatory
why: The Sibyl names her own half-mortal birth, then speaks from her tombstone: 'A maiden once gifted with voice, but now for ever voiceless.'

title: Description of Greece
author: Pausanias
lyrics:
Maenalia is storm-swept, where lies Arcas, from whom all Arcadians are named, In a place where meet three, four, even five roads; Thither I bid you go, and with kind heart Take up Arcas and bring him back to your lovely city. There make Arcas a precinct and sacrifices. This place, where the grave of Arcas is, they call Altars of the Sun.
Adrastus, son of Talaus, son of Cretheus, The very first of the Danai to drive his famous horses, Swift Caerus and Areion of Thelpusa, Whom near the grove of Oncean Apollo Earth herself sent up, a marvel for mortals to see.
Azanian Arcadians, acorn-eaters, who dwell In Phigaleia, the cave that hid Deo, who bare a horse, You have come to learn a cure for grievous famine, Who alone have twice been nomads, alone have twice lived on wild fruits. It was Deo who made you cease from pasturing, Deo who made you pasture again After being binders of corn and eaters of cakes, Because she was deprived of privileges and ancient honors given by men of former times. And soon will she make you eat each other and feed on your children, Unless you appease her anger with libations offered by all your people, And adorn with divine honors the nook of the cave.
style: delphic prophecy chant, aulos and hand drum, harsh male voice, ominous, building
why: Demeter's threat to the acorn-eaters of Phigaleia — famine, cannibalism, and a bargain, all in hexameters.

title: Description of Greece
author: Pausanias
lyrics:
Dwellers in the land of Pelops and in Achaia, who to Pytho Have come to inquire how ye shall take a city, Come, consider what daily ration, Drunk by the folk, saves the city which has so drunk. For so ye may take the towered village of Phana.
On this day the Attic contingent surpassed the other Greeks in courage. Of the Athenians themselves the bravest was Cydias, a young man who had never before been in battle. He was killed by the Gauls, but his relatives dedicated his shield to Zeus God of Freedom, and the inscription ran: Here hang I, yearning for the still youthful bloom of Cydias, The shield of a glorious man, an offering to Zeus. I was the very first through which at this battle he thrust his left arm, When the battle raged furiously against the Gaul.
style: votive hymn, kithara and soft percussion, clear tenor, measured, elegiac
why: A dead man's shield speaks from the wall, and Homer is told he has no fatherland, only a motherland.

title: Juliana
author: Cynewulf
lyrics:
Hark! We have heard it, a history for heroes,
of days long departed, when a dark power reigned.
Merciless Maximian, a man who held mastery
over the wide world, a wicked emperor
who raised up terror, a relentless persecution,
and hunted God's people. He harried the righteous,
spilling their sacred blood, servants of glory.
He tore down God's temples, and turned them to ruin,
and kindled his pyres for the Christian believers,
who held to the holy truth. He hewed them down,
felled the faithful in front of his idols.
There was a reeve then, a rich and powerful man,
who ruled in the city of Nicomedia.
Eleusius he was called, an eager persecutor.
This lord of the heathens loved idols and treasure,
and his heart was hardened. He held a great hatred
style: old english scop, bowed lyre and frame drum, low male chant, stark, declamatory
why: 'Hark! We have heard it' — the alliterative opening sets the persecution and the whole world of the poem in sixteen lines.

title: Juliana
author: Cynewulf
lyrics:
were sunk by the waters, drowned in the flood-tide,
under the rushing stream by my crafts.
Some I delivered to the cross, so that they, grieving,
gave up their lives on the high gallows.
Some I drew with my teachings, drove them to strife,
so that they suddenly renewed old grudges,
drunk on beer. I poured them strife from a cup,
so that in the wine-hall, by the grip of a sword,
they sent their souls from their bodies,
fated to fall, beset by sorrows.
Some, whom I found without Gods sign,
careless, unblessed, I boldly struck
with my own hands, with cunning thoughts,
through various torments. I cannot recount,
though I were to sit for a summer-long day,
all the evils I have ever worked with deceit,
style: dark ritual chant, bowed lyre and rasping drone, growling male voice, ominous, driving
why: The devil's inventory of his own work: strife poured from a cup in the wine-hall, souls sent out by the sword.

title: Juliana
author: Cynewulf
lyrics:
with his troop of fiends, sought the sea-stream by ship,
and tossed over the flood for a long while
on the swans road. Death took them all,
that host of men, and himself with them,
before they had reached the land,
through a terrible torment. There thirty-four
of that warrior-kin were deprived of their lives
by the waves surge, lowly with their lord,
bereft of joy, without hope they sought hell.
Those thanes had no need to expect, in that dark home,
that company in the deep abyss, that their treasure-giver
would grant them rings in the wine-hall,
apple-gold from the beer-bench.
It was far different for the holy one. Her body was led
with songs of praise, by a great company,
to its grave of earth. A great host of people
style: anglo-saxon elegy, solo bowed lyre, hollow male voice, slow, cold
why: Drowned on the swan's road, with no treasure-giver to hand them apple-gold from the beer-bench — the great Old English image of the lost hall.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Warton
lyrics:
From their firm base, increase the mould'ring mass.
Far as the sight can pierce, appear the spoils
Of sunk magnificence! a blended scene
Of moles, fanes, arches, domes, and palaces,
Where, with his brother Horror, Ruin sits.
O come then, Melancholy, queen of thought!
O come with saintly look, and stedfast step,
From forth thy cave embower'd with mournful yew,
Where to the distant curfeu's solemn sound
List'ning thou sitt'st, and with thy cypress bind
Thy votary's hair, and seal him for thy son.
But never let Euphrosyne beguile
With toys of wanton mirth my fixed mind,
Nor in my path her primrose-garland cast.
Tho' 'mid her train the dimpled Hebe bare
Her rosy bosom to th' enamour'd view;
style: gothic chamber song, viola da gamba and chamber organ, dark tenor, slow, brooding
why: The invocation of Melancholy from her yew-bowered cave, with Ruin sitting among sunk magnificence.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Warton
lyrics:
Th' unshaken Britomart; or Milton knew,
When in abstracted thought he first conceiv'd
All heav'n in tumult, and the Seraphim
Come tow'ring, arm'd in adamant and gold.
Let others love soft summer's ev'ning smiles,
As, list'ning to the distant water-fall,
They mark the blushes of the streaky west;
I choose the pale December's foggy glooms.
Then, when the sullen shades of ev'ning close,
Where thro' the room a blindly-glimm'ring gleam
The dying embers scatter, far remote
From Mirth's mad shouts, that thro' th' illumin'd roof
Resound with festive echo, let me sit,
Blest with the lowly cricket's drowsy dirge.
Then let my thought contemplative explore
This fleeting state of things, the vain delights,
style: winter nocturne, solo cello and muted piano, low male voice, unhurried, wistful
why: 'I choose the pale December's foggy glooms' — dying embers and the cricket's drowsy dirge, a complete mood in itself.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Warton
lyrics:
O bid my well-rang'd numbers rise
Pervious to none but Attic eyes;
O give the strain that madness moves,
Till every starting sense approves!
What felt the Gallic traveller,
When far in Arab-desert drear
He found within the catacomb,
Alive, the terrors of a tomb?
While many a mummy thro' the shade,
In hieroglyphic stole array'd,
Seem'd to uprear the mystic head,
And trace the gloom with ghostly tread;
Thou heardst him pour the stifled groan,
Horror! his soul was all thy own!
O mother of the fire-clad thought,
O haste thee from thy grave-like grot!
style: gothic ode, tremolo strings and distant horn, urgent tenor, restless, eerie
why: The traveller shut alive in a catacomb while the mummies seem to rise — the strongest image in the poems.

title: Poems
author: (Mary) Matilda Betham
lyrics:
Who prizes more the diamond's glow,
Than all in humbler vest array'd.
Sweet is the rural festive song,
Which sounds so wildly o'er the plain,
When thoughtless mirth the notes prolong,
And heart-felt pleasure pours the strain.
Sweet is the dance where light and gay,
The village maiden trips along;
Her simple robe in careless play,
As her fleet step winds round the throng.
Sweet is the labourer's blazing fire,
When evening shades invite to rest;
Though weary, home does joy inspire,
And social love dilates his breast.
His rural lass with glee prepares,
The dainties fondness made her hoard;
style: pastoral folk ballad, acoustic guitar and fiddle, warm female vocal, unhurried, sweet
why: Built on 'Sweet is...' anaphora — village dance, labourer's fire, concrete and already half a song.

title: Poems
author: (Mary) Matilda Betham
lyrics:
There will, at some far-distant spot,
A streak of light appear,
Or, when the sullen vapours break,
The ether will be clear.
And if the sun illumes the east,
And sheds his gladsome ray,
Some boding mist, or passing cloud
Will threat the rising day.
The heart rejoicing in the view,
And dancing with delight,
Oft feels the touch of palsied fear,
And sinks at thought of night.
So Hope's bright torch more clearly shines,
Amidst surrounding gloom,
And, beldame Fortune vainly throws
Her mantle o'er the tomb.
style: hymn-metre reflection, parlour piano and soft strings, gentle soprano, steady, hopeful
why: Clean common-metre stanzas on light breaking through cloud, ending 'Hope's bright torch more clearly shines, amidst surrounding gloom.'

title: Poems
author: (Mary) Matilda Betham
lyrics:
Though still she clasp'd her hero's valued corse,
She slowly rais'd her languid, streaming eyes,
And own'd astonishment's resistless force,
Viewing the stranger with a wild surprize.
The form was clad in robes of purest white,
That swept with solemn dignity the ground;
Contrasting with the blackest gloom of night,
Which reign'd in awful majesty around.
The silver beard did reverence demand,
And told her that a holy bard was there,
Whose shrivell'd fingers grasp'd a flaming brand,
Which threw a lustre on the waving hair.
His eye possess'd the brilliant fire of youth,
United with the wisdom of the sage;
And speaking, with the simple voice of truth,
He blended the solemnity of age.
style: gothic ballad, harp and low strings, hushed female voice, mysterious, slow
why: The white-robed bard appearing out of black night with a flaming brand — the one genuinely visual passage.

title: Poems
author: Charles Parrott
lyrics:
At length descends a browner shade;
At length the glimm'ring objects fade:
'Till all submit to NIGHT'S impartial reign,
And undistinguish'd darkness covers all the plain.
No more the ivy-crowned oak
Resounds beneath the wood-man's stroke.
Now Silence holds her solemn sway;
Mute is each bush, and ev'ry spray:
Nought but the sound of murm'ring rills is heard,
Or from the mould'ring tow'r, NIGHT'S solitary bird.
Hail sacred hour of peaceful rest!
Of pow'r to charm the troubled breast!
By thee the captive slave obtains
Short respite from his galling pains;
Nor sighs for liberty, nor native soil;
But for a while forgets his chains, and sultry toil.
style: georgian nocturne ode, chamber strings and flute, calm tenor, slow, tender
why: Night falling over the plain, the woodman's axe silent, and the slave briefly forgetting his chains.

title: Poems
author: Charles Parrott
lyrics:
Pomp and pow'r, and tinsel state,
Those false pageants of the great,
Crowns and scepters, envied things,
And the pride of Eastern kings,
Are but childish empty toys,
When compar'd to Love's sweet joys,
Love alone can pleasure give,
Only while we love, we live.
style: valentine air with refrain, harpsichord and recorder, light soprano, dancing, playful
why: Real refrain lines that circle back: 'Only while we love we live, love alone can pleasure give.'

title: Poems
author: Charles Parrott
lyrics:
No horrors hast thou in thy train,
No scorpion lash, no clanking chain.
When the pale murd'rer round him spies
A thousand grisly forms arise,
When shrieks and groans arouse his palsy'd fear,
'Tis guilt alarms his soul, and conscience wounds his ear.
The village swain whom Phillis charms,
Whose breast the tender passion warms,
Wishes for thy all-shadowing veil,
To tell the fair his love-sick tale:
Nor less impatient of the tedious day,
She longs to hear his tale, and sigh her soul away.
Oft by the covert of thy shade
LEANDER woo'd the THRACIAN maid;
Thro' foaming seas his passion bore,
Nor fear'd the ocean's thund'ring roar.
style: baroque love song, lute and viol, ardent tenor, flowing, warm
why: Leander crossing the roaring sea for the torch hung out of the tower — a whole myth in six lines.

title: De Officiis
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
lyrics:
There is no fellowship inviolate,
No faith is kept, when kingship is concerned;
Gold will I none, nor price shall ye give; for I ask none;
Come, let us not be chaff'rers of war, but warriors embattled.
Nay; let us venture our lives, and the sword, not gold, weigh the outcome.
Make we the trial by valour in arms and see if Dame Fortune
Wills it that ye shall prevail or I, or what be her judgment.
Hear thou, too, this word, good Fabricius: whose valour soever
Spared hath been by the fortune of war-their freedom I grant them.
Such my resolve. I give and present them to you, my brave Romans;
Take them back to their homes; the great gods' blessings attend you.
Who kindly sets a wand'rer on his way
Does e'en as if he lit another's lamp by his:
No less shines his, when he his friend's hath lit.
style: roman martial recitation, war horn and low drum, commanding baritone, stately, resolute
why: Pyrrhus refusing ransom — 'the sword, not gold, weigh the outcome' — and then the lamp lit from another's lamp.

title: Burke
author: John Morley
lyrics:
"The muse nor can, nor will declare, What is my work, and what my studies there."
That pious moralist, that reasoning saint! Can I of worth like thine, Eusebius, speak? The man is willing, but the muse is weak.
When France in wrath her giant limbs upreared, And with that oath, which smote air, earth, and sea, Stamped her strong foot, and said she would be free.
Oro parumper Attendas quantum de legibus ipse queratur Fatorum et nimio de stamine, quum videt acris Antilochi barbam ardentem: quum quaerit ab omni Quisquis adest socius, cur haec in tempora duret, Quod facinus dignum tam longo admiserit aevo.
style: revolutionary art song, solo piano and cello, declamatory baritone, slow, gathering
why: Only candidate; the Coleridge lines on France stamping her strong foot carry it.

title: Protagoras
author: Plato
lyrics:
In hands and feet and mind foursquare,
Fashioned without reproach.
That word of Pittacus
And yettwas a sage who spakeHard, quoth he, to be good.
style: greek lyric fragment, solo lyre, single unaccompanied male voice, sparse, aphoristic
why: Only candidate; the Simonides fragment on the foursquare man and Pittacus' 'Hard to be good' — the axis of the dialogue.

title: Mahābhārata
author: Vyāsa
lyrics:
In Krttika, the first of mansions, a fierce planet, blazing and stealing away forms with its glare, stands like a smoking comet.
Through all three of the earlier mansions, O lord of peoples, Budha (Mercury) repeatedly speeds, engendering exceedingly great fear.
A fourteenth-day moon, a fifteenth-day moon, and once even a sixteenth I have known; but this new moon falling on a thirteenth day I have never known before.
Both moon and sun eclipsed within a single month, on the thirteenth day and out of their proper season  these two seizures shall bring the peoples to ruin.
All the quarters are wrapped in dust, with showers of grit on every side; and dreadful portent-clouds rain down blood in the night.
Again, on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, at midnight, there came a fierce and most terrible rain of flesh, whereat the raksasas glutted themselves unsated.
style: sanskrit apocalyptic recitation, tanpura drone and heavy mridangam, deep male voice, ominous, building
why: The portents before Kurukshetra — sun and moon eclipsed in one month, clouds raining blood, a rain of flesh at midnight.

title: Mahābhārata
author: Vyāsa
lyrics:
Then once that great ascetic, taking no food and feeding on air alone, stood still as a log, unmoved, and stirred not at all.
While he stood thus, become like a tree-stump, motionless, O Bharataa pair of kulinga sparrows, O king, made a nest upon his head.
That compassionate brahmin-seer watched the mated pair as they fashioned their little nest there in his matted locks with strands of grass.
And since that great ascetic, become like a stump, stirred not at all, the two birds, grown wholly trusting, dwelt there in ease.
Then, when the rains had passed and the autumn season had come, the pair, made trusting and overcome by desire, after the manner ordained of Prajapati,
those two skyfarers, O king, let fall their eggs upon his head; and that splendid brahmin of strict vows became aware of them.
style: gentle sanskrit chant, tanpura and bamboo flute, warm male voice, slow, tender
why: The ascetic standing still as a tree-stump until sparrows nest and lay their eggs in his matted hair.

title: Mahābhārata
author: Vyāsa
lyrics:
Beside Drona, slain by the son of Drupada, O slayer of Madhu, Krpi sits in piteous grief, her senses overborne by sorrow.
Behold her, weeping and anguished, her hair unbound, her face cast down, attending upon her slain husband Drona, best of those who bear arms.
Beside Drona, his armor pierced through by the arrows of Dhrstadyumna, O Kesava, sits she upon the field, her hair matted, faithful and chaste.
And Krpi, delicate and renowned, stricken and forlorn, strives to perform the funeral rites of her lord slain in battle.
Bringing the sacred fires as the rite ordains and kindling the pyre on every side, the chanters of the Saman lay Drona upon it and sing the three Saman melodies.
And these matted-haired celibate students heap the pyre with bows, with spears, and with the framework-seats of chariots, O Madhava.
style: sanskrit funeral lament, sarangi and low drone, keening female-led voices, slow, grieving
why: Kṛpī with unbound hair beside Droṇa's pyre, students heaping it with bows and spears while the Sāman is sung.

title: Bacchae
author: Euripides
lyrics:
nearby, raving Satyrs were fulfilling the rites of the mother goddess, and they joined it to the dances of the biennial festivals, in which Dionysus rejoices.
Chorus:
He is sweet in the mountains, whenever after the running dance he falls on the ground, wearing the sacred garment of fawn skin, hunting the blood of the slain goat, a raw-eaten delight, rushing to the
Phrygian, the Lydian mountains, and the leader of the dance is Bromius, evoe! The plain flows with milk, it flows with wine, it flows with the nectar of bees.
style: ancient ecstatic chorus, frame drums and shrill aulos, layered female voices, accelerating, wild
why: The parodos itself: 'The plain flows with milk, it flows with wine, it flows with the nectar of bees.'

title: Bacchae
author: Euripides
lyrics:
Chorus:
Io! Io! Master, master! Come now to our company, Bromius.
Dionysus:
Shake the worlds plain, lady Earthquake!
Chorus:
Oh! Oh! Soon the palace of Pentheus will be shaken in ruin.
Dionysus is in the halls.
Revere him.
We revere him!
Did you see these stone lintels on the pillars falling apart? Bromius cries out in victory indoors.
Dionysus:
Light the fiery lamp of lightning!
Burn, burn Pentheus home!
Chorus:
Oh! Oh! Do you not see the the fire, do you not perceive, about the sacred tomb of Semele, the flame that Zeus thunderbolt left?
Cast on the ground your trembling bodies, Maenads, cast them down, for our lord, Zeus son, is coming against this palace, turning everything upside down.
style: ritual call and response, deep drums and low horns, antiphonal voices, frenzied, thunderous
why: The palace miracle — 'Shake the world's plain, lady Earthquake!' — already written as call and response.

title: Bacchae
author: Euripides
lyrics:
When they did not succeed in their toils, Agave said: Come, standing round in a circle, each seize a branch, Maenads, so that we may catch the beast who has climbed aloft, and so that he does not make public the secret dances of the god. They applied countless hands to the pine and dragged it up from the earth. Pentheus fell crashing to the ground from his lofty seat, wailing greatly: for he knew he was in terrible trouble.
His mother, as priestess, began the slaughter, and fell upon him. He threw the headband from his head so that the wretched Agave might recognize and not kill him. Touching her cheek, he said: It is I, mother, your son, Pentheus, whom you bore in the house of Echion.
Pity me, mother, and do not kill me, your child, for my sins.
But she, foaming at the mouth and twisting her eyes all about, not thinking as she ought, was possessed by Bacchus, and he did not persuade her.
style: tragic messenger lament, single aulos and low strings, stark solo voice, slow, harrowing
why: Pentheus throwing off the headband so his mother might know him — the most terrible recognition in Greek tragedy.

title: Poems
author: Ambrose Philips
lyrics:
Whose Fate he wept, a faithful Shepherd he.
Awake my Pipe; in ev'ry Note express
Fair Stella's Death, and Colinet's Distress.
O woful Day! O Day of Woe! quoth he;
And woful I, who live the Day to see!
That ever she could die! O most unkind,
To go, and leave thy Colinet behind!
And yet, why blame I her? Full fain would she,
With dying Arms, have clasp'd her self to me:
I clasp'd her too; but Death was all too strong,
Nor Vows, nor Tears could fleeting Life prolong.
Teach me to grieve, with bleating Moan, my Sheep;
Teach me, thou ever-flowing Stream, to weep;
Teach me ye faint, ye hollow Winds, to sigh,
And let my Sorrows teach me how to die:
Now Flock, nor Stream, nor Winds can e'er relieve
style: pastoral dirge with refrain, oboe and muted strings, plaintive tenor, slow, mournful
why: Built on repeated 'Teach me' lines and a returning refrain: 'Awake my Pipe; in ev'ry Note express fair Stella's Death.'

title: Poems
author: Ambrose Philips
lyrics:
HOBBINOL.
I love in secret all a beauteous Maid,
And have my Love in secret all repaid.
This coming Night she does reserve for me.
Divine her Name; and thou the Victor be.
LANQUET.
Mild as the Lamb, unharmful as the Dove,
True as the Turtle, is the Maid I love.
How we in secret love, I shall not say.
Divine her Name, and I give up the Day.
HOBBINOL.
Soft on a Cowslip Bank, my Love and I
Together lay: A Brook ran murm'ring by.
A thousand tender things to me she said;
And I a thousand tender Things repaid.
LANQUET.
style: alternating shepherds' duet, recorder and lute, two light voices trading verses, lilting, courting
why: Amoebean couplets swapped between two singers — cowslip bank, murmuring brook, love kept secret.

title: Poems
author: Ambrose Philips
lyrics:
From my fond Heart the racking Pains of Love.
LANQUET.
What profits me, that I in Charms have skill,
And Ghosts and Goblins order as I will;
Yet have, with all my Charms, no Pow'r to lay
The Sprite, that breaks my Quiet Night and Day.
HOBBINOL.
O that, like Colin, I had Skill in Rhymes:
To purchase Credit with succeeding Times!
Sweet Colin Clout! who never yet had Peer,
Who sung thro' all the Seasons of the Year.
LANQUET.
Let me like Wrenock sing; his Voice had Pow'r
To free the clipsing Moon at Midnight Hour:
And, as he sung, the Fairies, with their Queen,
In Mantles blue came tripping o'er the Green.
style: fairy pastoral, harp and soft flute, clear tenor, gentle, enchanted
why: Ends on the singer whose voice freed the eclipsed moon and brought the fairy queen tripping over the green in blue mantles.

title: Poems
author: William Shenstone
lyrics:
Written at an INN on a particular Occasion.
TO thee, fair Freedom! I retire,
From flattery, feasting, dice, and din;
Nor art thou found in domes much higher
Than the low cot, or humble inn.
'Tis here with boundless power I reign,
And every health which I begin,
Converts dull port to bright champain;
For Freedom crowns it at an inn.
I fly from pomp, I fly from plate,
I fly from Falshood's specious grin;
Freedom I love, and form I hate,
And chuse my lodgings at an inn.
Here, waiter! take my sordid ore,
Which Iacqueys else might hope to win;
It buys what courts have not in store,
style: english tavern air, fiddle and cittern, hearty baritone, steady, convivial
why: 'To thee, fair Freedom! I retire' — Shenstone's most quoted poem, four square stanzas made for singing at a table.

title: Poems
author: William Shenstone
lyrics:
Only purest on the plain!
Peers can no such charms discover,
All in stars and garters drest,
As, on Sundays, does the lover
With his nosegay on his breast.
Pinks and roses in profusion,
Said to fade when Chloe's near;
Fops may use the same allusion,
But the shepherd is sincere.
Hark to yonder milk-maid singing,
Cheerly o'er the brimming pail;
Cowslips all around her springing
Sweetly paint the golden vale.
Never yet did courtly maiden
Move so sprightly, look so fair;
Never breast with jewels laden
style: pastoral folk ballad, acoustic guitar and fiddle, warm female vocal, unhurried, bright
why: Trochaic and already tuneful: the milkmaid singing over the brimming pail with cowslips springing around her.

title: Poems
author: William Shenstone
lyrics:
SAYS Richard to Thomas (and seem'd half afraid)
I am thinking to marry thy mistress's maid:
Now because Mrs. Martha to thee is well known,
I will do't if thou bidst me, or let it alone.
Nay don't make a jest on't, 'tis no jest to me;
For faith I'm in earnest, so prithee be free.
I have no fault to find with the girl since I knew her.
But I'd have thy advice, ere I tye myself to her.
Said Thomas to Richard  to speak my opinion,
There is not such a bitch in king George's dominion!
And I firmly believe, if thou knew'st her as I do,
Thou would'st chuse out a whipping-post, first, to be ty'd to.
She's peevish, she's thievish, she's ugly, she's old,
And a lyar, and a fool, and a slut, and a scold
Next day Richard hasten'd to church and was wed,
And ere night had inform'd her what Thomas had said.
style: comic broadside ballad, banjo-like plucked strings and bodhran, wry male voice, brisk, deadpan
why: A complete joke with a punchline — Richard asks advice, is warned off, marries her, and tells her what Thomas said.

title: Lysistrata
author: Aristophanes
lyrics:
CHORUS OF ATHENIANS
Bring on the dance, summon the Graces, call upon Artemis, and her twin, the chorus-leading Healer, gracious, and the Nysian one, who flashes Bacchic fire among his maenads, and Zeus blazing with fire, and the blessed queen his consort; and then the divinities whom we'll call as witnesses, not forgetful, of gentle-minded Peace, which the goddess Cypris made. Alalai! Hurrah for the Healer! Leap up highhurrah!as for victoryhurrah! Euoi, euoi, euai, euai!
CHORUS OF SPARTANS
style: greek festival dance, double pipes and clashing cymbals, massed voices with cries, fast, jubilant
why: The closing hymn — Spartan girls like fillies kicking dust beside the Eurotas, hair tossing, feet beating.

title: Lysistrata
author: Aristophanes
lyrics:
CHORUS OF WOMEN
Fly, fly, Nicodice, before Calyce and Critylla are burned upblown about by cruel winds and by deadly old men. But I'm afraid of this: have I come too late to help? For just now I filled my pitcher at dawn, with difficulty, at the fountain, amid the crowd and the uproar and the clatter of pots, jostled by slave-girls and branded knavesand snatching it up eagerly I bring water to help my fellow-townswomen who are being burned.
CHORUS OF WOMEN
For I heard that some doddering old men were on the move, carrying logs to the citadel as if to heat a batha three-talent weightuttering the most dreadful threats, that the loathsome women must be reduced to charcoal by fire. O goddess, may I never see them burningbut rather see them rescuing Greece and the citizens from war and madness! That is why, O gold-crested guardian of the city, they have taken their seats in your shrine. And I call you to my aid, Tritogeneia: if any man sets those women alight, help us carry water!
style: urgent women's chorus, hand drums and reed pipe, quick female voices, running tempo, breathless
why: The water-carrying chorus racing the fire, with the fountain, the jostling, and the prayer to Tritogeneia.

title: Lysistrata
author: Aristophanes
lyrics:
CHORUS OF OLD MEN
I want to tell you a tale, which I once heard myself when I was still a boy. There was a young man called Melanion, who, fleeing marriage, came to the wilderness and lived in the mountains. He hunted hares, weaving nets, and kept a dogand he never came back home again, out of hatred. So loathing of women had he, that fellow; and we who are chaste are no less than Melanion.
CHORUS OF WOMEN
And I want to tell you a tale in answer to your Melanion. There was a certain Timon, a roamer with no fixed home, his face fenced about with impassable thorns, an offshoot of the Furies. So this Timon went off out of hatred, hurling many curses at wicked men. So that man hated your wicked men forever, in return, but to the women he was dearest.
CHORUS OF OLD MEN
In dreadful misery, poor wretch, your soul wears away, deceived. And I pity youalas! For what kidney could hold out, what soul, what testicles, what loins, what backside, stretched taut and getting no screwing at dawn?
style: comic antiphonal chorus, plucked lyre and clappers, two opposing groups of voices, brisk, mocking
why: Melanion answered by Timon — two rival tales traded between choruses, built for alternating verses.

title: Ab urbe condita
author: Titus Livius (Livy)
lyrics: City. Regarding this as a favourable opportunity for mischief, they despatched some light-armed cohorts to harry the Roman territory, in the belief that the Romans would either let the outrage pass unpunished to avoid having another war on their shoulders, or would resent it with a small and weak force. The Romans felt more indignation than anxiety at the raid, and without making any great effort, took prompt steps to avenge it. A. Postumius and L. Julius raised a force, not by a regular levy for they were obstructed by the tribunes of the plebs but consisting mostly of volunteers whom they had induced by strong appeals to come forward. With this they advanced by cross marches through the territory of Caere and surprised the Tarquinians as they were returning heavily laden with booty. They slew great numbers, stripped the whole force of their baggage, and returned with the recovered possessions from their farms to Rome. Two days were allowed for the owners to identify their property; what was unclaimed on the third day, most of it belonging to the enemy, was sold under the spear, and the proceeds distributed amongst the soldiers. The issues of the other wars, especially of that against Veii, were still undecided, and the Romans were already despairing of success through their own efforts, and were looking to the Fates and the gods, when the embassy returned from Delphi with the sentence of the oracle. It was in accord with the answer given by the Veientine soothsayer, and ran as follows:  See to it, Roman, that the rising flood At Alba flow not o'er its banks and shape Its channel seawards. Harmless through thy fields Shalt thou disperse it, scattered into rills. Then fiercely press upon thy foeman's walls, For now the Fates have given thee victory. That city which long years thou hast besieged Shall now be thine. And when the war hath end, Do thou, the victor, bear an ample gift Into my temple, and the ancestral rites Now in disuse, see that thou celebrate Anew with all their wonted pomp.
style: roman oracular recitation, low drone and single horn, grave male voice, measured, prophetic
why: Only candidate; the Delphic response about the Alban flood and the fall of Veii closes it in real verse.

title: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
author: Max Weber
lyrics:
They, looking back, all the eastern side beheld Of paradise, so late their happy seat, Waved over by that flaming brand; the gate With dreadful faces thronged and fiery arms. Some natural tears they dropped, but wiped them soon: The world was all before them, there to choose Their place of rest, and Providence their guide.
 ... Only add Deeds to thy knowledge answerable; add faith; Add virtue, patience, temperance; add love, By name to come called Charity, the soul Of all the rest: then wilt thou not be loth To leave this Paradise, but shall possess A Paradise within thee, happier far.
style: english devotional art song, chamber organ and viol, solemn baritone, slow, valedictory
why: Only candidate, and it is the close of Paradise Lost: 'The world was all before them.'

title: The Natural and Artificial Right of Property Contrasted
author: Thomas Hodgskin
lyrics:
Who see God in clouds, and hear him in the storm,
Tongues in trees, books in the running brooks,
Sermons in stones, and good in every thing,
style: pastoral hymn, solo acoustic guitar, soft tenor, spacious, reverent
why: Only candidate; two famous lines about finding tongues in trees and sermons in stones — short but whole.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
author: Vālmīki
lyrics:
The ascetic Valmiki questioned Narada  the foremost among those devoted to austerity and sacred study, the best of the eloquent, the bull among sages.
"Who in this world today is truly virtuous, and also mighty? Who knows righteousness, and is grateful, truthful in speech, and steadfast in his vows?
Who is endowed with noble character, and who is a benefactor to all creatures? Who is learned, who is capable, and who is ever pleasant to behold?
Who is self-possessed, who has conquered anger? Who is radiant and free from envy? Whom do even the gods fear when his wrath is aroused in battle?
I wish to hear of such a one  my curiosity is boundless. O great seer, you are capable of knowing such a man."
Having heard these words of Valmiki, Narada  who has knowledge of the three worlds  addressed him saying "Hear me!" and, delighted, spoke thus:
style: sanskrit invocation, tanpura drone and bamboo flute, deep male voice, slow, questioning
why: The question that starts the whole epic — 'Who in this world today is truly virtuous?' — a litany of questions that stands alone.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
author: Vālmīki
lyrics:
The sky was filled with bands of great seers, Gandharvas, Nagas, and Yaksas; it was clear and pure and wide, frequented by Visvavasu.
He moved through the sky traversed by the elephant of the king of gods, along the path of the moon and the sun, the auspicious canopy of the world of the living, spread out and fashioned by Brahma.
Frequented on all sides by heroes and by noble hosts of Vidyadharas, great clouds blazed as the monkey drew them in his wake.
Darting into masses of clouds and bursting out again and again, he shone like the moon in the rainy season, emerging and entering in turn.
But seeing him flying, a raksasi named Simhika, enormous and able to assume any form at will, thought within her mind:
"Today, after a long time, I shall eat my fill; this great creature has come within my power after so long."
style: soaring sanskrit chant, tanpura and rapid tabla, bright male voice, fast, exhilarated
why: Hanumān flying the moon's path, bursting in and out of cloud-banks, with Siṃhikā waiting below.

title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
author: Vālmīki
lyrics:
"Today the king Vaivasvata is even more honoured by me  he by whom you, O mighty-armed one, have today been united with the law of time."
"This is the path of great warriors even among all the hosts of immortals: the man who is slain for his master's sake attains heaven."
"Today all the hosts of gods, the world-guardians, and the sages will sleep in peace and without fear, having seen Indrajit slain."
"Today the three entire worlds and the earth with all its forests, bereft of Indrajit alone, seem void to me."
"Today I shall hear in the inner apartments the wailing of the raksasa women, like the trumpeting of a herd of female elephants in a mountain cave."
"O scorcher of foes, the crown-princeship, Lanka, the raksasas, your mother, me, and your wife  where have you gone, abandoning us all?"
style: sanskrit lament, sarangi and low drone, grieving male voice, slow, heavy
why: Rāvaṇa over Indrajit, each line beginning 'Today' and ending 'where have you gone, abandoning us all?'

title: Persa
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
(Enter TOXILUS and SAGARISTIO, on different sides..)
TOXILUS:
(to himself.)
He who, falling in love, destitute of means, has first entered upon the paths of love, has in his own labours exceeded all the labours of Hercules. For with the lion, and with the Hydra, with the stag, with the Aetolian boar, with the birds of Stamphalus, with Antaeus, would I rather contend than with love. So wretched am I become with hunting after money to borrow; and yet, those whom I ask know of nothing to answer me, except I have got none.
SAGARISTIO:
(apart.)
The servant that is desirous faithfully to serve his master, i troth, it surely does behove him to treasure up full many a thing in his breast which he may think will please his master, both present and abroad.
I neither serve with cheerfulness, nor am I quite to my masters satisfaction; but, as though from a running eye, my master is still unable to keep his hands off me, in giving me his commands, in making me the support of his affairs.
style: roman comic aria, double pipes and hand drum, exasperated male voice, brisk, mock-heroic
why: The penniless lover claiming his labours outdo Hercules' — lion, Hydra, stag, boar, birds of Stymphalus.

title: Persa
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
(to himself.)
The old and ancient calling of my forefathers do I follow, and hold, and cultivate with great care.
For never was there any one of my forefathers, but that by acting the parasite they filled their bellies: my father, grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather, his father, and his grandfather, just like mice, always fed on the victuals of others, and in love of good eating no one could excel them.
Hard Heads was their surname. From them have I derived this calling, and the station of my forefathers; nor do I wish myself to turn informer, nor indeed does it become me, without risk of my own, to go seize upon the goods of other people; nor do those persons please who do so; Im speaking out.
For whoever does this, more for the sake of the public than of his own benefit, my mind can be induced to believe that he is a citizen both faithful and deserving; but if he should not prosecute to conviction the breaker of the laws, let him pay one half of the intended penalty to the public. And let this, too, be written in that law;
style: patter song, plucked lyre and clappers, fast male voice, rattling, boastful
why: The parasite's ancestral trade recited down the generations: 'just like mice, always fed on the victuals of others.'

title: Persa
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
from which spot Ill cause all to become merry, joyous, and delighted, by the aid of whom those things which I wished to be effected have been rendered for me easy to be done; for worthless is the man who knows how to receive a kindness, and knows not how to return it.
(Enter LEMNISELENE, SAGARISTIO, and PAEGNIUM, from the house.)
LEMNISELENE:
My Toxilus, why am I without you? And why are you without me?
TOXILUS:
Come then, my own one, approach me, and embrace me, please.
LEMNISELENE:
Indeed I will.
(Embraces him.)
TOXILUS:
O, nothing is there more sweet than this.
But, theres a dear, apple of my eye, why dont we at once betake us to the couches?
LEMNISELENE:
Everything that you wish, the same do I desire.
TOXILUS:
Its mutual. Come, come-come then. You, Sagaristio, recline in the upper place.
style: roman banquet duet, tibiae and tambourine, two warm voices, lilting, amorous
why: 'Why am I without you? And why are you without me?' — a love duet that walks straight to the couches.

title: Poems
author: Lady Mary Chudleigh
lyrics:
When he was doom'd by his own Hand to die,
She beg'd him with the Sentence to comply;
Told him a wretched Life deserv'd no Care,
And that a Roman never ought to fear:
Bid him remember with what noble Pride
The valiant Curtius, and the Decii dy'd;
And how th' immortal Brutus Death's griefly Form defy'd:
But when she saw her Reasons could not move,
She gave a vast, a wondrous Proof of Love:
With hast she snatch'd his Poniard from his Side,
And with her dearest Blood the fatal Weapon dy'd;
Then drawing it undaunted from her Breast,
And with a Look that no Concern exprest,
She smiling gave it to his trembling Hand,
And said, O Petus, thus, thy Fate command:
Thus, Csar's Malice, and thy Stars defie;
style: baroque dramatic aria, harpsichord and strings, steady soprano, measured, unflinching
why: Arria stabs herself first and hands back the dagger smiling: 'O Petus, thus, thy Fate command.'

title: Poems
author: Lady Mary Chudleigh
lyrics:
From whence with blameless Scorn she views
The Follies of Mankind;
And smiles to see how each pursues
Joys fleeting as the Wind.
Yonder's the little Ball of Earth,
It lessens as I rise;
That Stage of transitory Mirth,
Of lasting Miseries:
My Scorn does into Pity turn,
And I lament the Fate
Of Souls, that still in Bodies mourn,
For Faults which they create:
Souls without Spot, till Flesh they wear,
Which their pure Substance stains:
While they th' uneasie Burthen bear,
They're never free from Pains.
style: visionary art song, chamber organ and viol, clear high voice, slow, rising
why: The soul climbing away from earth — 'Yonder's the little Ball of Earth, it lessens as I rise.'

title: Poems
author: Lady Mary Chudleigh
lyrics:
On the Death of his Highness the Duke of Glocester.
I'LE take my Leave of Business, Noise and Care,
And trust this stormy Sea no more:
Condemn'd to Toil, and fed with Air,
I've often sighing look'd towards the Shore:
And when the boistrous Winds did cease,
And all was still, and all was Peace,
Afraid of Calms, and flatt'ring Skies,
On the deceitful Waves I fixt my Eyes,
And on a sudden saw the threatning Billows rise:
Then trembling beg'd the Pow'rs Divine,
Some little safe Retreat might be for ever mine:
O give, I cry'd, where e'er you please,
Those Gifts which Mortals prize,
Grown fond of Privacy and Ease,
I now the gaudy Pomps of Life despise.
style: pindaric sea ode, cello and harpsichord, warm alto, swelling, restless
why: A whole storm-at-sea figure for a life of business, ending in the plea for a safe retreat.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Holcroft
lyrics:
When May-Day Garlands deck'd the Pole?
Or, Prize propos'd to glide the Green,
Who sooner reach'd the distant Goal?
How slow and feeble now my Tread!
Those Feet which erst have won the Prize
Are only swift to reach the Bed
Where, undistinguish'd, Merit lies.
This Arm athletic once could raise
The massy Beam, the pond'rous Stone;
Loud echo'd forth the Village Praise
When I the whirling Quoit have thrown.
Behold it wither'd, now, and weak,
