Its brawny Texture quite forgot;
Its languid Pulse, slow winding, seek
The Mansion where to rest and rot!
When I into the Circle sprung,
style: village lament ballad, solo fiddle and guitar, aged male voice, slow, rueful
why: The old athlete counting what his arm could once lift, now 'wither'd, weak' — plain quatrains, real grief.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Holcroft
lyrics:
And learning is, still, something worse;
You've form'd one comprehensive curse,
More vast, and certain to engulph us,
Than that erst utter'd by Ernulphus.
The more we search, the more we find,
We're feeble, foolish, vain, and blind;
This only certain seems to be,
We're all absurd uncertainty.
Our joys are false, and false our tears,
False are our hopes, and false our fears.
Our pleasure, like the rainbow, shews
Then only beauteous when not close;
Tho', glorious in its shining birth,
It seems to reach from heav'n to earth,
Approach to touch it, and you'll see
'Twill vanish in nonentity!
style: skeptic's air, spare piano and cello, dry baritone, unhurried, wry
why: 'Our joys are false, and false our tears' — and the rainbow that vanishes when you reach it.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Holcroft
lyrics:
ELEGY.
AH! what avails the fancied Lore of Man,
Or all the envied Gifts the Gods bestow?
His Wisdom Folly, Length of Time a Span,
His Life is Vanity, his Death is Woe!
Could Wit protect, had Genius power to save,
Did they immortal Life with Fame impart,
Alexis ne'er had known a dreary Grave,
Death ne'er had drench'd an Arrow in his Heart.
Mourn, mourn, ye Spirits, who delight in Mirth;
In yonder Tomb Alexis breathless lies;
The Soul of Wit, that gave your Laughter Birth,
Inhabits, once again, her native Skies.
How fix'd those Features which so well pourtray'd
The Cobweb Virtues of the canting Saint;
How dull those Eyes that could so well upbraid,
style: georgian elegy, string quartet, plaintive tenor, slow, formal
why: A clean elegy opening: 'His Wisdom Folly, Length of Time a Span, his Life is Vanity, his Death is Woe.'

title: Quaestiones Convivales
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
And Sophocles more plainly: Old men are slow in talk, they hardly hear; Far off they see; but all are blind when near.
Ulysses says to Alcinous, You bid me tell what various ills I bore, That the sad tale might make me grieve the more.
And Oedipus says to the chorus,Tis pain to raise again a buried grief. But Euripides on the contrary, How sweet it is, when we are lulled in ease, To think of toils!when well, of a disease!
Again, a complaint that implies thankfulness for a received favor is pleasant raillery. Thus Diogenes of his master Antisthenes: That man that made me leave my precious ore, Clothed me with rags, and force. me to be poor; That man that made me wander, beg my bread, And scorn to have a house to hide my lead.
And in his answer he makes the old man impertinently brag: I cuffing conquered Oinops famous son, With Anceus wrestled, and the garland won, And outran Iphiclus.
style: greek symposium song, lyre and soft aulos, conversational tenor, easy, reflective
why: A run of pungent quoted verses on old age, buried grief, and the sweetness of remembering past toils.

title: Quaestiones Convivales
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
And again he brings in Ulysses challenging the Phaeacians To cuff, to wrestle, or to run the race; and Alcinous answers: Neither in cuffing nor in wrestling strong, But swift of foot are we.
What is your opinion at present, Sossius Senecio, of the pleasures of mind and body, is not evident to me; Because us two a thousand things divide, Vast shady hills, and the rough oceans tide.
And Callimachus is plainer and more express, when he makes Hercules speak thus of parsley, This at Isthmian games To Neptunes glory now shall be the crown; The pine shall be disused, which heretofore In Corinths plains successful victors wore.
As we were at supper in Chaeronea, and had all sorts of fruit at the table, one of the company chanced to speak these verses, The fig-trees sweet, the apple-trees that bear Fair fruit, and olives green through all the year.
style: banquet air, kithara and hand drum, light male voice, gentle, abundant
why: Ends on the orchard line — 'The fig-trees sweet, the apple-trees that bear fair fruit, and olives green through all the year.'

title: On the Sublime
author: Longinus
lyrics:
8. Far better than these scenes of the Battle of the Gods are the passages that present the divine as something undefiled and great, truly pure and unmixed, such as the lines on Poseidon, a passage worked out by many before us:
The long mountains and the forest trembled,
and the peaks and the city of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans
beneath the immortal feet of Poseidon as he went.
He set out to drive over the waves, and the sea-beasts gambolled beneath him
from every side out of their lairs, and knew their lord.
The sea parted for joy, and the horses flew on.
2. He seems to me equal to the gods,
that man, whoever he is, who sits facing you,
and close at hand listens to your sweet speaking,
and your lovely laughterwhich truly has set
the heart in my breast a-flutter;
style: sublime greek hymn, deep drone and struck strings, resonant male voice, vast, surging
why: Poseidon striding, the sea-beasts gambolling from their lairs, the sea parting for joy — then Sappho's 'he seems to me equal to the gods'.

title: On the Sublime
author: Longinus
lyrics:
truly, often, lifting their hands to the gods,
they pray, while their inward parts heave wretchedly.
It is plain to all, I think, that there is more flowery prettiness than terror in these words.
5. But Homerhow? Let one example out of many be given:
He fell upon them, as when a wave falls upon a swift ship,
a furious wave reared by the winds from beneath the clouds, and the whole ship
is hidden in foam, and the terrible blast of the wind
roars in the sail, and the sailors tremble in their hearts
in fear; for they are borne but a little way out of the reach of death.
style: storm ode, low strings and rolling percussion, urgent voice, driving, fearful
why: The Homeric wave burying the ship in foam, the sailors borne a little way out of reach of death.

title: De saltatione
author: Lucian of Samosata
lyrics:
Returns a gladder and a wiser man.
To one the God hath given warlike deeds:
But to another dance and lovely song.
Their dainty feet round the dark waters dance, about the altar of Zeus.My dear sir, your onslaught upon the dance is little short of blasphemy.
Dumb though he be, and speechless, he is heard by the spectator.
As that sea-beast, whose hue
With each new rock doth suffer change,
So let thy mind free range
Through evry land, shaping herself anew.
That lulls all pain and wrath.
Strange, that my drugs have wrought no change in thee!
When so he will, and rouses them that sleep.
style: greek dance song, aulos and finger cymbals, light voices, quick, circling
why: Only candidate; a chain of lines about dancing, with 'their dainty feet round the dark waters dance, about the altar of Zeus.'

title: Institutes of Roman Law
author: Gaius
lyrics:
Here touched Achaean barks in quest of wine.
They purchased it with copper and with steel,
With hides, with horned cattle, and with slaves.
style: sea-trader's chant, bowed lyre and low drum, rough male voice, steady, working
why: Only candidate; three lines of barter at a harbour — copper, steel, hides, cattle, slaves — concrete and chantable.

title: Rigveda
author: Aufrecht (ed.)
lyrics:
Agni I laud, the divine household-priest of the sacrifice, the seasonal officiant, the Hotr, the most generous bestower of treasures.
Agni, lauded by the ancient seers and by those of today  may he convey the gods hither.
Through Agni may one attain wealth and prosperity day by day  wealth glorious and abounding in heroes.
O Agni, whatever unblemished sacrifice you encompass on all sides  that one truly reaches the gods.
May Agni the Hotr, of poet-wisdom, true, most rich in varied fame, come hither as a god among the gods.
Whatever good, O Agni, you will bestow upon the worshipper  that is indeed your truth, O Angiras.
To you, O Agni, day by day, at the dusk and at the dawn, we come with prayer bearing homage.
To him who reigns over the sacrifices, the guardian of rta who shines bright, who grows mighty in his own house
style: vedic hymn, tanpura drone, deep male voice, slow, reverent, sparse
why: The opening hymn of the Rigveda — Agni praised at dusk and dawn, the first words of the tradition.

title: Rigveda
author: Aufrecht (ed.)
lyrics:
The seven who stand on this seven-wheeled chariot  seven horses draw it. Seven sisters call out together, where the seven names of the cattle are set down.
Who saw the one being born first, the one with bones, which the boneless one bears? The earth's vital breath, blood, and soul  where are they? Who has gone to the wise one to ask this?
Childlike I ask, not knowing in my mind  what are the hidden tracks of the gods there? The poets have stretched out, as if for weaving, seven threads upon the young calf  so they say.
Not knowing, even among the knowing, I ask the poet-seers here for the sake of knowledge, I who do not know  what is the one thing that in the form of the unborn has propped up these six spaces apart?
Let him speak here who truly knows the hidden track of this lovely bird. The cows milk milk from his head; clothed in wrappings they have drunk water with their feet.
style: riddle chant, tanpura and low frame drum, hushed male voice, slow, enigmatic
why: The Riddle Hymn: seven-wheeled chariot, seven sisters, 'Childlike I ask, not knowing in my mind.'

title: Rigveda
author: Aufrecht (ed.)
lyrics:
Growing great on the pressed, exhilarating drink of Trita, he has struck down the myriad serpents. Indra with the Angirases has turned the sun like a wheel; he has cloven Vala.
Now may that bountiful right hand of yours, O Indra, yield to your singer the choicest gift. Grant aid to the praisers; let our share not be consumed. May we speak great words at the assembly, possessed of heroes.
He who, as soon as born, was the first thinker, the god who encompassed the gods with his power of will  from whose might the two world-halves trembled in fear at the greatness of his manly force  he, O people, is Indra.
He who made firm the trembling earth; he who stilled the mountains when they were enraged; he who measured out the atmosphere more widely; he who propped up the sky  he, O people, is Indra.
style: vedic praise hymn with refrain, drone and hand-struck drum, strong male voice, building, emphatic
why: Built on the great refrain — he who stilled the mountains, who propped up the sky, 'he, O people, is Indra.'

title: Poems
author: Robert Lowth
style: baroque seduction aria, harpsichord and viol, honeyed soprano, languid, coaxing
why: Sloth's whole seduction speech: 'Rough is the road to fame, thro' blood and war; smooth is my way, and all my paths are peace.'

title: Poems
author: Robert Lowth
style: allegorical art song, chamber strings and oboe, clear tenor, stately, expectant
why: The two enormous women appearing on the road to the young Hercules — one striking awe, one winning love.

title: Poems
author: Robert Lowth
lyrics:
Marches off with some friends that will ply the brisk glass;
Gives us liquor enough, and a good pleasant seat,
And damns your fine taste, and your finical lass:
Al fresco, my lads, we'll carouse and we'll drink,
Take your bottle each man, and away to the Link.
Not so gentle Collin, whom love holds in thrall,
To Molly he steals all in silence away;
And when nought can be heard but the rude water-fall,
And the woodbine breathes sweetest at close of the day,
He takes her soft hand, and he tips her the wink,
Come, my dear, let us take a cool walk on the Link.
But, O ye fair maidens, be sure have a care,
Nor lay yourselves open to love's cruel dart;
Of the hour and the place and the season beware,
And guard well each passage that leads to your heart;
Sly Cupid will steal in at some little chink,
style: english country ballad, fiddle and cittern, bright male voice with chorus, brisk, roguish
why: A genuine ballad with a returning refrain — 'away to the Link' and 'a cool walk on the Link'.

title: Poems
author: John Dyer
lyrics:
A little rule, a little sway,
A sun beam in a winter's day,
Is all the proud and mighty have
Between the cradle and the grave.
And see the rivers how they run,
Thro' woods and meads, in shade and sun,
Sometimes swift, sometimes slow,
Wave succeeding wave, they go
A various journey to the deep,
Like human life to endless sleep!
Thus is nature's vesture wrought,
To instruct our wand'ring thought;
Thus she dresses green and gay,
To disperse our cares away.
Ever charming, ever new,
When will the landskip tire the view!
style: pastoral octosyllabic song, acoustic guitar and recorder, warm tenor, unhurried, reflective
why: Dyer's most quoted lines — 'a little rule, a little sway... between the cradle and the grave' — and the rivers running to endless sleep.

title: Poems
author: John Dyer
lyrics:
AN EPISTLE TO A FRIEND IN TOWN.
BY MR. DYER.
HAVE my friends in the town, in the gay busy town,
Forgot such a man as John Dyer?
Or heedless despise they, or pity the clown
Whose bosom no pageantries fire?
No matter, no matter  content in the shades
(Contented?  why, every thing charms me)
Fall in tunes all adown the green steep, ye cascades,
Till hence rigid virtue alarms me.
Till outrage arises, or misery needs
The swift, the intrepid avenger;
Till sacred religion, or liberty bleeds,
Then mine be the deed, and the danger.
Alas! what a folly, that wealth and domain
We heap up in sin and in sorrow!
style: anapaestic country air, fiddle and hand drum, easy baritone, swinging, good-humoured
why: Already a song rhythm: 'Have my friends in the town, in the gay busy town, forgot such a man as John Dyer?'

title: Poems
author: John Dyer
lyrics:
Sits piping with his oaten reed; as erst
There pip'd the shepherd to his nibbling sheep,
When th' humble roof Anchises' son explor'd
Of good Evander, wealth-despising king,
Amid the thickets: so revolves the scene;
So time ordains, who rolls the things of pride
From dust again to dust. Behold that heap
Of mould'ring urns (their ashes blown away,
Dust of the mighty) the same story tell;
And at its base, from whence the serpent glides
Down the green desert street, yon hoary monk
Laments the same, the vision as he views,
The solitary, silent, solemn scene,
Where Caesars, heroes, peasants, hermits lie,
Blended in dust together; where the slave
Rests from his labours; where th' insulting proud
style: ruins elegy, low strings and distant horn, grave male voice, slow, hollow
why: The monk over the tombs where 'Caesars, heroes, peasants, hermits lie, blended in dust together'.

title: Poems
author: Anne Hunter
lyrics:
WHILE I behold the moon's pale beam,
Her light, perhaps, reflects on thee,
As wand'ring near the silver stream,
Thy sad remembrance turns to me.
Ah, to forget! the wish were vain!
Our souls were form'd thus fond to be;
No more I'll murmur and complain,
For thou, my love, wilt think on me.
Silent and sad, I take my way,
As fortune deigns my bark to steer;
Of hope a faint and distant ray
Our far divided days shall cheer.
Ah! to return, to meet again!
Dear blissful thought! with love and thee!
No more I murmur and complain,
For thou, my love, wilt think on me.
style: georgian canzonetta, fortepiano and cello, tender soprano, gentle, aching
why: A finished song with a returning refrain: 'No more I'll murmur and complain, for thou, my love, wilt think on me.'

title: Poems
author: Anne Hunter
style: mad song, harp and sparse strings, unsteady female voice, shifting tempo, haunted
why: The Maniac's Song — 'I had a friend, she prov'd unkind; I had a love, he prov'd untrue' — and a passing bell.

title: Poems
author: Anne Hunter
lyrics:
Ah! while he wanders far from home,
How can I hail the festive May?
THE SONG AT MARIA'S GRAVE.
IN TWO PARTS.
COME, gentle maidens, gather round.
Bring sprigs of rosemary and rue,
Strew virgin lilies on the ground,
And the wild rose embalm'd in dew.
Emblem of hope, upon the thorn
Their transient beauties bloom and die,
While yet their sweets perfume the morn,
They on Maria's grave shall lie.
For she was fair, as fairest flower,
And gentle as the breath of peace;
But now her charms exist no more,
And soon their memory shall cease.
style: funeral dirge, string quartet and soft voices, clear female lead, slow, processional
why: Rosemary, rue, virgin lilies and wild rose strewn on a grave — a dirge already written for singers.

title: Poems
author: James Barclay
lyrics:
"And she, meek daughter of the vale,
" That growing scents the passing gale,
"Not less revives the ravish'd sense,
" When rooted and remov'd from hence.
"On Chloe's breast still seen to blow,
" Adds whiteness to the dazzling snow:
"And dealing sweetness, tho' in death,
" Perfumes e'en Chloe's fragrant breath. "
THE INVITATION.
BY THE SAME.
AWAKE, my fair, the morning springs,
The dew-drops glance around,
The heifer lows, the blackbird sings,
The echoing vales resound.
The simple sweets would STELLA taste,
That breathing morning yields,
style: morning pastoral ballad, fiddle and flute, bright female vocal, lively, fresh
why: 'Awake, my fair, the morning springs' — the heifer lows, the blackbird sings; ballad metre made for singing.

title: Poems
author: James Barclay
lyrics:
In youth, compound of curls and lace,
Of giggle, fidget, and of froth;
One simper dimpled in his face,
No butterfly more void of wrath.
Pleas'd with himself, with all well-pleas'd,
The flutterer scarce could give offence:
Or if he teaz'd, with nought he teaz'd,
But simple, pure, impertinence.
Now view him in declining age,
Assume the four satyric frown:
On friends and foes discharge his rage,
The very SCARECROW of the town.
So Flies, in frisk, and buzz, and play,
That harmless through the summer past,
When ready to be swept away,
Grow blind, and sting us at the last.
style: satirical parlour song, harpsichord and pizzicato strings, arch baritone, brisk, cutting
why: Witwoud young against Witwoud old, closing on flies that grow blind and sting us at the last.

title: Poems
author: James Barclay
lyrics:
THE TULIP AND LILY.
BY MR. BY.
HIGH o'er the bed, conspicuous seen,
A Tulip rose, the garden's queen.
Never on Holland's foggy strand
Was taller rear'd by Dutchman's hand:
Never was Flora known t' imprint
On Tulip's leaf a brighter tint,
Or lead with more fantastic freak,
On Tulip's leaf the varying streak.
Beneath the tow'ring Tulip's shade,
In nought but simple white array'd,
And shelter'd from th' intruding view,
A Lily of the valley grew;
The humblest plant of all the train
That deck the mountain or the plain,
style: garden fable air, lute and recorder, light tenor, courtly, playful
why: The tall tulip lording it over the lily of the valley — the fable set up in one clean scene.

title: Themistocles
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
Who came from sacred Athens; since Leto loathes Themistocles,
The liar, cheat, and traitor, who, though Timocreon was his host,
By knavish moneys was induced not to bring him back
Into his native Ialysus,
But took three talents of silver and went cruising off,to perdition,
Restoring some exiles unjustly, chasing some away, and slaying some,
Gorged with moneys; yet at the
Isthmus he played ridiculous host with the stale meats set before his guests;
Who ate thereof and prayed Heaven no happy return of the day for Themistocles!
Much more wanton and extravagant was the raillery which Timocreon indulged in against Themistocles after the latters own exile and condemnation. Then he composed the song beginning: O Muse grant that this song
Be famed throughout all Hellas,
As it is meet and just.
style: greek invective song, lyre and hard-struck drum, biting male voice, driving, sardonic
why: Timocreon's attack song in full — three talents of silver, stale meats, and guests praying against their host.

title: Themistocles
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
He made himself hateful to the allies also, by sailing round to the islands and trying to exact money from them. When, for instance, he demanded money of the Andrians, Herodotus says he made a speech to them and got reply as follows: he said he came escorting two gods, Persuasion and Compulsion; and they replied that they already had two great gods, Penury and Powerlessness, who hindered them from giving him money.
Timocreon, the lyric poet of Rhodes, assailed Themistocles very bitterly in a song, to the effect that for bribes he had secured the restoration of other exiles, but had abandoned him, though a host and a friend, and all for money. The song runs thus: Come, if thou praisest Pausanias, or if Xanthippus,
Or if Leotychidas, then I shall praise Aristides,
The one best man of all
style: greek satirical air, kithara and light percussion, wry male voice, moderate, mocking
why: The Andrians answering Persuasion and Compulsion with their own two gods, Penury and Powerlessness.

title: Pro lapsu inter salutandum
author: Lucian of Samosata
lyrics:
Joy to thee, Lord of this Tirynthian land!
Achilles, Joy! We lack not fair repast so says Odysseus discharging his embassy. And even at parting:
Joy be with you! And henceforth know me God,
No longer mortal man,
Joy with you! for the darkness closes on me.
Hail to thee, joy be thine which puts health before rejoicing clearly enough. And says Alexis: All hail, my lord; after long time thou comest.
Again Achaeus: I come in sorry plight, yet wish thee health.
And Philemon: Health first I ask, and next prosperity,
Joy thirdly, and to owe not any man.
Health, with thee I mean to live.
style: greek toast song, lyre and hand drum, warm male voice, easy, convivial
why: Only candidate; a chain of greetings ending in a drinking-toast order — health first, then prosperity, then joy.

title: Demonax
author: Lucian of Samosata
lyrics:
Admetus husk earth holds, and Heaven himself.
Idle or busy, death takes all alike.
The games are done,
The crowns all won;
No more delay,
style: greek epitaph chant, single lyre, unaccompanied male voice, sparse, final
why: Only candidate; short but complete — 'the games are done, the crowns all won; no more delay.'

title: Kunjarakarna Dharmakathana
author: Mpu Dusun
lyrics:
1. The steadfast one, seeking battle on the field of austerities and vows, warring against the six heroic enemies within,
His battle-array is the quality of truth in meditation; his chariot, the practice of compassion and more.
The sacred hand-gestures are his banner, the lion's roar his chanted spell, the supreme bow his inconceivable contemplation;
The highest arrow is enlightenment-wisdom, annihilating the foe, bearing the fruit of *dharma*-*sunyata*.
2. Such a one is the visible form of the Lord Sakyamuni, victor over Mara.
He stands as a blessing for those who would compose poetry, who bow in devotion, heads bowed to the dust of his feet.
My praise is like a consecrated image, set forth as a diadem of rule, seeded with syllables.
May my spirit never be parted from his feet in all my lives to come.
style: old javanese kakawin invocation, bronze gamelan, suling flute, low male chant, slow, ceremonial, incense-heavy
why: The whole poem's opening praise, built as one sustained metaphor of the inner war fought with meditation, compassion and wisdom.

title: Kunjarakarna Dharmakathana
author: Mpu Dusun
lyrics:
Not in vain are its evil deeds reckoned; their end is in the cauldron."
14. "The proof is that they all flock to Yama's realm, without cease.
There was a path you traveled on your way here, clean and well-trodden.
And the city of the Iron Earth, a league wide, was filled
with the many who were unrighteous, evil-doers, base people in the world of mortals."
15. "But not so is the path of the soul that comes to the abode of the gods; it is faint.
Overgrown and tangled are the sprouts of grass and vines, rustling softly.
It is still, lonely, and desolate, as if it were a phantom city.
It is difficult for a person to find his way to the worthy assembly of the gods' abode."
16. "So, that is the reason for the base and sinful in the abode of Yama.
But what is the cause of their living again, when they have truly died?
style: javanese temple chant, gong and rebab, solemn male voice, sparse, ominous, measured
why: The road to hell is broad and well-trodden, the path to the gods faint and overgrown — a self-contained turn of thought.

title: Kunjarakarna Dharmakathana
author: Mpu Dusun
lyrics:
> When your time comes to be taken by force, may your brother be deep within you, your protector.
>
> 8. If you become an asana tree, my dear, I will become the cloud that approaches bringing rain.
> Enjoy my love, which becomes a drizzle; if it thunders, it is to greet the seeds of your longing.
> Let me see the joy of my love in full blossom, that you may know my passion.
> And as a bee, I will never cease to approach your beauty, to be remembered by my kisses."
9. Such was the song of the departed one that she read, over and over, reading it aloud.
The heart of the celestial woman was pained, crushed, as if she had lost her very soul.
Her pain could no longer be held back, like a fire consuming blazing straw.
Her cries were piteous as she repeatedly wiped her tears, forgetting that her sarong was slipping.
style: kawi love lament, gender wayang metallophones, breathy female vocal, slow, tender, rain-soft
why: A dead lover's song read over and over: if you become a tree, I will become the rain-cloud.

title: Georgics
author: P. Vergilius Maro (Virgil)
lyrics:
What makes the cornfield smile; beneath what star
Maecenas, it is meet to turn the sod
Or marry elm with vine; how tend the steer;
What pains for cattle-keeping, or what proof
Of patient trial serves for thrifty bees;
Such are my themes. O universal lights
Most glorious! ye that lead the gliding year
Along the sky, Liber and Ceres mild,
If by your bounty holpen earth once changed
Chaonian acorn for the plump wheat-ear,
And mingled with the grape, your new-found gift,
The draughts of Achelous; and ye Fauns
To rustics ever kind, come foot it, Fauns
And Dryad-maids together; your gifts I sing.
And thou, for whose delight the war-horse first
Sprang from earth's womb at thy great trident's stroke,
style: latin georgic invocation, lyre and pan pipes, warm baritone, stately, sunlit, processional
why: The famous opening — what makes the cornfield smile — naming the whole poem's themes and calling the rustic gods to dance.

title: Georgics
author: P. Vergilius Maro (Virgil)
lyrics:
Supply new kings and pigmy commonwealth,
And their old court and waxen realm repair.
Oft, too, while wandering, against jagged stones
Their wings they fray, and 'neath the burden yield
Their liberal lives: so deep their love of flowers,
So glorious deem they honey's proud acquist.
Therefore, though each a life of narrow span,
Ne'er stretched to summers more than seven, befalls,
Yet deathless doth the race endure, and still
Perennial stands the fortune of their line,
From grandsire unto grandsire backward told.
Moreover, not Aegyptus, nor the realm
Of boundless Lydia, no, nor Parthia 's hordes,
Nor Median Hydaspes, to their king
Do such obeisance: lives the king unscathed,
One will inspires the million: is he dead,
style: pastoral recitation, cello drone, hurdy-gurdy, warm male voice, measured, elegiac
why: The bees: each life narrow and brief, yet the race deathless, counted backward from grandsire to grandsire.

title: Georgics
author: P. Vergilius Maro (Virgil)
lyrics:
Nay to the jaws of Taenarus too he came,
Of Dis the infernal palace, and the grove
Grim with a horror of great darknesscame,
Entered, and faced the Manes and the King
Of terrors, the stone heart no prayer can tame.
Then from the deepest deeps of Erebus,
Wrung by his minstrelsy, the hollow shades
Came trooping, ghostly semblances of forms
Lost to the light, as birds by myriads hie
To greenwood boughs for cover, when twilight-hour
Or storms of winter chase them from the hills;
Matrons and men, and great heroic frames
Done with life's service, boys, unwedded girls,
Youths placed on pyre before their fathers' eyes.
Round them, with black slime choked and hideous weed,
Cocytus winds; there lies the unlovely swamp
style: underworld lament, solo lyre, low strings, hushed tenor, slow, funereal, echoing
why: Orpheus at the jaws of Taenarus, the shades trooping up like birds driven from the hills by winter.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Parnell
lyrics:
Ye Fields, ye Forests, own Dione's Reign,
And Delia, Huntress Delia, shun the Plain.
Let those love now, who never lov'd before,
Let those who always lov'd, now love the more.
Gay with the Bloom of all her opening Year,
The Queen at Hybla bids her Throne appear;
And there presides; and there the fav'rite Band
(Her smiling Graces) share the great Command.
Now beauteous Hybla! dress thy flow'ry Beds
With all the Pride the lavish Season sheds,
Now all thy Colours, all thy Fragrance yield,
And rival Enna's Aromatick Field.
To fill the Presence of the gentle Court
From ev'ry Quarter rural Nymphs resort,
From Woods, from Mountains, from their humble Vales,
From Waters curling with the wanton Gales.
style: baroque pastoral hymn, strings and harpsichord, bright soprano, dancing triple time, refrain-driven
why: The Pervigilium Veneri refrain — let those love now who never loved before — already built as a song.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Parnell
lyrics:
That Steeple guides thy doubtful sight
Among the livid gleams of Night.
There pass with melancholy State,
By all the solemn Heaps of Fate,
And think, as softly-sad you tread
Above the venerable Dead,
Time was, like thee they Life possest,
And Time shall be, that thou shalt Rest.
Those Graves, with bending Osier bound,
That nameless heave the crumbled Ground,
Quick to the glancing Thought disclose
Where Toil and Poverty repose.
The flat smooth Stones that bear a Name,
The Chissels slender help to Fame,
(Which e'er our Sett of Friends decay
Their frequent Steps may wear away.)
style: graveyard elegy, chamber organ, bass viol, grave contralto, slow, hushed, tolling
why: The Night-Piece on Death: walking the churchyard by steeple-light, time was and time shall be.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Parnell
lyrics:
In trailing Purple o'er the Ground:
Or in a Soul exalted high,
To range the Circuit of the Sky,
Converse with Stars above, and know
All Nature in its Forms below;
The Rest it seeks, in seeking dies,
And Doubts at last for Knowledge rise.
Lovely, lasting Peace appear!
This World it self, if thou art here,
Is once again with Eden bless'd,
And Man contains it in his Breast.
'Twas thus, as under Shade I stood,
I sung my Wishes to the Wood,
And lost in Thought, no more perceiv'd
The Branches whisper as they wav'd:
It seem'd, as all the quiet Place
style: english devotional air, lute and recorder, gentle tenor, unhurried, serene
why: The Hymn to Contentment's turn — peace makes this world Eden again, and man contains it in his breast.

title: Poems
author: Edward Moore
lyrics:
A BALLAD.
BY THE SAME.
HARK, hark, 'tis a voice from the tomb,
Come, Lucy, it cries, come away,
The grave of thy Colin has room
To rest thee beside his cold clay.
I come, my dear shepherd, I come,
Ye friends and companions adieu,
I haste to my Colin's dark home,
To die on his bosom so true.
All mournful the midnight bell rung,
When Lucy, sad Lucy, arose;
And forth to the green turf she sprung,
Where Colin's pale ashes repose.
All wet with the night's chilling dew,
Her bosom embrac'd the cold ground,
style: 18th century broadside ballad, acoustic guitar and fiddle, plaintive female vocal, minor key, steady, mournful
why: A complete ballad opening — a voice from the tomb calling Lucy to lie down beside Colin's clay.

title: Poems
author: Edward Moore
lyrics:
While stormy winds over her blew,
And night-ravens croak'd all around.
How long, my lov'd Colin, she cry'd,
How long must thy Lucy complain?
How long shall the grave my love hide?
How long ere it join us again?
For thee thy fond shepherdess liv'd,
With thee o'er the world would she fly;
For thee has she sorrow'd and griev'd;
For thee would she lie down and die.
Alas! what avails it how dear
Thy Lucy was once to her swain!
Her face like the lily so fair,
And eyes that gave light to the plain.
The shepherd that lov'd her is gone;
That face and those eyes charm no more;
style: graveside ballad lament, solo fiddle, near-unaccompanied female voice, slow, keening
why: The lament proper, built on the repeated 'How long' — the most singable stretch in the collection.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Percy
lyrics:
Eager to wrest and represent them wrong;
Yet shall your conduct, circumspect and clear,
Nor baleful touch, nor fangs envenom'd fear.
A SONG.
By T. P***CY.
O Nancy, wilt thou go with me,
Nor sigh to leave the flaunting town:
Can silent glens have charms for thee,
The lowly cot and russet gown?
No longer dress'd in silken sheen,
No longer deck'd with jewels rare,
Say can'st thou quit each courtly scene,
Where thou wert fairest of the fair?
O Nancy! when thou'rt far away,
Wilt thou not cast a wish behind?
Say canst thou face the parching ray,
style: scottish pastoral song, fiddle and small harp, warm tenor, gentle lilt, refrain
why: O Nancy, wilt thou go with me — Percy's best-known song, with its 'fairest of the fair' refrain intact.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Percy
lyrics:
Nor shrink before the wintry wind?
O can that soft and gentle mien
Extremes of hardship learn to bear,
Nor sad regret each courtly scene,
Where thou wert fairest of the fair?
O Nancy! can'st thou love so true,
Thro' perils keen with me to go,
Or when thy swain mishap shall rue,
To share with him the pang of woe?
Say should disease or pain befal,
Wilt thou assume the nurse's care,
Nor wistful those gay scenes recall
Where thou wert fairest of the fair?
And when at last thy love shall die,
Wilt thou receive his parting breath?
Wilt thou repress each struggling sigh,
style: border ballad, clarsach and low whistle, plain male voice, slow, tender, question-and-refrain
why: The song's rising questions — hardship, sickness, the deathbed — each answered by the same refrain.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Percy
lyrics:
Ye know, the curling breeze, or gilded fly
That idly wantons in the noon-tide air,
Was not so free, was not so gay as I,
For ah! I knew not then or love, or care.
Witness ye winged daughters of the year,
If e'er a sigh had learnt to heave my breast
If e'er my cheek was conscious of a tear,
'Till Cynthia came and rob'd my soul of rest!
O have you seen, bath'd in the morning dew,
The budding rose its infant bloom display;
When first its virgin tints unfold to view,
It shrinks and scarcely trusts the blaze of day.
So soft, so delicate, so sweet she came,
Youth's damask glow just dawning on her cheek:
I gaz'd, I sigh'd, I caught the tender flame,
Felt the fond pang, and droop'd with passion, weak.
style: georgian parlour elegy, fortepiano, soft tenor, wistful, chamber
why: The budding rose that shrinks from the blaze of day, and the moment love first landed.

title: De musica
author: Pseudo-Plutarch
lyrics: In like manner Menalippides the lyric poet, Philoxenus and Timotheus, all forsook the ancient music. For whereas until the time of Terpander the Antissaean the harp had only seven strings, he added a greater number, and gave its notes a wider range. The wind-music also exchanged its ancient plainness for a more copious variety. For in ancient times, till Menalippides the dithyrambic came into request, the wind-music received salaries from the poets, poetry holding the first rank and the musicians being in the service of the poet. Afterwards that custom grew out of date; insomuch that Pherecrates the comedian brings in Music in womans habit, all bruised and battered, and then introduces Justice asking the reason; to which Music thus replies: Music.Tis mine to speak, thy part to hear, And therefore lend a willing ear; Much have I suffered, long opprest By Menalippides, that beast; He haled me from Parnassus springs, And plagued me with a dozen strings. His rage howeer sufficed not yet, To make my miseries complete. Cinesias, that cursed Attic, A mere poetical pragmatic, Such horrid strophes in mangled verse Made the unharmonious stage rehearse, That I, tormented with the pains Of cruel dithyrambic strains, Distorted lay, that you would swear The right side now the left side were. Nor did my miseries end here; For Phrynis with his whirlwind brains, Wringing and racking all my veins, Ruined me quite, while nine small wires With harmonies twice six he tires. Yet might not he so much be blamed, From all his errors soon reclaimed; But then Timotheus with his freaks Furrowed my face, and ploughed my cheeks. Justice. Say which of them so vile could be? Music. Milesian Pyrrhias, that was he, Whose fury tortured me much more Than all that I have named before; Whereer I walk the streets alone, If met by him, the angry clown, With his twelve cat-guts strongly bound, He leaves me helpless on the ground.
style: greek comic parody song, aulos and lyre, sardonic female vocal, brisk patter, mock-lament
why: Music herself, bruised and battered, listing by name the poets who racked her strings — comic verse already in rhyme.

title: An seni respublica gerenda sit
author: Plutarch
lyrics:
And it is said of Sophocles, that, to avoid being condemned of dotage at the instance of his children, he repeated the entrance song of the Chorus in his tragedy of Oedipus in Colonus, which begins thus: Welcome, stranger, come in time To the best place of this clime, White Colonus, which abounds With brave horses. In these grounds, Spread with Natures choicest green, Philomel is often seen. Here she her hearers charms with sweetest lays, Whilst with shrill throat And warbling note She moans the sad misfortunes of her former days:
and again, Let us not cease to benefit mankind.
style: attic tragic chorus, lyre and aulos, layered voices, solemn, flowing, birdsong-bright
why: The Colonus chorus Sophocles recited to prove he was not senile — white Colonus, its horses and its nightingale.

title: Sophist
author: Plato
lyrics: Str. Because he says somewhere: Never shall this thought prevail, that not-being is; Nay, keep your mind from this path of investigation,
style: philosophical incantation, low drone, single male voice, austere, slow, oracular
why: Only candidate, but it is the Parmenides prohibition itself: keep your mind from this path.

title: Vīramitrodaya
author: Mitra Miśra
lyrics:
May that unprecedented body of the Man-Lion (Nrhari) protect uswhose terrifying frown is made dreadful by the fierce movement of His brow, which dances with the bristling and spreading of His mane in a fit of rage; whose dreadful gaze roams about; before whom the mountain-like serpent bows down completely; from the fearsome expanse of whose tearing apart of His enemy's naked body, the edge of the great cauldron of the golden cosmic egg shatters. // 1 //
May that Nrsimha, whose great and furious impetuosity is kindled by the great demon's attack, which is repelled by the drops of nectar flowing from the moon entangled in the tips of His mane; who licks the entire circle of the horizons with His tongue, which is like a flame of sacrificial firemay He, with His force, quell my sin, which is like a rutting elephant. // 2 //
style: sanskrit invocation chant, tanpura drone, mridangam, fierce deep male voice, building, ritual, incantatory
why: The opening benediction to Nṛsiṃha — mane, frown, tongue like sacrificial flame, the cosmic egg splitting.

title: Vīramitrodaya
author: Mitra Miśra
lyrics:
Having worshipped the lotus-face of his preceptor, and spurned the dance on the faces of the Four-Faced (Brahma), Sarasvati, here, adorned with figures of speech, full of aesthetic sentiment, and endowed with virtues, performs her dances upon his tongue. // 44 //
The line of smoke from his sacrifices appeared to the deer-eyed women of the horizons like a line of hair on the belly, a single line of collyrium on the boundary of the eyes, a musk-leaf design on the tablet of the forehead, a parting of the hair on the head, or a swarm of bees above, agitated by the desire for the fragrance of their tresses. // 45 //
From that Parasurama Misraa repository of brilliant fame, a repository of flawless knowledge, a repository of beautiful poetry, a repository of *smrti* (sacred tradition), and a repository of the splendor of *sruti* (revealed scripture)was born in this world, through the merit of his good deeds, Mitra Misra, whose dignity was no less than his father's. // 46 //
style: sanskrit court panegyric, sitar and tabla, ornamented male voice, moderate, courtly, flowing
why: Sarasvatī dancing on the poet's tongue, and sacrifice-smoke read as a line of collyrium on the horizon's face.

title: Vīramitrodaya
author: Mitra Miśra
lyrics:
> Austerity is supreme in the Krta Yuga; in the Treta, knowledge is the highest. /
> In the Dvapara, they say only sacrifice; in Kali, charity, compassion, and self-control. //
> Austerity is the *dharma* in the Krta Yuga; knowledge is established in the Treta Yuga. /
> In the Dvapara, sacrifice is proclaimed; in Tisya, charity, compassion, and self-control. //
> Meditation is supreme in the Krta Yuga; in the Treta, the worship of the linga. /
> In the Dvapara, study; in Tisya, the praise of Mahadeva. //
> Meditation is supreme in the Krta Yuga; in the Treta, sacrifice. /
> In the Dvapara, the worship of the linga; in Kali, the praise of Sankara. //
> Knowledge is supreme in the Krta Yuga; and in the Treta, it is more so. /
> And in the Dvapara, likewise, sacrifice; consecration, however, is in the Kali Yuga. //
style: vedic litany chant, drone and hand cymbals, unison male voices, slow, hypnotic, repetitive
why: The yuga refrain — austerity, knowledge, sacrifice, charity — restated four ways, a chant by construction.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Chatterton
lyrics:
ETHELGAR,
A SAXON POEM.
'TIS not for thee, O man! to murmur at the will of the Almighty. When the thunders roar, the lightnings shine on the rising waves, and the black clouds sit on the brow of the lofty hill; who then protects the flying deer, swift as a sable cloud, tost by the whistling winds, leaping over the rolling floods, to gain the hoary wood: whilst the lightnings shine on his chest, and the wind rides over his horns? When the wolf roars; terrible as the voice of the Severn; moving majestic as the nodding forests on the brow of Michel-stow; who then commands the sheep to follow the swain, as the beams of light attend upon the morning?  Know, O man! That God suffers not the least member of his work to perish, without answering the purpose of their creation. The evils of life, with some, are blessings: and the plant of death healeth the wound of the sword.  Doth the sea of trouble and affliction overwhelm thy soul, look unto the Lord, thou shalt stand firm in the days of temptation, as the lofty hill of Kinwulf; in vain shall the waves beat against thee; thy rock shall stand.
style: ossianic bardic chant, bowed lyre and low drone, grave male voice, slow, stark, windswept
why: A complete Saxon homily: thunder, wolf, flying deer, and the promise that thy rock shall stand.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Chatterton
style: graveyard elegy, viol and chamber organ, dark tenor, slow, mounting, funereal
why: A litany of apostrophes turned self-destructive — noxious vapours, adders, toads, blasting meteors called down on the mourner.

title: Poems
author: Thomas Chatterton
style: african eclogue, hand drums and kora, urgent male vocal, driving, cinematic, hot
why: The tiger hunt told as a love gift — I stripped his carcase, on this shall my loved Cawna lie.

title: An Assorted Collection of Eighteenth-Century Poetry
author: Various
lyrics:
To disturb me with fair Charlotte Lynes.
The pastures, the sheep,
Shall exchange for the deep,
And mackrel shall grow on the vines;
The sun shall burn blue,
Ere my heart proves untrue,
Or forgets to love fair Charlotte Lynes.
THE WISH.
SHOULD I e'er become parson (for so I'm inclin'd)
May I get a snug benefice pat to my mind,
Large enough to allow of a wife at my table,
A cow in my yard, and a nag in my stable.
May my flock n'er embroil me in quarrels and strife,
In good humour I'd live all the days of my life,
And die before tir'd of myself or my wife.
With a friend or two near me of equal degree,
style: english drinking-song, fiddle and box accordion, hearty male vocal, brisk, lilting, refrain-driven
why: The impossibility-oath — mackerel on the vines, the sun burning blue — before the heart proves untrue.

title: An Assorted Collection of Eighteenth-Century Poetry
author: Various
lyrics:
Those eyes no longer can divine
Each secret of my breast.
What pleases now, or grieves my mind,
What makes me sad, or gay,
It is not in thy power to give,
Nor canst thou take away:
Each pleasant spot without thee charms,
The wood, the mead, the hill;
And scenes of dullness, even with thee,
Are scenes of dullness still.
Judge, if I speak with tongue sincere;
Thou still art wond'rous fair;
Great are the beauties of thy form,
But not beyond compare:
And, let not truth offend thine ear,
My eyes at length incline
style: georgian parlour ballad, harpsichord and viola, cool female vocal, plain, unhurried, wry
why: A clear-eyed falling-out-of-love: scenes of dullness, even with thee, are scenes of dullness still.

title: An Assorted Collection of Eighteenth-Century Poetry
author: Various
lyrics:
And when it came, borne to our peaceful grave
By the plain villager; what tho' no tomb
Of sculptur'd marble call'd the passing eye
To read our story, yet the cottage tear
Should on our ashes fall, and the good heart
O'erflow sincerely for a neighbour lost:
Upon our bier the virgin troop would hang
Fresh-woven chaplets of the sweetest flowers:
Green turf should deck our grave; and every year
In spring-time would some friendly hand with care
Bind the fresh briar around, to guard the place
From the rude insult of the careless step;
And faithful Memory to late time record,
We were the happiest pair of human kind.
THE THREE WARNINGS:
A TALE.
style: pastoral elegy, acoustic guitar and soft strings, warm tenor, gentle, elegiac
why: No sculptured marble, only cottage tears and a briar bound fresh each spring — we were the happiest pair of human kind.

title: Poems
author: Mary Alcock
lyrics:
Till time shall be no more
AN AUNT'S LAMENTATION FOR THE ABSENCE OF HER NIECE.
WRITTEN FROM HASTINGS.
Like as the dove I sit alone,
Dejected, pale, and wan,
Without a friend to hear me moan
The loss of Marianne.
Now on the raging deep I gaze,
And all it's wonders scan,
Yet still my thoughts revert always
To thee, my Marianne.
Now o'er my book, my work I pore,
But do whate'er I can,
My book, my work will charm no more,
I've lost my Marianne.
The other morn the fifers play'd,
style: 18th century parlour lament, fortepiano and cello, plaintive female vocal, slow, tender, refrain
why: Like as the dove I sit alone — every stanza falling back onto the lost Marianne.

title: Poems
author: Mary Alcock
style: comic patter song, harpsichord and pizzicato strings, bright arch soprano, brisk, buoyant, refrain
why: The balloon ascent as satire, with its returning boast: and leave the wondering multitude below.

title: Poems
author: Mary Alcock
lyrics:
Oft have I seen, come to careen,
Many an honest tar,
With batter'd hide by scurvy dried,
Yet cur'd at Swandling Bar.
I've seen a fair who might compare
With Venus in her car,
Approach the rill and drink her fill
Each day at Swandling Bar.
Here lords from town, of high renown,
With garter and with star,
Decrepid come, yet brisk go home,
Such power hath Swandling Bar.
Late have I seen, of graceful mien,
A nymph from Mullingar,
So fair, so bright, she caught the sight
Of all at Swandling Bar.
style: spa-town drinking ballad, fiddle and tabor, cheerful female vocal, jaunty, internal-rhyme swing
why: Swandling Bar's cast of tars, lords and nymphs, carried on a strong internal-rhyme refrain.

title: San Hyan Kamahayanikan
author: Mpu Shri Sambhara Surya Warama
lyrics:
*Come, child, I shall teach you the Great Vehicle, the method of the Path of the Master of Mantras. You are a worthy vessel for the Great Path.*
*The Buddhas who have passed, and likewise those who are yet to come, and the Lords who are present, stand for the welfare of the world.*
*By all these heroes, having known this supreme method of mantras, the vajra, All-Knowingness was attained at the root of the Bodhi tree, which is without characteristics.*
*By this incomparable application of mantra, the great and terrible army of Mara was broken by the Lion of the Sakyas, the Protector.*
*Therefore, set your mind on this path to attain All-Knowingness. Listen, O good-hearted one, always concentrating your mind and dispelling all imaginings.*
*This is the excellent, glorious path, the Mahayana of great prosperity, by which you shall go forth and become Tathagatas.*
style: buddhist tantric chant, bronze bell and drone, low male voice, slow, solemn, initiatory
why: The teacher's opening address — come, child — naming the vajra path and the breaking of Māra's army.

title: San Hyan Kamahayanikan
author: Mpu Shri Sambhara Surya Warama
lyrics:
*OM. Bajrasatwa himself is now intent on opening your eyes. He, the all-seeing, opens the unsurpassable vajra-eye.*
*Behold this mandala and generate faith now. You are born into the family of the Buddhas, empowered by all the mantras.*
*All fortunes are facing you, and the paths of yogic accomplishment are yours. Uphold the samaya for siddhi; be diligent in the mantras.*
*IM OM To the Bajra-Eye, remove, remove the veil in the heart. The veil of ignorance, O child, has been removed for you by the Jinas, with the probes of the supreme king of physicians, just as the worlds blindness is removed.*
*Phenomena are like reflections: clear, pure, and untroubled. They are ungraspable and inexpressible, arising from cause and action.*
*Having thus known these phenomena to be essenceless and pure, work for the incomparable welfare of beings, for you are born as the true son of the Protectors.*
style: javanese esoteric chant, singing bowls and gong, hushed male voice, sparse, luminous, unhurried
why: The eye-opening rite: remove the veil in the heart, phenomena are like reflections.

title: San Hyan Kamahayanikan
author: Mpu Shri Sambhara Surya Warama
lyrics:
*One should always serve ones own Samaya-Master, even with ones own life, with un-giveable things like wife and children, let alone with fleeting riches.*
*Because he gives, in this very life, Buddhahood to the diligent onea state which is always extremely difficult to obtain over countless billions of kalpas.*
*Today your birth is fruitful, for you are well-established in this. Today you are born as equals of the Self-Born Gods.*
*Today, O long-lived ones, you are consecrated by all the Buddhas with their Vajras. You are established as sovereign emperors in the great kingdom of the three realms.*
*Today, having conquered Mara, you have entered the supreme city. Buddhahood has been attained by you this very day; there is no doubt in this.*
*Therefore, make your mind a vajra of clarity. Devote yourselves to your samaya, which bestows the bliss of the void-like exhaustion of karma. In this world of fleeting pleasures, you will become equal to all Buddhas, having attained the state of eternity.*
style: consecration chant, gamelan gongs and hand drum, layered male voices, rising, triumphal, ceremonial
why: Anaphora on 'today' — today your birth is fruitful, today, having conquered Māra, you have entered the supreme city.

title: The Heroic Deeds of the Emperor Constantius
author: Julian
lyrics:
"Son of Atreus, has this then proved better for us both,
For you and for me . . ."
"And lordly Agamemnon rose,
Holding the sceptre that Hephaestus toiled to make,
And gave to Zeus; and he to the son of Maia and himself,
And lord Hermes gave it to Pelops,
And Pelops gave it to Atreus, shepherd of the people;
And Atreus dying left it to Thyestes rich in flocks,
And he again left it to Agamemnon to bear,
To be lord over many islands and over all Argos."
"Whether they fitted him, and his glorious limbs moved freely within."
"Who then was far the best of these, tell me, O Muse,
Of the men and the horses, that followed the sons of Atreus?
Of the men by far the best was Telamonian Ajax,
While Achilles was wroth; for he was far the strongest."
"Ajax, who in form and in deeds was fashioned
style: homeric rhapsody, phorminx lyre, resonant male voice, measured, formal, hall-lit
why: The sceptre passed hand to hand from Hephaestus down to Agamemnon — the one fully coherent stretch among these quotations.

title: Divus Augustus
author: Suetonius
lyrics:
Sexque deos vidit Mallia, sexque
deas
Impia dum Phoebi Caesar mendacia ludit,
Dum nova divorum coenat adulteria:
Omnia se a terris tunc numina declinarunt:
Fugit et auratos Jupiter ipse thronos.
When Mallia late beheld, in mingled train,
Twelve mortals ape twelve deities in vain,
Caesar assumed what was Apollo's due,
And wine and lust inflamed the motley crew.
At the foul sight the gods avert their eyes,
Aliquando ut vincat, ludit assidue aleam.
Twice having lost a fleet in luckless fight,
To win at last, he games both day and night.
style: roman satiric epigram, tibia pipes and lyre, sardonic male voice, brisk, mocking, tavern-loud
why: The street lampoon on the banquet of the twelve gods — at the foul sight the gods avert their eyes.

title: Orationes 25
author: Aelius Aristides
lyrics:
"Asclepius shall heal you of your sickness and cure you,
honouring the famed town of Telephus,
not far from the streams of the Caicus."
style: greek oracular chant, single lyre, clear high voice, slow, hieratic, sparse
why: Only candidate, but a complete oracle: Asclepius shall heal you, by the streams of the Caicus.

title: Phoenissae
author: Euripides
lyrics:
Chorus:
O snow-capped Cithaeron, dear to Artemis, holy vale of leaves, crowded with wild animals, would that you had never reared the one exposed to die, Oedipus, Jocastas child, when as a baby he was cast forth from his home, marked with a golden brooch; and would that the Sphinx, that winged maid, monster from the hills, had never come as a grief to our land with her inharmonious songs, she that once drew near our walls and snatched the sons of Cadmus away in her taloned feet to the untrodden light of heaven, sent by Hades from hell to plague the men of Thebes; once more unhappy strife is coming into bloom between the sons of Oedipus in home and city. For never can wrong be right, nor can there be good in unlawful children, their mothers birth pangs, their fathers pollution; she came to the bed of her son....
style: ancient greek chorus, lyre and frame drum, layered female voices, solemn, keening, building
why: The Cithaeron ode — the exposed child with the golden brooch, and the Sphinx's inharmonious song.

title: Phoenissae
author: Euripides
lyrics:
wherever I live, I shall seem base.
No, by Zeus and all his stars, by Ares, god of blood, who established the Sown-men that sprung one day from earth as lords of this land! I will go, and standing on the topmost battlements, will sacrifice myself over the dragons deep, dark den, the spot the seer described, and will set my country free. I have spoken. Now I go to make the city a present of my life, no mean offering, to rid this kingdom of its affliction.
For if each were to take and expend all the good within his power, contributing it to the common good of his country, our states would experience fewer troubles and would prosper for the future.
Exit Menoeceus.
Chorus:
style: tragic chorus, aulos and low drums, massed voices with a lead, driving, incantatory, dark
why: You came, you came, O winged creature — the Sphinx ode, built on repetition and mourning of mothers, mourning of maidens.

title: Phoenissae
author: Euripides
lyrics:
Oh, Polyneices! you were rightly named, after all; woe to you, Thebes!
Your strifenot strife, but murder on murder has brought the house of Oedipus to ruin with dire and grim bloodshed. What harmonious or tuneful wailing can I summon, for my tears, my tears, oh, my home! oh, my home! as I bear these three kindred bodies, my mother and her sons, a welcome sight to the Fury? She destroyed the house of Oedipus, root and branch, when his shrewdness solved the Sphinxs unsolvable song and killed that savage singer. Alas for you, father! What other Hellene or barbarian, what mortal from a noble line ever endured the anguish of such visible afflictions?
Ah! poor girl, how piteous is your cry!
What bird, perched on the high-leaved branches of oak or pine, will come to mourn with me, left motherless? With cries of woe,
style: solo tragic lament, single lyre, unaccompanied female voice, slow, raw, echoing
why: Antigone over three bodies, asking what bird on the high branches will come to mourn with her.

title: Curculio
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
PALINURUS:
By my faith, he who is in love, if he is in want as well, is afflicted with a dreadful malady.
PHAEDROMUS:
Such is not the case with me; for I feel sure that this very day my Parasite will come hither to me with the money.
PALINURUS:
You attempt something mighty, if you expect that which nowhere exists.
PHAEDROMUS:
What if I approach the door, and trill a carol?
PALINURUS:
If you choose; I neither bid nor request you, since, my master, I see that you are of manners and disposition thus changed.
PHAEDROMUS:
(sings.)
Bolts, O ye bolts, with pleasure do I salute you. I love you, I court you, I seek you, and you entreat; most kindly lend your aid to me in love;
become, for my sake, as though play-actors from foreign climes; leap upwards pray, and send out of doors this fair one, who drains my blood for me distractedly in love. (Addressing PALINURUS.) Look at that, how those most accursed bolts sleep on, and none the quicker for my sake do they bestir themselves.
style: roman comic serenade, tibia pipes and lyre, tipsy tenor, swaying, mock-passionate, theatrical
why: The serenade to the door-bolts — Plautus's famous drunken paraclausithyron, marked in the text as sung.

title: Curculio
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
There, at the old shops, are these who lend and those who borrow at interest. Behind the Temple of Castor there are those to whom unguardedly you may be lending to your cost. There, in the Etrurian street, are those men who hold themselves on sale. In the Velabrum youll find either baker, or butcher, or soothsayer; either those who sell retail themselves, or supply to others things to be sold by retail.
Rich sinning husbands youll find at the house of Oppian Leucadia. But, meantime, the door makes a noise; I must curb my tongue.
(Exit.)
(Enter, from the house of CAPPADOX, CURCULIO, leading PLANESIUM, followed by LYCO and CAPPADOX.)
CURCULIO:
Maiden, do you go before; what is behind me I cannot keep my eye upon. Both the trinkets of gold, and all the clothing that she had, were his own, he said.
style: latin patter song, hand drum and pipes, fast wry male vocal, brisk, streetwise, rattling
why: The tour of Rome by vice — the Etrurian street, the Velabrum, the perjurers behind Castor's temple.

title: Curculio
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
CAPPADOX:
Save you, Palinurus.
PALINURUS:
O source of villanies, save you; how are you?
CAPPADOX:
Im just alive.
PALINURUS:
Just as you deserve, I suppose? But whats the matter with you?
CAPPADOX:
My spleen is killing me, my reins are in torment, my lungs are being torn asunder, my liver is being tortured, my heart-strings are giving way, all my intestines are in pain.
PALINURUS:
The liver complaint is afflicting you, then.
CAPPADOX:
My spleen is expanded.
PALINURUS:
Take walking exercise; thats the best thing for the spleen.
style: comic lament, plucked lyre and clacking percussion, groaning bass voice, mock-tragic, lurching
why: The pimp's catalogue of ailments, spleen to intestines, answered with the advice to take a walk.

title: Poems
author: John Gambold
lyrics:
The Mystery of Life.
SO many Years I've seen the Sun,
And call'd these Eyes and Hands my own,
A thousand little Acts I've done
And Childhood have and Manhood known:
O what is Life! and this dull Round
To tread, why was a Spirit bound?
So many airy Draughts and Lines,
And warm Excursions of the Mind,
Have fill'd my Soul with great Designs,
While Practice grovel'd far behind:
O what is Thought! and where withdraw
The Glories which my Fancy saw?
So many tender Joys and Woes
Have on my quiv'ring Soul had Pow'r;
Plain Life with height'ning Passions rose,
style: english hymn, chamber organ and viol, plain tenor, slow, questioning, devotional
why: So many years I've seen the sun — the poem's anaphora and its refrain of unanswered questions.

title: Poems
author: John Gambold
lyrics:
My Soul an unknown Path shall tread,
And strangely leave, who strangely fills
This Frame, and waft me to the Dead:
O what is Death?  'tis Life's last Shore,
Where Vanities are vain no more;
Where all Pursuits their Goal obtain,
And Life is all retouch'd again;
Where in their bright Result shall rise
Thoughts, Virtues, Friendships, Griefs and Joys.
EPITAPH.
ASK not, who ended here his Span?
His Name, Reproach and Praise, was Man.
Did no great Deeds adorn his Course?
No Deed of His, but shew'd him worse:
One Thing was great, which GOD supply'd,
He suffer'd Human Life  and Dy'd.
style: funeral hymn, low organ and cello, grave baritone, hushed, resolving, benedictory
why: The close of the same poem into the epitaph: his name, reproach and praise, was Man.

title: Poems
author: John Gambold
lyrics:
On CLEMENS ALEXANDRINUS'S Description of a Perfect Christian.
HERE from afar the finish'd Height
Of Holiness is seen:
But O what heavy Tracts of Toil,
What Deserts lie between?
Man for the Simple Life Divine
What will it cost to break;
Ere Pleasure soft and wily Pride
No more within him speak?
What lingring Anguish must corrode
The Root of Nature's Joy?
What secret Shame and dire Defeats
The Pride of Heart destroy?
Learn Thou the whole of Mortal State
In Stilness to sustain;
Nor sooth with false Delights of Earth
style: common-meter hymn, four-part voices and harmonium, sober, steady, austere
why: Here from afar the finished height of holiness is seen — and the deserts that lie between.

title: Poems
author: James Boswell
lyrics:
ODE.
IF e'er my fingers touch'd the lyre,
In satire fierce, in pleasure gay,
Shall not my THRALIA'S smiles inspire?
Shall SAM refuse the sportive lay?
My dearest lady! view your slave,
Behold him as your very SCRUB,
Eager to write as authour grave,
Or govern well the brewing tub.
To rich felicity thus rais'd,
My bosom glows with amorous fire;
Porter no longer shall be prais'd;
'Tis I MYSELF am Thrale's Entire!
PIOZZI once alarm'd my fears,
Till beauteous MARY'S tragick fate
And RIZZIO'S tale dissolv'd in tears
style: mock-heroic drawing-room ode, harpsichord and strings, arch male vocal, brisk, satirical, sparkling
why: The burlesque ode in Johnson's voice — behold him as your very Scrub, 'tis I myself am Thrale's Entire.

title: Poems
author: James Boswell
lyrics:
Praise thy past life, and, while they praise, admire
And wail their charming friend, alas! no more.
No costly monument adorns thy tomb,
No panegyric spreads thy humble fame;
Nor verses, carv'd upon the sculptur'd dome,
Transmit to after times thy virtuous name.
Oft as the circling sun returns the day
On which thou mounted to th' realms of rest,
Unto thy lonely grave I'll yearly hie,
And bid the turf lie easy on thy breast.
I'll sprinkle flowers of ev'ry richest dye,
And deck thy grave with wreaths of liveliest hue,
Then shed a tear, and breathe the heaving sigh
To sacred friendship; sure so much is due.
Farewell, my charmer, peace attend thy rest,
Thou, who in virtue did so much excel;
style: 18th century elegy, fortepiano and viola, soft tenor, slow, tender, valedictory
why: No monument, no panegyric — only flowers strewn yearly and the wish that the turf lie easy.

title: Poems
author: James Boswell
lyrics:
How do the streams of pity flow?
How does the breast with throbs spontaneous beat?
How is compassion found so strangely sweet?
Hail! father of the British stage!
Shakespear! to whom shall still belong
Thro' each successive wond'ring age,
The glories of immortal song!
Melpomene, with aspect mild,
With joyful hope exulting smil'd,
What time on Avon's banks she saw
Thee young thy first rude sketches draw
Of richest poesy, whose strains sublime
Already aim'd th' empyreum's height to climb.
Genius unbounded as the sky,
That spreads itself from pole to pole,
Disdains a formal course to fly,
style: pindaric ode, baroque orchestra with trumpet, declamatory tenor, stately, rising
why: Hail, father of the British stage — the Shakespeare strophe, Melpomene smiling over Avon.

title: Fragmenta
author: Bion of Smyrna
lyrics:
Blessed are they who love, when they are loved in equal return.
Blessed was Theseus while Pirithous was at his side,
even though he went down to pitiless Hades.
Blessed was Orestes among the harsh Inhospitable peoples,
because Pylades chose to share his roads with him.
Blessed was Achilles, the grandson of Aeacus, while his comrade lived;
and blessed was he in dying, because he warded off a dread fate from him.
Hesperus, golden light of lovely Aphrodite,
Hesperus, dear holy ornament of the dark-blue night,
as much fainter than the moon as you are foremost among the stars,
hail, friend, and as I lead a revel to the shepherd,
give me your light in place of the moon, since she
today, but newly risen, too quickly set. I do not go
to steal, nor to trouble those who travel by night;
style: hellenistic bucolic hymn, single lyre and syrinx, warm tenor, slow, luminous, evening-lit
why: Blessed are they who love and are loved in return, then the hymn to Hesperus asked to light a lover's way.

title: Fragmenta
author: Bion of Smyrna
lyrics:
May spring, thrice-longed-for, be with me through the whole year round,
when neither cold nor sun weighs heavy upon us.
In spring all things conceive, in spring all sweet things bloom,
and night for men is equal and alike to day . . .
A fowler-boy, still in the leafy grove,
hunting birds, saw the wayward Love
seated upon the branch of a box-tree; and when he saw him,
rejoicing because the bird seemed a great one to him,
joining together all his rods one upon another,
this way and that he lay in wait for Love as he hopped about.
And the boy, vexed, when no end of it came,
threw down his rods and went to an old plowman
who had taught him this craft, and told him,
and showed him Love sitting there. But the old man,
smiling, shook his head and answered the boy:
"Spare yourself the hunt, and do not go after that bird.
style: pastoral idyll, syrinx and soft frame drum, bright male voice, unhurried, sunlit, dancing
why: Spring thrice-longed-for, all things conceiving — then the boy who tries to snare Love with birdlime.

title: Fragmenta
author: Bion of Smyrna
lyrics:
Flee far away. An evil thing is that creature. You will be blessed
so long as you do not catch him; but if you come to a man's full measure,
this very one who now flees and hops away, of his own accord
coming suddenly, will settle upon your head."
Great Cypris stood beside me as I yet slept,
leading the infant Love by his fair hand,
with eyes cast down to the ground, and spoke to me this word:
"Take Love, dear herdsman, and teach him to sing."
So she spoke; and she departed, and I, fool that I was,
taught Love whatever herdsmen's lore I knew, as one willing to learn:
how Pan invented the cross-flute, how Athena the pipe,
how Hermes the lyre, how sweet Apollo the cithara.
These things I kept teaching him; but he heeded not my words,
and instead himself sang me songs of love, and taught me
style: greek bucolic song, kithara and pipes, gentle mid-range voice, lilting, wry, tender
why: Cypris hands the infant Love to a herdsman to be taught song, and Love does the teaching instead.

title: Philosophy and Religion: Six Lectures Delivered at Cambridge
author: Hastings Rashdall
lyrics: Once more to distant ages of the world Let us revert, and place before our thoughts The face which rural solitude might wear To the unenlightened swains of pagan Greece. --In that fair clime, the lonely herdsman, stretched On the soft grass through half a summer's day, With music lulled his indolent repose: And, in some fit of weariness, if he, When his own breath was silent, chanced to hear A distant strain, far sweeter than the sounds Which his poor skill could make, his fancy fetched, Even from the blazing chariot of the sun, A beardless Youth, who touched a golden lute, And filled the illumined groves with ravishment. The nightly hunter, lifting a bright eye Up towards the crescent moon, with grateful heart Called on the lovely wanderer who bestowed That timely light, to share his joyous sport: And hence, a beaming Goddess with her Nymphs, Across the lawn and through the darksome grove, (Not unaccompanied with tuneful notes By echo multiplied from rock or cave), {43} Swept in the storm of chace; as moon and stars Glance rapidly along the clouded heaven, When winds are blowing strong. The traveller slaked His thirst from rill or gushing fount, and thanked The Naiad. Sunbeams, upon distant hills Gliding apace, with shadows in their train, Might, with small help from fancy, be transformed Into fleet Oreads sporting visibly. The Zephyrs fanning, as they passed, their wings, Lacked not, for love, fair objects whom they wooed With gentle whisper. Withered boughs grotesque, Stripped of their leaves and twigs by hoary age, From depth of shaggy covert peeping forth In the low vale, or on steep mountain side; And, sometimes, intermixed with stirring horns Of the live deer, or goat's depending beard,-- These were the lurking Satyrs, a wild brood Of gamesome Deities; or Pan himself, The simple shepherd's awe-inspiring God!
style: pastoral blank-verse setting, acoustic guitar and soft strings, warm narrating voice, unhurried, sunlit
why: Only candidate, and a strong one: how pagan Greece peopled its hills with Apollo, Diana, naiads and Pan.

title: A Short History of Greek Philosophy
author: John Marshall
lyrics:
Thou wilt not leave us in the dust: Thou madest man, he knows not why; He thinks he was not made to die; And Thou hast made him: Thou art just,
Deus immortalis haberi Dum cupit Empedocles, ardentem frigidus Aetnam Insiluit. HOR. *Ad Pisones*, 464 *sqq*.
Naturam expellas furca, tamen usque recurret,
Lead me, O Zeus most great, And thou, Eternal Fate: What way soe'er thy will doth bid me travel That way I'll follow without fret or cavil. {237} Or if I evil be And spurn thy high decree, Even so I still shall follow, soon or late.
style: stoic hymn, low drone and plucked lyre, steady male voice, austere, resolute, slow
why: Only candidate, but it carries Cleanthes' prayer — lead me, O Zeus, that way I'll follow without fret or cavil.

title: Jewish History: An Essay in the Philosophy of History
author: Simon Dubnow
lyrics:
"To die was not his hope; he fain Would live to think and suffer pain."
"The hammer shivers glass, But iron by its blows is forged."
style: eastern european folk lament, solo violin and low male voice, sparse, minor key, resolute
why: The hammer shivers glass but iron by its blows is forged — a whole philosophy of history in a couplet.

title: Viṣṇu Smṛti
author: Viṣṇu
lyrics:
When the night of Brahma had passed, and the Lotus-born had awakened,
Visnu, desiring to create beings, and knowing the Earth was submerged in water, || Vi_1.1 ||
Took on the auspicious form of the Boar, delighting in sport in the water, as in previous cosmic ages,
And lifted up the Earth. || Vi_1.2 ||
He, the great ascetic, whose feet were the Vedas, whose tusks were the sacrificial post, whose teeth were the sacrifice, whose mouth was the fire-altar,
Whose tongue was the sacrificial fire, whose bristles were the sacred *darbha* grass, and whose head was the highest Brahman; || Vi_1.3 ||
The divine one, whose eyes were day and night, whose ornaments were the ancillary Vedic texts in his ears,
Whose nostrils were the clarified butter offering, whose snout was the sacrificial ladle, the great one whose grunt was the chant of the Sama Veda; || Vi_1.4 ||
style: sanskrit cosmogonic chant, tanpura drone and deep frame drum, resonant male voice, slow, vast, ritual
why: The Boar lifting the drowned earth, his whole body read as a sacrifice — tusks the sacrificial post, grunt the Sāma chant.

title: Viṣṇu Smṛti
author: Viṣṇu
lyrics:
Having been thus addressed, the blessed one said, "So be it." // Vi_98.3 //
Vasudha, having obtained her desire, did so. // Vi_98.4 //
And she praised the god of gods. // Vi_98.5 //
Om, salutation to you. // Vi_98.6 //
O god of gods. // Vi_98.7 //
O Vasudeva. // Vi_98.8 //
O primeval god. // Vi_98.9 //
O god of love. // Vi_98.10 //
O protector of love. // Vi_98.11 //
O protector of the earth. // Vi_98.12 //
O you without beginning, middle, or end. // Vi_98.13 //
O lord of creatures. // Vi_98.14 //
O good lord of creatures. // Vi_98.15 //
O great lord of creatures. // Vi_98.16 //

O lord of speech. // Vi_98.18 //
style: namavali litany, harmonium and hand cymbals, call-and-response male voices, steady, hypnotic, devotional
why: A litany of names of the god — already built to be sung antiphonally: O you without beginning, middle, or end.

title: Viṣṇu Smṛti
author: Viṣṇu
lyrics:
He may eat flowers. // Vi_95.7 //
He may eat fruits. // Vi_95.8 //
He may eat vegetables. // Vi_95.9 //
Or he may eat leaves. // Vi_95.10 //
Or he may eat barley-gruel once at the end of a fortnight. // Vi_95.11 //
Or he may subsist on lunar penances. // Vi_95.12 //

> This entire world of gods and men has austerity (*tapas* ()) as its root, /
> Austerity as its middle, and austerity as its end; and by austerity it is thus supported. || Vi_95.15 ||
>
> What is hard to practice, what is hard to obtain, what is distant, and what is difficult to do, /
> All that is achievable by austerity (*tapas* ()); for austerity is indeed insurmountable. || Vi_95.16 ||
Then, having been purified of his passions in the three stages of life, having performed the Prajapatya sacrifice and given his entire wealth as a sacrificial fee, he shall become a renunciant (*pravrajyasrami* ()). // Vi_96.1 //
style: ascetic chant, single drone and finger cymbals, austere male voice, sparse, unhurried, resolute
why: The tapas couplets: austerity as root, middle and end of the world, and nothing insurmountable to it.

title: Poems
author: Moses Mendez
lyrics:
As thro' the heavens he speeds his burning way:
The sultry lion rages for his prey.
Ah Phoebus, quench thy wild destroying fire,
Each flower, each shrub doth sink beneath thy ray,
Save the fresh laurel, that shall ne'er expire.
The leaves that crown a bard may brave celestial ire.
Or shall I hie to mine own hermitage,
Round which the wanton vine her arms doth wind,
There may I lonely turn the sacred page,
Improve my reason, and amend my mind;
Here 'gainst Life's ills a remedy I find.
An hundred flowers emboss the verdant ground;
A little brook doth my sweet cottage bind,
Its waters yield a melancholy sound,
And sooth to study deep, or lull to sleep profound.
The playful insect hopping in the grass
style: spenserian pastoral, lute and recorder, warm tenor, gentle, unhurried, sunlit
why: The hermitage stanza — vine-wound cottage, hundred flowers, a brook that lulls to sleep profound.

title: Poems
author: Moses Mendez
lyrics:
For oft when poets dream, their readers sleep.
On a wide champian, where the surges beat
Th' extended beach, then sullenly retreat,
A dismal cottage rear'd its turfy head,
O'er which a yew her baleful branches spread;
The owl profane his dreadful dirges sung,
The passing bell the foul night-raven rung;
No village cur here bay'd the cloudless moon,
No golden sunshine chear'd the hazy noon,
But ghosts of men by love of gold betray'd,
In silence glided thro' the dreary shade.
There sat pale Grief in melancholy state,
And brooding Care was trusted with the gate,
Within, extended on the cheerless ground,
An old man lay in golden fillet bound;
Rough was his beard, and matted was his hair,
style: gothic ballad, viol and low drone, dark baritone, slow, eerie, brooding
why: The turf cottage under the yew, the owl's dirge, and the old miser bound in a golden fillet.

title: Poems
author: Moses Mendez
lyrics:
'Till I should full three hundred nymphs attain,
Whose hearts should aye with Virtue's lessons glow,
And to all swains but one cry out for ever, No.
To find the fortilage that ne'er will yield
Is not an easy matter, good sir Knight;
Troy town, they say, is now a grass-grown field,
That long withstood the force of Grecian might;
And castles fall tho' deep in earth empight;
Ne ought so strong is found but what may fail,
The sun at last shall lose his glorious light,
And vows or bribes o'er women may prevail;
Their hearts are made of flesh, and mortal flesh is frail.
With heavy heart, and full of cark I go
And take my conge of my blooming maid,
I kiss'd her hond, and, louting very low,
To her behest at length myself array'd:
style: archaic ballad, harp and fiddle, plain male voice, measured, wry, elegiac
why: Troy town is now a grass-grown field — the sun itself shall lose its light, and mortal flesh is frail.

title: Hymn 5 to Aphrodite
author: Homeric Hymns
lyrics:
Muse, tell me the deeds of golden Aphrodite the Cyprian, who stirs up sweet passion
in the gods and subdues the tribes of mortal men and birds that fly in air and all the many
creatures that the dry land rears, and all that the sea: all these love the deeds of
rich-crowned Cytherea. Yet there are three hearts that she cannot bend nor yet ensnare.
First is the daughter of Zeus who holds the aegis, bright-eyed Athena; for she has no
pleasure in the deeds of golden Aphrodite, but delights in wars and in the work of Ares, in strifes and battles and in
preparing famous crafts. She first taught earthly craftsmen to make chariots of war and cars
variously wrought with bronze, and she, too, teaches tender maidens in the house and puts knowledge of goodly arts in each one's mind. Nor does laughter-loving
style: homeric hymn, phorminx lyre and light drum, clear male voice, stately, invocatory, flowing
why: The proem: the goddess who subdues gods, mortals, birds of the air and everything the sea rears.

title: Hymn 5 to Aphrodite
author: Homeric Hymns
lyrics:
golden-throned Eos, the early-born, by the streams of Ocean, at the ends of the earth; but
when the first grey hairs began to ripple from his comely head and noble chin, queenly Eos kept away from his bed, though she cherished him in her house and
nourished him with food and ambrosia and gave him rich clothing. But when loathsome old age
pressed full upon him, and he could not move nor lift his limbs, this seemed to her in her heart the best counsel: she laid him in a room and put to
the shining doors. There he babbles endlessly, and no more has strength at all, such as once
he had in his supple limbs. I would not have you be deathless among the deathless gods and live continually after such sort. Yet if you could live on such as now you are
in look and in form, and be called my husband, sorrow would not then enfold my careful
style: greek lament, single lyre and low drone, ageing male voice, slow, hollow, haunted
why: Tithonus granted deathlessness without youth — shut in a room, babbling endlessly, unable to lift a limb.

title: Hymn 5 to Aphrodite
author: Homeric Hymns
lyrics:
with immortals:
long indeed do they live, eating heavenly food and treading the lovely dance among
