author: Jonathan Swift
lyrics:
VERSES Wrote in a LADY'S Ivory Table-Book.
Anno. 1698.
PERUSE my Leaves thro' ev'ry Part,
And think thou seest my owners Heart,
Scrawl'd o'er with Trifles thus, and quite
As hard, as sensless, and as light:
Expos'd to every Coxcomb's Eyes,
But hid with Caution from the Wise.
Here you may read (Dear Charming Saint)
Beneath (A new Receit for Paint)
Here in Beau-spelling (tru tel deth)
There in her own (far an el breth)
Here (lovely Nymph pronounce my doom)
There (A safe way to use Perfume)
Here, a Page fill'd with Billet Doux;
On t'other side (laid out for Shoes)
style: satirical chamber song, harpsichord and viol, arch mezzo, clipped, sly
why: The lady's table-book, with love notes and shoe accounts alternating line by line.

title: Hymn to Apollo
author: Callimachus
lyrics:
How the laurel-branch of Apollo trembled!
How the whole shrine trembled! Away, away with whoever is sinful!
And now surely Phoebus knocks at the doors with his fair foot.
Do you not see? The Delian palm has nodded sweetly,
all at once, and the swan sings beautifully in the air.
Now of yourselves draw back, you bolts of the gates,
and you, the keys; for the god is no longer far off.
And you young men, make ready for the song and for the dance.
Apollo does not appear to all, but only to whoever is good;
whoever sees him, that man is great; whoever sees him not, that man is lowly.
We shall see you, Far-shooter, and we shall never be lowly.
Let not the children keep the lyre silent, nor their step soundless,
now that Phoebus has come to dwell among us,
if they mean to accomplish their marriage and to cut their grey hair,
style: hellenistic processional hymn, kithara and aulos, young chorus, ecstatic, ringing, quickening
why: The laurel shakes, the palm nods, the swan sings — the god is at the door. Nothing better in the batch.

title: Hymn to Apollo
author: Callimachus
lyrics:
and that the wall may stand upon its ancient foundations.
I marvel at the children, since the tortoise-shell is no longer idle.
Keep holy silence as you hear, at the song of Apollo.
Even the sea keeps silence, when the singers celebrate
either the lyre or the bow, the gear of Lycorean Phoebus.
Nor does Thetis, his mother, wail her dirges for Achilles,
whenever she hears the cry "Hie Paieon, Hie Paieon."
And even the weeping rock holds back its sorrows,
that wet stone set fast in Phrygia,
the marble in place of a woman, gaping in some lament.
Cry "Hie, hie"; it is an evil thing to strive with the blessed gods.
Whoever fights the blessed gods, let him fight my king;
whoever fights my king, let him fight Apollo too.
The chorus that sings to Apollo what is after his heart
he will honour; for he has the power, since he sits at the right of Zeus.
style: ritual hymn with refrain, lyre and hand drum, layered voices, hushed then crying out
why: Even the sea and the weeping rock fall silent at the paean — with the Hie Paieon refrain built in.

title: Hymn to Apollo
author: Callimachus
lyrics:
"Great is the stream of the Assyrian river, but it draws
much refuse of the earth and much rubbish upon its water.
And not from every source do the Bees carry water to Deo,
but only that which, pure and undefiled, creeps up
from a holy spring, a little drip, the choicest of all."
Hail, lord; and let Blame go where Envy is.
style: spare lyric, solo kithara, clear tenor, poised, aphoristic, unhurried
why: The Assyrian river of refuse against the little pure drip the bees carry — Callimachus's poetic creed.

title: Placita Philosophorum
author: Pseudo-Plutarch
lyrics:
Afterwards by the sanction of laws wickedness was suppressed; but by reason that laws could prohibit only public villanies, yet could not hinder many persons from acting secret impieties, some wise persons gave this advice, that we ought to blind truth with lying disguises, and to persuade men that there is a God: Theres an eternal God does hear and see And understand every impiety; Though it in dark recess or thought committed be.
But this poetical fable ought to be rejected, he thought, together with Callimachus, who thus saith: If you believe a God, it must be meant That you conceive this God omnipotent.
EMPEDOCLES believes that Nature is nothing else but the mixture and separation of the elements; for thus he writes in the first book of his natural philosophy: Nature gives neither life nor death, Mutation makes us die or breathe. The elements first are mixed, then all Do separate: this mortals Nature call.
style: presocratic chant, drone and hand drum, grave male voice, slow, elemental
why: The Empedocles quatrain — nature gives neither life nor death, only mixture and separation.

title: Necyomantia
author: Lucian of Samosata
lyrics:
Menippus All hail, my roof, my doors, my hearth and home! How sweet again to see the light and thee!
Menippus Deaths lurking-place I leave, and those dark gates
Where Hades dwells, a God apart from Gods.
Menippus Not so; a living guest in Hades I.
Menippus Youth drew me ontoo bold, too little wise.
Menippus Dear friend, to Hades realms I needs must go,
To counsel with Tiresias of Thebes.
Troubled at heart, with welling tears, we went.
So he, and sought the lawn of asphodel.
style: mock-tragic aria, lyre and low drone, theatrical baritone, wry, declamatory
why: Only candidate; Menippus back from the dark gates, hailing his own roof and the light.

title: Individualism: A System of Politics
author: Wordsworth Donisthorpe
lyrics: Grata populo est Tabella, qu frontes aperit hominum, mentes tegit, dat-que earn libertatem ut quid volrnit faciant.
style: latin motet, small a cappella choir, austere, slow, sustained
why: Only candidate; a single Latin line on the secret ballot that opens men's faces and hides their minds.

title: Yājñavalkya Smṛti
author: Yājñavalkya
style: sanskrit shloka chant, tanpura drone, deep male voice, slow, austere, unadorned
why: The forest ascetic in five fires and wet winter cloth, the same to thorns and to sandalwood.

title: Yājñavalkya Smṛti
author: Yājñavalkya
lyrics:
Just as the conditions of embodied beings in their bodies are endless,
so too are the forms of those beings here in all wombs. // Yj_3.132 //
For some, the fruition of `*karma*` occurs after death; for others, it is born here in this life.
For still others, it is here or in the hereafter; one's state of being is the determining factor. // Yj_3.133 //
One who covets the property of others, contemplates evil,
and adheres to falsehood is born into other wombs. // Yj_3.134 //
A man who speaks untruth, is a slanderer, is harsh in speech,
and engages in idle talk is born among beasts and birds. // Yj_3.135 //
One who delights in taking what is not given, who commits adultery with another's wife,
and who unlawfully inflicts harm is born among immovable things. // Yj_3.136 //
A knower of the Self, pure, self-restrained, ascetic, with conquered senses,
style: sanskrit recitation, drone and small hand cymbals, grave male voice, measured, hypnotic
why: The rebirth verses — the slanderer among beasts and birds, the thief among immovable things.

title: Yājñavalkya Smṛti
author: Yājñavalkya
lyrics:
through these, the Self is known as the wealth and cause of the world. // Yj_3.173 //
Ego, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, happiness, fortitude,
the activity of the inner sense, desire, retention, and life; // Yj_3.174 //
heaven, dream, the impulse of thoughts, the movement of the mind,
the blinking of an eye, consciousness, effort, and the taking on of the five elements // Yj_3.175 //
because these signs of the supreme Self are seen,
therefore there exists a Self beyond the body, all-pervading, the Lord. // Yj_3.176 //
The organs of knowledge with their objects, the mind, the organs of action,
the ego, the intellect, and the elements beginning with earth; // Yj_3.177 //
the Unmanifest, and the Self, the knower of the fieldthis is said of this field.
He is the Lord, situated in all beings, who is being, non-being, and both being and non-being. // Yj_3.178 //
style: upanishadic chant, tanpura and bansuri, low voice, spacious, reverent, slow
why: The catalogue of inner signs closing on a Self beyond the body, all-pervading, seated in all beings.

title: Adelphi
author: Terence
lyrics:
(Enter MICIO, calling to a servant within.)
MICIO:
Storax! Aeschinus has not returned home from the entertainment last night, nor any of the servants who went to fetch him. (To himself.) Really, they say it with reason, if you are absent anywhere, or if you stay abroad at any time,twere better for that to happen which your wife says against you, and which in her passion she imagines in her mind, than the things which fond parents fancy. A wife, if you stay long abroad, either imagines that you are in love or are beloved, or that you are drinking and indulging your inclination, and that you only are taking your pleasure, while she herself is miserable.
As for myself, in consequence of my son not having returned home, what do I imagine? In what ways am I not disturbed? For fear lest he may either have taken cold, or have fallen down somewhere, or have broken some limb. Oh dear! that any man should take it into his head, or find out what is dearer to him than he is to himself!
style: roman comic recitative, tibia and lyre, warm conversational baritone, wry, unhurried
why: Micio waiting up for his son, marvelling that a man can find something dearer to him than himself.

title: Adelphi
author: Terence
lyrics:
He has broken open a door, and forced his way into another persons house, beaten to death the master himself, and all the household, and carried off a wench whom he had a fancy for. All people are exclaiming that it was a most disgraceful proceeding. How many, Micio, told me of this as I was coming here? It is in everybodys mouth. In fine, if an example must be cited, does he not see his brother giving his attention to business, and living frugally and soberly in the country? No action of his is like this. When I say this to him, Micio, I say it to you. You allow him to be corrupted.
MICIO:
Never is there any thing more unreasonable than a man who wants experience, who thinks nothing right except what he himself has done.
DEMEA:
What is the meaning of that?
MICIO:
style: roman comic patter, tibiae and light drum, quick tenor, brisk, arch
why: The liberal father's defence — it was poverty, not virtue, that kept us from doing the same.

title: Adelphi
author: Terence
style: roman recitative, solo tibia and low strings, rueful baritone, slow, self-mocking
why: Demea's turn: a whole life of thrift and rigour repaid with dislike, renounced in one speech.

title: Mostellaria
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
(Enter PHILOLACHES, from the house of THEUROPIDES.)
PHILOLACHES:
(to himself.)
Ive often thought and long reflected on it, and in my breast have held many a debate, and in my heart (if any heart I have) have revolved this matter, and long discussed it, to what thing Im to consider man as like, and what form he has when he is born?
Ive now discovered this likeness. I think a man is like unto a new house when he is born. Ill give my proofs of this fact. (To the AUDIENCE.) And does not this seem to you like the truth? But so Ill manage that you shall think it is so.
Beyond a doubt Ill convince you that it is true what I say. And this yourselves, Im sure, when you have heard my words, will say is no otherwise than just as I now affirm that it is. Listen while I repeat my proofs of this fact;
style: plautine song, tibiae and hand drum, boisterous baritone, patter, comic, bouncing
why: Philolaches announcing his great discovery — that a man newly born is like a new house.

title: Mostellaria
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
Servants who, though they are free from fault, still stand in awe of punishment, those same are wont to be serviceable to their masters.
But those who fear nothing, after they have merited punishment, hit upon foolish plans for themselves: they exercise themselves in running; they take to flight. But, if they are caught, they acquire from punishment a hoard, which by good means they cannot.
They increase from a very little, and from that they lay by a treasure. The resolution thats in my mind is to be determined to be on my guard against punishment, before my back comes to lose its state of soundness. As hitherto it has been, so does it become my hide still to be, without a bruise, and such that I should decline its being beaten.
style: servant's aria, tibia and plucked strings, sly tenor, jaunty, conspiratorial
why: The slave's philosophy of the whip — as servants wish their master to be, such is he wont to be.

title: Mostellaria
author: Plautus, Titus Maccius
lyrics:
I went that way (pointing) slily through the lane to our garden. At the entrance to the garden thats in the lane, I opened the door; and by that road I led out all the troop, both men and women. After, from being in a state of siege, I had led out my troops to a place of safety, I adopted the plan of convoking a senate of my comrades, and when I had convoked it, they forthwith banished me from the senate. When I myself perceived that the matter must be decided by my own judgment, as soon as ever I could, I did the same as many others do, whose affairs are in a critical or a perplexed state; they proceed to render them more perplexed, so that nothing can be settled.
But I know full well, that now by no means can this be concealed from the old man.
But hows this, that our next neighbours door makes a noise? Why, surely this is my master: Id like to have a taste of his talk.
style: comic monologue song, tibiae and tambourine, breathless baritone, fast, farcical
why: Tranio convening a senate of his fellow slaves, who promptly banish him from it.

title: Poems
author: William Gerard Hamilton
lyrics:
ODE TO SLEEP.
BY MR. H.
FRIEND to the gloomy shade of night!
Vast source of fanciful delight!
Power! whose care-dissolving sway,
The slave that pants o'er Indian hills,
The wretch whom snow-girt Zembla chills,
And wide creation's fertile race obey;
The joyous choristers that flit in air,
The mutes that dwell beneath the silver flood,
The savage howling o'er th' affrighted wood,
And man, th' imperious lord of all, thy power declare.
Thy magic wand can oft restrain
The miser's sordid hopes of pain;
Can make each heart-felt trouble cease:
Or from the sickening thought suspend
style: english ode, chamber strings and flute, gentle tenor, hushed, nocturnal
why: The Ode to Sleep's invocation, reaching from Indian hills to snow-girt Zembla — a proper hymn opening.

title: Poems
author: William Gerard Hamilton
style: gothic ode, low strings and chamber organ, dark baritone, storm-driven, eerie
why: Spectres, opening charnels and blustering winds, ending on pour thy loved horrors o'er my soul.

title: Poems
author: William Gerard Hamilton
lyrics:
Shall whisper thro' the shade:
"Stranger, draw near!  To Sorrow true
" With me these lonesome walks review,
"Where Horror's charms invite;
" Daughter of Joy!  I know thy air!
"Retract thy hurry'd steps!  nor dare
" Profane each hallow'd rite!
"To mix with Mirth's mad train be thine:
" The dismal drearier task be mine
"'Mid these lorn scenes to weep!
" My days in these still bowers immur'd,
"By no false flattering hopes allur'd,
" Shall one sad tenor keep.
"Let Grief no more thy youth consume,
" Nor sighing o'er the silent tomb
"Thy piteous murmurs breathe.
style: graveside elegy, solo viola and harp, mourning female voice, slow, austere
why: The voice in the shade warning the daughter of Joy back from the hallowed rite of grief.

title: Tusculan Disputations
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
lyrics: 20. But let us look at Hercules himself, who was broken by pain at the very time when by death itself he was seeking immortality. What words does he utter in Sophocles, in the Trachiniae! When Deianira had put upon him the tunic dyed with the Centaur's blood, and it had cleaved to his flesh, he says: \"O things grievous to tell, harsh to endure, / Which, drained out, I have borne in body and in soul! / Neither did Juno's relentless terror, / Nor sullen Eurystheus, bring me so much ill / As one frenzied woman, the child of Oeneus' birth. / She has snared me unawares in a robe of madness, / Which, clinging to my sides, rends my flesh with its bite / And, pressing hard, draws off the breath of my lungs: / Already it has sucked up all my discoloured blood. / Thus my body, consumed by horrible ruin, has wasted away; / I myself, fast bound, am slain by a woven plague. / This neither an enemy's hand, nor the Earth-born / Mass of the Giants, nor the Centaur with his double-formed onset / Inflicted upon my body, / No power of Greece, no barbarian savagery, / No fierce race banished to the ends of the earth, / Through all of which, ranging, I drove out every wildness  / But I, a man, am slain by a woman, by a woman's hand. / O son, lay true claim to this name for your father, / Let not a mother's love prevail over my death. / Snatch her hither to me, torn from those dutiful hands; / Now shall I see whether you hold her or me the dearer.
style: roman tragic aria, low strings and drone, anguished bass, slow, harrowing
why: Hercules in the burning robe — no giant, no centaur, but a woman's hand kills him.

title: Tusculan Disputations
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
lyrics: 23. Let Aeschylus come forward, who was not a poet only, but a Pythagorean too  for so we have been told. How, in him, does Prometheus bear the pain which he undergoes for the theft from Lemnos  \"whence fire is famed to have been secretly parcelled out to mortals; the cunning Prometheus stole it by guile, and paid the penalties to Jove by supreme decree\"? Paying these penalties, then, fastened to the Caucasus, he says this: \"Offspring of the Titans, sharers of our blood, / Begotten of Heaven, behold me bound to the rugged / And fettering rocks, as on a roaring strait / Timid sailors, fearing the night, make fast their ship. / Thus has Saturnian Jupiter fixed me, / And the will of Jove enlisted the hands of Mulciber. / These wedges, driving them in by cruel craft, / He drove through my limbs; whereby, wretched, by such skill / Transfixed, I dwell in this fortress of the Furies.
style: tragic lament, bowed drone and struck metal, deep male voice, stark, chained, slow
why: Prometheus wedged into the Caucasus, moored like a ship by frightened sailors on a roaring strait.

title: Tusculan Disputations
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
lyrics:
24. Now too, on this third dread day, / With grim swoop, tearing me with his hooked talons, / Jove's minion mangles me with savage feeding. / Then, glutted and sated to the full on my rich liver, / He pours forth a vast cry and, soaring on high, / With feathered tail he fawns upon my blood. / But when the gnawed liver is renewed by swelling, / Then again, greedy, he betakes himself to his foul repasts. / Thus I feed this guardian of my mournful torment, / Which fouls me, living, with unending misery. / For, as you see, fettered by Jove's chains, / I cannot keep the dread bird from my breast.
25. Thus, bereft, I myself receive these anxious plagues, / Seeking in love of death an end to my ill; / But far from death I am driven back by the will of Jove, / And this ancient, doom-laden calamity, heaped up through ages of horror, / Is fixed upon my body; / From which there fall drops melted by the sun's heat, / Which drip without ceasing upon the rocks of Caucasus.\" We seem, then, scarcely able to say that a man so afflicted is not wretched  and, if now wretched, then surely pain is an evil.  You are still pleading my case; but this I shall see to presently;
style: tragic aria, low strings and sparse percussion, ravaged baritone, grinding, unrelenting
why: The eagle fawning on his blood, the liver renewed, the drops melting onto the rock forever.

title: Tiberius
author: Suetonius
lyrics:
Et dic, Roma perit: regnabit sanguine multo,
Ad regnum quisquis venit ab exsilio.
Obdurate wretch! too fierce, too fell to move
The least kind yearnings of a mother's love!
No knight thou art, as having no estate;
Long suffered'st thou in Rhodes
an exile's fate,
No more the happy Golden Age we see;
The Iron's come, and sure to last with thee.
Instead of wine he thirsted for before,
He wallows now in floods of human gore.
Reflect, ye Romans, on the dreadful times,
Made such by Marius, and by Sylla's crimes.
Reflect how Antony's ambitious rage
Twice scar'd with horror a distracted age.
And say, Alas! Rome 's blood in
style: roman satirical ballad, lyre and drum, sneering tenor, driving, caustic
why: The street lampoon on Tiberius in full — the golden age exchanged for iron, wine for human gore.

title: Lesser Hippias
author: Plato
lyrics: Zeus-born son of Laertes, wily Odysseus, I must speak out the word without refraining, as I shall act and think will be accomplished. For hateful to me as the gates of Hades is he who hides one thing in his heart and says another. But I shall speak that which shall be accomplished. In these lines he makes plain the character of each of the men, that Achilles is true and simple, and Odysseus wily and false for he represents Achilles as saying these lines to Odysseus.
style: epic recitation, lyre drone, stern male voice, measured, adamant
why: Achilles' line — hateful as the gates of Hades is the man who hides one thing and says another.

title: The Wages Question
author: Francis Amasa Walker
lyrics:
"Upon one pair of English legs did march three Frenchmen."
"From the rising of the lark to the lodging of the lamb,"
style: english folk air, solo lute, light tenor, sprightly, brief
why: Only candidate; from the rising of the lark to the lodging of the lamb is at least a real line of verse.

title: Hymn 4 to Hermes
author: Homeric Hymns
lyrics:
Muse, sing of Hermes, the son of Zeus and Maia, lord of Cyllene and Arcadia
rich in flocks, the luck-bringing messenger of the immortals whom Maia bare, the rich-tressed nymph, when she was joined in
love with Zeus,
a shy goddess, for she avoided the company of the blessed gods, and lived within a
deep, shady cave. There the son of Cronos used to lie with the rich-tressed nymph, unseen by
deathless gods and mortal men, at dead of night while sweet sleep should hold white-armed
Hera fast.
And when the purpose of great Zeus was fulfilled, and the tenth moon with her was
fixed in heaven, she was delivered and a notable thing was come to pass. For then she bare a
son, of many shifts, blandly cunning, a robber, a cattle driver, a bringer of dreams, a watcher by night, a thief at the gates, one who was soon to show forth wonderful
style: archaic greek hymn, phorminx lyre and frame drum, bright rhapsode tenor, steady processional, incantatory
why: The invocation plus the litany of epithets — robber, cattle driver, bringer of dreams, watcher by night — is a built-in refrain.

title: Hymn 4 to Hermes
author: Homeric Hymns
lyrics:
deed at once. He cut stalks of reed to measure and fixed them, fastening their ends across
the back and through the shell of the tortoise, and then stretched ox hide all over it by
his skill.
Also he put in the horns and fitted a cross-piece upon the two of them, and
stretched seven strings of sheep-gut. But when he had made it he proved each string in turn
with the key, as he held the lovely thing.
At the touch of his hand it sounded marvelously; and, as he tried it, the god sang
sweet random snatches, even as youths bandy taunts at festivals. He sang of Zeus the son of
Cronos and neat-shod Maia, the converse which they
had before in the comradeship of love, telling all the glorious tale of his own begetting.
He celebrated, too, the handmaids of the nymph, and her bright home, and the tripods
style: playful greek lyre song, solo kithara with hand percussion, light agile tenor, quick, mischievous, dancing
why: The birth of the lyre itself: strings tried one by one, and the god singing his own begetting in sweet random snatches.

title: Hymn 4 to Hermes
author: Homeric Hymns
lyrics:
known but you,O thievish son of Maia. What skill is this?
What song for desperate cares? What way of song? For verily here are three things to hand
all at once from which to choose, mirth, and love, and sweet sleep.
And though I am a follower of the Olympian Muses who love dances and the bright
path of song the full-toned chant and ravishing thrill of flutes yet I never cared for any
of those feats of skill at young men's revels, as I do now for this:
I am filled with wonder, O son of Zeus, at your sweet playing. But now, since you,
though little, have such glorious skill, sit down, dear boy, and respect the words of your
elders For now you shall have renown among the deathless gods, you and your mother also.
This I will declare to you exactly:
by this shaft of cornel wood I will surely make you a leader renowned among the
style: greek hymn of wonder, layered lyre and soft aulos, warm high voice, slow, rapt, swelling
why: Apollo undone by music — 'mirth, and love, and sweet sleep' is the line the whole hymn turns on.

title: Elene
author: Cynewulf
lyrics:
The host was heart-shaken, horror-struck,
as nights dark shadow descended upon them.
Then as the battle-king slumbered in sorrow,
surrounded by thanes, a dream descended.
A shining spirit appeared in his sleep,
a heavenly herald, handsome of feature,
who called out his name through the closing darkness.
The king looked up, and saw in his vision,
held by the herald, a holy symbol,
a tree of glory, transcendently bright.
He saw the sign of the Saviors Rood,
gleaming with gold, with gems adorned,
a beacon of brightest wood, brilliantly shining.
Letters of light were laced upon it,
written in wonder, a radiant message.
The messenger of glory spoke with majesty,
style: old english alliterative chant, bowed lyre and low drone, deep male voice, hushed then rising, visionary
why: The dream of the Rood in the night camp — a tree of glory with letters of light laced upon it.

title: Elene
author: Cynewulf
lyrics:
Two hundred winters had wound their way,
and three and forty told in number,
since the Wielder of Glory, the world's true Light,
was born among men to bring us solace.
Then Constantine ruled, the Caesar commanded,
helm of the Romans, a righteous ring-giver.
The lord of legions was loved by his people,
a shield to his warriors, strong in his reign.
Then word was brought to the war-leaders ear
of a gathering horde, a grim invasion.
The Hunnish people and Hrethgoths hardened,
Franks and Hugas, a fearsome force,
had mustered their might by the rivers margin,
on Danubes dark bank, a host of darkness.
Their banners billowed, their byrnies glittered,
they shook their spears, swore oaths of slaughter.
style: nordic folk war-verse, bowed lyre and frame drum, stark low chant, driving, cold, martial
why: Banners billowing, byrnies glittering, oaths of slaughter on the Danube's dark bank — hard alliterative drive.

title: Elene
author: Cynewulf
lyrics:
the eternal kingdom of angels revealed,
a joy without ceasing, and their share assigned
with Mary, for all who take to mind
the day-honoring of the dearest Rood
under the heavens, on which the mightiest
over-ruler of all spread out his arms.
Thus I, old and ready for my journey,
through this frail house have woven word-craft
and wondrously gathered, at times I pondered
and sifted my thoughts in the narrow night.
I did not know the truth of the Rood
until a roomier thought, through that glorious might,
unveiled wisdom in my minds chamber.
I was stained by my deeds, shackled by sins,
worn down by sorrows, bitterly bound,
beset by troubles, until the mighty King
style: solitary old english lament, single bowed lyre, aged male voice, very slow, bare, inward
why: The poet's own signature: old and ready for his journey, weaving word-craft in the narrow night.

title: Poems
author: Mary Leapor
lyrics:
Now the Rivers smoother flow,
Now the op'ning Roses glow,
The Woodbine twines her odorous Charms
Round the Oaks supporting Arms:
Lilies paint the dewy Ground,
And Ambrosia breathes around.
Come, ye Gales that fan the Spring;
Zephyr, with thy downy Wing,
Gently waft to Mira's Breast
Health, Content, and balmy Rest.
Far, O far from hence remain
Sorrow, Care, and sickly Pain.
Thus sung Mira to her Lyre,
Till the idle Numbers tire:
Ah! Sappho sweeter sings, I cry,
And the spiteful Rocks reply,
style: georgian pastoral air, harpsichord and recorder, clear light soprano, lilting, gentle, dancing
why: A true song in tetrameter — rivers, roses, woodbine, and Zephyr called to waft rest to Mira's breast.

title: Poems
author: Mary Leapor
lyrics:
DORINDA at her Glass.
DORINDA, once the fairest of the Train,
Toast of the Town, and Triumph of the Plain;
Whose shining Eyes a thousand Hearts alarm'd,
Whose Wit inspired, and whose Follies charm'd:
Who, with Invention, rack'd her careful Breast
To find new Graces to insult the rest,
Now sees her Temples take a swarthy Hue,
And the dark Veins resign their beauteous Blue;
While on her Cheeks the fading Roses die,
And the last Sparkles tremble in her Eye.
Bright Sol had drove the sable Clouds away,
And chear'd the Heavens with a Stream of Day,
The woodland Choir their little Throats prepare,
To chant new Carols to the Morning Air:
In Silence wrap'd, and curtain'd from the Day,
style: georgian parlour song, harpsichord and viola da gamba, expressive mezzo, measured, wistful, chamber
why: Dorinda at her glass: 'the fading Roses die, / And the last Sparkles tremble in her Eye.'

title: Poems
author: Mary Leapor
lyrics:
And wanton out their Age of half a Day:
In those small Groves the smaller Birds may sing,
And share like us their Winter and their Spring.
Pluck off you Acorn from its Parent Bough,
Divide that Acorn in the midst  and now
In its firm Kernel a fair Oak is seen
With spreading Branches of a sprightly Green:
From this young Tree a Kernel might we rend,
There wou'd another its small Boughs extend.
All Matter lives, and shews its Maker's Power;
There's not a Seed but what contains a Flower:
Tho' unobserv'd its secret Beauty lies,
Till we are blest with Microscopick Eyes.
When for blue Plumbs our longing Palate calls,
Or scarlet Cherries that adorn the Walls;
With each plump Fruit we swallow down a Tree,
style: english baroque devotional air, chamber organ and lute, warm soprano, unhurried, bright, contemplative
why: 'There's not a Seed but what contains a Flower' — and with each plump fruit we swallow down a tree.

title: Poems
author: Francis Coventry
lyrics:
And Phebe pales her lamp of night,
Still let me wander forth anew,
And print my footsteps on the dew,
What time the swain with ruddy cheek
Prepares to yoke his oxen meek,
And early drest in neat array
The milk-maid chanting shrill her lay,
Comes abroad with milking pail;
And the sound of distant flail
Gives the ear a rough good-morrow,
And the lark from out his furrow
Soars upright on matin wings,
And at the gate of heaven sings.
But when the sun with fervid ray
Drives upwards to his noon of day,
And couching oxen lay them down
style: georgian pastoral ode, baroque strings and recorder, warm tenor, flowing, fresh, morning-bright
why: Milk-maid, flail, and the lark that soars upright and sings at the gate of heaven.

title: Poems
author: Francis Coventry
lyrics:
The sloping lawns, and zephyrs mild,
The clouds that blush with ev'ning red,
Or meads with silver fountains fed,
The fragrance of the new-mown hay,
And black-bird chanting on the spray;
The calm farewel of parting light,
And Ev'ning sad'ning into Night.
Nor wearied yet my roving feet,
Tho' Night comes on amain, retreat;
But still abroad I walk unseen
Along the star-enlighten'd green;
Superior joys my soul invite,
Lift, lift to heav'n the dazzled sight.
Lo, where the moon enthron'd on high,
Sits steady empress of the sky,
Enticing nations to revere,
style: english pastoral ballad, acoustic strings and soft flute, warm low voice, unhurried, dusk-lit, fading
why: New-mown hay, blackbird on the spray, 'the calm farewel of parting light, / And Ev'ning sad'ning into Night.'

title: Poems
author: Francis Coventry
lyrics:
And proudly vain of pagan fear;
Or where thro' clouds she travels fast,
And seems on journey bent in haste,
While thousand hand-maid stars await,
Attendant on their queen of state.
'Tis now that in her high controul,
Ambitious of a foreign rule,
She stirs the Ocean to rebel,
And factious waters fond to swell
Guides to battle in her carr,
'Gainst her sister Earth to war.
Thus let me muse on things sublime,
Above the flight of modern rhyme,
And call the soul of Newton down,
Where it sits high on starry throne,
Inventing laws for worlds to come,
style: sublime baroque ode, full strings and chamber organ, declamatory tenor, stately, swelling, awed
why: The moon as empress with a thousand hand-maid stars, stirring the ocean to rebel against her sister Earth.

title: Liber Protrepticus ad Nepotem
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: 22.po. To his Grandson Ausonius. The Muses too have their sports: leisure is mingled with the songs, my honey-sweet grandson; nor does the imperious voice of the harsh master ever exercise the boys without ceasing, but rest and the turns of study keep their fixed times. And it is enough for a retentive boy to have read gladly, and it is allowed to pause. School is named by a Greek name (schole, leisure): let just leisures be granted to the toil-bearing Muses. Wherefore learn the more gladly that alternating play surely follows: we give the intervals that shall soothe the long labour. A boy's zeal grows weary, unless glad things be varied with austere, holidays with workdays. Learn gladly, and do not detest, grandson, the reins of a stern teacher: never is the look of a master a thing of horror. Though he, sad with age and not serene of voice, threaten the harsh quarrels of a knit brow, he will never be monstrous, who has once steeped his face in a placid habit. He will love the wrinkles of his nurse who flees his mother; grandfathers and trembling grandmothers the late-born prefer to their fathers  grandsons, a new care. So neither did Chiron, mingled with the Thessalian horse, terrify Achilles son of Peleus, nor the pine-bearing Atlas the boy son of Amphitryon (Hercules), but each, gentle, soothed his tender charges with mild addresses. Do you too not fear, although the school resound with many a stroke and the old master wear a truculent face: fear convicts degenerate spirits; but do you stand firm, undismayed, and let no shout and sounding blows, no dread under the morning hours, agitate you. That the sceptre of the rod is brandished, that there is much furniture of switches, that the deceitful soft leather covers the scourge, that your benches seethe with anxious tumult  these are the pomp of the place, and the scene is painted with a vain terror. These things once your father and your mother followed, and soothed my untroubled old age into peace for me. Do you, who bear your grandfather's name, in your first promise, my first grandson, hold out to me, whether in reality or in hope, an old age  whatever, as the years glide on, the fates shall give  to be enjoyed. Now I shall behold you a boy, soon in your youthful years, and now a man, if chance so bid; or if there be envy in it, I shall hope nonetheless, nor shall my prayers grow weary, that, mindful both of your father and of me, you may ever, eloquent, desire the lofty rewards of the Muses, and one day walk this road, on which we went before, and which your father the proconsul, your great-uncle the prefect, press upon. Read through whatever is memorable; I shall give the first counsels. The author of the Iliad and the lovely beginnings of Menander must be unrolled by you: do you, with the bending and keenness of your voice, bring out the numberless numbers (rhythms) with learned accents, and, as you read, put on the feelings: division increases the sense, and the intervals give vigour to the dull. And when shall those gifts fall to my old age? When will you renew for me, declaiming, so many poems forgotten, and so many strung through the ages of history  the comic shoes and the curtains of kings, the melic and lyric measures  and make the senses, overlaid in an old man, grow young again? With you leading the way, grandson, it is right to learn over again the measured poems of Flaccus (Horace) and high-sounding Maro. And you, dear Terence, who run over the stages in chosen speech, courteous, in the tight-laced sock of Latium, compel my scarce-remembering old age to your new dialogues. Now your crime, Catiline, and the tumult of Lepidus; now, beginning from Lepidus and Catulus, the affairs and times of Rome I connect in a series through twice six years. Now I read of the war mingled with civil strife, which Sertorius the exile stirred up with his Iberian ally. Nor do I, an unskilled grandfather, give these counsels; but, having trained a thousand talents, I myself, in my boastful years, reared many; and, cherishing them in my bosom and loosing their murmurs, I snatched their tender age from the coaxing nurses; soon, by soft admonition and gentle fear, I enticed the boys, that, mild, they might seek their advancement through hard things, about to pluck the sweet fruit of a bitter root. The same boys, taking on the toga in the stir of grown age, I led forward to good morals and arts and the vigour of speech, although they refused to bear the rein upon their neck, and would not offer their mouths to the inserted bits. Hard is the temperance, hard the experience, rare the outcome, proved by a long use of affairs, that a mild censorship should rule unteachable youth  which was endured by me, until at last the toil grew pleasant, and good habit, by use, lightened the labour; until I was summoned to the pious duties of the Augustan instruction, and, increased, was girded with various honour, when I was bidden to obey at the golden palace. Let Nemesis stand aloof, and let Fortune bear with me as I jest: I presided over the empire, while the prince, still wearing the boy's gown in the purple, set before himself, with his sceptre and his throne, the rights of his master, and Augustus thought our honours the greater. These, soon ripe, he brought forth with lofty increase: that I should be made quaestor to the Augusti, father and son; that I should put on a double prefecture and the curule chair, the consular robe and the embroidered toga  my rewards, a consul  and be held foremost in my own annals. By these I sought for my grandson how great a merit, a consul and grandfather, and I shine forth as the light of your life. Although you have long been famous by your father's name, and could be held adorned, or could be held burdened; yet from us a renowned honour has accrued. Now do you bring it to pass that it be no burden, that through yourself, striving upward to the heights, you may climb, and may hope for your own fasces with you as consul.
style: late antique latin recitation, soft harp and low strings, avuncular baritone, measured, warm, conversational
why: The only candidate, and it carries a real turn: a grandfather telling a frightened boy that the schoolmaster's terror is only painted scenery.

title: Epithalamium Achillis et Deidameiae
author: Bion of Smyrna
lyrics:
neither of the Mycenaeans nor of Elis nor of the Laconians,
stayed at home in his hall, fleeing wretched war.
But hidden among the daughters of Lycomedes was Achilles alone,
and instead of arms he was learning to handle wool, and in his white hand
he held a maiden's task, and seemed like a girl;
for he made himself womanly as they were, and so great a bloom
flushed his snowy cheeks, and with the gait
of a maiden he walked, and covered his hair with a veil.
But the heart of a man he had, and the love of a man he had;
and from dawn to night he would sit beside Deidameia,
and at times he kissed her hand, and often
he lifted up her fair warp-thread, and praised her intricate webs;
and he ate with no other companion, and did all things
hastening toward their shared sleep. He spoke this word too to her:
style: hellenistic bucolic idyll, panpipes and soft lyre, high tenor, languid, honeyed, tender
why: Achilles veiled among the girls at the loom — 'the heart of a man he had, and the love of a man he had.'

title: Epithalamium Achillis et Deidameiae
author: Bion of Smyrna
lyrics:
MYRSON
Will you now sing me, Lycidas, some sweet Sicilian strain,
lovely, honey-hearted, amorous, such as the Cyclops
Polyphemus sang to Galatea by the shore?
LYCIDAS
I too, Myrson, am glad to pipe; but what shall I sing?
MYRSON
The Scyrian love, Lycidas, the sweet love men envied,
the secret kisses of the son of Peleus, the secret bed,
how the boy put on a robe, and how he belied his form,
and how among the daughters of Lycomedes, heedless,
Deidameia came to know Achilles within the bridal chamber.
LYCIDAS
Once the herdsman carried off Helen, and led her to Ida,
a bitter grief to Oenone. And Lacedaemon was wroth,
and gathered all the Achaean host, and no Greek,
style: sicilian pastoral duet, syrinx and plucked lyre, two soft voices trading lines, gentle, sunlit, unhurried
why: A shepherd asking for a song and naming exactly what he wants: the Scyrian love, the secret kisses, the secret bed.

title: Instituta Laconia
author: Plutarch
lyrics: Archilochus the poet, when he arrived in Sparta, they ordered to depart that very instant because they learned that he had written in his verses that it is better to throw away ones arms than to be killed: Shield that was mine, fair armour, now gladdens the heart of some Saian; Sorry I left it behind tangled in brush in my path; But for myself I escaped from the clutches of Death. Let perdition Take the old shield, for no worse surely Ill get the next time.
style: archaic greek soldier's song, aulos and hand drum, wry baritone, brisk, marching, defiant
why: Archilochus thrown out of Sparta, with the shield poem itself intact — 'no worse surely I'll get the next time.'

title: Capital, Volume One: The Process of Production of Capital
author: Karl Marx
lyrics: Acerba fata Romanos agunt Scelusque fraternae necis. [A cruel fate torments the Romans, and the crime of fratricide]
style: latin epode dirge, low male chorus and sparse frame drum, slow, ominous, unresolved
why: The only candidate in the work — a bleak Horatian tag on fratricide that at least stands alone as a line.

title: Electra
author: Sophocles
lyrics:
any in the house your nurse but I, and by you I was ever called sister. But now all this has vanished in a day with your death. Like a whirlwind you have swept everything away with you. Our father is gone; I am dead because of you; you yourself are dead and gone; our enemies laugh at us; and our mother, who is no mother, raves with joy. Unknown to her, you often sent me messages about her, saying that you yourself would appear for vengeance. But our evil fortune, yours and mine, has torn all that away, and has sent you back to me in this state, ash and a useless shade in place of your beloved form.
ah, me, ah, me! O pitiable body! Alas, dear one sent on a most dire journey, how you have destroyed me, destroyed me indeed, my brother!
Therefore accept me into this abode of yoursme, a nothing, into your nothingness,so that I may dwell with you hereafter below. For when you were on earth, we shared equally, and now I wish to die and not to be left out of your grave, since I see that the dead are relieved of pain.
style: greek tragic lament, solo aulos and sparse lyre, keening female voice, very slow, bare, desolate
why: Electra over the urn — 'accept me into this abode of yours, me, a nothing, into your nothingness.'

title: Electra
author: Sophocles
lyrics:
Chorus:
But never by weeping nor by prayer will you resurrect your father from the pool of Hades which receives all men.
No, by grieving without end and beyond due limits you will find cureless misery and your own ruin; in these actions there is no deliverance from evils. Tell us, why do you pursue such suffering?
Electra:
Foolish is the child who forgets a parents piteous death. No, closer to my heart is the
mourner who eternally wails, Itys, Itys, that bird mad
with grief, the messenger of Zeus.
Ah, all-suffering Niobe, you I count divine, since you weep forever in your rocky tomb!
Chorus:
Not to you alone of mortals, my daughter, has sorrow come, though you face it with less restraint than those girls inside, Chrysothemis and Iphianassa, whose parents and blood you share. They still live, as he, too, lives, sorrowing in his secluded youth, yet happy in that this famous realm of the Mycenaeans shall one day receive him as a
style: ancient chorus with soloist, lyre and frame drum, layered voices answering one voice, solemn, circling, building
why: The kommos on grief that will not end: the bird crying Itys, Itys, and Niobe weeping in her rock.

title: Poems
author: Edward Young
lyrics:
Night I. On life, death, and immortality.
Humbly inscribed to the right honourable Arthur Onslow, Esq., Speaker of the House of Commons.
Tired Nature's sweet restorer, balmy Sleep!
He, like the world, his ready visit pays
Where Fortune smiles; the wretched he forsakes;
Swift on his downy pinion flies from woe,
And lights on lids unsullied with a tear.
From short (as usual) and disturb'd repose
I wake: how happy they who wake no more!
Yet that were vain, if dreams infest the grave.
I wake, emerging from a sea of dreams
Tumultuous; where my wreck'd desponding thought,
From wave to wave of fancied misery,
At random drove, her helm of reason lost:
Though now restored, 't is only change of pain,
(A bitter change!) severer for severe.
style: solemn georgian nocturne, chamber organ and low strings, grave baritone, slow, hushed, funereal
why: 'Tired Nature's sweet restorer, balmy Sleep!' — the most famous opening in the graveyard school, and it holds alone.

title: Poems
author: Edward Young
lyrics:
All accident apart, by Nature sign'd,
My warrant is gone out, though dormant yet;
Perhaps behind one moment lurks my fate.
Must I then forward only look for Death?
Backward I turn mine eye, and find him there.
Man is a self-survivor every year.
Man, like a stream, is in perpetual flow.
Death's a destroyer of quotidian prey.
My youth, my noon-tide, his; my yesterday;
The bold invader shares the present hour.
Each moment on the former shuts the grave.
While man is growing, life is in decrease,
And cradles rock us nearer to the tomb.
Our birth is nothing but our death begun;
As tapers waste that instant they take fire.
Shall we then fear lest that should come to pass,
style: english blank-verse meditation, viola da gamba and single bell, low male voice, measured, austere, tolling
why: 'Our birth is nothing but our death begun; / As tapers waste that instant they take fire.'

title: Poems
author: Edward Young
lyrics:
Of man's miraculous mistakes, this bears
The palm, "That all men are about to live,"
For ever on the brink of being born.
All pay themselves the compliment to think
They one day shall not drivel; and their pride
On this reversion takes up ready praise,
At least their own; their future selves applauds;
How excellent that life they ne'er will lead!
Time lodged in their own hands is folly's vails;
That lodged in Fate's, to wisdom they consign;
The thing they can't but purpose they postpone.
'T is not in folly not to scorn a fool;
And scarce in human wisdom to do more.
All promise is poor dilatory man,
And that through every stage: when young, indeed,
In full content we sometimes nobly rest,
style: georgian moral ode, harpsichord and strings, declamatory tenor, steady, ironic, gathering
why: 'That all men are about to live' — forever on the brink of being born, the whole poem's argument in one line.

title: Poems
author: Matthew Prior
lyrics:
And often took Leave; but was loath to Depart.
What frightens You thus, my good Son? says the Priest:
You Murther'd, are Sorry, and have been Confest.
O Father! My Sorrow will scarce save my Bacon:
For 'twas not that I Murther'd, but that I was Taken.
Pough! pr'ythee ne'er trouble thy Head with such Fancies:
Rely on the Aid You shall have from Saint Francis:
If the Money You promis'd be brought to the Chest;
You have only to Dye: let the Church do the rest.
And what will Folks say, if they see You afraid?
It reflects upon Me; as I knew not my Trade:
Courage, Friend; To-day is your Period of Sorrow;
And Things will go better, believe Me, To-morrow.
To-Morrow? our Hero reply'd in a Fright:
He that's hang'd before Noon, ought to think of To-night.
Tell your Beads, quoth the Priest, and be fairly truss'd up:
style: georgian comic ballad, fiddle and harpsichord, wry baritone patter, brisk, jaunty, gallows-humoured
why: The condemned man and the priest, ending on a real punchline: 'He that's hang'd before Noon, ought to think of To-night.'

title: Poems
author: Matthew Prior
lyrics:
In t'other, at his Hours of Leisure,
He smokes his Pipe, and takes his Pleasure.
And now your Matrimonial Cupid,
Lash'd on by Time, grows tir'd and stupid.
For Story and Experience tell Us,
That Man grows cold, and Woman jealous.
Both would their little Ends secure:
He sighs for Freedom, She for Pow'r.
His Wishes tend abroad to roam;
And Her's, to domineer at Home.
Thus Passion flags by slow Degrees;
And ruffl'd more, delighted less,
The busy Mind does seldom go
To those once charming Seats below:
But, in the Breast incamp'd, prepares
For well-bred Feints, and future Wars.
style: drawing-room satirical song, plucked harpsichord and light strings, arch mezzo, light, clipped, knowing
why: Marriage anatomised in couplets — 'He sighs for Freedom, She for Pow'r.'

title: Poems
author: Matthew Prior
lyrics:
Fav'rites of Heav'n, with happy Care protect
Their fleecy Charge; and joyous drink her Wave.
Thee, God, to Cnossus Neda brought: the Nymphs
And Corybantes Thee their sacred Charge
Receiv'd; Adraste rock'd Thy golden Cradle:
The Goat, now bright amidst her fellow-Stars,
Kind Amalthea, reach'd her Tett distent
With Milk, Thy early Food: the sedulous Bee
Distill'd her Honey on Thy purple Lips.
Around, the fierce Curetes (Order solemn
To thy foreknowing Mother!) trod tumultuous
Their Mystic Dance, and clang'd their sounding Arms;
Industrious with the warlike Din to quell
Thy Infant-Cries, and mock the Ear of Saturn.
Swift Growth and wond'rous Grace, O heav'nly Jove,
Waited Thy blooming Years: Inventive Wit,
style: classical hymn art song, baroque strings and harp, clear tenor, stately, bright, ceremonial
why: Infant Zeus in a golden cradle, the bee distilling honey on his lips while the Curetes clash their arms to drown his crying.

title: Poems
author: Rebekah Carmichael
lyrics:
Ah! she could tell thee such a tale!
Look not, Maria, with surprise,
Dim is the Star of Eden vale.
But why should I this tale relate,
Or what can sighs or tears avail?
Curse on a rival's ruthless hate,
Fall'n is the Star of Eden vale.
But I'll forbear to tell her name,
For that would turn Maria pale;
Yet never was she heard to blame,
But bless the Star of Eden vale.
With languid look, at close of day,
She walks alone by hill and dale;
And oft I've heard her sighing say,
The Sun is set in Eden vale.
A TALE
style: scottish parlour ballad, fiddle and small harp, plaintive female voice, slow, lilting, refrain-led
why: Built on a returning line — 'Dim is the Star of Eden vale' — closing on 'The Sun is set in Eden vale.'

title: Poems
author: Rebekah Carmichael
lyrics:
ON THE FATE OF CAPTAIN G*****
Sad on the margin of the deep,
I saw a lady sit and weep,
Arrayed in robes of white;
Below she mark'd the billows rise,
Above the dark unsettled skies,
Nor shiver'd at the sight.
No terror in her looks I trac'd,
While lightnings gleam wild o'er the waste,
And hideous thunders roar.
For O! the mind o'ercharg'd with care,
The heart-struck marble, in despair,
Alas! can feel no more.
But, like soft rains 'midst summer sun,
Her tears in mild composure run
From either beaming eye;
style: scots ballad lament, harp and low strings, clear female voice, unhurried, grey, sea-swept
why: A lady in white weeping on the shore while the lightning walks the waste and she does not flinch.

title: Poems
author: Rebekah Carmichael
lyrics:
In all the charms of youth;
Your face and figure e'er divine,
But, O! you've lost a tooth.
Ah! why that angry frown? for shame!
I only speak the truth:
It cannot hurt Eliza's fame
To say she's lost a tooth.
But search some hearts, perhaps you'll find
A greater fault forsooth;
O! it were well for woman kind
Were all their loss a tooth!
A ROMANTIC SCENE
Which happened in the year 1746.
Phenes and Hero far retir'd,
Without one wish to be admir'd,
Liv'd in a lonely den;
style: georgian comic air, harpsichord and pizzicato strings, arch female voice, quick, teasing, light
why: A whole joke with its own refrain — 'O! it were well for woman kind / Were all their loss a tooth!'

title: Orations
author: Dio Chrysostom
lyrics:
24. Muses of Pieria, who glorify with songs, come, tell of Zeus, your own father, hymning him, through whom mortal men are alike unspoken and spoken of, named and unnamed, by the will of great Zeus. For lightly he gives strength, and lightly he crushes the strong; lightly he diminishes the conspicuous and exalts the obscure, and lightly he makes straight the crooked and withers the proud  Zeus who thunders on high, who dwells in the loftiest halls.
23. The assembly was stirred like the long waves of the sea, of the Icarian deep, which the East Wind and the South Wind raise, rushing from the clouds of father Zeus; and another again: The people is a fickle evil, and like the sea is all whipped up by the wind; and in calm a brief breath rears it into crests. And if some pretext arise, it has swallowed up the citizen.
style: archaic greek hymn, kithara and low drone, deep male voice, slow, oracular, weighty
why: The Hesiodic hymn to Zeus — lightly he gives strength, lightly he crushes the strong — with its own hammering repetition.

title: Orations
author: Dio Chrysostom
lyrics:
13. somewhat consonant with this, calls upon a third, beyond the two witnesses, the prophetic Sibyl; and she, having received a clear voice from the god, sings very loudly: Happy is the pine-clad blessed neck of Ephyra, daughter of Ocean, where Poseidon, father of my mother Lamia, first set up a contest together with the Sun, and bore away the honours alone.
38. but the poet who made this epigram boasted vainly, which they say was written upon the tomb of Midas: I am a bronze maiden, and I lie upon the tomb of Midas. So long as water flows and tall trees flourish, remaining here on the much-wept tomb, I shall announce to those passing by that Midas is buried here.
style: greek epitaph chant, single lyre, distant clear voice, still, timeless, sparse
why: The bronze maiden on Midas' tomb: so long as water flows and tall trees flourish, she will keep saying it.

title: Aesthetical Essays
author: Friedrich Schiller
lyrics:
"Oh nobleness, oh generosity of the ancient manners of chivalry! These were rivals, separated by their faith, suffering bitter pain throughout their frames in consequence of a desperate combat; and, without any suspicion, behold them riding in company along dark and winding paths. Stimulated by four spurs, the horse hastens his pace till they arrive at the place where the road divides." ["Orlando Furioso," canto i., stanza 32.]
"'Thus, then, I am for thee a faithful host in Argos, and thou to me in Lycia, when I shall visit that country. We shall, therefore, avoid our lances meeting in the strife. Are there not for me other Trojans or brave allies to kill when a god shall offer them to me and my steps shall reach them? And for thee, Glaucus, are there not enough Achaeans, that thou mayest immolate whom thou wishest? But let us exchange our arms, in order that others may also see that we boast of having been hosts and guests at the time of our fathers.' Thus they spoke, and, rushing from their chariots, they seized each other's hands, and swore friendship the one to the other." [Pope's "Iliad," vi. 264-287.]
style: chivalric epic recitation, viol and lute, warm baritone, measured, noble, unhurried
why: Two enemies trading armour instead of blows, so that others may see they were hosts and guests in their fathers' time.

title: Letters
author: Plato
lyrics:
Bereft of friendsah! woe is meI die.
But not one of them has represented him as dying for lack of gold. This other poem also to men of judgement seemeth not amiss In this our human life, with halting hopes, It is not glittering gold that rarest is: Not diamond nor couches silver-wrought Appear so brilliant in the eyes of men: Nor do the fertile fields of earths broad breast, Laden with crops, so all-sufficing seem As gallant mens unanimous resolve.
style: classical greek gnomic song, lyre and soft drone, grave male voice, slow, reflective, plain
why: Not gold nor diamond nor loaded fields, but 'gallant men's unanimous resolve' — a complete argument in verse.

title: Symbolic Logic
author: Lewis Carroll
lyrics: "Jack Sprat could eat no fat: His wife could eat no lean: And so, between them both, They licked the platter clean."
style: victorian nursery rhyme, music box and pizzicato strings, bright playful voice, quick, light, sing-song
why: The only candidate, and it happens to be a finished song already — Jack Sprat, whole and singable.

title: Culex
author: Appendix Vergiliana
lyrics:
a judge who avenges, after death, the deeds of life.
But fortune, prevailing, had made him bold before.
Now the swift rivers had stood still, and the throng of wild beasts,
following his coaxing voice, had settled in Orpheus' region;
and now the oak had moved its deepest root high
from the green earth, the rivers had stood, and the sounding woods
of their own accord snatched his songs with their greedy bark.
The Moon too, gliding with two yoked horses through the stars,
checked her steeds: and you, monthly maiden, the running
ones you held, to hear the lyre, the night abandoned.
This same lyre could conquer for you the wife of Dis,
and grant Eurydice to be led back of her own accord: it was not lawful,
it was not appeasable for the goddess of death to grant return to life.
style: latin orphic lament, single lyre and low bowed drone, high plaintive voice, slow, spellbound, suspended
why: Orpheus stops the rivers and the beasts, and the Moon reins in her horses to listen — and it still is not enough.

title: Culex
author: Appendix Vergiliana
lyrics:
when, the flock driven together, the shepherd, the shadows doubling,
goes on, and prepares to give rest to his wearied limbs.
When sleep, the lighter, entered through his body,
and his languid limbs rested, slumber poured out,
the likeness of the gnat came to him, and to him,
sad at the outcome of its death, sang reproaches.
"Who," it said, "and to what fortune borne, am I forced
to undergo this bitter change? While your very life was dearer to me
than my own life, I am snatched through the void by the winds.
You, slack, refresh your pleasant limbs in rest,
snatched from foul disasters: but my shades
the gods compel to swim across the Lethean waters.
I am driven, the prey of Charon. I have seen how, blazing with torches,
all the thresholds shine in the infernal temples.
style: latin underworld song, hollow flute and dark strings, thin spectral voice, slow, hushed, reproachful
why: The ghost of the gnat wakes the shepherd to accuse him: 'I am driven, the prey of Charon.'

title: Culex
author: Appendix Vergiliana
lyrics:
Therefore, both to tell the cause of death and of life,
the savage Penalties force me with their lashes before the judge,
since you are the cause of my evil, nor are you present as a witness,
but care more bearably. Do you hear these things, unmindful?
Yet, when you have heard them, you will scatter all to the winds,
and my words will be snatched through the spreading breezes.
I depart, never to return. You, tend the spring
and the green woods of the groves and the pastures, glad."
It spoke, and sadly with its last word withdrew.
When the idleness of life dismissed him, anxious,
groaning heavily within, nor did he bear any longer
the grief poured into his senses at the gnat's death,
as much as his aged strength bestowed upon him
yet with which, fighting, he had conquered the hostile foe
style: roman pastoral farewell, reed pipe and soft lyre, warm baritone, unhurried, tender, fading
why: The parting line is a small perfect blessing: 'I depart, never to return. You, tend the spring and the green woods.'

title: Poems
author: James Thomson
lyrics:
SPRING.
COME, gentle SPRING, AETHEREAL MILDNESS, come,
And from the bosom of yon dropping cloud,
While music wakes around, veil'd in a shower
Of shadowing roses, on our plains descend.
O HERTFORD, fitted, or to shine in courts,
With unaffected grace; or walk the plain,
With INNOCENCE and MEDITATION join'd
In soft assemblage, listen to my song,
That thy own Season paints; when NATURE all
Is blooming, and benevolent like thee.
AND see where surly WINTER passes off,
Far to the north, and calls his ruffian blasts;
His blasts obey, and quit the howling hill,
The shatter'd forest, and the ravag'd vale:
While softer gales succeed, at whose kind touch,
style: georgian pastoral ode, baroque strings and flute, warm tenor, flowing, bright, welcoming
why: 'Come, gentle Spring, aethereal mildness, come' — an invocation built to be sung, with Winter walking off north behind it.

title: Poems
author: James Thomson
lyrics:
" Down thunders back the Stone with mighty Sweep,
"And hurls your Labours to the Valley deep,
" For-ever vain: come, and, withouten Fee,
"I in Oblivion will your Sorrows steep,
" Your Cares, your Toils, will steep you in a Sea
"Of full Delight: O come, ye weary Wights, to me!
"With me, you need not rise at early Dawn,
" To pass the joyless Day in various Stounds:
"Or, louting low, on upstart Fortune fawn,
" And sell fair Honour for some paltry Pounds;
"Or through the City take your dirty Rounds,
" To cheat, and dun, and lye, and Visit pay,
"Now flattering base, now giving secret Wounds;
" Or proul in Courts of Law for human Prey,
"In venal Senate thieve, or rob on broad High-way.
"No Cocks, with me, to rustic Labour call,
style: spenserian song of temptation, harp and viol, low seductive voice, languid, drowsy, hypnotic
why: The enchanter's call from the Castle of Indolence — 'O come, ye weary Wights, to me!' — a refrain with a hook already in it.

title: Poems
author: James Thomson
lyrics:
Of horrid prospect, shag the trackless plain:
Nor finds the river, nor the forest, hid
Beneath the white abrupt; but wanders on
From hill to dale, still more and more astray:
Impatient flouncing thro' the drifted heaps,
Stung with the thoughts of home; the thoughts of home
Rush on his nerves, and call their vigour forth
In many a vain effort. How sinks his soul!
What black despair, what horror fills his heart!
When for the dusky spot, that fancy feign'd
His tufted cottage rising thro the snow,
He meets the roughness of the middle waste,
Far from the tract, and blest abode of man:
While round him night resistless closes fast,
And every tempest, howling o'er his head,
Renders the savage wilderness more wild.
style: english winter ballad, low strings and sparse piano, grave baritone, slow, bleak, closing in
why: The man lost in the snow: 'the thoughts of home / Rush on his nerves,' and night shuts round him anyway.

title: Poems
author: Oliver Goldsmith
lyrics:
And parting summer's lingering blooms delay'd:
Dear lovely bowers of innocence and ease,
Seats of my youth when every sport could please,
How often have I loiter'd o'er thy green,
Where humble happiness endear'd each scene;
How often have I paus'd on every charm,
The shelter'd cot, the cultivated farm,
The never-failing brook, the busy mill,
The decent church that topt the neighbouring hill,
The hawthorn bush, with seats beneath the shade,
For talking age and whispering lovers made;
How often have I blest the coming day,
When toil remitting lent its turn to play,
And all the village train, from labour free,
Led up their sports beneath the spreading tree;
While many a pastime circled in the shade,
style: english pastoral elegy, acoustic guitar and soft strings, warm tenor, unhurried, nostalgic, evening-lit
why: The brook, the mill, the church on the hill, the hawthorn 'for talking age and whispering lovers made.'

title: Poems
author: Oliver Goldsmith
lyrics:
And even the story ran that he could gauge;
In arguing too, the parson own'd his skill,
For ev'n though vanquish'd, he could argue still;
While words of learned length, and thund'ring sound,
Amaz'd the gazing rustics rang'd around;
And still they gaz'd, and still the wonder grew,
That one small head could carry all he knew.
But past is all his fame. The very spot
Where many a time he triumph'd, is forgot.
Near yonder thorn, that lifts its head on high,
Where once the sign-post caught the passing eye,
Low lies that house where nut-brown draughts inspir'd,
Where grey-beard mirth and smiling toil retir'd,
Where village statesmen talk'd with looks profound,
And news much older than their ale went round.
Imagination fondly stoops to trace
style: village ballad, fiddle and tabor, genial baritone, brisk, affectionate, tavern-warm
why: 'And still they gaz'd, and still the wonder grew, / That one small head could carry all he knew.'

title: Poems
author: Oliver Goldsmith
lyrics:
THE HERMIT.
BY DR. GOLDSMITH.
"TURN, gentle Hermit of the dale,
" And guide my lonely way
"To where yon taper chears the vale
" With hospitable ray.
"For here, forlorn and lost I tread,
" With fainting steps and slow,
"Where wilds immeasurably spread
" Seem lengthening as I go. "
"Forbear, my son," the Hermit cries,
"To tempt the dangerous gloom,
" For yonder faithless phantom flies
"To lure thee to thy doom.
"Here to the houseless child of Want
" My door is open still;
style: english narrative ballad, harp and fiddle, two answering voices, plaintive, measured, candle-lit
why: 'Turn, gentle Hermit of the dale' — a ballad opening that sets a whole story going in eight lines.

title: Slokantara
author: Unknown
lyrics:
> *Burned and burned again, gold has a radiant color;*
> *Ground and ground again and again, sandalwood has a lovely fragrance;*
> *Cut and cut again and again, the sugarcane stalk is full of sweetness;*
> *Even at the end of existence, for the highest ones, primordial nature does not become modified.* || 75 ||
> *After happiness, there is suffering; after suffering, there is happiness.*
> *Like a wheel, all the world turns, the moving and the unmoving.* || 76 ||
> *The guest and the slanderer, these two are my kinsmen.*
> *The slanderer takes away sin; the guest is a guide to heaven.* || 77 ||
> *From the forehead is born the vipra; the ksatriya is born from the arms.*
> *From the thighs is born the vaisya; and the sudra is born from the feet.* || 78 ||
> *Some questions are for the sake of argument; some are the assertion of a child.*
style: javanese-sanskrit recitation, gamelan gongs and bamboo flute, measured male chant, slow, ceremonial, resonant
why: Gold burned, sandalwood ground, sugarcane cut — three hammer-blows of repetition, then the wheel of joy and grief turning.

title: Slokantara
author: Unknown
lyrics:
> *The sun is fierce; the moon has a body stained by a hare; the ocean has salty water;*
> *Visnu was a cowherd; Indra is exceedingly fickle; Sankara has a blue throat;*
> *All these have flaws; how much more so will people on earth have flaws?* || 47 ||
> *For five years, like a king; for ten years, like a servant;*
> *At sixteen years, like a friendthis is the rule for a son.* || 48 ||
> *From indulgence, many flaws; from discipline, many virtues.*
> *Therefore, for sons and pupils, discipline, not indulgence.* || 49 ||
> *In giving a daughter, in settling a debt, in giving charity, in acquiring wealth,*
> *In matters of enemies, knowledge, fire, and disease, one should not cause delay.* || 50 ||
> *Even a stranger, if helpful, is a kinsman; even a kinsman, if harmful, is a stranger.*
style: kawi didactic chant, soft gong and drone, low even voice, steady, wry, unhurried
why: A litany of the flaws of the sun, the moon, the ocean and the gods, ending: how much more so will people have flaws?

title: Slokantara
author: Unknown
lyrics:
> *A disease born of the body is harmful; a forest herb that helps is a friend.* || 51 ||
> *The lamp of the night is the moon; in the morning, the sun is the lamp.*
> *In the three worlds, the lamp is dharma; a good son is the lamp of the family.* || 52 ||
> *Born from the same womb, under the same star,*
> *They are not of the same conduct, like the thorns of the badara tree.* || 53 ||
> *For one bound by the serpent-noose of a wife, and accompanied by affection for a son,*
> *And burned by the fire of cravingrenunciation is the great medicine.* || 54 ||
> *An old and wealthy woman, and one who is ugly but exceedingly skillful,*
> *And one who is poor but endowed with beautythese three are to be served by the wise.* || 55 ||
> *Even one without wealth, if of good lineage; even a twice-born without knowledge of the Veda;*
style: devotional sanskrit chant, tanpura drone and small bell, warm male voice, slow, luminous, sparse
why: 'The lamp of the night is the moon... in the three worlds, the lamp is dharma' — a built refrain on one image.

title: Epigrams
author: Homer
lyrics:
Come all of you and sack the kiln-yard and the buildings: let the whole kiln be shaken up to the potters loud lament.
As a horses jaw grinds, so let the kiln grind to powder all the pots inside.
And you, too, daughter of the Sun, Circe the witch, come and cast cruel spells; hurt both these men and their handiwork.
Let Chiron also come and bring many Centaurs all that escaped the hands of Heracles and all that were destroyed:
let them make sad havoc of the pots and overthrow the kiln, and let the potters see the mischief and be grieved;
but I will gloat as I behold their luckless craft.
And if anyone of them stoops to peer in, let all his face be burned up, that all men may learn to deal honestly.
Let us betake us to the house of some man of great power, one who bears great power and is greatly prosperous always.
style: greek curse song, aulos and clattering percussion, ragged gleeful chorus, fast, wild, mocking
why: The poet's revenge on the cheating potters — Shatter, Smash, Charr, Crash and Crudebake summoned by name.

title: Epigrams
author: Homer
lyrics:
Open of yourselves, you doors, for mighty Wealth will enter in, and with Wealth comes jolly Mirth and gentle Peace. May all the corn-bins be full and the mass of dough always overflow the kneading-trough.
Now (set before us) cheerful barley-pottage, full of sesame
Your sons wife, driving to this house with strong-hoofed
mules, shall dismount from her carriage to greet you;
may she be shod with golden shoes as she stands weaving at the loom.
I come, and I come yearly, like the swallow that perches light-footed in the fore-part of your house. But quickly bring
If you will give us anything (well). But if not, we will not wait, for we are not come here to dwell with you.
HOMER:
Hunters of deep sea prey, have we caught anything?
FISHERMEN:
All that we caught we left behind, and all that we did not catch we carry home.
style: greek folk begging-song, syrinx and hand drum, bright chorus of young voices, quick, festive, door-to-door
why: 'I come, and I come yearly, like the swallow' — a real doorstep song, blessing and threat in the same breath.

title: Epigrams
author: Homer
style: archaic greek epitaph chant, single lyre, clear distant voice, still, timeless, sparse
why: The bronze maiden on Midas' tomb, speaking for as long as water flows and tall trees flourish.

title: Tyranni Triginta
author: Scriptores Historiae Augustae
lyrics: 11. Aureolus. This man too, governing the Illyrican armies in contempt of Gallienus, as did all at that time, compelled by the soldiers, assumed the empire; and when Macrianus, with his son Macrianus, came against Gallienus with very many men, he captured his army, and bound some, corrupted, to his own allegiance. And when he had become from this a strong emperor, and Gallienus had vainly tried to overcome the brave man, he made peace with him, intending to fight against Postumus. Of which most things both have been and will be said. This same Aureolus ClaudiusGallienus having already been killed and a battle joinedslew at that bridge which is now called the Bridge of Aureolus; and there, as a tyrant, he gave him a rather humble tomb. There exists even now a Greek epigram in this form: "By the gift of a tomb, victor after many battles of the tyrant, Claudius, now fortunate, attends Aureolus with a mortal gift, and by right surviving him whom he would wish to live, if the love of an excellent soldiery allowedwhich by right denied life to all the unworthy, and most of all to Aureolus. Yet he, merciful, preserving the last rites of the body, both dedicates the Bridge of Aureolus and the mound." These verses, translated by a certain grammarian, I have set down so as to keep faithnot that they could not have been better translated, but that historical fidelity might be preserved, which I have thought ought to be guarded above all else; for as to what pertains to eloquence, I care nothing. For I have proposed to deliver to you the matter, not the wordsespecially with so great an abundance of matters as in the Lives of thirty pretenders at once.
style: late latin funerary declamation, low brass drone and frame drum, sombre baritone, slow, martial, grim
why: The only candidate; its core is a real tomb-epigram — the victor burying the rival he would rather have kept alive.

title: History of the Peloponnesian War
author: Thucydides
lyrics:
O'er numerous islands and all Argos ruled.
that they should bring back the seed of the demigod son of Jupiter from a foreign land to his own; else they would plough with a silver share.
Pisistratus, the son of Hippias, here, In Pythian precinct, marked his archon year.
Beneath this dust Archedice finds peace, Whose sire was Hippias, peerless once in Greece. She, though of tyrants daughter, sister, bride, And mother, ne'er was lifted up with pride.
style: greek epitaph song, lyre and soft drone, clear female voice, slow, dignified, spare
why: Archedice's epitaph — daughter, sister, wife and mother of tyrants, and never once lifted up with pride.

title: The Ego and Its Own
author: Max Stirner
lyrics: I dare meet every foeman Whom I can see and measure with my eye, Whose mettle fires my mettle for the fight  etc.
style: defiant romantic art song, piano and low strings, bold baritone, martial, rising, brief
why: The only candidate, and it stands as a boast: every foeman he can see and measure with his eye.

title: Theogony
author: Hesiod
lyrics:
From the Heliconian Muses let us begin to sing, who hold the great and
holy mount of Helicon, and dance on soft feet about the deep-blue
spring and the altar of the almighty son of Cronos, and, when they have washed their tender
bodies in Permessus or in the Horse's Spring or Olmeius, make their
fair, lovely dances upon highest Helicon and move with vigorous feet.
Thence they arise and go abroad by night, veiled in thick mist, and utter their song with lovely
voice, praising Zeus the aegis-holder, and queenly Hera of Argos who
walks on golden sandals, and the daughter of Zeus the aegis-holder
bright-eyed Athena, and Phoebus Apollo, and Artemis who delights in
arrows, and Poseidon the
earth holder who shakes the earth, and revered Themis, and
quick-glancing Aphrodite, and Hebe with
style: archaic greek hymn, phorminx lyre and low drone, rhapsode tenor, stately, incantatory, processional
why: The Muses washing in the spring and dancing on soft feet before they go abroad by night, veiled in mist.

title: Theogony
author: Hesiod
lyrics:
great-souled Obriareus live,
trusty warders of Zeus who holds the aegis. And there, all in their
order, are the sources and ends of gloomy earth and misty Tartarus and
the unfruitful sea and starry heaven, loathsome and dank, which even
the gods abhor.
It is a great
gulf, and if once a man were within the gates, he would not reach the
floor until a whole year had reached its end, but cruel blast upon
blast would carry him this way and that. And this marvel is awful even
to the deathless gods. There stands the awful home of murky
Night wrapped in dark
clouds. In front of it the son of Iapetus stands immovably
upholding the wide heaven upon his head and unwearying hands, where
Night and Day draw near and greet one another as they pass the great
threshold of bronze: and
while the one is about to go down into the house, the other comes out
style: cold underworld chant, bowed drone and distant bell, low male voice, very slow, vast, echoing
why: The great gulf where a falling man needs a whole year to reach the floor, and Night and Day greet each other on the bronze threshold.

title: Theogony
author: Hesiod
lyrics:
from Olympus he came immediately, hurling his
lightning: the bolts flew thick and fast from his strong hand together
with thunder and lightning, whirling an awesome flame. The life-giving
earth crashed around in burning, and the vast wood crackled loud with
fire all about.
All the land
seethed, and Ocean's streams and the unfruitful sea. The hot vapor
lapped round the earthborn Titans: flame unspeakable rose to the
bright upper air: the flashing glare of the thunderstone and lightning
blinded their eyes for all that they were strong.
Astounding heat seized Chaos: and to
see with eyes and to hear the sound with ears it seemed even as if
Earth and wide Heaven above came together; for such a mighty crash
would have arisen if Earth were being hurled to ruin, and Heaven from
style: thunderous epic chant, deep drums and low brass drone, massed male voices, fast, cataclysmic, roaring
why: Zeus opening on the Titans — the sea seething, heat seizing Chaos, earth and heaven sounding as if hurled together.

title: Poems
author: Ann Yearsley
lyrics:
NIGHT.
To STELLA.
At this lone hour, when Nature silent lies,
And Cynthia, solemn, aids the rising scene,
Whilst Hydra-headed Care one moment sleeps,
And, listless, drops his galling chain to earth;
O! let swift Fancy plume her ruffled wing,
And seek the spot where sacred raptures rise;
Where thy mild form, relax'd in guiltless sleep,
Forgets to think, to feel; may dreams of bliss
Lull thy soft sense, nor paint the scene of woe,
I lately told; think not my spirit near,
Light airy shade, that would elude thine eye,
And shrink to nothing, conscious of thy worth.
Yet here I dare, in Fancy's boundless walk,
Invoke thy Muse, and hail thy song sublime.
style: georgian nocturne, harp and low strings, soft female voice, hushed, moonlit, slow
why: 'At this lone hour, when Nature silent lies' — and Hydra-headed Care drops his galling chain for one moment.

title: Poems
author: Ann Yearsley
lyrics:
There needs no more; the world to me is lost,
And all the whirl of life-unneeded thrift.
I sicken at the Sun, and fly his beams,
Like some sad ghost which loves the moonless night,
And pensive shuns the morn. The deep recess
Where dim-ey'd Melancholy silent sits,
Beckoning the poor desponding slighted wretch,
Suits well. 'Tis here I find a gloomy rest;
'Tis here the fool's loud clatter leaves me still,
Nor force unwilling answers to their tale:
But, ah! this gloom, this lethargy of thought,
Yields not repose; I sigh the hour away;
The next rolls on, and leaves me still opprest.
But, oh! swift-footed Time, thou ceaseless racer,
Thou who hast chac'd five thousand years before thee,
With all their great events, and minute trifles,
