style: melancholy english art song, viola and piano, low female voice, brooding, spare, unresolved
why: 'I sicken at the Sun, and fly his beams, / Like some sad ghost which loves the moonless night.'

title: Poems
author: Ann Yearsley
lyrics:
Thy jawless skeleton of Joppa's wood
Stares in my face, and frights my mental eye;
Not stiffen'd worse the love-sick Frederic stood,
When the dim spectre shriek'd the dismal cry.
But whilst the Hermit does my soul affright,
Love dies  Lo! in yon corner down he kneels;
I shudder, see the taper sinks in night,
He rises, and his fleshless form reveals.
Hide me, thou parent Earth! see low I fall,
My sins now meet me in the fainting hour;
Say, do thy Manes for Heaven's vengeance call,
Or can I free thee from an angry power?
Stella! if Walpole's spectres thus can scare,
Then near that great Magician's walls ne'er tread,
He'll surely conjure many a spirit there,
Till, fear-struck, thou art number'd with the dead.
style: gothic ballad, harpsichord and tremolo strings, urgent female voice, eerie, quick, shivering
why: A reader frightened by her own book — the fleshless form rising as the taper sinks, in tight singable quatrains.

title: Poems
author: Mary Collier
lyrics:
THE Woman's Labour:
TO Mr. STEPHEN DUCK.
Immortal Bard! thou Fav'rite of the Nine!
Enrich'd by Peers, advanc'd by Caroline!
Deign to look down on one that's poor and low,
Remembring you yourself was lately so;
Accept these Lines: Alas! what can you have
From her, who ever was, and's still a Slave?
No Learning ever was bestow'd on me;
My Life was always spent in Drudgery:
And not alone; alas! with Grief I find,
It is the Portion of poor Woman-kind.
Oft have I thought as on my Bed I lay,
Eas'd from the tiresome Labours of the Day,
Our first Extraction from a Mass refin'd,
Could never be for slavery design'd;
style: english work song, bare frame drum and fiddle, plain strong female voice, steady, driving, unadorned
why: 'No Learning ever was bestow'd on me; / My Life was always spent in Drudgery' — the whole address lands in ten lines.

title: Poems
author: Mary Collier
lyrics:
When bright Orion glitters in the Skies
In Winter Nights, then early we must rise;
The Weather ne'er so bad, Wind, Rain, or Snow,
Our Work appointed, we must rise and go;
While you on easy Beds may lie and sleep,
Till Light does thro' your Chamber Windows peep
When to the House we come where we should go,
How to get in, alas! we do not know:
The Maid quite tir'd with Work the day before,
O'ercome with Sleep; we standing at the Door
Oppress'd with Cold, and often call in vain,
E'er to our Work we can admittance gain:
But when from Wind and Weather we get in,
Briskly with Courage we our Work begin;
Heaps of fine Linnen we before us view,
Whereon to lay our Strength and Patience too;
style: winter labour ballad, low fiddle and hand drum, weathered female voice, slow, cold, insistent
why: Rising under Orion in the snow while 'you on easy Beds may lie and sleep' — the contrast is the song.

title: Poems
author: Mary Collier
lyrics:
Is not the worst we hapless Females do:
When Night comes on, and we quite weary are,
We scarce can count what falls unto our Share;
Pots, Kettles, Sauce-pans, Skillets, we may see,
Skimmers, and Ladles, and such Trumpery,
Brought in to make compleat our Slavery.
Tho' early in the Morning 'tis begun,
'Tis often very late before we've done;
Alas! our Labours never know no End,
On Brass and Iron we our Strength must spend;
Our tender Hands and Fingers scratch and tear:
All this, and more, with Patience we must bear,
Colour'd with Dirt and Filth we now appear;
Your threshing sooty Peas will not come near.
All the Perfections Woman once could boast,
Are quite obscur'd, and altogether lost.
style: kitchen work chant, clattering percussion and drone fiddle, rough female chorus, brisk, relentless, wry
why: Pots, kettles, saucepans, skillets, skimmers and ladles — a catalogue that beats like a work rhythm, ending on lost perfections.

title: Poems
author: Richard Graves
lyrics:
AN INVITATION TO THE FEATHERED RACE, MDCCLXIII.
WRITTEN AT CLAVERTON, NEAR BATH.
BY THE REV. MR. GRAVES.
AGAIN the balmy Zephyr blows,
Fresh verdure decks the grove,
Each bird with vernal rapture glows,
And tunes his notes to love.
Ye gentle warblers, hither fly,
And shun the noon-tide heat;
My shrubs a cooling shade supply,
My groves a safe retreat.
Here freely hop from spray to spray,
Or weave the mossy nest;
Here rove and sing the live-long day,
At night here sweetly rest.
Amidst this cool translucent rill,
style: english pastoral air, recorder and harpsichord, light soprano, gentle, springlike, lilting
why: An invitation sung to birds — hop from spray to spray, weave the mossy nest, sing the live-long day.

title: Poems
author: Richard Graves
lyrics:
BY THE SAME.
THIS bubbling stream not uninstructive flows,
Nor idly loiters to its destin'd main,
Each flower it feeds that on its margin grows,
And bids thee blush, whose days are spent in vain.
Nor void of moral, tho' unheeded, glides
Time's current stealing on with silent haste;
For lo! each falling sand his folly chides,
Who lets one precious moment run to waste.
ON THE ANCIENT CITY OF BATH.
WRITTEN ON THE FINISHING THE CIRCUS.
BY THE SAME.
'MIDST flowery meads and Avon's winding floods,
Romantic hills, wild rocks, and pendent woods,
Behold fair Bath her stately front advance,
In all the pomp of Latian elegance!
style: reflective baroque air, solo lute, quiet tenor, slow, still, meditative
why: The stream and the hour-glass in eight lines: 'each falling sand his folly chides, / Who lets one precious moment run to waste.'

title: Poems
author: Richard Graves
lyrics:
Or spoke but by a tear.
Now far from her and bliss I roam,
All nature wears a change:
The azure sky seems wrapt in gloom,
And every place looks strange.
Those flow'ry fields, this verdant scene,
Yon larks that towering sing,
With sad contrast increase my spleen
And make me loath the spring.
My books that wont to sooth my mind
No longer now can please:
There only those amusement find
That have a mind at ease.
Nay life itself is tasteless grown
From Lucy whilst I stray:
Sick of the world I muse alone
style: georgian song of absence, guitar and viola, warm male voice, plaintive, unhurried, evening-toned
why: Larks and flowery fields turned unbearable by one absence — 'Sick of the world I muse alone.'

title: Griphus Ternarii Numeri
author: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
lyrics: 1. The Riddle of the Number Three. Drink thrice, or as many times three: such is the mystic law, whether for one who drinks three, or for one who multiplies three by three, to weave the cube from nine uneven threes. The right of three is the same as that of thrice three: all things are in these  the form of a begun human being and the completion of a full birth; and that end of fate which holds the last of nine times nine. Three brothers, begotten of Ops; three sisters, born in order, of the female sex  Vesta, Ceres, and Juno. Hence Jove's thunderbolts are three-forked, hence Cerberus, hence the trident, and the threefold egg of Helen with her brothers. Thrice the new purple filled the spindles of Nestor, and the crow, three times more long-lived than that age; whom, gathering the generations in nine triple courses, the bronze-footed stags surpass three times Nestor's span, three of whose ages the bird of Phoebus (the raven) outlives, whom nine times older the bird of the Ganges goes before  the bird whose temples are radiant in their cinnamon nest (the Phoenix). Threefold is Hecate, three the faces of the maiden Diana; three the Graces, three the Fates, threefold the voice, threefold the elements, three the Sirens in Trinacria; all things by threes: three winged ones, three half-goddesses, three half-girls, bidden, three times three, to contend with the Muses for the palm, singing with mouth, hand, breath, with the boxwood pipe, with the lyre-string, with the voice. Three the parts of philosophy, three the Punic wars, three-month the turns of the years and of the sky, and through the shadow of night the threefold watches; thrice the late sentinel, when Mars is caught, sings the bright signs of the coming dawn. And he who, conceived in the evening of a tripled night (Hercules), fixed four times three rich spoils to his trophies. And the lyric bards are of the number of the Memnosynes (Muses), three of whom alone the right hand of Phoebus once held; but Cithaeron three times consecrated three of them in bronze, by the religion of the fathers, who feared to have scorned the six. The triple three-night festivals were celebrated in the Tarentine games, such as the triennial rites at Thebes for twice-born Bacchus. The first three battles of the Thracian gladiators, in three wars in order, the sons of Junius sent as offerings to their father's tomb. She too (the Sphinx), seeking marriages through three riddles  what was two-footed and four-footed and three-footed, all alone  terrified Aonia: a bird, a lion, a three-formed maiden  the Sphinx, with the wings of a bird, the feet of a beast, the face of a girl. Three partnerships gleam in the Tarpeian temple. Three kinds of arts make human dwellings: he who lays the stones for the walls, he who lays the beams on the roof, and he who adorns the plastering with the final touch. Hence the cask of Bromius (wine-measure) and hence the Sicilian medimnus: the practice of measuring unfolds the one by three, the other by twice three. In physics, three first things: God, the world, the form given; a triple of all kinds  begetter, begettress, begotten. Through three kinds of triangles the rule runs: equilateral, or with equal legs, or unequal in all. The perfect number coalesces into three parts, so that the same, by the assembled triple, is dissolved through thrice three. Three, the first, has an even, an odd, and a middle; but it alone, as it divides three, so also divides five and seven; and, set in the whole number under the point of the centre, it marks off the solid thirds as the cube proceeds, sundering the equal parts from the odd by its triple; and a triple middle is in even numbers, when of four and six and twice four the same navel (omphalos) is distinguished. Threefold law, which the four times three Tables (the Twelve Tables) ratified: the sacred, the private, and that which is the common property of the people anywhere. A triple kind of interdicts: "from which I shall have been driven by force," or "in which of two places it shall have been," or "of whose goods." Threefold liberty, and threefold the diminution of civil status. Threefold the kind of speaking: the sublime, the moderate, and that of a slender thread. Threefold too the manner of healing, whose names are by reason, or by method, or by experience; and medicine is threefold: to preserve, to prevent, to cure. Three the cultivations of the orators: that which Rhodes, ruled by its Colossus, and you, Attic Athens, loved; and that which prose of Asia drew from the stages to the stern benches, imitating in lawsuits the numbers of the choruses. Hence the tripods of Orpheus, because they are three  earth, water, flame. A triple consideration for the stars: position, distance, form. And music, both the measure and the mother of melodies, is threefold: mingled in books, secret in the stars, made common in the theatres. Martial Rome is threefold: in cavalry, plebs, and senate; by this number the tribes, and the tribunes of the sacred mount. Three squadrons of the knights, three names of the nobler sort. Three are the names for the lyre-strings, three the names for the month. The Geryons are threefold, threefold the framing of the Chimaera; Scylla is threefold, made of three  dog, maiden, fish. The Gorgons and the Harpalycae and the Furies are in a band of three; and the three prophetic Sibyls, of a common name, whose fatal songs are three books, which the cultivation of thrice five men preserves. Drink thrice. Three is the number above all things; three is the one God. Here too, lest the game run by with an inert number, let it have ten times three threes and ten times nine.
style: latin drinking incantation, hand drums and low pipes, chanting male voices, insistent, hypnotic, accelerating
why: The only candidate, and it is already a chant: 'Drink thrice' opening and closing a hammering litany of threes.

title: Lectures on the True, the Beautiful and the Good
author: Victor Cousin
lyrics:
"Est Deus in nobis, agitante calescimus illo."
"In vain against the Cid a minister is leagued, All Paris for Chimene the eyes of Rodrique," etc.
"After a little spot of earth, obtained by prayer, Forever in the tomb had inclosed Moliere," etc.
"At the feet of this altar of structure gross, Lies without pomp, inclosed in a coffin vile, The most learned mortal that ever wrote; Arnaud, who in grace instructed by Jesus Christ, Combating for the Church, has, in the Church itself, Suffered more than one outrage and more than one anathema," etc.
"Wandering, poor, banished, proscribed, persecuted; And even by his death their ill-extinguished rage Had never left his ashes in repose, If God himself here by his holy flock From these devouring wolves had not concealed his bones."
Juez combien ce coup frappe tous les esprits; La moitie s'epouvante et sort avec des cris; Mais ceux qui de la cour ont un plus long usage Sur les yeux de Cesar composent leur visage.
style: french baroque funeral air, viol consort and chamber organ, grave baritone, slow, dignified, austere
why: The epitaph at its centre stands alone — wandering, poor, banished, and even his ashes hidden from the wolves.

title: Brutus
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
lyrics:
To these is added an orator, Cornelius, sweet of speech,
Cethegus Marcus, colleague of Tuditanus,
Marcus's son
he was called by those of his countrymen of old,
the men who then were living and passing their time,
the chosen flower of the people
and the marrow of Persuasion.
which once the Fauns and seers used to sing,
when neither the crags of the Muses . . .
nor was anyone studious of learned words before this man
style: early latin saturnian chant, plucked lyre and hand drum, rough low voice, archaic, measured, sparse
why: The old Ennian praise of Cethegus — 'the chosen flower of the people, and the marrow of Persuasion.'

title: Orator
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
lyrics:
"How prettily your little phrases are set, like all the cubes
of art in a pavement and mosaic of inlaid work!"
style: latin epigram song, single lute and light hand percussion, wry tenor, light, quick, brief
why: One barbed image, whole in itself: phrases laid like the little cubes of a mosaic pavement.
